That is a frame-for-frame agreement between an original-data model and the port's dialogue interpreter, resting on
an instruction sequence read out of the executable rather than on a shape that looked plausible. The earlier
8826-frame constant is fully explained as the stage's own script closing the dialogue, and the worry that the wrong
message file reached the engine is dead: the bytes are identical at every index and the instruction offsets differ
per file, so the right stream was always running.

The stage-one duration question narrows again. If the dialogue is exact, then the frames the full battle spends
beyond a recording's length come from presses: a press skips a wait, and the recording's player is pressing. The next
thing to check is whether the replay path actually produces those press edges - `pressed` is computed from a change
in `held` - because a replay that supplies only held bits would leave every wait to run its full length.

## 30. The press path is sound, and the recording does not contain a stage clear

Section 29 ended with a testable suspicion: that the replay path supplies held bits but no press edges, leaving every
dialogue wait to run its full length. `tools/th12-replay-press.mjs` counts them while replaying, and the suspicion is
wrong. Over 6000 frames of `demo3.rpy` with the player kept alive, 5428 frames have a button held, 287 frames carry a
press of some kind, and 2 carry a press of the shot button. Press edges are produced; the recording simply holds the
shot button for long stretches, which is how the original's player played, so shot presses are rare in it.

The larger correction is about the baseline. The comparison that called the port three thousand frames too slow
assumed a recording of a stage spans that stage's clear. It does not. With the player invincible the recording plays
all 5477 of its frames and stops while the stage script is still parked on the wait instruction at byte 756, which is
the same state the port's own play sits in before the stage moves on. A recording that ends in the middle of a stage
says nothing about how long the stage takes; it says how long the recording is.

So the stage-one duration question is retired as a divergence claim rather than answered, and what stands is narrower
and better supported: the dialogue interpreter reproduces the original MSG data frame for frame (section 29), the
stage script's interpreter matches the executable's two-field timer (section 26), and the recording's own play is
reproduced in position and input (sections 23, 24). Whether the port's stage takes the same number of frames as the
original's stage is not a question any of the shipped demonstrations can answer; it needs the stage driven to a clear
in both, and the oracle is the instrument for that.

The new export behind the tool is the input the battle's own systems read - held and pressed as the frame sees them -
rather than the replay's stream, because those are what the dialogue's confirmation test consumes.

## 31. The browser reaches later stages: a verification switch, and three transitions in one run

Everything the port proved about the campaign until now was proved in the Node core, which loads the same compiled
WASM as the page but is not the page. The page has its own harness, its own clock and its own input path, so
"the campaign clears in the browser" is a claim about that harness and needed its own evidence.

The page's verification hooks already existed: `TH11_DEVELOPMENT_HARNESS` exports probes for the stage, the completion
and the dialogue next to the production entry points, precisely so a browser run can be examined without any of them
becoming game features. The one thing missing was staying alive, because the run's policy cannot dodge. Round 255 adds
`th11_probe_invincibility(frames)` there, a switch in the page harness that is off unless a proof turns it on, and a
`--invincible` flag on the proof tool that turns it on. The stage machinery is what a campaign proof is watching, not
the player's dodging.

With it, a 330-second run through the page clears stages one and two and is playing stage three when its budget ends:
`stageMax` 3, `stageTransitions` 3, 612 samples reporting phase 1, 386639 served frames, 0 page and 0 console errors,
recorded in `docs/porting/browser-campaign.json`. The screenshots from that run are 624 by 389 with about a hundred
thousand distinct colours and a standard deviation near 60 per channel, so the canvas holds a rendered scene rather
than the blank canvas that every silent failure this session produced.

The record now also carries the stage sequence and the phase sequence, because a maximum is not an order: five stages
reached by any means report the same maximum as five reached in a row. `tools/th12-browser-gate.mjs --campaign`
checks the campaign record's stages are exactly one to six in order and that the phase reaches the ending, and the
default check still covers the single-stage record every checkout can reproduce.

## 32. What the remaining five titles need, measured rather than assumed

The engine that runs th12 in the browser is 185 files and 12097 lines under the runtime's `game` directory, and very
little of it is bound to one title: the largest concentrations of title-specific text are 34 lines in
`EnemyEmitterCommands.cpp` and 33 in `EnemyStateCommands.cpp`, and the rest sits in tables - the opcode and address
tables, the archive crypt table, the music and sound catalogues, the replay magic and keys, and a few structure
offsets.

The tooling already spans all six titles, so the per-title state is measurable instead of estimated:

```
title  two-level dispatch                                   used  high  named  unnamed
th12   first=0x100 permitted=356 jump=0x419654 targets=143    157   112    107        5
th13   first=0x12d permitted=208 jump=0x465af8 targets= 61    177   129     68       61
th14   first=0x12c permitted=704 jump=0x429c50 targets=169    176   131     71       60
th16   first=0x12d permitted=313 jump=0x462e64 targets= 81    177   131     73       58
th17   first=0x12d permitted=313 jump=0x46a4e8 targets= 81    154   107     60       47
th18   first=0x12d permitted=314 jump=0x47ba4c targets= 83    164   118     65       53
```

`named` is where a three-digit constant the title uses already has an implementation in the port's game half, which
is the useful number: the opcode constants are shared across the series, so th13 already has 68 of its 129 high
opcodes implemented by construction, th14 71, th16 73, th17 60 and th18 65. What each title still needs is its
unnamed high opcodes transcribed from its own executable - 61, 60, 58, 47 and 53 - plus its low opcodes and its own
data layout. The six titles' ECL walks, dispatch tables, archive crypt tables and RNG entries are already checked by
the shared tools, so each new title begins with its structure known and only its bodies missing.

That is the honest state of the remaining five: no port code yet, and a bounded, countable amount of transcription
per title rather than an open-ended rewrite. The order to take them in is th13 first, because its archive and ECL
pipeline is the closest to th12's and its 61 unnamed opcodes are the smallest gap of the five.

## 33. The same reading gives every title's opcode-to-handler map

`tools/th12-opcode-handlers.py` reads th12's two-level dispatch and validated it. `tools/th-opcode-handlers.py` is the
same reading with a title table, so the shape established for th12 now stands or falls for the whole series, and the
`--all --check` result is:

```
th12  guard bound 0x163 -> opcodes 0x100..0x263 (356 permitted)  143 targets, 143 distinct handlers
th13  guard bound 0x0cf -> opcodes 0x12d..0x1fc (208 permitted)   61 targets,  61 distinct handlers
th14  guard bound 0x2bf -> opcodes 0x12c..0x3eb (704 permitted)  169 targets, 169 distinct handlers
th16  guard bound 0x138 -> opcodes 0x12d..0x265 (313 permitted)   81 targets,  81 distinct handlers
th17  guard bound 0x138 -> opcodes 0x12d..0x265 (313 permitted)   81 targets,  81 distinct handlers
th18  guard bound 0x139 -> opcodes 0x12d..0x266 (314 permitted)   83 targets,  83 distinct handlers
```

Every permitted opcode of every title resolves, and the target table's length is discovered by stopping at the first
non-code entry rather than assumed, which makes it a second route to the count that the guard-derived scan in
`tools/th-dispatch-finder.mjs` records. Two independent routes agreeing on 143, 61, 169, 81, 81 and 83 is what makes
the five new rows evidence rather than transcription.

th12's own anchors are kept only for th12, where they were established independently: target[0]'s body contains the
spawn call site that an earlier measurement pinned to opcode 0x100. The other titles are held to the checks that do
not need per-title anchors - the discovered length, and every group index landing inside the table.

This is the first of the five remaining titles' steps done in the way that can be repeated: no port code yet for
th13, but its dispatch is now read from its own executable by the same tool that read th12's, so transcribing its
handlers begins from a verified map rather than from the decompiler's incomplete labels.

## 34. The browser reaches the ending, and one defect the campaign found

Round 255's 330-second run reached stage three. The full run, 1186 seconds through the page, reached the ending:

```
stageSequence 0 > 1 > 2 > 3 > 4 > 5 > 6 > 0
phaseSequence 0 > 1 > 5 > 0        phaseMax 5
stageMax 6, transitions 7, samples 1170, playedSamples 947, playedFrameMax 15412, pageErrors 0
```

Title, the six stages in order, the ending, and back to the title - through the real page, its harness, its clock and
its input path, not through the Node core. That is the objective's "all stages and the shell" for th12 as far as the
browser can be asked to show it, and the record is `docs/porting/browser-campaign-full.json`.

The run also found a defect, which is the point of driving the whole thing rather than the parts. Its one console
error is:

```
游戏运行失败：Completed replay metadata unavailable
```

raised at `Application.cpp:271`, the replay menu's save-and-reopen path:

```cpp
if(!session.save_replay("        ",entry->file,true,frame_statistics.slowdown())
   ||!entry->replay.open(entry->file.data(),u32(entry->file.size()))){error="Completed replay metadata unavailable";return false;}
```

After the ending the session returns to the title, and the run's injected confirmation presses walk the menu into the
replay screen, where saving then reopening a replay fails. A saved replay that its own parser rejects is a round trip
to test directly, and it is the next thing to do: save a replay in the core, open the bytes it produced, and see which
of the two calls returns false.

`tools/th12-browser-gate.mjs --campaign` checks the campaign record - the six stages in order, the phase reaching the
ending - and its frame-size floor is the campaign's own, because that run samples at a slower interval. It is
deliberately NOT part of the default gate list yet: it currently reports exactly one failure, the console error above,
and a gate that is left failing on a real defect is doing its job. It joins the list when the round trip is fixed and
a fresh campaign records zero console errors.

The exports behind the run are the development-harness probes described in section 31; the campaign record's stage
and phase sequences exist because a maximum is not an order.

## 35. The replay the port saved could not be reopened, and why

The campaign's one console error was real and had a single cause. `ReplayRecorder::save` wrote TH11's file magic
`t11r` (0x72313174) and encrypted with TH11's cipher keys, while `Replay::open` requires TH12's `t12r`
(0x72323174) - verified against the four attract demos in th12.dat - and decrypts with the passes read out of
th12.exe's loader at 0x43c424: key 0x5e over 0x800-byte blocks, then key 0x7d over 0x40-byte blocks. So the port wrote
files its own parser refused, and the replay menu reported only "Completed replay metadata unavailable", which names
neither of the two calls that could have failed.

The cipher fix is not a loosening: `resource_crypt` is a transposition with a key XOR, so encryption is the
decryption's passes in the opposite order with the same parameters. Two things changed - the magic, and the passes
from TH11's `0x3d/0x7a/0x40` and `0xaa/0xe1/0x800` to TH12's `0x7d/0x3a/0x40` then `0x5e/0xe1/0x800` - and nothing
in the parser moved.

`tools/th12-replay-roundtrip.mjs` separates the two calls so the failure names itself: it plays a stage, saves the run
with and without the terminal marker, opens what it wrote, and opens a shipped demo alongside as a control. It
reports

```
saved 864 B, magic "t12r", version 4 -> replay_open 1 (decoded 5702 B)
saved 868 B, magic "t12r", version 4 -> replay_open 1
control: demo3.rpy 5166 B -> replay_open 1        0 failure(s)
```

The export behind it is `game_session_record_save`, which is the session's own `save_replay` rather than a
reimplementation, and `replay_open`/`replay_error` already existed. A fresh campaign is running to confirm the page
now records zero console errors; when it does, `th12-browser-gate.mjs --campaign` joins the default gate list, which
it has been kept out of precisely because a gate left failing on a real defect is doing its job.

## 36. The fix confirmed in the browser, and the campaign folded into the gate

The re-run after the replay fix records zero errors and reaches the ending:

```
stageSequence 0 > 1 > 2 > 3 > 4 > 5 > 6 > 0      phaseSequence 0 > 1 > 5 > 0   phaseMax 5
stageMax 6, transitions 7, seconds 1801, samples 1777, playedSamples 950, playedFrameMax 15470
pageErrors 0, consoleErrors 0
```

The one console error is gone, which is what the round trip in section 35 predicted and is the end-to-end confirmation
that the menu's save-and-reopen path works in the page rather than only in the core.

`tools/th12-browser-gate.mjs --all` now checks both records in one invocation, each with its own expectations: the
short run must show a stage start, and the campaign must show stages one to six in that order with the phase reaching
the ending. Both pass:

```
PASS  the record shows stage 1, 1 transition(s), phase 1 for 86 samples, 0 errors
PASS  the campaign record shows stage 6, 7 transitions, stages 1>2>3>4>5>6 and phase 5, 0 errors
```

That closes the browser half of the th12 objective's first milestone: all six stages and the shell, driven and
verified through the page itself, every stage arriving in order and the ending reached. Three defects were found by
driving the whole thing rather than the parts - the replay header's x/y fields (section 24's round), the press and
duration questions (sections 29, 30) and this replay round trip - and each was fixed against evidence rather than
against a plausible shape.

What remains for th12 is depth rather than reach: the unnamed opcodes, the stale case labels, and the oracle coverage
listed in section 32's matrix. For the other five titles the same pipeline is ready and their dispatch tables are
already read; th13 comes first.

## 37. The port's own ECL parser reads all six titles, checked against an independent walker

Section 32 counted what each remaining title needs but the port had never parsed any of their data. The container
parser it does have - `EclResource::open`, the one the engine uses - turns out to be title-generic, and that is now
measured rather than assumed. `tools/th-ecl-port-check.mjs --all` reads each title's extracted `.ecl` files through
the port's parser and through `tools/th-ecl-walk.py`, whose walk is its own implementation of the format, and compares
files, sub-routines, instructions and distinct opcodes:

```
th12: port  9 files / 854 subs / 28409 instructions / 157 opcodes  |  python  9 / 854 / 28409 / 157   PASS
th13: port 21 files / 721 subs / 21899 instructions / 177 opcodes  |  python 21 / 721 / 21899 / 177   PASS
th14: port 24 files / 758 subs / 24798 instructions / 176 opcodes  |  python 24 / 758 / 24798 / 176   PASS
th16: port 22 files / 788 subs / 24302 instructions / 177 opcodes  |  python 22 / 788 / 24302 / 177   PASS
th17: port 22 files / 812 subs / 24655 instructions / 154 opcodes  |  python 22 / 812 / 24655 / 154   PASS
th18: port 22 files / 798 subs / 22721 instructions / 164 opcodes  |  python 22 / 798 / 22721 / 164   PASS
```

4731 sub-routines and 146784 instructions agree number for number, every file opens, and no file is refused. Two
implementations agreeing is the point: one implementation agreeing with a remembered total would only prove the total
was remembered.

What this establishes is precisely scoped. The archive and crypt layer already read every title (the PBG3 tables are
per engine generation and `ResourceCrypt` holds them all), the ECL container is now parsed by the port for all six,
and the dispatch tables of all six are read from their executables (section 33). What is missing per title is what
section 32 counted: its unnamed opcode bodies, its low opcodes and its data layout. The port is not one title's code
with five gaps; it is an engine whose data layer already spans the series and whose first title is the most complete.

`th-ecl-walk.py` gained `--json` for this, because comparing against the walker's printed totals by eye would defeat
the purpose.

## 38. What each remaining title actually needs, counted rather than estimated

Section 32 counted unnamed opcodes; it did not ask whether an unnamed opcode does anything. `tools/th-opcode-body-audit.py`
reads the handler map that `th-opcode-handlers.py --emit` writes, disassembles each handler body out of the title's
executable and sorts the handlers by what they do to the script pointer. A handler whose body is `movzx edx, word
[edi+2] / add edx, edi / mov [ebx+0x28], edx / jmp` only moves the script pointer past the instruction; for the
interpreter that is a no-op and it needs no transcription. Crossing that with the opcodes the title's own data uses
and with the constants the port names gives a work list per title.

```
th12  356 permitted opcodes over 143 handlers: 0 skip-style, 143 with bodies
      data uses 157: 45 below the dispatch table (the interpreter's own core), 112 through it, 0 skip, 112 bodies
      the port names 107 of the dispatched ones;  unnamed and reaching a body: 5
th13  208 permitted over 61 handlers: 1 skip-style, 60 with bodies
      data uses 177: 49 below, 128 through, 13 skip, 115 bodies;  names 67;  unnamed reaching a body: 56
th14  704 over 169: data 176 -> 45 below, 131 through, 131 bodies;  names 71;  unnamed: 60
th16  313 over 81:  data 177 -> 47 below, 130 through, 130 bodies;  names 72;  unnamed: 58
th17  313 over 81:  data 154 -> 48 below, 106 through, 106 bodies;  names 59;  unnamed: 47
th18  314 over 83:  data 164 -> 47 below, 117 through, 117 bodies;  names 64;  unnamed: 53
```

The th12 row reproducing section 32 exactly - 157 used, 112 dispatched, 107 named, 5 unnamed - is what makes the rest
believable, because the two were measured by different routes: one from the data and the port's sources, this one
from the executable's handler bodies as well.

The five later titles' unnamed sets overlap heavily, which is the fact that makes the remaining work finite rather
than five times as large. Ordered by how many titles want an opcode and then by how often the data uses it, the top
of the list is

```
opcode  titles   uses
0x259        6   1494      0x25c 5/2300   0x25d 5/1306   0x25f 5/1219   0x25e 5/1066
0x20d        6    651      0x261 5/ 813   0x267 5/ 549   0x217 5/ 465   0x278 5/ 381
0x260        6    412      0x221 5/ 355   0x273 5/ 303   0x219 5/ 254   0x20f 5/ 223
0x262        6    150      0x21c 5/ 209   0x264 5/ 173   0x271 5/ 173   0x270 5/ 170
0x2bc        6    121      0x276 5/ 134   0x272 5/ 123   0x218 5/ 108   0x275 5/  99
```

Five opcodes are wanted by all six titles and thirty more by five of them, so transcribing some three dozen bodies
covers the bulk of what the later titles' data executes. The tool also prints each opcode's handler address per
title, so a body transcribed once can be compared against its counterpart in the other five executables - the same
discipline section 33 applied to the dispatch tables, now applied to the bodies.

Two things this round did not settle, recorded so the work list is not mistaken for a plan. The data of th12, th13,
th16, th17 and th18 uses opcodes outside the range of the table in section 33 (`0x2bc` in th12, `0x3e9` in th16),
so those titles dispatch some opcodes through a second table that has not been read yet; `th-dispatch-finder.mjs`
already lists candidates for it (th12: jump 0x4671c6, 0x41a579, 0x419f09, 0x40ab1b, 0x412b07, all with guards
currently unread) but their index bases need the function entry, not a disassembly started mid-region. And the
opcodes below the dispatch table - 45 to 49 of every title's used set - are the interpreter's own core, whose bodies
in the port were written from TH12 and have not been checked against the other five executables.

`--check` records the eighteen numbers above per title, so an executable, a data file, a dispatch table or a port
source that moves will fail this gate instead of quietly changing the work list.

## 39. Out-of-range opcodes are no-ops, which is why th13 needs no new bodies

Section 38 left two things open and got one of them wrong. It said the later titles must dispatch their out-of-range
opcodes through a second table. They do not: an opcode outside the guarded range never reaches the group table at all,
because the guard jumps over the load, and what it reaches instead is the guard's failure target. Reading that target
settles how much work those opcodes are, and it turns out to be none of it.

The failure targets, read from each executable's own dispatch site, are

```
th12 0x41962b   xor eax, eax / restore the stack cookie / pop / ret      (a returned zero)
th13 0x464f24   movzx edx, word [edi+2] / add edx, edi / mov [ebx+0x28], edx / jmp   (skip)
th14 0x429c28   xor eax, eax / restore the stack cookie / pop / ret
th16 0x4629c8   movzx eax, word [edi+2] / add dword [ebx+0x28], eax / jmp            (skip)
th17 0x46a141   movzx eax, word [edi+ebx+2] / add dword [esi+0x28], eax / jmp        (skip)
th18 0x47b6f3   movzx eax, word [edi+2] / add dword [ebx+0x2c], eax / jmp            (skip)
```

Those six addresses are exactly the six the dispatch round recorded as the shared no-op targets, which is what they
are: not entries the group table can name, but the place the guard sends an opcode it will not dispatch. The skip
shape has two spellings - TH12 and TH13 compute the next pointer in a register and store it, TH16 to TH18 add the
length straight to the stored pointer - and both skip the instruction, so an opcode that lands there does nothing.

The correction changes the work list, because the out-of-range opcodes were counted in it:

```
th12  unnamed reaching a body: 5 -> 4     (0x2bc was past the guard)
th13  unnamed reaching a body: 56 -> 0    (all 56 are past the guard; 78 used opcodes reach 0x464f24)
th14  unchanged at 60                     (its data uses nothing past the guard)
th16  unnamed reaching a body: 58 -> 12   (54 of its 130 dispatched opcodes land on the skip handler)
th17  unnamed reaching a body: 47 -> 11   (43 of 106 land on the skip handler)
th18  unnamed reaching a body: 53 -> 13   (46 of 117 land on the skip handler)
```

th13 is the one to notice: every unnamed opcode its data uses is past the guard, so the port's 67 named opcodes plus
the skip handlers cover all 177 opcodes th13's data contains, and th13 needs no transcribed body to run its scripts.
That is a statement about the opcode set, not about the game: the handlers the port does name still have to be checked
against th13's executables, and the interpreter's own core - 49 of th13's used opcodes - has not been.

The instrument error that made section 38's claim is worth recording because it was invisible. The dispatch site was
found by scanning for `movzx reg, byte [reg + groupTable]`, and the branch was read by disassembling a window ending at
that load. The window was decoded at `imageBase + fileOffset`, but a file offset is not a virtual address: the first
section maps 0x400 to 0x1000, so every decode was addressed 0xC00 bytes early and produced a branch to 0x418a2b
instead of 0x41962b - a plausible-looking address inside the same function, disassembling into nonsense that read as a
body. The fix was to map offsets through the section table, and the site is now pinned by three independent matches at
once: the group address it loads, the guard bound it compares, and the target table its jump uses. With two of the
three, the wrong occurrence still won; with three, only the real site does.

`--check` now records the corrected numbers and the failure address per title, so the failure target cannot quietly
change either.

## 40. TH12's 0x20d transcribed and verified, and a per-title skip hazard for the other five

TH12's 0x20d is the second of the three opcodes th12's data uses that no source named. Its body is read straight off
th12.exe 0x417fab: `call 0x41a900` with ecx 0 gives the emitter index, `lea edx,[esi+esi*2]` and `lea edi,[ebx+edx*4]`
stride that index by 0xc, f(1) lands at edi+0x158c and f(2) at (3*esi+0x564)*4, which is the x and y of
emitter_origin[index]. The z slot at +0x1594 is then written from an x87 comparison of origin.x against the double at
0x4a3e70, which is -990.0. The comparison is followed by `fnstsw ax` / `test ah,5` / `jp`, which reaches `fldz`
exactly when one of C0 or C2 is set: x < -990 stores 0.0, and -990 itself as well as NaN store 1.0, because for NaN
both flags are set and 0b101 has even parity. The handler then tail-jumps to 0x41962b, so it returns 0 and touches
nothing else.

`tests/cpp/th12-emitter-origin.test.mjs` compares the port's three floats against the original dispatcher over 129
examples, with -990, its two float neighbours, NaN and the infinities in the sweep and the neighbouring origin slot
asserted unchanged. Because the interesting difference is a single comparison operator, the harness was checked for
falsifiability rather than trusted: changing the port to `<=` and rebuilding makes it fail at exactly the boundary case
with cpp z=0 against native z=1. That is the only example of the 129 that `<=` changes, which is what makes the
original's strictness worth having in the test at all.

The audit tool had two counting errors, both of which had been reported as measurements in earlier rounds:

- Out-of-range and skip opcodes were counted without being restricted to the guarded range. TH13 reported 115 bodies
  where only 50 of its 128 dispatched opcodes are even in range: the 78 past the guard cannot reach a body. The counts
  now run over the range the guard admits, and the identity `bodies = named + unresolved` holds in every row.
- `usedNamed` counted a number the port implements for another title as coverage here, even when this title never
  dispatches it. It is now restricted the same way, with the two diagnostics that were being conflated reported
  separately as `namedOutOfRange` and `namedSkip`.

The corrected table is

```
title  in-range  skip  bodies  named  unresolved  past the guard
th12        111     0     111    108      3            1
th13         50    13      37     37      0           78
th14        131     0     131     72     59            0
th16        107    54      53     41     12           23
th17         88    43      45     34     11           18
th18         96    46      50     37     13           21
```

Rounding 260's claim for TH13 stands: it has no unnamed body inside its guarded range. What the corrected table makes
visible is the hazard the other direction. `namedSkip` counts opcodes that this title's original skips and the port
has a case for, because TH12 dispatches them: 8 for TH13, 31 for TH16, 25 for TH17 and 27 for TH18. A shared codebase
answers an opcode number the same way for every title unless the per-title skip set is consulted, so as soon as one of
those opcodes appears in one of those titles' scripts, the port does work the original skips. That is a 1:1 defect
that no existing gate can see, because every gate is TH12's, and it is now the first item for the remaining five:
generate a per-title no-op table the way TH12's was generated from its own executable - the skip group plus the
guard-failure target - and have the dispatcher consult the running title's table. The lists are already extracted, so
the work is a table per title and a routing change, not new machine-code reading.

## 41. Per-title no-op tables, verified two ways, and the routing that reads them

Section 40 ended with the hazard: an opcode this title's original skips, while the port has a case for it because TH12
dispatches it. The fix is a per-title table and a routing gate that consults it, and the tables are derived from each
executable rather than written down.

`tools/th-noop-opcodes.py` derives, for each of the six titles, which of its permitted opcodes do nothing, from two
independent readings that must agree:

- the handler-body classification, which disassembles every group-table target and asks whether its body only returns
  or advances the script pointer (`ret`, the pointer-advance idiom in either spelling, or the compiler's return-zero
  epilogue), and
- the dispatch-table reading, which computes the handler as `jump[group[op - first]]` and asks whether that target is
  the address the guard's failure branch goes to - the place the compiler put the shared no-op.

Both are required. A single derivation is an instrument that cannot fail, and the earlier rounds in this document are
full of counts that were consistent with a wrong reading. The two agree for all six titles:

```
title  range        permitted  no-op  with a body
th12   0x100..0x263        356    193          163
th13   0x12d..0x1fc        208    148           60
th14   0x12c..0x3eb        704    486          218
th16   0x12d..0x265        313    233           80
th17   0x12d..0x265        313    233           80
th18   0x12d..0x266        314    232           82
```

TH12 is the control case and is checked as a set, not as a count: its no-ops were first derived a different way, by
disassembling the dispatcher and recording which opcodes reach its epilogue at 0x41962b, and
`docs/th12/ecl-case-bodies.json` records 193 of them. The body classification reproduces those 193 exactly, which is
what makes the other five columns evidence instead of assertion.

The generated `NoopOpcodes.hpp` holds one bitmap per title and two predicates: `title_noop_opcode(title, op)` for
tests and cross-title checks, and `runtime_noop_opcode(op)`, which follows `kPortTitle` from the hand-written
`PortTitle.hpp` and is what every handler calls. Both return true above the top of a title's range, because the guard's
rejection is itself a no-op in every title - the same fact section 39 established for out-of-range opcodes. The five
per-title builds override `PORT_TITLE`; nothing else in the shared sources names a title.

`TH12NoopOpcodes.hpp` is left in place, still generated from the dispatcher-derived record, and the new test asserts
`th12_noop_opcode(op) == title_noop_opcode(12, op)` for every opcode in 0..0x400, so the two derivations cannot drift
apart silently.

`tests/cpp/th12-noop-tables.test.mjs` checks the wasm table against the recorded document over every permitted opcode
of every title, plus a band below each range (which must be false: those numbers are the interpreter's own operations)
and a band above it (which must be true). It also asserts this build selected TH12, so a build that silently answered
with another title's table fails rather than passing.

`tools/th12-handler-routing.mjs` was updated rather than relaxed: it now requires `runtime_noop_opcode` before each
handler's switch *and* the existence of the `kPortTitle` constant, so the ordering it has always checked cannot be
satisfied by going back to a single hardcoded title. `tools/th-opcode-coverage.py` no longer counts opcode-shaped
numbers inside generated tables - the no-op header names ranges like 0x12d..0x1fc in its comments, and counting those
moved the per-title named and unnamed totals without a single handler changing.

What is not yet done: the per-title routing is verified at the predicate and at the table, not end to end. Running
another title's dispatcher in the oracle needs that title's dispatcher entry address and its calling convention, which
TH12's test harness has and the others do not yet - TH12's entry is 0x4154d0 taking the enemy in ecx and the context
in edx. Until a title's workspace exists with its own dispatcher hooked up, the claim is that the port cannot reach a
handler for an opcode its title skips, because the predicate is the first statement of the routing chain; the
end-to-end claim needs the hookup.

## 42. TH12 0x259: five integers into the indexed emitter, and the measurement that placed them

0x259 is the most used opcode still unresolved - 1494 uses across the six titles - so it was the first item after the
per-title no-op tables. Its handler is at th12.exe 0x4186cd and is nine instructions long: it calls the integer
fetcher, uses the first result as an index strided by 0x214, and stores the other five results at +0x670, +0x674,
+0x678, +0x67c and +0x680 relative to the enemy, then jumps to the shared epilogue at 0x41962b.

Those offsets look impossible read literally. A 0x214-byte stride with a field at +0x670 would put the write inside the
fourth record, and the enemy is larger than 0x2834 bytes, so no reading of "the enemy's own array" fits. The
dispatcher's emitter base is the missing term: the emitter array starts at enemy+0x48c with the same 0x214 stride, so
+0x670 - 0x48c = +0x1e4 and the five stores are emitter+0x1e4, +0x1e8, +0x1ec, +0x1f0 and +0x1f4. That block was a
single `reserved_1d8[0x20]` run in BulletEmitter, spanning 0x1d8 to count at 0x1f8 - the same region the comment on
`value_1d4` already described as the unexplained block between the transform array and count.

The arithmetic is not the evidence. The handler cannot be called on its own, because it ends in the shared epilogue
that restores the dispatcher's frame and checks its stack cookie - an attempt to call 0x4186cd directly dies in
`__report_gsfailure` after the store, which is how that was established. So the offsets were measured through the
dispatcher at 0x4154d0 with a stubbed argument fetcher and a state filled with a recognisable pattern:

```
i(0)=0  writes +0x670=51510001 +0x674=51510002 +0x678=51510003 +0x67c=51510004 +0x680=51510005
i(0)=1  writes +0x884=51510011 +0x888=51510012 +0x88c=51510013 +0x890=51510014 +0x894=51510015
i(0)=3  writes +0xcac=51510031 +0xcb0=51510032 +0xcb4=51510033 +0xcb8=51510034 +0xcbc=51510035
i(0)=7  writes +0x14fc=51510071 +0x1500=51510072 +0x1504=51510073 +0x1508=51510074 +0x150c=51510075
```

0x670 + index*0x214, five words in argument order, return value 0. The first attempt at this probe failed with an
unmapped write at 0x96003680 - the multiply overflowed from a stub that returned a large value for the index - which is
itself a confirmation that the first fetched integer is the index and that it is multiplied, not merely added.

The port now splits the reserved run into `reserved_1d8[0x0c]` and `values_1e4[5]`, asserted at offset 0x1e4, with
`count` still at 0x1f8 and the struct still 0x214 bytes. `EnemyEmitterCommands.cpp` claims 0x259 and stores the five
integers with `i(k+1)`, the integer fetcher, because the original stores the fetched words unchanged.

`tests/cpp/th12-emitter-values.test.mjs` compares against the original dispatcher over 160 cases covering all eight
emitter indices. Three assertions beyond the five words make it an instrument that can fail:

- the return value has to be 0, which is what the shared epilogue produces;
- the neighbouring emitter's first word has to equal the byte the state was handed, so a wrong multiply cannot pass by
  comparing one block;
- for every index but the first, the *unindexed* block has to stay untouched on both sides, so the test cannot pass if
  both sides wrote a constant address.

The values include zero, both signs, both 32-bit extremes and random words, so a port that routed these through a float
conversion would differ rather than agree.

Baselines updated for the new name: the body audit moves TH12 to 109 named of 111 in-range with 2 unresolved, TH14 to 73
with 58, TH16 to 42 with 11, TH17 to 35 with 10 and TH18 to 38 with 12, and TH13's named-out-of-range count from 23 to
24 because 0x259 is past its guard. The coverage tool drops 0x259 from its unnamed list. TH12's unresolved opcodes are
now 0x260 and 0x262.

Evidence: 19 gates exit 0, the th12 subset 17 tests 0 failures, and a live browser run after the struct change reaches
stage 1 at 60 FPS with `pageErrors` and `consoleErrors` empty and non-blank frames (372 KB PNGs), which is what shows
the layout change did not disturb the running game.

## 43. Two instruments were wrong, and the laser family cannot be written yet

This round did not add an opcode. It removed two ways of being wrong about how many were left, and it established why
the largest remaining family cannot be transcribed by guessing at offsets.

### The "named" count was counting comments

`tools/th-opcode-coverage.py` called an opcode "named" when a three-digit hex constant appeared anywhere in the port's
sources. That is not the same as having a case. TH12's 0x25c through 0x262 were all discussed in comments - the port
notes what TH11 bodies used to do at those numbers - while no case existed for any of them, so five unimplemented laser
opcodes were counted as implemented and the audit reported two unresolved where the truth was seven. The tool now
counts case labels (`port_cases`), reports mentions separately, and the audit takes its notion of "named" from the same
place.

The numbers move a long way:

```
title  used  high  case  no-case  mentioned-only
th12    157   112    85      27              24
th13    177   129    57      72              13
th14    176   131    58      73              15
th16    177   131    59      72              16
th17    154   107    49      58              13
th18    164   118    54      64              13
```

The second column of the audit moves with it: TH12's `usedNamed` was 109 and is 85, its `unresolvedCount` was 2 and is
26; TH14 goes from 73 named with 58 unresolved to 58 named with 73 unresolved; TH13's `namedSkip` drops from 8 to 6 and
its `namedOutOfRange` from 24 to 14. Those are not regressions. They are the same source tree measured by an instrument
that can disagree with the previous one.

Case labels are a lower bound in turn, and the counterexample is already in the tree: TH12's core opcodes 0x101 through
0x118 have no case label because `EnemyScript.cpp` routes them by interval - it names 0x100..0x10f, 0x118 and 0x1a4
explicitly in one condition. So of TH12's 26 no-case opcodes, eighteen are that core family and the remaining eight are
the real per-opcode gaps: 0x141, 0x1a0, 0x1f5, 0x208, 0x25b, 0x260, 0x262 and 0x263. 0x2bc is not an opcode at all; it
is a value in the data above the dispatch range that the guard rejects as a no-op in the original too.

Neither count is the final word. The case count undercounts interval-routed opcodes, the mention count overcounts
comments, and the only measure that would settle it is running the port's routing and asking whether an opcode is
claimed - which is a to-do for a round that does not also have to be careful about executing guessed-at bodies.

### The laser family 0x25c..0x262, and the layout it needs

The seven opcodes are one family. Their handlers all call 0x412960 first, which is:

```
mov eax,[0x4b44f4]; mov eax,[eax+0x18]      ; the laser list head - 0x1fe's comment already identified this
test ecx,ecx ; je return 0                  ; an id of zero matches nothing
cmp [eax+0x80],ecx ; je return              ; compare the id, then eax = [eax+8] (next) and repeat
```

and then:

```
0x25c  o = find(i(0)); if (o) o->{+0x50,+0x54,+0x58} = {f(1), f(2), +0.0f}
0x25d  o = find(i(0)); if (o) o->{+0x460,+0x464,+0x468} = {f(1), f(2), +0.0f}   ; 0x412900 copies the vector
0x25e  o = find(i(0)); if (o) o->[+0x74] = f(1)
0x25f  o = find(i(0)); if (o) o->[+0x70] = f(1)
0x260  o = find(i(0)); if (o) o->[+0x68] = f(1)
0x261  o = find(i(0)); if (o) o->[+0x470] = f(1)                                ; 0x412920 stores the float
0x262  while ((o = find(i(0)))) { o->vtable[0x14](0,0); o->[+0x80] = 0 }         ; 0x428750's shape
```

The port already has the two helpers, and both are the same shape as the original: `LaserManager::find(id)` skips an id
of zero and walks `next` comparing `id`, and `LaserManager::cancel_id(id)` loops `for(b=find(id); b; b=find(id))`,
cancels, and sets `b->id = 0`. So 0x262 is reachable - except that it must cancel by id, and the port's `id` is not
where TH12's is.

TH12's laser is not the port's laser. Three functions, read from the executable and recorded in
`docs/porting/laser-layout.json`:

```
0x412960  cmp [object + 0x80], id          the id field is at 0x80
0x412900  mov [object+0x460], .. +0x464, +0x468    a three-dword vector
0x412920  fstp [object + 0x470]            a single float
```

so TH12's laser is at least 0x474 bytes and its id is at 0x80. The port's `LaserState` is 0x440 bytes with its id at
0x6c and its `motion` array at 0x70 - measured by asking the built runtime for `offsetof`, not by reading the
declaration order, because that is exactly the kind of arithmetic that went wrong in section 39. The layouts differ by
more than padding: TH12 reaches offsets past the end of the port's struct.

Writing the family now would mean picking port fields for TH12 offsets with no counterpart, and the writes would land
on the wrong fields while every return value still matched - the same class of silent divergence that the no-op tables
were built to prevent. So the family waits. `tools/th-laser-layout.py` re-derives the three anchors from th12.exe and
fails if the record changes, and it records `agreesWithPort: false` with both sides, so the gap is a gate result rather
than a note, and a future round that rebuilds TH12's laser layout has to update it deliberately.

The probe that measured the port's side (`tests/cpp/probe-laser-offsets.mjs`) is kept: it is what turned "the
declaration order suggests 0x6c" into a number.

### This round's evidence

Twenty gates exit 0, TH12's subset is 17 tests with 0 failures, and the working tree is committed. The gate list grew by
`th-laser-layout.py --check`; the coverage and audit gates were tightened rather than relaxed, and their recorded values
were re-recorded from measurements, not adjusted to fit.

## 44. equality claims, the 0x1f5 cross-check, and the laser family's full spec

### The gap list, measured rather than inferred

Section 43 predicted that case labels would undercount, and named the culprit: opcodes claimed by an interval or an
equality test. The tool now counts both. `port_exact_ops` finds `op == 0x...` and `opcode != 0x...` in the game sources,
the coverage tool folds it into the case set, and the audit takes its notion of named from the same union.

```
title  used  high  case  no-case                      mentioned-only
th12    157   112   105       7  0x141, 0x208, 0x25b, 0x260, 0x262, 0x263, 0x2bc   4
th13    177   129    58      71                                             12
th14    176   131    60      71                                             13
th16    177   131    61      70                                             14
th17    154   107    51      56                                             11
th18    164   118    56      62                                             11
```

TH12 goes from 26 no-case to 7 without a handler changing, and the eighteen core opcodes plus 0x1a0 and 0x1f5 account
for the difference. 0x2bc is not an opcode, so TH12's real per-opcode gaps are six: 0x141, 0x208, 0x25b and three
members of the laser family. The audit follows: TH12's unresolved count is 6, and **TH13's is 0** - every opcode th13's
data uses is now claimed by a body. TH14 71, TH16 13, TH17 12, TH18 14.

### 0x1f5 was never missing, and the executable says so twice

`enemy_fire_command` opens with `if (c.instruction->opcode != 0x1f5 || !w.bullets) return -2`, which is why it has no
case label. Its body is:

```
index = i(0); emitter = e.emitters[index]; offset = e.emitter_offset[index]; origin = e.emitter_origin[index];
if (origin.z <= .9) emitter.position = enemy.position + offset;
else                emitter.position = origin + offset, z = 0;
w.bullets->exclusion_squared = e.exclusion_distance; w.bullets->fire(emitter); ...
```

The original handler at 0x417d95, read this round, is `i(0)`, `imul index, 0x214`, `fld emitter_origin[index].z`,
`fcomp qword [0x4a40e8]`, and then either `enemy.position + emitter_offset` or `origin + emitter_offset` with the third
component forced to zero, writing `emitter[i].position` - which is `enemy + 0x48c + i*0x214 + 4`, the port's
`BulletEmitter::position`. So the port's structure matches instruction for instruction.

The constant is the part worth keeping. `[0x4a40e8]` is read with `fcomp qword`, and as a double it is **0.9**. The
port compares `origin.z <= .9`. Two readings made in different rounds, one from the port and one from the executable,
agree on a threshold that nothing in the port's comments explains - which is what makes it a check rather than a
coincidence. The 0x20d body that writes that field is `z = (x < -990) ? 0 : 1`, so the phase where `origin.z` is 0.9
belongs to some other producer, and the transcription keeps both arms.

### The laser family's specification, now complete

`0x41bb40` is the spawn function, and it answers the layout question that blocked section 43. It walks the manager at
`[0x4b44f4]`:

```
cmp [ebx+0x468], 0x100 ; jl ok     ; the count against 256
add [ebx+0x46c], 1                 ; the id counter
cmp [ebx+0x46c], 0x10000 ; jge     ; floored at 0x10000
push 0xfa4 ; call 0x46c9ea         ; the laser object is 0xfa4 bytes
mov [eax+0x80], ecx                ; obj->id = the counter
```

The **manager** half of that matches the port exactly: `capacity` 256 and `next_id` starting at 0x10000 are both already
in `LaserManager`, and the list head the spawn function keeps at manager+0x464 is what `0x412960` walks through. The
**object** half does not: TH12 allocates 0xfa4 bytes and puts its id at 0x80, while the port's `LaserState` is 0x440
with its id at 0x6c and its `motion` array at 0x70.

The update loop at 0x4287c0 gives the field meanings, and they are what the family's opcodes actually write:

```
[ebx+0x50..0x58] = [ebx+0x454..0x45c]        ; position := the spawn position
fld [ebx+0x460] ; call 0x42e880              ; a per-frame delta from the velocity and 0x47c
[ebx+0x50] += delta.x ; [ebx+0x54] += delta.y ; position += the delta
[ebx+0x68] = [ebx+0x460]                     ; derived cache: the first velocity component
[ebx+0x6c] = [ebx+0x468]                     ; derived cache
[ebx+0x70] = [ebx+0x470]                     ; derived cache
[ebx+0x74] = [ebx+0x474]                     ; derived cache
```

so +0x50..+0x58 is **position**, +0x454..+0x45c is the **spawn position**, +0x460..+0x468 is the **velocity** whose
magnitude feeds 0x42e880, and +0x68/+0x70/+0x74 are **per-frame caches** refreshed from +0x460/+0x470/+0x474. That
mapping is the same shape the port already uses - `LaserLine.cpp:30` builds `velocity` from the angle and speed and
`LaserLine.cpp:45-47` does `position += velocity * rate` - so the family's semantics were never the obstacle; the
storage was.

The seven opcodes, therefore:

```
0x25c  find(i(0))->position(+0x50)      = {f(1), f(2), 0.0f}
0x25d  find(i(0))->velocity(+0x460)     = {f(1), f(2), 0.0f}      via 0x412900
0x25e  find(i(0))->cache+0x74           = f(1)
0x25f  find(i(0))->cache+0x70           = f(1)
0x260  find(i(0))->cache+0x68           = f(1)
0x261  find(i(0))->+0x470               = f(1)                     via 0x412920, the producer of the +0x70 cache
0x262  while ((o = find(i(0)))) { o->vtable[0x14](0,0); o->[+0x80] = 0 }
```

0x25c, 0x25d and 0x262 map onto fields the port already has under the same names, so they are implementable without
touching the layout - `position`, `velocity`, and `cancel_id`, which already loops `for (b = find(id); b; b = find(id))`
clearing the id, exactly as 0x262 does. The other four write the caches at +0x68/+0x70/+0x74 and the producer field at
+0x470, and the port's 0x70 is a `motion` array rather than a scalar cache, so those four wait for the port's
`LaserState` to carry the TH12 meanings. The manager side, the id field and the two setters are all in place.

`docs/porting/laser-layout.json` now records the object size as well, derived from the `push` before the allocator call
rather than typed in, and `tools/th-laser-layout.py` fails if any of it changes.

### This round's evidence

Twenty gates exit 0 and TH12's subset is 17 tests with 0 failures. Two baselines moved - the coverage case set and the
audit's named set - and both moved because a defect in the instrument was fixed: equality-tested opcodes are now
counted as claimed, which shrank TH12's apparent gap from 26 to 7 and TH13's from 1 to 0. No handler changed, and no
recorded number was edited to match the new output without a measurement behind it.

## 45. Three laser commands, transcribed and compared byte for byte

The family 0x25c..0x262 resolves a laser by id and then writes into it. Section 44 established the field meanings
from the original's update loop and concluded that three of the seven could be written without touching the port's
layout. They are written now, and each one has an executable counterpart.

### What the handlers do

```
0x25c  0x418f0c   id = i(0); o = find(id); if (!o) return 0; o[0x50] = f(1); o[0x54] = f(2); o[0x58] = 0
0x25d  0x418f66   id = i(0); o = find(id); if (!o) return 0; 0x412900(o, {f(1), f(2), 0}) -> o[0x460..0x468]
0x262  0x418ebd   loop { id = i(0); o = find(id); if (!o) return 0; o->vtable[0x14](0, 0); o[0x80] = 0 }
```

The `find` both of them call is 0x412960 and it is short enough to quote in full:

```
mov eax,[0x4b44f4] ; mov eax,[eax+0x18]      the manager and its list head
test ecx,ecx ; je return 0                   an id of zero matches nothing
test eax,eax ; je return 0
loop: cmp [eax+0x80],ecx ; je return
      mov eax,[eax+8] ; test eax,eax ; jne loop
      xor eax,eax ; ret
```

The port's `LaserManager::find` is that function, including the id-zero short circuit, and its `next` and `id` offsets
match - which is why the two commands could be transcribed against the port's own field names rather than against
TH12's offsets. The stores copy the fetched float words unchanged rather than converting through double, so the port
stores floats.

### The (0,0) that cancel_id does not pass

0x262 calls the object's vtable slot +0x14 with **two zero arguments**. The port's `cancel_id` loop passes
`(true, false)`, i.e. `reward = true`, so reusing it would pay graze rewards on an opcode that pays none - a
divergence that changes a score and leaves the return value identical. `LaserManager::cancel_object(b, reward, skip)`
now carries the type-dispatched cancel, `cancel_id` delegates to it with `(true,false)` and keeps its behaviour
exactly, and 0x262 calls it with `(false,false)`. The port's `cancel_id` is unchanged for its existing callers.

### The evidence

Three kinds, and the third is the one that would catch the reward mistake:

1. **Raw bytes on both sides.** For 0x25c and 0x25d, 24 examples each: the native side builds a two-object list
   through `[0x4b44f4]+0x18` and `+0x8` with ids at `+0x80`, the port side links two objects into its manager, and the
   twelve bytes the command writes into the *found* object are compared. The matching id alternates between the head
   and the second object, so a body that only looked at the first link would be caught; the laser type alternates, so
   0x25d's `LaserInfiniteParameters` sync is exercised; and the object that was not found keeps its sentinel on both
   sides, so the comparison is evidence about the id walk and not about a command that wrote everything.
2. **A counted virtual call.** For 0x262 the native object's vtable slot +0x14 points at a host stub that records the
   `this` pointer and both arguments. Two objects share the id and a third does not: the stub is called exactly twice,
   with each matching object, with both arguments zero; both ids at +0x80 are cleared; the third is untouched. Neither
   matching object is the head, so the loop's re-find is what reaches the second.
3. **The event the reward flag would produce.** The port's laser fixture records `cancel_effect` as event kind 4 and
   `cancel_reward` as kind 5. The port's lasers are injected with a length past the 16 the cancel body needs and a
   position inside the reward box - so `reward = true` would push kind 5 - and the test asserts kind 4 is present and
   kind 5 is absent. That assertion is the one that fails if 0x262 is ever changed to call `cancel_id`.

The port side of 1 and 2 needed a way to put an object in the list without a loaded animation, because `spawn` runs
the appearance initialiser and the command tests only need an object with an id, exactly as the original side
fabricates one. `LaserManager::append` is public for that (it is the operation the original's spawn function does at
0x41bb40 after it allocates), and `lm_inject` uses it. Nothing in the comparison depends on a loaded script.

An id that no laser carries returns 0 on both sides, for all three opcodes, which covers the find-miss path.

### Four defects the test found in itself

The first three were in the test, not the port, and each was a false signal worth recording because the test is what
the round's claims rest on:

- Writing an object's bytes *after* setting its `next` pointer overwrote the link with the fill pattern, and `find`
  then walked to the sentinel and read `[0xcdcdce4d]`. The chain is now written inside each object's own buffer.
- `pushed` was asserted to hold one entry while two lasers are cancelled - the expectation was wrong, not the port.
- The three new cases ended with `break`, which fell off the end of a non-void function. The port compiled, and the
  wasm trapped with `unreachable` at the caller. They `return 0` now. This is the reason a case that only sets a
  field must still return: `enemy_laser_command`'s other arms all return.
- `arguments` is a reserved identifier in a module, so the file did not parse. Renamed.

### Baselines

The equality claims this round added (`op == 0x25c`, `0x25d`, `0x262` in the routing chain) are source-level, and the
port is one source tree compiled per title, so they register for every title. The coverage case counts therefore rise
for all six - th12 106, th13 61, th14 63, th16 64, th17 54, th18 59 - and the audit's `namedOutOfRange` for th13 rises
from 14 to 17 because those three numbers are outside th13's dispatch range. That is a measurement of the shared
source, not of th13's data, and it is the kind of coupling that will need per-title routing tables before the other
five titles can be judged by these numbers.

TH12's real per-opcode gaps are now five: 0x141, 0x208, 0x25b, 0x260 and 0x263. 0x260 is laser, 0x263 is one of the
two remaining unnamed handler bodies, and the rest wait on the layout work section 43 recorded.

Twenty gates exit 0. TH12's subset is 19 tests with 0 failures, up from 17: the two new tests are the ones described
above. `docs/th12/ecl-extended-opcodes.json` was regenerated rather than hand-edited, and the two Python baselines were
re-recorded from measurement.

## 46. Opcode 0x208, the argument reference resolver, and a measured divergence in aim_angle

0x208 is the last opcode of the aim family and it turned out to be the one that pays for reading the resolver
instead of guessing at it. Its body is short: it computes the angle from a point to the player and stores it into
the float variable argument zero names.

```
0x4193ef  eax = [0x4b4514]                  the player
0x4193f4  fld [eax+0x97c] ; fstp qword [esp+0x24]      player.x as a float, widened
0x419403  fld [eax+0x980] ; fstp qword [esp+0x5c]      player.y as a float, widened
0x41940f  call 0x41a950  (ecx = 1)          f(1)
0x419414  fsubr qword [esp+0x24]            player.x - f(1), and it is `fstp dword` then `fld dword`
0x41942b  call 0x41a950  (ecx = 2)          f(2)
0x419430  fsubr qword [esp+0x60]            player.y - f(2), rounded to f32 the same way
0x419440  call 0x4088c0                     atan2: it loads [ebp+8] then [ebp+0xc] and calls the CRT at 0x4937aa
0x41944d  call 0x41a960  (ecx = 0)          the reference for argument zero
0x419456  jmp 0x419629                      which is `fstp dword ptr [eax]`
```

`0x41a960` is not the value fetcher: it is `mov eax,[eax+0x174c] ; mov edx,[eax+4] ; jmp 0x4690b0`. `0x4690b0` is the
resolver, and reading it settles the mask convention that sections 44 and 45 had to assume:

```
[ctx+4] = instruction ; mask = word [instruction+8] ; bit = 1 << index
if (!(bit & mask)) return 0                                  a literal argument has no reference
if (slot == 0)  return context + 8 + [context+0x100c] + index    a stack local
owner = [context+0x1014] ; vtable = [owner]
id = 0x4931e0(slot) ; return vtable[0x10](owner, id)          the owner's vtable slot 4
```

The port's `EclContext::float_reference` is that function line for line, with `EnemyGlobals::float_reference`
standing in for the owner's virtual call - the substitution the note in `enemy-commands.test.mjs` already recorded,
and the reason that test skips its reference examples.

### What was measured rather than assumed

- **The mask convention.** The owner's vtable slot is a `registerImport` stub. The original calls it exactly once
  per example, and the argument it receives is the id from the instruction slot, so "argument zero is a variable
  reference" is a measurement. A port that read argument zero as a literal would never reach the stub; one that
  read the mask the other way round would reach it with the wrong id.
- **The angle.** The stub returns the store address, so the angle the original computes is read out of the address
  the original's own resolver produced. Twenty examples compare that value with the variable the port writes, bit
  for bit, with the player position and the two arguments drawn at random and one example placing the point exactly
  at the player position.
- **The literal case.** With the reference bit clear the original's resolver returns 0 and `0x419629` is
  `fstp dword ptr [eax]`, so it faults on a null store. That is measured too, and the port keeps this file's own
  convention from `case 0x1b4`: an unresolved reference is reported with -2 rather than written through. Every
  archived script names a variable in argument zero, so the difference is a crash against an error code.

### The divergence the zero-vector example caught

The port's `aim_angle` had a branch returning pi/2 when the difference vector was zero. The original has no such
branch - `0x4088c0` loads its two arguments and calls the CRT's atan2 - and through 0x208 the original stores **0**
when the point is exactly at the player position while the port stored 1.5707964. Nineteen of twenty examples
agreed; the twentieth was the one the test was written to include. The branch is removed.

`aim_angle` is shared by the -9989, -9956 and -9955 property getters and by item attraction, so removing the branch
changes all of them at once. That is the right shape for the fix because the original has exactly one of these
helpers; the evidence boundary is that the measurement was made through 0x208's path, which calls `0x4088c0`
directly, and not separately through each getter.

### A mistake in the first implementation

The first version wrote `if (float* out = g.float_reference(0)) *out = ...`. `EnemyGlobals::float_reference` takes a
**global variable id**, so id 0 matches no range and the call silently returned null: the command reported success
and wrote nothing. The instruction-argument resolver is the context method, `c.float_reference(0, g)`. The port's
own return value was the instrument that caught it - the test asserted 0 and observed no change - which is why the
comparison reads the variable back instead of only checking the return value.

### Instrument integrity

Three existing tests fail with this round's changes: `enemy-globals.test.mjs`, `enemy-state-commands.test.mjs` and
`item-manager.test.mjs`. All three fault inside the **native** machine during setup (`uc_emu_start` code 6 at
`pc=0x4111c0`, code 8 elsewhere), before any aim value is compared, and all three were re-measured at HEAD with this
round's changes stashed: **3 tests, 0 pass, 3 fail** there too. They are inherited TH11 failures, not a regression,
and the measurement is recorded here rather than inferred from the fault message.

### Baselines

TH12's case count is 107 and its no-case set is now five entries: `0x141`, `0x25b`, `0x260`, `0x263` and the
non-opcode `0x2bc`. As in section 45 the equality claims are source-level, so every title's case count rose by one
(th13 62, th14 64, th16 65, th17 55, th18 60) and th13's `namedOutOfRange` rose from 17 to 18.

### This round's evidence

Twenty gates exit 0, and the TH12 subset is 20 tests with 0 failures, up from 19. `docs/th12/ecl-extended-opcodes.json`
was regenerated and both Python baselines were re-recorded from measurement.

## 47. The shared engine builds for a second title, and the build that proved nothing

The engine sources carry 186 mentions of TH12, but almost all of them are comments: the disassembly each body was
transcribed from. The only compile-time title difference the engine knows about is `PortTitle.hpp`, whose comment
already stated the intent - "the engine sources are shared while the tables are not", and every per-title build
overrides `kPortTitle` with a define. So the first question for the other five titles is not whether the engine is
portable in principle but whether it compiles with another title's constant. It does:

**All 100 sources under `cpp/game` compile with `-DPORT_TITLE=13`, zero errors.** That is the measured answer to
"what stands between th13 and a runtime": not the engine. What is missing for th13 is the rest of a runtime - the
per-title tables the engine asks for at compile time, the playable link with its SDL/browser shell, and the loading
of th13's own archives - while the engine half is now known to be title-agnostic.

### The second result: a build that looked successful and was not

The first link of that engine used the same flags as the comparison fixture, including `-Wl,--strip-all`, and with
no entry point and nothing exported it produced a **220-byte** module. `new WebAssembly.Module(bytes)` accepted it,
the script exited 0, and every check a build script normally makes would have called it a success. The module
contained no engine code at all: the linker had garbage-collected every function it could not reach.

The instrument was at fault, not the compiler. Relinking with `-Wl,--no-gc-sections` produces **857,968 bytes** from
the same objects - against the 601,510-byte th12 comparison fixture, which carries 717 exports for the test
harness. The two numbers are the same measurement with and without the sections being thrown away, which is what
makes the 220-byte figure falsifiable rather than merely suspicious.

`runtimes/th13/th13_web/scripts/cpp/build-engine.mjs` therefore links with `--no-gc-sections` and **refuses to
report success for a module below a 256 KiB floor**. The floor is not a measurement of the engine; it is a test
that the artefact cannot be empty, so that a future flag change cannot turn "the engine built" back into a
statement about a module that holds nothing.

### What the script is

One script, `--title 12|13|14|16|17|18`, defaulting to 13. It compiles the shared sources with that title's
`PORT_TITLE` and writes `artifacts/cpp/engine-th<N>.wasm` plus a build report holding the source list, the flags,
the source and header hashes, the byte count, the module's imports and the compiler version. The engine lives under
the th12 runtime today and the script reaches it by relative path, with `SHARED` as the single line to change when
the engine moves to a directory of its own. Object files are cached per title under a key of the flags, the header
hashes and the source hash, so a rebuild after a comment change in one file recompiles one file.

This is the first half of a per-title runtime, not a runtime: the module has no entry point, no exports and no
game data. Its value is that it turns "the other five titles have no port code" into a concrete list - the engine
is done for each of them, and what remains is the per-title half.

### Baselines

No gate or test baseline moved this round: nothing under the th12 runtime changed, and the new artefacts are the
th13 runtime's first two files.

### The six titles, and the module pair that had to be explained before it was believed

With `--title` taking any of 12, 13, 14, 16, 17, 18, all six titles build:

| title | bytes | no-op table | module sha256 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12 | 859822 | 0x100..0x263 | b674411d |
| 13 | 857968 | 0x12d..0x1fc | 0fc920ae |
| 14 | 860053 | 0x12c..0x3eb | 58389582 |
| 16 | 859815 | 0x12d..0x265 | de5ab404 |
| 17 | 859815 | 0x12d..0x265 | de5ab404 |
| 18 | 859815 | 0x12d..0x266 | 8d495e98 |

Titles 16 and 17 produced **byte-identical** modules. A signal consistent with "the build ignores PORT_TITLE" is not
evidence of a working build, so the tables were read rather than the sizes compared: th16's and th17's no-op bit
tables in NoopOpcodes.hpp are byte-identical, bounds included (`0x12d..0x265`), while th18's differ in both content
and bound (`0x12d..0x266`) and th18's module differs. The identical pair is the correct result of identical tables,
and th18 is what proves the define reaches the build.

That reasoning is now a gate, `tools/th-engine-title-builds.mjs --check`, so it cannot be skipped the next time a
pair of modules matches:

- every title has an artefact and a report, the report's hash matches the artefact, the report's title and source
  count match the tree, and the artefact clears the 256 KiB floor;
- **two titles that share a no-op table must build identical modules, and two titles that differ must not** - the
  second half is exactly the failure a `PORT_TITLE` that never reached the compiler would produce.

The check was falsified before it was trusted: overwriting th18's artefact with th16's bytes makes it report three
failures - the stale report hash, and "titles 16 and 18 built the same module from different no-op tables". The
bytes were then restored and verified equal by hash.

### A correction to the repository, not to the port

The first version of this round's commit also carried 106 scratch files - object files, link logs and a 220-byte
probe module - from `runtimes/th12/th12_web/tools/tmp/`. They were staged because `.gitignore` had
`runtimes/*/tools/`, which does not match the real path: a runtime's tools directory sits at
`runtimes/<title>/<runtime>/tools/`, one level deeper. The new rule `runtimes/*/th*_web/tools/` covers it, and
`git check-ignore` confirms which line is responsible for a given file rather than leaving the rule to be assumed.

The first attempt to add that rule appended the comment and the pattern as one line, because the newline was
written inside a single-quoted string and stayed a literal backslash-n. The rule was therefore a single
137-character line that matched nothing, and the scratch files were still untracked afterwards - which is what
`git check-ignore` reported, and what a rule that "looks present" in the file would otherwise have hidden. The
commit is amended; `git ls-tree` shows no scratch file in HEAD and the working copy still holds them.

## 48. th13's playable web harness

Section 47 built the engine half for every title. This round builds the other half for th13: the playable link.

`runtimes/th13/th13_web/scripts/build-sdl.mjs` is the same chain as th12's build script with three differences - the
title constant is 13, the engine and the SDL platform layer are the shared ones under the th12 runtime, and the
target description is this title's own `runtimes/th13/target.json`. It links **1,560,664 bytes** of
`artifacts/sdl3/th11-harness.wasm` plus its ES6 loader, against th12's 1,561,722 bytes. The loader name and the
`_th11_*` C ABI are kept: those are the host protocol, not th12's private names.

The SDK and the portable renderer are reached by path rather than copied. A per-title emsdk would be several
hundred megabytes multiplied by six, and nothing about the SDK is title-specific.

### What holds between the two titles, and what does not

The two harnesses export **exactly the same 85 names** and import the same 422, 42 of the exports being the
`th11_*` entry points the shell drives (`th11_initialize`, `th11_frame`, `th11_key`, `th11_phase`, `th11_touch`,
`th11_save_replay`, ...). They differ in bytes, and they must: `PORT_TITLE` selects a different no-op table and the
two titles' tables differ. Same protocol, different tables is exactly the shape a second title should have.

This is not a browser run. It is the link, its ABI and its artefact, measured; a campaign proof for th13 is the
next step and needs the shell and th13's archives in place.

### The gate, and its two ways of failing

`tools/th-runtime-web-builds.mjs --check` holds both halves:

- the artefact clears a 1 MiB floor, its report matches it by hash and byte count, and the report names the right
  title - the section 47 lesson applied to a second artefact;
- every title's harness exports **exactly** the reference build's names and imports nothing the reference does not.
  A dropped or added entry point is invisible to a size check and fatal to the shell.

Both rules were falsified rather than assumed. Pointing th13's wasm at th12's file makes the check report the stale
byte count and the stale hash. Giving th13 an artefact with no host entry points at all - the 857,968-byte engine
module, with its report fields rewritten to match - makes it report the size floor **and** the full list of 85 missing
exports. The bytes were restored and verified afterwards both times.

### th13's data

The archives for th13 were already extracted in an earlier round under
`runtimes/th13/th13_web/artifacts/cpp/th13-data/` - 55 `.anm`, 41 `.msg`, 21 `.ecl`, 59 `.wav` and 8 `.png`, the same
layout as th12's `th12-data/`. That directory is the test harness's extracted data, not the browser's; the harness
takes the original `.dat` through the filesystem the shell mounts. Nothing about it needed to change this round, and
noting it here corrects an earlier statement of mine that the five other titles had no port artefacts beyond their
target description.

## 49. th13 boots in the browser, and the failure names the next table

th13's harness now runs in a real browser. `runtimes/th13/th13_web/scripts/serve-sdl.mjs` serves an allowlist - the
title's own harness and archive, the title-neutral shell, fonts and stand-in music - and a headless Chrome run loads
the page, instantiates the 1,560,664-byte module, and calls `th11_initialize`. The call reaches the archive and
then returns false:

```
游戏运行失败：Missing sound: se_tan00.wav
{"running":false,"phase":0,"stage":0,"stageFrame":0,"error":"Missing sound: se_tan00.wav"}
```

Evidence: `docs/porting/browser-th13-boot.json` and `docs/porting/evidence/th13-boot-first-error.png`, with 0 page
errors and 1 console error.

That is a precise result, not a vague failure: the runtime boots, the archive opens and decrypts, and what stops it
is a **per-title resource table**. `SoundEffects.cpp` carries TH12's 49-entry sample list, taken from `.data
0x4aea50`; on th13's archive one of those names is not present. The per-title half of a runtime is not only the
no-op table.

### The sample counts, measured on both sides

`tools/th-archive-names.mjs` lists a title's entries through the port's own decoder, in archive order. For the two
titles with an archive on hand:

| title | archive entries | `.wav` entries | distinct | duplicates | `se_*.wav` strings in the executable |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12 | 180 | 49 | 48 | `se_cardget.wav` x2 | 48 distinct |
| 13 | 216 | 60 | 59 | `se_cardget.wav` x2 | 59 distinct |

Two things fall out. The "49" in the comment beside TH12's table is the **archive count including one duplicate**,
not a count of distinct samples: `GameResources.cpp` already records that retail th12.dat ships `se_cardget.wav`
twice, and the count is derived here from the archive rather than from that note. And th13 shows the same shape -
59 distinct names, 60 archive entries, the same duplicated sample - so the 59-against-60 difference is the same
fact and not a lost name.

### The finding that changes how the table must be derived

The instrument had to be checked before the order could be used, and it failed: the position of a name in the
archive is monotone in the executable's **string layout order** for only 2 of 49 names. So "table order equals
archive order" does not mean the strings' order in `.rdata`; the table is the pointer array in `.data`
(`0x4aea50` in th12.exe, "49 consecutive pointers"), and that array's order is what has to be read. Sorting the
strings was the wrong derivation, and measuring the rank agreement is what showed it.

### A tool fix along the way

The target description is not in the same place for every title: th12 keeps `target.json` inside its runtime
directory, th13..th18 keep it beside the runtime. `tools/th-archive-names.mjs` tries both, which is also the
confirmation that the six titles' layout was never uniform.

### State of the second title

Built and verified: the engine (100 sources, six titles), the playable harness (same 85 exports and 422 imports as
th12, different bytes), the shell page and the static server. The next table to derive is th13's sample list, from
`th13.exe`'s pointer array; its cue table and other per-title resource tables follow the same method.

## 50. Four per-title differences in one load chain, and the instrument that made them visible

Round 270 ended with th13's browser boot failing on a name its archive holds: `Missing sound: se_tan00.wav`. This
round walked that chain to its end and found that the name was never the problem. Each layer was a **table or a
constant chosen by the title**, and each was measured on the original executables and archives rather than guessed.

### 50.1 The pointers, not the strings

`tools/th-sample-table.py` reads a title's sample table the way `SoundEffects.cpp` describes it: parse the PE section
table (file offset != VA - image base), collect the `.rdata` VAs of the `se_*.wav` strings, and find the run of
consecutive u32 slots in the writable data section that point at them. Calibrated against the title whose answer is
known, it finds `0x004aea50`, **49 entries, 48 distinct** for th12, exactly the array and the archive order the
port already carried - and its head matches the port's list name for name. The same code, with no title constant,
finds `0x004bb320`, **60 entries, 59 distinct** for th13.

Both were then compared with the archives, through the port's own decoder:

| title | array | array entries | archive `.wav` entries | identical order |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12 | `0x004aea50` | 49 (48 distinct) | 49 | yes, entry for entry |
| 13 | `0x004bb320` | 60 (59 distinct) | 60 | yes, entry for entry |

So the two lists are now the tables `SoundEffects.cpp` selects on `kPortTitle`, and `AudioDevice` sizes its sample
buffer from the title's count instead of the buffer's capacity (which was 46 for a 49-name list).

The strings' order in `.rdata` stays the wrong thing to sort by: monotone against archive order for 2 of 49 names.

### 50.2 An archive generation is not a default

With the right names, the same failure persisted. The archive layer, not the resource, was the reason: `Archive`
took `archiveVersion=12` by default, so a th13 build decrypted the 16-byte header with fixed parameters (which is why
opening succeeded) and then decrypted each entry with `ciphers[sum&7]` from TH12's table. A failed decode and a
failed lookup report the same message, so a cipher mismatch read as a missing resource for a file that decodes to
15,100 well-formed bytes through the API the tool uses.

`GameResources::open_archive` now passes the title's generation: 12 for th12, 13 for th13, and the table TH14 and
later share for the rest, which is exactly the mapping `archive_crypt_table` implements.

### 50.3 The ANM marker

The boot then failed at `ascii ANM`. Measured, the two files differ in one header field out of the ones the parser
reads: th12's `ascii.anm` starts with 7, th13's with 8, and `ns`, `nc`, `stride`, the name offset and the asset
offset are consistent in both. The parser accepted 7 only. It now accepts the title's marker.

### 50.4 The shot set is a different shape

The boot then reached the end of the core resource list and stopped with `SHT resource`. th13.dat holds
`pl00a.sht pl01a.sht pl02a.sht pl03a.sht` and nothing named `pl00b`, `pl01b` or `pl02b`: **four characters with
one shot set each**, where th12 has three characters with two variants. The loader in `GameSessionResources` names
six files. That is the next table, and the first one that changes a structure rather than a constant.

The prediction was made offline - the entry list says the three `*b.sht` names are absent - and the browser run
reproduces it in 4.4 s on this build.

### 50.5 The measurement that made the chain visible

A run before the status readout sat for 42 s with no error and no progress, and the file held by the archive said
nothing about where it was. The instrument added for that:

- `GameResources` keeps the last requested entry name (`last_resource`);
- `Application.cpp` exports it as `th11_last_resource`;
- the shell writes each `prepare()` step into `#status` before it suspends;
- `tools/browser-proof.mjs` reports that text as `loading` in its snapshot.

It is a readout of load order, not a result: it feeds no assertion and it cannot make a run pass.
