- `hook_add(2)` is rejected outright: `uc_hook_add failed with code 9: Invalid hook type`.
- `hook_add(112|1024|2048|4096|...|265216)` - the module's own bits OR-ed - is accepted, its
  callback still fires zero times, and the failure changes shape:
  `RuntimeError: null function or function signature mismatch` at `pc=0x402523`.

So the first two numbers are masks this build rejects or ignores, and "no events" from a memory hook
is not evidence about the guest here.

### 67.4 Where the trap sits, with the memset mounted in a fresh process

One fresh process, `m.replace(0x477420,'memset',handler,3)` and one `m.call(0x402520)`:
the trace now runs *through* the call and reaches `0x477447` (the memset body's own `jmp 0x48b39a`)
before the trap, while the host handler ran **zero** times. So the failure is not "before the call";
it is in the path the call takes through the memset - the filler at `0x48b39a`, which the same
engine runs happily when the memset is called on its own with the same arguments.

### 67.5 The next step, named

Snapshot registers from a code hook that reaches `0x48b39a` in the *in-call* context (the same
engine, fresh process, per-instruction snapshot of `esp/ebp/ecx/edx/edi` plus the accessed range)
and let the last snapshot name the exact instruction; the direct-memset runs at the same arguments
are the control. This is one instrument with one control, and it is the only thing standing
between the oracle suite and a whole-corpus run - so the fixture suites also need the per-process
rule: one case per process, or a reset the poison survives.
## 68. The engine's refusal, measured case by case

### 68.1 The boundary is real and survives the one-process-per-measurement rule

One fresh process per line (`tests/cpp`):

```
m.call(0x402545) -> wasm trap, and its code hook saw 0x402545, 0x402546, 0x402548 first
m.call(0x40254c) -> wasm trap, one event (the call); the memset runs, the trap follows it
m.call(0x402551) -> wasm trap, ZERO events
m.call(0x402553) -> wasm trap, ZERO events
m.call(0x402557) -> wasm trap, ZERO events
m.call(0x40255a) -> wasm trap, ZERO events
m.call(0x40255e) -> wasm trap, ZERO events
m.call(0x402560) -> wasm trap, ZERO events
m.call(0x402561) -> ordinary emulation (the guest faults later on its own)
m.call(0x402564) -> ordinary emulation
m.call(0x40256d) -> ordinary emulation
```

Six consecutive entry points refuse to start, six bytes apart in the last case, and the next one
runs. The head instruction of the refusing window is `fld1` (`d9 e8` at `0x402551`); the first
accepting entry is `fst dword [esi+0x50]` (`d9 56 50` at `0x402561`).

### 68.2 Argument count is not the cause

`m.call(0x402520)` with `args` of length **0, 1, 3, 4 and 5**, one fresh process each, traps with
the same error every time. The initialiser's own stack contract is self-contained: it does its own
`push`es before `call memset`, cleans them with `add esp,0xc`, restores `edi/ebp/ebx`, skips
`0x10` bytes and returns - so pass anything.

### 68.3 Not the harness: a bare engine with a proper frame does the same

With the harness's two hooks deleted (`for(const hook of m.hooks) m.cpu.hook_del(hook)`) and the
stack prepared the same way the harness prepares it (`esp = 0x07efff00`, the return address on top),
a direct

```
m.cpu.emu_start(entry, 0x07f00000, 0, 200000)
```

gives: entry `0x402551` -> the wasm trap; `0x402561` -> ordinary emulation; `0x402520` -> the wasm
trap (it reaches its own `call` and returns to `0x402551`). No `m.call`, no hook, no fixture.

### 68.4 The bytes matter, but bytes alone are not the rule

Minimal assemblies, each in a fresh process at a scratch address, with the same frame, through
`uc_emu_start`: `fst dword [esi+0x50]; ret`, `fld1; fst dword [esi+0x50]; ret`,
`mov edx,[esp+0x18]; ret`, and the **exact sixteen bytes of the refusing window**
(`d9 e8 8b 54 24 18 d9 56 40 8b 44 24 24 d9 56 44`) - all four run, and the first and third were
repeated to show it is not flaky.

Then the same sixteen bytes **copied** to the heap run, while at `0x402551` they trap; and the
sixteen bytes at `0x402561` copied to the same heap slot **trap**. So the engine accepts or refuses
on more than the instruction bytes: both an address effect and a first-bytes effect are present.

The in-call control is quieter than the rest: `memset(0x477420)` itself runs for sizes `1, 0x10,
0xff, 0x100, 0x101, 0x200, 0x4b4`, and so do its helpers `0x48b343`/`0x48b39a` called on their
own. A register snapshot on the failing path puts the last instruction at the memset filler's own
`ret` (`0x48b428`, `esp=0x7effed0`, `ebp` already popped): the word it pops is `0x402551`, and
`0x402551` is measured (68.1) to fail on its own.

### 68.5 The artifact: an acceptance table, and the tool to grow it

`docs/porting/oracle-engine-acceptance.json` collects the 21 measured cases with, for each, the
entry, how it was measured, and the verdict, under one sentence of method: **one case per node
process**, because of section 67. It also records the two limits: no repetitions except the
minimal forms, and no model yet.

`tools/th-callers.py <exe> <0xVA>` is the other half of a transcription: it lists a virtual
address's raw `e8` sites with the caller's own code window, so the argument pushes come from the
caller's bytes. For `0x402520`, th12 has 33 raw hits (the first two windows only disassemble
cleanly after a few bytes, so a raw hit is a candidate, not a call site); for its memset there are
192. The tool's docstring says which part is which.

### 68.6 The next step, named

Grow the table mechanically instead of arguing: a batch runner that starts one node process per case
(the rule from section 67), over a grid of (entry address, byte pattern, frame), and appends the
verdicts, so that either an accepted **shape** the fixture can use emerges, or the interval of
accepted shapes is small enough to conclude that this build cannot run the oracle and the bounded
Unicorn build named in `helpers.mjs` is the route. The fixture cases that already depend on it are
the first `m.call` of `anm-oracle.mjs` (`0x454190`, an ordinary guest fault today because its data
is still th11's) and every fixture row built from the code table of section 64.
## 69. A minimal reproducer, a box of one-at-a-time cases, and which fixture entries the engine accepts

### 69.1 Eight lines, the shipped bytes, no fixture

```js
const bytes=readFileSync(resolve(root,target.executable));
const m=await NativeMachine.create(bytes);          // no helpers.oracle(), no replace(), no bring-up
m.reg('ESP',m.stack); m.u32(m.stack,m.returnAddress); m.reg('ESI',heap);
m.cpu.emu_start(0x402551, m.returnAddress, 0, 200000);   // wasm trap
m.cpu.emu_start(0x402561, m.returnAddress, 0, 200000);   // ordinary emulation
```

`resetThreadFPU()` or not, hooks present or deleted, before or after the fixture's bring-up: the two
lines say the same thing. `helpers.oracle()`'s whole bring-up, the four `replace()` stubs, the
argument list of the call, the harness `call()` - none of them is needed to reproduce it, and none
of them changes it. That is what `tests/cpp/engine-case.mjs` runs.

### 69.2 A box that holds one case per process

`tests/cpp/engine-case.mjs` takes one spec as JSON and prints one JSON line; `tests/cpp/
engine-acceptance.mjs` runs a grid of specs through it, one node process each (section 67's rule),
prints a table, and with `--out` appends the run to `docs/porting/oracle-engine-acceptance.json`
under `runs`. Commands: `case` (one spec), `window` (a byte range), `prefix` (a byte string cut
to lengths with a `ret`, the cut-length bisect), `sample` (a spread of `.text` addresses). A run
records the grid it covered, so a table can be re-measured instead of quoted.

### 69.3 It is the bytes, not the address

The 33 entries `0x402548..0x402568`, one process each, with the shipped bytes:

```
tally: {trap: 23, guest: 10}
```

The traps are not a contiguous window: `0x402548,0x402549,0x40254a` trap, `0x40254b` is an
ordinary guest fault, `0x40254c` traps, `0x40254d..0x402550` are guest faults, and from
`0x402551` on traps and guest faults alternate at byte resolution (`0x402561` is a guest fault,
`0x402562` traps, `0x402563/0x402564` are guest faults, `0x402565..0x402567` trap). Then the
same 33 entries with **one byte (`0xc3`, a `ret`) written over the entry**: `tally: {ok: 33}`.
The address is fine at every one of them; the shipped instruction stream is not.

That also corrects 68.1's shape: "the 16-byte window" was the harness reading of a phenomenon
that is not contiguous, though every number 68.1 recorded is reproduced exactly here.

### 69.4 It happens before a single instruction

`limit 1` (one instruction):

```
uc_emu_start(0x402551, until, 0, 1) -> trap, and the code hook saw ZERO instructions
uc_emu_start(0x402561, until, 0, 1) -> stopped after exactly one: eip=0x402564, hook saw one
```

So the engine refuses at **entry/translation** time for that byte stream, in a machine with both
harness hooks deleted. A `ret` written over the entry, the same 16 bytes copied to a heap address,
or the exact same bytes assembled at a scratch address all run (68.4) - the stream the shipped image
has from `0x402551` is the case the engine will not start.

### 69.5 Which fixture entries the engine accepts

The fixture's game-facing calls mapped into th12 (`fixture-addresses.mjs`'s `touch`, applied to the
addresses `anm-oracle.mjs` uses), each one process in `--mode oracle` - the fixture's own machine,
with the bring-up and the stubs:

| fixture role | th12 address | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| template initialiser (`0x401fd0` in the fixture) | `0x402520` | **wasm trap** |
| ANM resource load (`0x454190`) | `0x45fc90` | ok |
| ANM chunk read (`0x4545a0`) | `0x4600a0` | ok |
| animation spawn (`0x455a00/0x455df0/0x455bc0/0x456020`) | `0x44bf6a` | ok |
| overlay update (`0x455480`) | `0x460fe0` | ok |
| overlay update, overlay branch (`0x455560`) | `0x4610d0` | ordinary guest fault (it wants game state) |

**Five of six are accepted, and the one that is refused is the fixture's first game call.** That is
the whole of the oracle suite's blocker, and it is one address, not the engine as a whole.

### 69.6 The next step, named

Two in parallel, and the box is the instrument for both:

1. Aligned cut-length bisect of the refusing stream (the `prefix` command with boundaries that fall
   between instructions, `ret` included), to name the shortest prefix the engine refuses and - if a
   `fld`/`fst` shape is the trigger - to check it against the fixture-relevant cases.
2. The fixture side: since only `0x402520` is refused, the cheapest route to a whole-corpus run is
   a measured host stand-in for the five instructions at `0x402551..0x402560` (the sub-block the
   initialiser re-enters after its own `call memset`), or an entry at `0x402561` with the first
   five instructions host-written - and either way the template's `0x434` bytes are compared against
   the oracle's own `initialized` buffer, which `anm-oracle.mjs` already keeps, so the stand-in is
   verified rather than asserted.
## 70. The refused block, relocated: the fixture's first call now runs

### 70.1 The shape the engine does accept

`m.write(0x402551, {0xeb,0x0e, nop x14})` - a two-byte jump over the five instructions to
`0x402561` - and the entry is accepted. Measured with the box (`engine-acceptance.mjs case
--entry 0x402551 --implant eb0e9090...`), the code hook then sees `0x402551 0x402561 0x402564
0x40256a`: the jump itself, then the shipped continuation, exactly where the disassembly says it
resumes.

### 70.2 Two shapes of the stand-in leave the same template

`tests/cpp/template-standin.mjs`, one process per variant:

| variant | what it does | verdict | template sha256 (first 16) |
|---|---|---|---|
| S | jump at `0x402551` to a heap copy of the five, which ends `jmp 0x402561` | wasm trap | `e174d832bbc0b665` |
| P | jump over the five, with `edx`/`eax` read from the block's own frame and `ST(0)=1.0` set by executing `fld1; ret` in the heap | ok | `0a12ba04f0167bf7` |
| P again | the same, second process | ok | `0a12ba04f0167bf7` |
| Q | jump over the five, with the five executed at a heap address (`template-standin.mjs` variant Q) | ok | `0a12ba04f0167bf7` |

P and Q do **not** share the mechanism: P seeds the three values the block produces, Q executes the
block's own bytes. They agree byte for byte on the whole `0x434`-byte template, and P reproduces
itself across processes. (S shows a relocation of the *block itself* is not enough: the engine
refuses those same bytes when entered as a block, which is why the stand-in here skips them and
executes them with `m.call`, either way ending in the accepted continuation.)

### 70.3 The fixture change is one call and a new module

`tests/cpp/engine-block-standin.mjs` exports `initialiseTemplate(m,{entry,block,size,template})`:
it copies `0x10` bytes at `block` into the heap, appends `ret`, writes the jump over the block,
executes the heap copy with the block's own frame, then calls `entry` exactly as the fixture did.
`anm-oracle.mjs`'s line 20 keeps the fixture's own addresses (`touch(0x401fd0)`,
`touch(0x434)`) and passes `block=0x402551` - the block the box measured as refused in this image,
addresses only, no title.

Before, and after (same command, `node --test dialogue.test.mjs`):

```
before: Error: RuntimeError: memory access out of bounds
        at NativeMachine.call (.../machine.mjs:69)
        at animationOracle (.../anm-oracle.mjs:20)
        at ... dialogue.test.mjs:6
after:  Error: Unicorn.js: Function uc_emu_start failed with code 6
        at NativeMachine.call (.../machine.mjs:69)
        at ... dialogue.test.mjs:7
        payload {"type":19,"address":"0x0","size":4,"pc":"0x45fbff",
                 "stack":["0x460125","0x0","0x27c0a80",...]}
```

The wasm-side trap is gone and the failure has moved to the fixture's own next line, as an ordinary
guest fault: a four-byte read of address `0` at `pc=0x45fbff`, in the ANM loader.

### 70.4 Eight suites, after the stand-in

| suite | verdict | first guest payload |
|---|---|---|
| `th12-rng.test.mjs` | **pass 2 / fail 0** | - |
| `dialogue.test.mjs` | fail | read of `0x0` (4) at `0x45fbff` |
| `damage-area.test.mjs` | fail | read of `0x8` (1) at `0x27c9db0` |
| `anm-scripts.test.mjs` | fail | (no guest payload) |
| `bullet-manager.test.mjs` | fail | (no guest payload) |
| `hud.test.mjs` | fail | write of `0x1` (1) at `0x41a6d0` |
| `score-popups.test.mjs` | fail | write of `0x0` (1) at `0x0` |
| `screen-fade.test.mjs` | fail | read of `0x24` (4) at `0x4489f1` |

**No wasm-side trap in any of them.** The engine now runs the fixture; what the eight meet is
guest data - null pointers, unwritten globals, unloaded resources - which is ordinary oracle
bring-up work and no longer an engine limitation. The box (`engine-acceptance.mjs`) stays the
instrument for any new "the engine refuses X" claim.

### 70.5 The next step, named

Take the first of them on its own terms: the four-byte read of address `0` at `0x45fbff` in the
ANM loader, reached from `dialogue.test.mjs`'s `o.load('text.anm')`. Its caller chain is in the
payload's stack (`0x460125`, `0x46d9b2`) and the register snapshot/dump of that one call is the
next measured item; the globals/constants tables of section 66.7 are the place a missing
fixture-side write would come from.
## 71. The ANM load's null read is the D3D8 device: a named chain, a mount, and an argument count that had to be measured

### 71.1 The chain, from the fixture's own call to the null

`dialogue.test.mjs` line 7 calls `o.load('text.anm')`, which is one `m.call` of
`touch(0x454190)` -> `0x45fc90`. The first fault in the load was a four-byte read of address `0`
at `pc=0x45fbff`, whose stack named the caller `0x460125`. That address is inside `FUN_004600a0`,
which the fixture itself calls as its chunk reader (`touch(0x4545a0)`), and the decomp of that
function names its callee:

```c
/* FUN_0045fbf0 @ 0045fbf0 */
*(uint *)(unaff_ESI + 0x10) = *(uint *)(unaff_ESI + 0x10) | 1;
(**(code **)(*DAT_004ce8f0 + 0x5c))(DAT_004ce8f0,DAT_004ce9dc,DAT_004ce9e0,1,1,DAT_004ce9e4,0);
*(uint *)(unaff_ESI + 0xc) = (uint)(DAT_004ce9e4 == 0x16) * 2 + 2;
```

and the raw bytes at `0x45fbf0..0x45fc34` (th12.exe, `tools/th-code-region.py`):

```
0x45fbf4  mov edx, [0x4ce9e4]      0x45fbfa  mov eax, [0x4ce8f0]
0x45fbff  mov ecx, [eax]           0x45fc01  push 0        ... nine pushes ...
0x45fc1a  mov eax, [ecx + 0x5c]    0x45fc1d  call eax      0x45fc34  ret
```

So the null pointer is the **D3D8 device singleton** and the indirect call is a `CreateTexture`
(the parallel site `0x45fba0` is the decomp's `D3DXCreateTexture(DAT_004ce8f0, ...)`).

`tools/th-writers.py` (new, this round) disassembles the whole image with capstone and reports
every instruction whose memory operand is an absolute reference to one address, classified by
whether it is the destination:

```
  H:/Games/th/12/th12.exe  0x4ce8f0: 273 absolute site(s)
    write   0x44fc24  mov dword ptr [0x4ce8f0], ebx
```

**One writer and 272 readers.** The writer is inside the teardown around `0x44fb8d` (`xor ebx,ebx`
at `0x44fb97`, then a run of `call [eax+8]` destructors), i.e. it writes **zero**, on shutdown.
The value the loader expects is therefore not established by any constructor in the image at all:
the game creates it through the `d3d8.dll` import path, which is exactly what this fixture
substitutes. Instrument caveat, kept explicit: the tool is a linear sweep with `skipdata`, so a
site in unaligned data is reported too; the single `write` is nonetheless the total over the
image, and it agrees with the measurement (the fixture's machine reads zero at `0x45fbff`).

### 71.2 The mount

`tests/cpp/anm-oracle.mjs` already substitutes "host allocation and GPU resource creation"; the
device belongs beside its three texture stubs:

```js
const deviceVtable=m.allocate(0x100),device=m.allocate(0x20);m.u32(device,deviceVtable);
m.u32(deviceVtable+0x5c,m.registerImport({dll:'fixture',name:'d3d device create texture',argc:9,handler:()=>0}));
m.u32(touch(0x4c3288),device);
```

`touch(0x4c3288)` is the fixture's own globals table entry - a measurement it has carried since
section 66.7 - which maps that source address to th12's `0x004ce8f0` (40 references, 8 agreeing
sites). The object layout is the COM one the raw code assumes: `[global]` is the interface
pointer, `*interface` is its vtable, and slot `+0x5c` is the method.

### 71.3 The measured effect

`tests/cpp/anm-load-fault.mjs` (new keeper: one loading call per process, then the payload, the
registers and the stack) before and after the mount, `text.anm`:

```
before: read of 0x0 (4) at pc=0x45fbff   EAX=0x0                       <- the device global is zero
after:  read of 0x0 (4) at pc=0x46024a   stack ["0x0","0x27c0ba0",...] <- the load runs on
```

`0x46024a` is `mov edx,[ecx]` where `ecx` came from `mov edx,[edi+0x120]; mov ecx,[edx+ebx]`
- a null entry in the loader's **texture table** (`param_1[0x48] + index` in the decomp's
terms). Six hundred bytes of original chunk-reading code now execute before it.

The sweep of the same eight suites as section 70.4, after the mount: `th12-rng` **pass 2 / fail
0**, and dialogue, damage-area, anm-scripts, bullet-manager, hud, score-popups and screen-fade fail
on guest data again (`pc 0x46024a`, `0x27c9ed0`, `0x41a6d0`, `pc 0`, `0x4489f1`) - **no
wasm-side trap in any of them**.

### 71.4 The argument count was measured, not assumed

`FUN_0045fbf0` pushes nine dwords before the indirect call. Guessing eight is silent in the
obvious way: the callee cleans four bytes too few, so the loader's own `ret` pops an argument as
its return address. `tests/cpp/anm-load-device.mjs` mounts a `CreateTexture` stub whose `argc`
comes from `CT_ARGC` and reports:

```
CT_ARGC=8 -> pc=0x0        (the loader's return address was popped as an argument)
CT_ARGC=9 -> pc=0x46024a   (the loader returns cleanly; the load reaches the texture table)
```

Two instrument lessons from that run, both worth keeping:

* `machine.mjs:39-46` keys a stub by `dll!name` and **overwrites** the map entry for one that
  exists. A fixture and a probe that register the same key therefore share a stub, and the
  **last** registration's `argc` governs calls already wired to it. The probe above uses a
  distinct key (`probe!create texture argc N`) so that the number under test is the one measured.
* The first version of the probe passed `--device` and tested `argv.includes('device')`, which is
  false for `--device`; the readback made the mistake visible (`afterWrite: 0x0` next to a
  successful `touch`). A readback of the value written is cheap and catches it.

### 71.5 The next step, named

**`0x46024a`.** The same substitution is missing its second half: `CreateTexture` has an output
pointer among its nine arguments, and the table the loader walks holds texture objects whose
`+0x44` slot it calls (`call ecx`, `mov ecx,[edx+0x44]`) - the slot the fixture already mounts
as `'texture dimensions'`. So the next experiment writes the created texture into the argument the
game expects, and re-runs `anm-load-fault.mjs` to see the load pass the table.
## 72. The ANM loader runs: the record write-back, and 47 of 47 shipped files

### 72.1 What the CreateTexture call has to leave behind

Section 71 ended on `pc=0x46024a`, a read of address 0. The chunk reader's own sequence says what
the missing value is (`tools/th-code-region.py`, th12.exe):

```
0x46023e  mov edx, [edi + 0x120]    ; the table of texture records
0x460244  mov ecx, [edx + ebx]      ; record = table + index*0x14 (computed at 0x460201)
0x46024a  mov edx, [ecx]            ; the record's first dword is the texture interface
0x46024c  mov eax, [eax]            ; the same interface, as the call's first argument
0x460253  mov ecx, [edx + 0x44]     ; its vtable's +0x44 slot
0x460259  call ecx                   ; (interface, 0, out)
```

and the create function section 71 identified (`FUN_0045fbf0`) is handed that record: it ORs 1
into `[esi+0x10]`, writes `[esi+0xc]`, and `esi` itself is one of the nine pushed argument
dwords. So the device method is expected to **store the created texture interface into the record**
- an output pointer the fixture's stub was not filling.

Which argument is the record was measured, not reasoned about: `anm-load-device.mjs` (this round,
`CT_WRITE`) reads a stack slot and stores the texture interface at the address it finds.

| `CT_WRITE` | outcome |
|---|---|
| unset | read of `0x0` at `pc=0x46024a` (the record stays null) |
| `0x24` | identical (the ninth argument is 0) |
| `0x20` | **the record fills, `0x46024a` no longer faults**, and execution reaches the call at `0x460259` |

`0x20` is the eighth argument, the `esi` push.

### 72.2 The fixture

`anm-oracle.mjs`'s CreateTexture stub keeps the address the game looked at:

```js
m.u32(deviceVtable+0x5c,m.registerImport({dll:'fixture',name:'d3d device create texture',argc:9,
  handler:()=>{const record=m.u32(m.reg('ESP')+0x20);if(record>0x10000)m.u32(record,texture);return 0;}}));
```

The `texture` object is one the fixture already builds two lines above, and its vtable already
carries `+0x44` as `'texture dimensions'` - so the game's own `call [edx+0x44]` lands on the
fixture's host stub, reads the ANM's chunk header for the size, and the load continues.

### 72.3 The measurement: the load returns

`tests/cpp/anm-load-fault.mjs` (one loading call per process):

```
text.anm   -> verdict ok   original=0x27c6860   heap=0x27c8140
front.anm  -> verdict ok
pl00.anm   -> verdict ok
```

and `tests/cpp/anm-load-all.mjs` (new keeper: every `reference/assets/*.anm`, one call per file,
first wasm trap stops the run):

```
assets=47 requested=47 tally={'ok': 47}
```

**All 47 shipped animation files load through the original's own loader in the oracle.** The ANM
stage of the fixture is no longer a gate: the suites below it now exercise their own subjects.

### 72.4 The suites, after

Same eight-suite sweep shape as 70.4/71.3, with a couple of neighbours added; every row is now
past the load, and the failure addresses are ordinary game code:

| suite | verdict | first guest payload |
|---|---|---|
| `th12-rng.test.mjs` | **pass 2 / fail 0** | - |
| `dialogue.test.mjs` | fail | `pc=0x41cfe0` |
| `anm-scripts.test.mjs` | fail | (node-side) |
| `hud.test.mjs` | fail | `pc=0x41a6d0` |
| `enemy-animations.test.mjs` | fail | `pc=0x412e30` |
| `player-animations.test.mjs` | fail | (node-side) |
| `title-selection.test.mjs` | fail | `pc=0x407700` |
| `budget-render.test.mjs` | fail | (node-side) |

None of them was anywhere near these addresses before: the loader used to die at `0x45fbff`, in
`0x45`-space. `0x41a6d0`/`0x41cfe0`/`0x412e30`/`0x407700` are the game's own logic and render
paths, and no wasm-side trap appears in any row.

### 72.5 The next step, named

Take `enemy-animations.test.mjs` (`pc=0x412e30`) or `dialogue.test.mjs` (`pc=0x41cfe0`) and make
each the subject of its own round with the same shape as this one: the payload's pc and registers,
then the decomp and the disassembly of that site, then the one substitution or the one global the
fixture must supply, then re-measure. The load's own instrument (`anm-load-fault.mjs`,
`anm-load-all.mjs`) stays in place as the regression for the stage that was just made whole.
## 73. Why a fixture suite can die in the wrong title: source addresses, measured twins, and field offsets

### 73.1 The audit

`tests/cpp/fixture-address-audit.mjs` (new) reads a fixture file, collects every `0x4xxxxx`
literal, and asks `touch()` what each maps to. A fixture is th11-shaped: the shipped tables map a
source address to the target image's, and a fixture that writes the *native* machine (`m.*`) must
write the mapped address - the same literal in a *core* accessor belongs to the port's own
(source) naming. A raw source address written into the native machine is the quiet kind of wrong:
the game reads the mapped address, finds zero, and dies somewhere unrelated. The audit's first run,
over the two suites of section 72.4 that fail late:

```
enemy-animations.test.mjs: 4 mapped literal(s) of 8
  0x4a7948 x1 -> 0x4b2ed0
  0x4a8d7c x1 -> 0x4b43dc
  0x4c2ef8 x1 -> 0x4ce560
  0x4c2f00 x1 -> 0x4a3ce0
dialogue.test.mjs: 15 mapped literal(s) of 26
  0x4a5714 x1 -> 0xc900d8b   0x4a5728 x1 -> 0x4b0cb0   0x4a5730 x1 -> 0x4b0cb8
  0x4a5738 x1 -> 0x48c       0x4a7948 x1 -> 0x4b2ed0   0x4a8d7c x1 -> 0x4b43dc
  0x4a8d84 x1 -> 0x4b43e4   0x4a8e94 x1 -> 0x4b44f4   0x4a8eb4 x1 -> 0x4b4514
  0x4a8ec8 x1 -> 0x4b452c   0x4c2ef8 x1 -> 0x4ce560   0x4c2f00 x1 -> 0x4a3ce0
  0x4c3808 x1 -> 0x1074     0x4c93c0 x1 -> 0x4d49d0   0x4c93cc x1 -> 0x4d49dc
```

`enemy-animations.test.mjs` writes `0x4a8d7c` into the native machine for the enemy manager, and
`0x4a7948` into the native enemy record; both are source addresses. Both now go through
`touch()`, as do the two RNG globals it compares natively (`0x4c2ef8`, `0x4c2f00`).

### 73.2 The bigger miss: the suite named a source *call target*

`enemy-animations.test.mjs` drives the port's ECL command executor and compares it against
`m.call(0x412e30, ...)`. `touch()` at first returned that address unchanged, so the native call
landed **mid-instruction in th12**: measured, the run read address 0 at `pc=0x412e30` and never
executed a single prologue byte. In th11 the same address is a real entry - `int3` padding, then
`push ebp; mov ebp,esp; and esp,-8; push -1; ...; sub esp,0x310` - and five suite files call it,
so the fixture is right and the *table* was short one measurement.

`tools/th-twin-find.py` (self-checked first: the identical-title round trip names `0x402520` at a
run of 48/48 literals) gives:

```
0x412e30 -> th12: 3 candidate(s), run >= 8  (span 64)
  run 9/64 literals 52  0x004154d0  55 8b ec 83 e4 f8 6a ff 68 ce 76 49
  run 9/64 literals 52  0x004049a0  55 8b ec 83 e4 f8 6a ff 68 4c 75 49
  run 8/64 literals 52  0x00404992  ...
```

The prologue alone is **ambiguous**: two th12 functions share `push ebp; mov ebp,esp; and
esp,-8; push -1; push imm32; 64 a1 00 00 00 00; 50; 81 ec imm32`. The body window decides it
(`--span 96` from th11 `0x412ea0`): a single candidate at a run of 21 literals, landing `0x6c`
into `0x004154d0`, and the frame size agrees with the shift - th11 `sub esp,0x310`, `0x004154d0`
`sub esp,0x308`, while the other candidate's frame is `0xa0` and the body hit is not inside it.

The row is added to `docs/porting/oracle-th11-th12.json` (`0x412e30 -> 0x004154d0`, span 96,
with the two windows and the frame-size argument recorded as evidence). `touch(0x412e30)` now
returns `0x4154d0`, and the suite's call is routed through it.

### 73.3 Acceptance by use, and the next translation the measurement exposed

With the call routed, the suite no longer dies at a garbage address: the executor's own prologue
runs and the fault moves to `pc=0x415518`, inside the function the twin search picked. That
address is the function's third instruction of substance:

```
0x415510  mov ebx, ecx                     0x412e??  mov ebx, ecx
0x415512  mov esi, [ebx + 0x174c]          0x412e??  mov esi, [ebx + 0x1614]
0x415518  mov eax, [esi + 4]      <-- null 0x412e78  mov eax, [esi + 4]
0x41551b  mov edi, [eax + 4]               0x412e7b  mov edi, [eax + 4]
0x41551e  movzx eax, word [edi + 4]        0x412e7e  movzx eax, word [edi + 4]
```

Byte for byte the two titles run the same function; the field offset moved (**0x1614 -> 0x174c**).
The fixture copies the 0x163c-byte enemy record (a th11-shaped structure, and the suite's
`normalize()` lists its fields) into the native machine, so the native read at `+0x174c` finds
the zero the two functions are looking past. The measurement above is the acceptance evidence
that the twin is right, and the offset is the next translation the fixture needs - the same shape
as the address tables: measure it (a field-offset row per structure), record the source, and let
the suite's own differential comparison decide.

After this round the audit reports five mapped literals in `enemy-animations.test.mjs`
(`0x412e30 -> 0x4154d0`, the two globals, and the two RNG globals), and the suite's first
failure is the field offset above rather than the call.
## 74. A moved field is a measurable row; the oracle's own budget is measurable too

### 74.1 The instrument for the next translation

Section 73 ended with a byte-level measurement: th12 `mov esi,[ebx+0x174c]` where th11 has
`mov esi,[ebx+0x1614]`, and the four instructions after it identical. A structure field that
moved is the same kind of fact as a function that moved, so it gets the same treatment: measure
it with a tool and ship the row.

`tools/th-twin-fields.py` (new) decodes the two copies of one function from their entries, walks
both streams, and pairs instructions. The pairing resynchronises on shape, and a pair counts only
when the two instructions have the same mnemonic and the same SIZE and **the same bytes outside
their numeric fields** (capstone reports each immediate's and displacement's offset). It prints the
alignment ratio and the operand-shape agreement with every answer, and it self-checks on an
identical-title round trip.

```
self-check: th12 0x402520 -> th12 0x402520 (span 0x120)
  decoded: 60 and 60 instructions, aligned 60
  alignment: 1.000 of the longer stream paired, 1.000 of pairs share operand shape
  field displacements that moved: 0

the executor: th11 0x412e30 -> th12 0x004154d0 (span 0x300)
  decoded: 200 and 198 instructions, aligned 164
  alignment: 0.820 of the longer stream paired, 1.000 of pairs share operand shape
  field displacements that moved: 32 (of 164 aligned pairs)
    0x412e72 -> 0x415512   [+0x1614 -> +0x174c]   mov esi, dword ptr [ebx + 0x1614]
    0x412ef1 -> 0x41558d   [+0x1580 -> +0x16b8]   test dword ptr [ebx + 0x1580], 0x400000
    0x412e51 -> 0x4154f1   [+0x308 -> +0x300]     mov dword ptr [esp + 0x308], eax
    0x412ed1 -> 0x41556d   [+0x298 -> +0x290]     lea eax, [esp + 0x298]      x6
```

Two things make the answer trustworthy beyond the tool's own report. The frame displacements all
move by exactly the amount the frame itself moved (`sub esp,0x310` against `sub esp,0x308`):
the alignment is witnessed by the shift it should produce. And the two record fields move by the
**same +0x138** - a coincidence that a wrong pairing would not produce. `0x412ef1` also shows a
constant of the same structure differently spelled (`0x400000` against `0x2000000`), which is
what `--constants` reports separately.

The rows go into `docs/porting/oracle-fields-th11-th12.json` (two rows, both shift 0x138, each
with the aligned pair and the acceptance note), and `fixture-addresses.mjs` grows a second,
separate map with `touchField()`: a fixture that writes a source-shaped record into the native
machine translates each measured field with it, exactly as it already routed addresses.

### 74.2 What that did to the suite

`enemy-animations.test.mjs` now routes its native call through `touch()`, moves the two measured
record fields and seeds the two RNG globals at their mapped addresses. Measured effect, same
suite, three runs of the same command:

```
before: guest fault, pc=0x412e30 (mid-instruction in th12), read of address 0, 1 native call
after:  native call 14, no guest unmapped-memory fault at all
```

In between the suite reached its own differential comparison and agreed: `c.ea_command(f,cc)`
against `m.call(...)` for opcode 0x102 returned equal, and the run continued through further
commands of the same sample. The executor's entry is now a measured address and the record's
fields reach the offsets the title reads.

### 74.3 The trap that follows, and the numbers that name it

The suite still fails, and now at a different layer: one `m.call` ends in a wasm-side
`RuntimeError: memory access out of bounds` with **no** guest fault recorded (the MEM_UNMAPPED hook
never fired), and the payload that used to say only "pc and stack" names this now:

```
{"pc":"0x7effc48","stack":["0x41c6d4","0x287ec2c","0x7effef8", ...],
 "calls":14,"entry":"0x4154d0",
 "stubs":[{"key":"kernel32.dll!GetProcAddress","registered":1,"calls":97},
          {"key":"kernel32.dll!TlsGetValue","registered":1,"calls":90},
          {"key":"kernel32.dll!GetModuleHandleW","registered":1,"calls":87},
          {"key":"kernel32.dll!EnterCriticalSection","registered":1,"calls":23},
          {"key":"kernel32.dll!LeaveCriticalSection","registered":1,"calls":23},
          {"key":"kernel32.dll!InterlockedIncrement","registered":1,"calls":18}]}
```

`machine.mjs` counts `m.call`s and, on the trap, reports the call count, the entry address and
the import census (registered from how many call sites, called how many times). The counts say
this is not a long run that wore the emulator down: the 14th call is *the executor itself*, and
inside that one call the guest runs an import-resolution loop (GetProcAddress 97 times). The guest's
EIP is a stack address while the CPU's `[esp]` holds `0x41c6d4`, the return of `call 0x4621c0`
at `0x41c6cf`, and the enter/leave pair is balanced 23/23 - so the next question is measured and
narrow: what does that resolution loop store, and where does the guest go when it uses what it
stored. The stub census - which also showed every one of the six imports registered exactly once
with the argument count it really has (`GetProcAddress` 2, the rest 1) - is the instrument for it.

Also in this round: `close()` in `machine.mjs` no longer turns a teardown trap into a suite failure.
One run's worth of `uc_emu_start` traps (the POISON rule) can leave a later `hook_del` trapping; the
handles it happened on are now collected into `machine.teardown` instead of being thrown.
## 75. A code row must name an instruction boundary, and the trace says so before the crash does

### 75.1 The trace, and the instrument's own integrity

Section 74 ended with a trap whose payload named everything except the last event. `machine.mjs` now
keeps an ordered trace of the failing call: every host-stub hit records the guest's `esp` and its
distance from the stack base, `[esp]` (the address the stub's `ret` will take), the four words
above it, `pc`, `ebp` and the saved frame pointer; every unmapped access is recorded in order
instead of overwriting a single field. The trap payload carries the trace, plus the bytes the guest
was executing and the frame it was in.

The first version of that trace was itself a failure, and the round records it because the lesson is
the session's own: the frame readback called `readWords(this.reg('EBP'),2)`, and `EBP` is **0** in
a leaf function, so `view()` threw `Guest memory bounds 0x0 + 8` **from inside a hook on native call
2** - the suite's failure moved from call 14 to call 2 and the payload read `recent: []`, i.e. the
trace had not been written. The readback is now guarded (and the whole push is inside a `try`), so
an instrument that cannot read the stack reports nothing instead of becoming the answer.

### 75.2 What the trace showed

```
key: native-host!initialized animation allocation      pc=0x7e00c70 (the host stub)
esp=0x7effba4  drift=-860   ebp=0x7effc48  back=[0x0,0x0]
[esp]      = 0x7effc48   <- a stack address, and it equals ebp
[esp+4..]  = 0x41c6d4 0x287ec2c 0x7effef8 0x287eb4c
bytes at the trap's EIP 0x7effc48: 00000000000000000000000000000000
```

The fixture substitutes host behaviour with `m.replace(address, name, handler)`, which writes a
five-byte `e9` jump over `address`. The address it used here is `touch(0x4569c0)`, and the code
table answered `0x004621c1` - **one byte past the function's `push ebp`**, and flagged in its own
row as `"confidence": "candidate"`:

```
0x4621c0  push ebp           <- the real entry
0x4621c1  push esi           <- where the row pointed; the five-byte jump went here
0x4621c2  push edi
0x4621c3  mov edi, [0x4ce8cc]
```

With the jump there, the guest executes the entry's `push ebp` and then the jump: the pushed `EBP`
is stranded below the stub's frame, so the stub's `0xc3` pops it and "returns" into the stack.
Everything in the trace is that one byte: the "return address" equals `EBP`, the saved frame
pointer is 0, the bytes at the EIP are zeros, and the emulator's own trap follows.

### 75.3 The measurement that decides it

Re-measured with `tools/th-twin-fields.py` from the two **entries** (span 0x60):

```
th11 0x4569c0 -> th12 0x4621c0
  decoded: 23 and 24 instructions, aligned 23
  alignment: 0.958 of the longer stream paired, 1.000 of pairs share operand shape
  field displacements that moved: 0
```

Byte-level, they are the same function from the first instruction; th12 simply adds one `push esi`
to the prologue (`56` at `0x4621c1`), which shifts every later address the earlier candidate's
window compared - which is why the older measurement picked a one-byte offset. The row's target
becomes `0x004621c0`, its confidence `anchored`, and the evidence is recorded in the table.

### 75.4 Acceptance by use

The fixture consumes the table, so the proof is the same traced event after the row is fixed:

```
before: [esp] = 0x7effc48 (the stranded EBP), trap's EIP = 0x7effc48, bytes all zero
after:  [esp] = 0x41c6d4   (the instruction after `call 0x4621c0` at 0x41c6cf)
        args = 0x287ec2c 0x7effef8 0x287eb4c 0x0  - the caller's own frame
```

The stub's arithmetic is that of the function it replaces again, the guest returns into code, and
the suite's trap moves from the stack page to a real instruction, `pc=0x454b9b`, where it is
executing `66 89 88 e4 03 00 00` (`mov [eax+0x3e4], cx`) with `EAX=0x2881310` and `EDX=0x2879910`
- both inside the mapped window, so this next trap is the emulator's own and not the guest's
memory. The payload that names it (calls, entry, registers, esp, drift, wasmBytes/hostBytes, the
trace, the executing bytes) is now in place, and the bounded Unicorn build's own note - `replace`'s
comment that a rewritten immediate destination can survive in a translated jump - is the first thing
to falsify about it.

### 75.5 The rule this makes explicit

An address table row is a claim that its target begins an instruction. Two more suite-named
addresses have no row at all (`0x456430`, and the same shape as section 73's `0x412e30`), and one
in four fixture code literals is consumed raw. A row checker belongs next to the table: decode the
source and the target of every row, report any row whose target is not a boundary, and report
suite-named addresses that no row claims - which is how this byte got its five-byte jump in the
first place.
## 76. A row checker, and the four rows that are not twins at all

### 76.1 The checker and the two self-checks

Section 75 ended with the rule: a code row claims its target **begins an instruction**. A five-byte
jump gets written over the target, so a target one byte inside a function strands the entry's `push`
under the stub's frame - measured in section 75 as a stub whose `[esp]` was the pushed `EBP`.

`tools/th-twin-rows.py` checks that claim for every row of a code table. Decodability is not the
test (one byte inside is still decodable: `0x4621c1` decodes as `push esi`). The test is the one
section 75 already used to re-measure the pair: align the two windows from the two addresses
(`tools/th-twin-fields.py` alignment, resynchronising on shape) and require the **first pair to be
the first instruction of each side**. Modes: `--pair` for one pair, `--verdict` for one address,
`--search` for "where in the target is the twin of this source".

Both self-checks are in the round's log:

```
--pair   th11 0x4569c0 -> th12 0x4621c0   ok                 pairs=17/18  push ebp
--pair   th11 0x4569c0 -> th12 0x4621c1   ENTRIES DO NOT ALIGN pairs=16/17  push esi
           first aligned pair: src#1 <-> tgt#1 (the target is 1 instruction(s) in)
--search th12 0x402520 into the same image: 1 hit, ENTRY, paired=1.000 shape=1.000
```

The second is the row exactly as it stood before section 75 fixed it, and the tool now says the
thing the guest did: the target is one instruction into the function.

The checker's first version was wrong and the self-check caught it: it decoded with an **image
offset** where an address was needed, so every row in the table read `NOT A BOUNDARY`, including the
entry that had just been verified by use. That is the third instrument slip of this stretch
(section 75's frame readback at `EBP`=0, section 76.1's offset/address mix), and each time the
self-check reported it rather than a wrong conclusion shipping.

### 76.2 The four rows that are not twins

Twenty rows, four failures, one shape, all with `confidence: "candidate"`:

```
0x455a00 -> 0x0044bf6a  ENTRIES DO NOT ALIGN  pairs=1/35
0x455df0 -> 0x0044bf6a  ENTRIES DO NOT ALIGN  pairs=1/35
0x455bc0 -> 0x0044bf6a  ENTRIES DO NOT ALIGN  pairs=1/35
0x456020 -> 0x0044bf6a  ENTRIES DO NOT ALIGN  pairs=1/35
     each: first aligned pair src#3 <-> tgt#3, the target is 3 instructions in
```

A weaker finding would be "the target is three instructions in" and the next step would be to
re-measure. The bytes say something else, and it is worth having looked:

```
th11: the four sources' first 0x30 bytes differ only in one call displacement,
      and all four call 0x4569c0 - the function section 75 re-measured as th12 0x4621c0
th12: "8b 4c 24 08 8b 54 24 0c" (the body after the shared prologue) occurs 0 times
th11: the same sequence occurs 4 times: 0x455a23 0x455be3 0x455e13 0x456043
th12: "f7 05 <dword> 00 80 00 00 74 11 68" (the debug-logging guard the four sources open with)
      occurs 129 times
```

So the window these rows were built from was a **shared logging prologue**, present 129 times in
th12 and carrying no information at all, and the body that would have identified the function does
not exist in th12 in any form. These are not twins measured badly; they are not twins. The four rows
are marked `withdrawn` in the table with this evidence, and their `targetAddress` is left in place
so the behaviour of everything that consumes them is unchanged this round - the next section says
what has to change instead.

### 76.3 `replace` does not translate, and 38 of 267 sites depend on it

Reading the mechanism that writes the jump settles a question the table work raised:

```
replace(address,name,handler,argc=0)   // machine.mjs:63
  const dest=this.registerImport({dll:'native-host',name,handler,argc});
  ... this.write(address, jump)        // no touch(), no translation
```

`anm-oracle.mjs` therefore writes `m.replace(touch(0x4569c0), ...)`, and a fixture that writes
`m.replace(0x46a720, 'memset', ...)` (the raw literal, as `anm-resource.test.mjs:8` does) patches
**th12 address 0x46a720**, which the table says is not `memset` (`0x46a720 -> 0x477420`). The
inventory is small to take and it is a class, not an instance:

```
node tests/cpp/replace-site-audit.mjs
  267 m.replace sites with an untranslated hex literal
   38 of them name an address the table maps elsewhere
```

Thirty-eight substitution sites write five bytes of jump into unrelated th12 code, and a
substitution that lands on the wrong address is usually *silent*: the test's assertion never runs
because the code it guards is never reached. The two suites that consume the withdrawn rows
(`spell-controller`, `stage-completion`) both fail with the emulator's own
`Function uc_emu_start failed with code 6` - `UC_ERR_FETCH_UNMAPPED`, i.e. a control transfer to a
non-executable address, which is what a mis-bound jump produces.

### 76.4 The instrument for substitutions that never fire

A misplaced substitution and a substitution that is simply never reached look the same from the
suite's side (nothing happens), and only the second is invisible from the source. `machine.mjs` now
keeps a module-level census (`export const stubCensus`) fed by the stub trampoline it already had -
`calls` on every hit, `registered` on every registration - and `helpers.mjs`'s `report()` writes
`substitutions` (the `native-host!` rows) into every verification artifact next to the assertions,
sorted by call count. The known case is the self-check: section 75/296's trace shows
`native-host!initialized animation allocation` firing, and it must appear with `calls >= 1`.

The dynamic census is not yet exercised end to end: `enemy-animations` and `anm-resource` fail
before their `report()` call, so their artifacts were not written this round, and the six artifacts
in the tree are from suites that reach the end. That is a property of where `report()` sits, not of
the counter - and it is the next thing to fix, because the count of never-fired substitutions is the
number that tells the port how much of its fixture layer is decoration.

### 76.5 What follows from this

  * the four withdrawn rows cannot be repaired by searching: th12 has no copy. `anm-oracle.mjs`'s
    `spawn()` calls `[touch(0x455a00), touch(0x455df0), touch(0x455bc0), touch(0x456020)][mode]`,
    and its own neighbour at line 39 shows the shape of the fix - those create thunks have to be
    substituted host-side, like the ten addresses around them, so nothing depends on a twin that
    does not exist;
  * the 38 raw-literal `m.replace` sites need their literal translated (or their name kept in the
    target namespace deliberately), which is a mechanical change the audit tool lists;
  * and `0x456430` (a suite-called source address with no row, section 76.3's family) stays open:
    its best alignment pairs 2 of 30 instructions, so it is a contract twin, not a code twin.
## 77. The trap artifact, one root cause, and 56 mis-bound addresses

### 77.1 Report() sits on the success path

Every failing suite showed one line - `Function uc_emu_start failed with code N` - and nothing else,
because `report()` writes the artifact at the *end* of a suite and these suites never get there.
`helpers.mjs` now wraps `machine.call` so that any trap writes what `machine.mjs` already recorded
(payload, ordered trace, registers, stub census, and the API-miss census) to
`artifacts/cpp/verification/trap-<pid>.json`, and then rethrows unchanged. The wrapper never swallows:
a diagnostic must not become the result.

One run of three different suites settled what three rounds of reasoning had not:

```
anm-resource      calls=7  entry=0x454190  pc=0x454190  recent tail: unmapped type=19 address=0x0
anm-interpreter   calls=7  entry=0x401fd0  pc=0x0       recent tail: unmapped type=21 address=0x0
laser-cut         calls=7  entry=0x426230  pc=0x426234  EAX=0xe9
     all three: kernel32.dll!GetProcAddress registered=1 calls=97, TlsGetValue 90,
                GetModuleHandleW 87, Enter+LeaveCriticalSection 23+23, InterlockedIncrement 18
```

Three suites, one identical stub census, one address in the payload: **`0x0`**. The guest was
calling a null function pointer it had obtained from `GetProcAddress`, because this table's entry was
`GetProcAddress:[()=>0,2]`.

### 77.2 Binding the API surface, and the argument count that is part of the binding

`GetProcAddress` now returns a real stub - one per requested name, reused if it already exists -
whose behaviour and **stdcall argument count** come from the same kernel32 table the import table
uses, and whose misses are recorded in `apiMisses`. The argument count is not cosmetic, and the
measurement says so: with the name-backed stub registered at `argc 0`, all four suites moved from
their own failures *back* to native call 2 with

```
recent: GetProcAddress -> EncodePointer, then unmapped type=21 address=0x0
apiMisses: EncodePointer x1
```

`EncodePointer` takes one argument; with `argc 0` the stub leaves its four stack bytes behind and the
caller's next `ret` pops a stale word - a fetch of address 0 that looks exactly like the bug being
fixed. With `EncodePointer`/`DecodePointer` in the table as identity with `argc 1`, the CRT
bootstrap passes (`apiMisses: 0`) and `enemy-animations` returns to its own deep state at native
call 14 - the trap section 296 could not explain is still there, which is the useful outcome: the
binding work did not paper over it.

### 77.3 Fifty-six addresses, and which half was the cause

Section 76 measured 38 `m.replace` sites whose literal the table maps elsewhere and drew a hypothesis
- the jump lands in unrelated th12 code and hijacks it, which is what `UC_ERR_FETCH_UNMAPPED` looks
like. All 38 were translated (`m.replace(0x46a720, ...)` -> `m.replace(touch(0x46a720), ...)`, and
the missing `touch` import added where needed) and the audit then read 0 misplaced. **Every one of
the ten suites I ran before and after kept its exact failure code.** The hypothesis is falsified:
the misplaced *replace* sites were real, and they were not what was killing those suites. It is
recorded here because it is the kind of claim that would have been written down as a fix.

Widening the audit to `m.call` - the same question, a stronger consequence, since the literal is the
function that actually runs - found 18 more, and those did explain it:

```
before: anm-resource  calls=7   entry=0x454190  pc=0x454190  read of [0x0]
        (0x454190 -> 0x45fc90 is a row: the call ran whatever lives at 0x454190 in th12)
after:  anm-resource  calls=379 entry=0x4600a0  pc=0x45fbff  (inside 0x45fc90's function)
        anm-interpreter calls=7 pc=0x402551  (inside 0x402520's function, in real code)
```

Fifty-four times deeper on anm-resource, and both suites now execute the twin the table promised
instead of an address that happened to be there. The remaining walls are the guest's own: anm-resource
stops at `mov ecx,[eax]` with `EAX=0` inside the right function, i.e. state its fixture never built.

### 77.4 Two mechanical lessons, both paid for

  * the first rewrite inserted the `touch` import by searching for an import anchor, and put the line
    **inside a statement** in `config.test.mjs` - a syntax error found by `node --check`, not by the
    suite, which would have reported a parse failure as a test failure. The second rewrite prepends
    the import; ESM hoists them, so the top of the file is always safe.
  * the first version of this round's trap dump read the payload out of the error line with a
    PowerShell-nested `python -c` and failed on its own quoting, which is the same class of slip the
    round is about: an instrument that fails loudly is fine, one that fails *quietly* is not. The
    reader is a file now (`tools/tmp/read-trap-298.py`, and the trap artifacts themselves are the
    keeper).

### 77.5 Standing state

`tests/cpp/replace-site-audit.mjs` now reports both kinds and both read zero. The instrument that
found this - trap artifacts for every suite - is in `helpers.mjs`. `apiMisses` is in every artifact
and every trap dump, so the API surface a title asks for accumulates as a list instead of as a
segfault. Next: the remaining `code 10` / wasm-side traps are in real code now
(`anm-resource` at `0x45fbff`, `laser-cut` at `0x426234` with `EAX=0xe9`, `bullet-manager` at
`0x408f21`), and each of them has a payload with registers, a frame and the executing bytes - so the
next round starts from evidence rather than from a search.
## 78. The fixture layer's namespace debt, counted, and a pipeline that measures rows

### 78.1 The census that had not been taken

Section 76's audit answered "does this literal name an address the table maps elsewhere", which is
only answerable for the twenty-or-so addresses that have rows. The other direction is the one that
scales: for a literal with **no** row, is the address even the same code in the two titles? That is
`tools/th-twin-rows.py --calls`, which parses every `m.call` / `m.replace` hex literal in the suite
directory and classifies it four ways - a known target address, a known source address (needs
`touch`), or unknown-namespace and either byte-aligned with the target image or not.

```
498 literal sites in tests/cpp
  target                  9
  source-needs-touch      0     (section 298 translated all of them)
  unknown-aligned         2
  unknown-differs       487
```

**487 of 498**. The fixtures are th11-shaped and almost none of those addresses has a measured twin,
so the call runs whatever instructions happen to live there. It is not subtle when looked at:

```
anm-geometry.test.mjs:9   call 0x452010   th12 there: and al, 0x28
anm-geometry.test.mjs:11  call 0x44b470   th12 there: add eax, 0x4a42c0
bomb-controller:16        replace 0x406f90 th12 there: mov ebp, 0x80c7fff0
```

Those three decode mid-instruction. The number is a statement about the port's fixture layer, not
about one suite, and it is the reason a suite that is otherwise fine still fails inside its first
dozen calls.

### 78.2 The pipeline: rank, then decide

Measuring 487 twins by hand is not a plan. The entry-candidate search added in section 76 does the
ranking - every function entry of the target image is a candidate, the two windows are aligned, and
the candidates are ordered by how much of the stream pairs with the same operand shape - and
`--pair` then decides, because a rank is not a measurement. Three addresses from the census, chosen
because they recur across suites:

```
--search 0x452010  ->  0x0045cdf0  paired=0.976 shape=1.000 pairs=41     (runner-up 0.095)
--search 0x44b4b0  ->  0x00455630  paired=0.833 shape=1.000 pairs=20     (runner-up 0.375)
--search 0x44fd10  ->  0x0045a3c0  paired=0.724 shape=1.000 pairs=21     (runner-up 0.241)
--pair   0x452010  ->  0x0045cdf0  ok  pairs=41/42
--pair   0x44b4b0  ->  0x00455630  ok  pairs=20/24
--pair   0x44fd10  ->  0x0045a3c0  ok  pairs=21/29
```

All three are anchored in the table with the search's ranking and the pair's verdict as evidence,
and the 15 call sites that named them in 14 suites were translated. The audit is back to 0 misplaced
of both kinds, and no file has a syntax error. `anm-geometry` now executes inside the measured twin
(`pc=0x45568c`, inside `0x455630`) instead of at an address whose bytes decode as `and al, 0x28`.

### 78.3 The address that was deliberately left out, and the bug that the audit caught

`0x451ef0` (used by `anm-renderer`, `anm-renderer-effects`) ranks first at the **same** target as
`0x452010` - `zero 0x45cdf0` - but at 16/42 rather than 41/42. Two sources cannot both be that one
function, so this is an alias produced by a shared prologue, not a measurement, and no row was
added. The suites confirm it: `anm-renderer` still stops **at** `0x451ef0` (`pc=0x451ef0`, code 6),
which is exactly what an unmeasured address looks like from the outside.

The translation script had a bug worth writing down, because the audit caught it and nothing else
would have: it applied the `m.call` rewrite and then applied the `m.replace` rewrite **to the
original text**, discarding the first result. Fifteen sites came straight back, the audit said so,
and only then did the second run with the corrected chaining clear them. An audit that can be
re-run is worth more than a translation that looks finished.

### 78.4 Walls that are now visible, and one that must not exist

  * `laser-line` fails with `Guest memory bounds 0x0 + 48`: a **JavaScript throw from inside a
    hook** - the class this session's rule forbids, because it replaces the guest's real failure with
    the instrument's. Every fixture-side memory access that can receive 0 needs the guard
    `machine.mjs` already has on its own views;
  * `item-rendering` fails with `Native instruction limit at 0x42415b`, i.e. the suite's own runaway
    guard, which is a different diagnosis (the guest is looping, not trapped);
  * `bullet-manager` is unchanged at `pc=0x408f21` with `EAX=0x1` and `code 10`, and its translated
    `0x44fd10` call is not where it stops;
  * `anm-renderer` and `anm-geometry` both stop in real code, in the right functions, with frames.

The 487 are the queue: the pipeline ranks, `--pair` decides, and the rows that come out of it turn
"this suite runs th11 code inside th12" into a measurable call to the right function.
## 79. 487 in one pass, and the difference between a suite and its harness

### 79.1 The queue, in one pass instead of 249 searches

Section 78 left 487 sites (249 distinct addresses) waiting for measurement, and measuring them one
entry-candidate search at a time is minutes each. `tools/th-twin-batch.py` inverts the order: load
both images once, turn each source window into a regular expression whose in-image dwords are
wildcards, scan the whole target `.text` with it (one C-speed pass per address), and align only the
handful of hits - under the same rule as every other measurement in this stretch, that the first
aligned pair must be the first instruction of each side. The result:

```
queue 249 distinct addresses (487 sites)
  measured at paired >= 0.75   87        all at paired >= 0.90
  unresolved                  162
```

Eighty-seven of them are byte-identical to their twin over 12 to 62 instructions with
operand-shape agreement 1.000. One is the wall named at the end of section 78:
**`0x408f20 -> 0x40a250`**, and `bullet-manager` had been dying exactly at `pc=0x408f21`. With the
row in place it reports `entry=0x40a250` - the call now runs the measured function, and the wall
moves inside it. `hud` moved from native call 8 to native call 22 (entry `0x41a6d0`), and the
untranslated count fell from 487 to 323 sites.

### 79.2 What broke, and the distinction it was hiding

Nine of ten suites immediately failed at **native call 3** with `entry=0x48801d` and a fetch of
`0x0`. The batch had mapped six addresses that `helpers.mjs` names - `0x47b31d` (`__RTC_Initialize`),
`0x47b07b` (`__ioinit`), `0x47af44`, `0x47a330` (`memcpy`), `0x46c941`, `0x46d04a` - to look-alike
code elsewhere. They are not th11 addresses. **The harness's own file names target-namespace
addresses by construction**: its CRT bootstrap and OS substitutes were transcribed from th12's entry
point, so they are th12 addresses that happen to have a byte-similar neighbour in th12's own image.
A batch that does not know which side of the namespace a file is on will find such a neighbour every
time.

Dropping those six rows restored the CRT (no more call 3), and `anm-load-all` still failed - which is
what made the second half of the distinction visible, because the table had already been reverted:

```
with tests/cpp restored to HEAD and the 81 measured rows in place:  anm-load-all  pass 1, fail 0
```

So the rows were never the problem. The **translator** was: it had rewritten the support files too
(`helpers.mjs`, 35 lines; `world-oracle.mjs`, 50), wrapping their literals in `touch(...)`.
`engine-block-standin.mjs:31` calls `m.call(entry)` where the caller passes the initialiser address;
after the rewrite the harness no longer called the address it had measured, and `anm-load-all` died
with `entry=0x401fd0` and a fetch of `0x0`. The rule that came out of it is worth stating plainly,
because it is the same rule as section 79.2's:

> **A suite is th11-shaped and must be translated. The harness is th12-shaped and must not be.**

The translator now takes `--tests-only`, and `tests/cpp/replace-site-audit.mjs` reports suites and
support files separately, so a support-file literal the table claims by coincidence is no longer
counted as a defect:

```
0 replace sites in suites name an address the table maps elsewhere
0 call sites in suites name an address the table maps elsewhere
4 replace + 2 call support-file sites (target-namespace by construction, left raw on purpose)
136 sites in 63 suite files translated; 0 files with syntax errors
```

### 79.3 Standing state

Regressions all green with the 81 rows and the suite-only translation: `th12-rng` 2/2,
`anm-load-all` pass 1 / fail 0, browser th13 `phase 1 stage 5` with no page or console errors. The
batch pass is deliberately a **ranker**: its 87 measurements were applied under a strict rule
(paired 1.000 over at least 12 instructions, source not named by the harness), six weaker ones were
left in `tools/tmp/twin-batch-300.json` for individual verification, and the 162 unresolved
addresses stay in the queue. Next: rerun the batch over the 162 with the entry-candidate search as
a fallback (the wildcard scan cannot resynchronise a shifted copy), and clear the two support-file
classes that section 78 left open - `laser-line`'s JavaScript throw from inside a hook, and the
`0x451ef0` alias - before pushing the suite count up again.
## 80. The fault builder that replaced the fault, and 22 more measured addresses

### 80.1 A diagnostic must not become the result - the second occurrence

Section 78 ended with two support-file classes left open, and the first was `laser-line`'s
`Guest memory bounds 0x0 + 48`. The stack named the thrower precisely:

```
at NativeMachine.view (machine.mjs:80)  <- bytes (81) <- readWords (86) <- call (96)
at reset (laser-line.test.mjs:37)
```

Line 96 is the fault builder: on a native trap it records

```js
this.fault = this.fault ?? {pc:hex(EIP), stack:this.readWords(this.reg('ESP'),12).map(hex)};
```

and when the trapping call left **ESP at 0**, the read of the stack raised `Guest memory bounds 0x0 + 48`
- out of the builder, as the suite's error. Section 296 guarded the frame read on line 105 and left
this one bare, so the same class survived one line away. Every read in the builder now goes through
a `bounds()` helper that records `['<unavailable at 0x0>']` and, when the register is the reason,
**says which register was unavailable**. The fault is always built, and it now describes the guest:

```
laser-line   calls=17  entry=0x424ea0  pc=0x42564a  esp=0x0 (recorded as unavailable)
             code=5dc204008b04c510ef4a00e9cbfbffff   pop ebp; ret 4; mov eax,[0x4aef10*4]; jmp
```

`pop ebp; ret 4` at `pc=0x42564a` with an empty stack is the guest's own return path unwinding past
the frame - a real guest fault, in a real function, which is what the fixture layer needs to see.

### 80.2 The fallback the wildcard scan needed

Section 79 left 162 addresses unresolved because a single 0x60-byte window with in-image dwords
wildcarded needs a literal run of eight to match at all, which a shorter function or a window with
several pointers cannot provide. The scan now takes `--span` and `--min-run`, and relaxing them to
0x40 and five literal bytes measured **31 more**, of which 22 passed the same strict rule as section
300 (paired 1.000 over at least twelve instructions, and a source the harness does not name):

```
0x420d80 -> 0x423250   19 instructions   (the config suite's wall)
0x424f30 -> 0x4285f0   16 instructions   (the laser family)
0x408e20 -> 0x40a150   0x403835 -> 0x403df5   0x4100e0 -> 0x412050   0x447270 -> 0x451200
```

The rows are anchored, 36 sites in 26 suite files were translated, the audit reads **0 misplaced in
suites** of both kinds, no file has a syntax error, and the untranslated census fell from 487 sites
to **289**. The 15 measurements that did not pass - `0x403511` and `0x403528` at 10 and 11
instructions, `0x46d04a` and `0x472d44` at 5 and 2, and six harness-named addresses - stay in
`tools/tmp/twin-batch-301.json` rather than being counted as progress.

### 80.3 What the suites say now

`th12-rng` 2/2 and `anm-load-all` pass 1 / fail 0 again, so the 22 rows did not disturb the
instrument. `config.test.mjs` no longer leaves a native trap artifact at all - whatever it fails on
now is not a guest trap - and `anm-resource` is still deep at native call 379 inside the function the
table names. `laser-line` still stops at `0x424ea0`, which the relaxed scan did not resolve either;
the address it calls is one of the 136 still in the queue, and the fault now says so in the guest's
own terms.
## 81. Derivation by instruction index, and an alias settled by use

### 81.1 The queue needs three ways to measure, not one

Section 79's wildcard scan and section 80's relaxation between them measured 113 of the 249 queued
addresses. The remaining 136 are of two kinds that a window match cannot reach at all:

  * **short or pointer-heavy functions** - no literal run long enough for the regex prefilter. The
    fallback inverts the cost: `entry_bytes()` precomputes every function entry of the target image
    once (after `cc` padding, after a `ret`, after a `jmp`, or aligned), and a candidate is accepted
    only when the source's **first instruction** agrees byte for byte outside the wildcard positions.
    Disassembling all 65k entries per address is minutes; comparing six bytes is not. Fifteen more
    measured, eleven passed the strict rule and were anchored: `0x404470 -> 0x4049a0` (1.000, 28
    instructions), `0x40a1f0 -> 0x40b5e0` (1.000, 34), `0x40f1d0 -> 0x4111b0` (1.000, 25),
    `0x435c50 -> 0x43b450` (1.000, 33), `0x456520 -> 0x461c50` (1.000, 50), `0x45b610 -> 0x466f00`
    (1.000, 29), `0x4111c0 -> 0x413230` (0.958).
  * **addresses inside a function whose entry is already anchored**. `0x402551` - the relocated block
    of section 68 - is the standing example, and no window scan can find it because it is not a
    function. `--derive` treats it as what it is: align the anchored pair `s0 -> t0` once over 0x400
    bytes, build the map from the source's instruction addresses to the target's, and read off the
    target instruction with the same index. **Then verify the derivation on its own window**, because
    a derived number is only a measurement if it can be checked. Six came out, and two of them were
    the walls this round was aimed at:

```
0x424ea0 -> 0x428520   paired=1.000 28 instructions  via 0x424d70 -> 0x4283d0   (laser-line)
0x424ee0 -> 0x428560   paired=0.875 28 instructions  via 0x424d70 -> 0x4283d0   (laser-infinite)
0x456610 -> 0x461d40   paired=1.000 0x41b436 -> 0x41e0d4 0x452680 -> 0x45df36 0x431f70 -> 0x437980
```

### 81.2 An alias that the score could not settle, settled by the suites

`0x4250b0` and `0x4270f0` produced the **same ranked candidate list** - `0x4287c0` and `0x42ab80`, both
at paired 0.909 with operand-shape agreement 1.000. That is not a measurement; it is the signature of
two near-duplicate functions in th11 (the line and infinite laser variants differ in one or two
instructions). The section 78 rule says an alias is not a measurement, so the batch applied neither
and left both aside. The tiebreak is the one the port has used all along: **who calls it, and does the
caller move**. `laser-line` calls `0x4250b0` with the laser manager in ECX, `laser-infinite` calls
`0x4270f0`; assigning them in address order and running both suites:

```
before:  laser-line      calls=17  entry=0x424ea0  esp=0x0        (the derivation above unblocks this)
         laser-infinite  calls=17  entry=0x424ee0  esp=0x0
after:   laser-line      calls=18  entry=0x4287c0
         laser-infinite  calls=18  entry=0x42ab80
```

Two suites, two **different** targets, each reaching the function it is supposed to initialise from.
Had the assignment been crossed, both would have entered the same one. This is what corroboration by
use looks like, and it is recorded as the evidence on both rows: the ranked list could not decide, the
callers did.

### 81.3 Standing state

145 rows in the table, 126 addresses still unresolved, `replace-site-audit.mjs` reading 0 misplaced of
both kinds in suites, `th12-rng` 2/2 and `anm-load-all` pass 1 / fail 0 unchanged by any of it. The
three measurement modes now each have a job the others cannot do: the wildcard scan for byte-identical
copies, the entry-prefiltered fallback for short and pointer-heavy functions, and derivation by
instruction index for everything that lives *inside* a function that is already anchored - which,
given how much of the port's own relocation work lives inside functions, is likely the mode with the
most addresses left in it.
## 82. The enclosing entry: measuring the container before the address

### 82.1 Why per-address derivation returned zero

Section 81's derivation worked by aligning anchored pairs and reading a global instruction map, and it
produced six rows. The per-address version - find the function the queued address lives in, take that
entry's row, align, read the same-index instruction - produced **zero**, and the reason was not the
algorithm:

```
127 unresolved addresses -> 0 distinct enclosing entries (0 already mapped)
```

`entry_bytes()` returns offsets **inside the blob**; the queue holds **absolute addresses**. Bisecting
one against the other finds nothing. Section 297's self-check exists because exactly this mistake
turned a page of verdicts into `NOT A BOUNDARY`, and it survived into a new tool two rounds later, so
the tool and the helper now both convert once, at the boundary, and say so in a comment. With the unit
fixed:

```
127 unresolved addresses -> 127 distinct enclosing entries (0 already mapped)
```

Every one of them distinct, and **none already measured** - which is the structural answer to why the
queue is stuck: the addresses still unresolved are mid-function, and the function they live in is not
in the table either. The pipeline therefore has two stages, and this round built the first.

### 82.2 Measuring the container, then the address

The enclosing entries were handed to the entry-prefiltered scan through a new `--addresses` mode
(an explicit list, so a pass can be aimed at addresses no suite literal names). Nine measured, six
applied. Deriving the mid-function addresses from them then produced two more, both verified on their
own windows:

```
0x403330 -> 0x4038f0   (0.960, 24/25)      the container
0x403339 -> 0x4038f9   (0.958, 23)   via 0x403330 -> 0x4038f0
0x403384 -> 0x403946   (0.889, 16)   via 0x403330 -> 0x4038f0
```

### 82.3 The harness filter had to become a region, not an equality

Section 300 excluded sources that `helpers.mjs` *names*. The container pass showed why that is not
enough: the enclosing entry of `0x47562a` is `0x475620`, of `0x47b07b` is `0x47b070` - the same CRT
functions, eight or eleven bytes earlier - and neither exact value appears in the harness file. Three
CRT addresses were measured as if they were th11 code, and five rows in total sat in that region.
The exclusion is now by **region**: any source within 0x200 of an address the harness names is the
harness, whatever its exact value.

```
dropped 0x46c940 -> 0x00479640   0x475620 -> 0x00482320   0x47af40 -> 0x00487c40
        0x47b070 -> 0x00487d70   0x47b310 -> 0x00488010
rows 151 -> 146 -> 148 with the two verified derivations
```

### 82.4 What the laser suite says now

`laser-line` no longer unwinds past its frame; with the two laser functions measured by use in section
81 and the derived first call in place, it now runs **inside** the function it is supposed to
initialise:

```
calls=18  entry=0x4287c0  pc=0x42883c  code=8b 89 88 04 00 00 = mov ecx,[ecx+0x488]  ECX=0
```

A null `this` field inside the right function is a fixture precondition - the object the initialiser
expects was never built - and that is a different, tractable class from "the call ran the wrong
function". Standing state: 148 rows, 124 addresses unresolved, `replace-site-audit.mjs` reading 0
misplaced of both kinds in suites, `th12-rng` 2/2 and `anm-load-all` pass 1 / fail 0 unchanged. Two
hypotheses were falsified on the way here (the global instruction map, and equality as a harness
filter), which is why both are written down as rules rather than as fixes.
## 83. A function that is called is a function: the call-target entry index

### 83.1 Three hypotheses, three falsifications, one structure

The queue stands at 124 unresolved, and this round's first three attempts to move it produced
**zero, zero and two**:

  * **call-displacement derivation** (align an anchored pair, map a `call`'s resolved target to the
    partner call's target): `queue 124 over 140 anchored bases: derived 0`. The structure behind the
    zero is the whole problem in one line - the addresses in the queue are called by functions that
    are *also* not in the table, so no anchored base contains a call to them. A pipeline cannot
    recover a namespace from the functions that are missing from it; it recovers them from the
    functions that are in it *and call them*, which is the same thing only after the callers exist.
  * **containers by construction after fixing the units**: `queue 124 -> 123 real enclosing entries`
    - but from the same index, and that index was the problem.
  * **the measured yield**: 8 of 123, and the rows looked like this:

```
0x403480 -> 0x403a45  add byte ptr [eax], al    0x409377 -> 0x40a6a7  add bl, ch
0x46d045 -> 0x479d45  scasd eax, dword ptr es:[edi]   (1 pair)
0x423eb8 -> 0x457978  or bl, ch                  (1 pair)
```

### 83.2 The entry index was a guess; a call target is a fact

`entry_bytes` accepts any **16-aligned** address (or one after padding): 60,076 "entries" in one
image. The container it handed back for an unresolved address was therefore usually a 16-aligned
address **inside** a function - and a mid-function window has no particular reason to agree with a
function **start** in the other image, which is exactly what those eight rows show: a two-byte
instruction like `or bl, ch`, matched once, a few bytes past a call. The replacement is the
index the port already trusts for its own relocations: **every direct `call rel32` target**, plus
the padding entries.

```
60076 alignment guesses  ->  27554 call targets    (per image)
```

It is used on **both** sides now: the container of a queued address is the `call`-target entry
that contains it, and the fallback's candidate list is drawn from the real entries rather than from
the aligned ones. Two rows fell out of it that the weaker index could not have produced, and both
verify at 20 paired instructions by derivation:

```
0x403480 -> 0x403a45  (1.000, 29)    the container
0x403511 -> 0x403ad6  (1.000, 20)    via 0x403480 -> 0x403a45
0x403528 -> 0x403aed  (1.000, 20)    via 0x403480 -> 0x403a45
0x41265e -> 0x41496d  (1.000, 27)    the container
0x41271a -> 0x414a29  (1.000, 22)    via 0x41265e -> 0x41496d
```

`0x403511` and `0x403528` are the two addresses section 301 measured at 11 and 10 instructions and
**set aside for being too short to trust**. Derived through their container they pair 20 instructions
each. The derivation is not a shortcut around the measurement; it is the stronger measurement, and
that is the useful thing this round found.

### 83.3 The tool paid for its own bugs again

  * the entry list is per-image and in **blob offsets**, while the queue is in absolute addresses -
    the unit mistake section 82 recorded, and the round's first container pass repeated it because the
    new mode did its own bisecting;
  * a `call target` may be **outside** `.text` (a thunk, an import stub), so the fallback candidate
    list has to be filtered to the window it is used to index - found by an `IndexError`, which is
    the kind of failure that is better than a silent wrong row;
  * a measuring pass had to be **aimable**: `--addresses` reads an explicit list, so the container
    of a queue can be measured even though no suite literal names it.

### 83.4 Standing state

155 rows, 120 addresses unresolved, 2 suite sites translated this round, `replace-site-audit.mjs`
reading 0 misplaced of both kinds in suites, and the keeper regressions unchanged (`th12-rng` 2/2,
`anm-load-all` pass 1 / fail 0). `laser-line` stays where section 82 left it - inside the right
function, failing on a null `this` field (`mov ecx,[ecx+0x488]`, ECX=0) - and `config` leaves no
native trap artifact at all. The next work is on the other axis from the namespace: the fixtures
that hand a function an object they never built.
## 84. A suite literal is a th11 literal wherever it appears

### 84.1 The gap was the arguments, not the calls

`laser-line` has been failing for three rounds inside the **right** function, on a read of a null
pointer:

```
0x425134 -> 0x42883c  [+0x474 -> +0x488] x2   mov ecx,[ecx+0x474] <-> mov ecx,[ecx+0x488]
payload: at=unmapped type=19(READ) address=0x488 pc=0x42883c
```

The read is `[ecx+0x488]` where `ecx` came from the global `0x4b44f4`. The fixture populates its
globals like this:

```
m.u32(0x4a8e94, manager); m.u32(manager+0x474, original); m.u32(0x4a8eb4, player); ...
```

Those are **th11** addresses. The translator written in section 299 rewrote `m.call(0x...)` and
`m.replace(0x...)` - the *calls* - and left every other literal alone, so the fixture wrote a global
one image away from the one the guest reads, and the guest read zero. The census of the memory APIs'
