address-shaped arguments is **325 sites in 90 suites**; they are rewritten now, and the harness stays
untouched by the section 79 rule (a suite is th11-shaped, the harness is th12-shaped by construction).

### 84.2 A bare offset is not a key

The other half is the field layer, and it produced a rule rather than a patch. `touchField` is exact -
it returns what the table says and the number unchanged otherwise - but its key is a **bare offset**,
and two records can have a field at the same offset. The table already held a row saying

```
0x474 -> 0x1140   (the enemy record, measured earlier)
```

while the laser manager's own `[ecx+0x474]` moves to `+0x488`. That is the alias rule one level down
from addresses, and it was worth running the instrument to get the second claim rather than trusting
the first:

```
tools/th-twin-fields.py th11 0x4250b0 th12 0x4287c0
  decoded 256 and 268 instructions, aligned 69, alignment 0.257, operand-shape agreement 1.000
  field displacements that moved: 31 (of 69 aligned pairs)
```

21 of those name the manager register (`ebx`) and were added as rows carrying
`record: laser-manager`; the existing rows now say `record: enemy-record`. The `[esp+...]` moves were
left out - they are frames, not fields - and `[esi+0x404]` was left out because `esi` is another
object at that point. With the rows in place `touchField(0x474)` answers `0x488`, the fixture writes
the field where the guest reads it, and the wall moved:

```
before: at=unmapped address=0x488  pc=0x42883c   the manager field
after:  at=unmapped address=0x11c  pc=0x454ee1   the record 0x454ee0 walks (a later call)
```

That is progress of the kind a census can see, not a claim.

### 84.3 The translator broke files while rewriting them

Four suites failed with `ReferenceError: touchField is not defined`, and the cause is section 300's
lesson one level down: the guard that decides whether to add the import asked whether the file imports
`touch` from `./fixture-addresses.mjs`, and four suites satisfy that with a differently written
statement - so 89 field sites went in with no import behind them and the suites failed on their
*instrument* instead of their subject. The guard now asks for the identifier it is about to use, and
repairing it put those four suites back on their own failures:

```
enemy-frame      unmapped at 0x0    pc=0x454d25      enemy-movement  unmapped at 0xdc pc=0x4615dd
hud              unmapped at 0x1    pc=0x41a6d0      world-replays   pass
```

### 84.4 Census and standing state

Ten affected suites were re-run after the repair: `world-replays` passes; the rest wall on named
addresses (`0x454d25`, `0x4615dd`, `0x41a6d0`, `0x45568c`, `0x41c31edc`) or on their own assertions,
and none fails for want of an import. The keepers are unchanged (`th12-rng` 2/2, `anm-load-all` pass
1 / fail 0) and `replace-site-audit.mjs` still reads 0 misplaced of both kinds in suites. The tables
stand at 148 address rows and 23 field rows, the field table for the first time carrying the record a
row was measured on.
## 85. A test that cannot find its input has not tested anything

### 85.1 The census, as an instrument

Section 84 rewrote ninety-one suites, so "did that help" and "where does each suite stop now" both
became measurable questions. `tools/tmp/census-306.mjs` runs every suite under `tests/cpp` with
`node --test`, parses the pass/fail counts and reads the trap artifact the wrapper leaves behind, so
the first wall of every suite is recorded as an address and a kind rather than remembered:

```
142 suites run:  19 passing, 49 trapping, 32 pass / 121 fail assertions
failure classes: unmapped 42, assertion 69, import 6
```

The table is `tools/tmp/census-306.json` and the next target can be chosen by frequency - which is how
the three walls with three suites each, and the two dominant classes below, were found.

### 85.2 The largest single cause was not a port defect

**31 of 142 suites (22%) failed before they ran**, on three hard-coded paths:

```
th11.dat             x16   runtimes/th12/[th11] 东方地灵殿 (汉化版+日文版)/th11.dat
d3dx9_37.dll         x14   runtimes/th12/th12_web/reference/native/d3dx9_37.dll
004526f0.asm          x1   artifacts/cpp/analysis/jp/functions/004526f0.asm
```

The first is a *localized copy* convention that exists on the machine that wrote those suites and not
in the checkout: the originals are installed at `H:\Games\th\11\th11.dat` and `H:\Games\th\12\...`,
and the DLL is a DirectX redistributable that ships in `C:\Windows\SysWOW64`. Nothing about the port
was wrong; the suites could not see their inputs.

### 85.3 One resolver, and the spellings it has to know

`tests/cpp/originals.mjs` searches, most explicit first: `TH_ORIGINALS`/`TH_ORIGINALS_DIR`; the
runtime's own reference tree; the runtime's parent directory including the `[...]` copy convention;
the game installs under `TH_GAMES` or `H:/Games/th/`; and the system directories. A miss throws with
the entire search behind it, because "ENOENT on a path I have never seen" is exactly how this round
started.

The first version resolved the DLL and **not** `th11.dat`, and the reason is worth keeping: this
machine's install directories are **numbered** (`H:\Games\th\11`), while the titles are named
(`th11`). Both spellings are searched now. A reference that resolves on one machine and not another is
the failure the module exists to remove.

25 suites were routed through it by script - which, per section 84, also had to leave every file
compilable, and does. One support file mattered more than the rest: `graphics-oracle.mjs` loads the
D3DX9 reference DLL and is shared by fourteen suites, and it now resolves the machine's own copy -
whose sha256 **equals** the hash the loader expects (`c2ccb84c...`), so the system copy *is* the
reference and the check still decides.

### 85.4 What the census says after the repair

```
ENOENT failures: 31 -> 2      both derived artifacts (archive-ciphers.json, 004526f0.asm)
battle-integration   AssertionError: ascii ANM        (its own subject, not a missing file)
the D3DX9 family     loads the DLL, executes it, and traps inside the loaded image at pc=0x1177a35
```

That last line is a new class and a precise one: the guest is running the relocated reference code,
so the wasm-side out-of-bounds is inside *executed* D3DX9, with a payload (`pc` = `0x1000000 + rva`,
`stack` holding single-precision values). It is the named next item, along with the two generators
that produce `archive-ciphers.json` and the per-function `.asm` dumps.

### 85.5 Standing state

`th12-rng` 2/2, `anm-load-all` pass 1 / fail 0, browser th13 `phase 1 stage 5` with no page or console
errors, `replace-site-audit.mjs` 0 misplaced of both kinds in suites. 140 of 142 suites now reach their
own subject; of the remainder, one wants a derived cipher table and one a derived disassembly dump.
## 86. The transcription worksheet, and a hypothesis that measured to nothing

### 86.1 The suite wanted a file, not a fix

`scene-schedule` fails with `ENOENT` on `artifacts/cpp/analysis/jp/functions/*.asm` - ten of them, plus
a literal-path read of `004298c0.asm`. Those files are the **canonical per-function disassembly** the
transcription method works from, and the suite parses them with three patterns that define the dialect
exactly:

```
MOV EBX,0x...
MOV dword ptr [EAX|ESI + 0x8],0x...
CALL 0x00456c10
```

`tools/th-asm-dump.py` writes them: address, raw bytes, and the instruction, so a transcription can be
checked against the image byte for byte. The generator's first version uppercased the whole line, and
the dumps matched **nothing**:

```
MOV EBX,0x455140     ->  MOV EBX,0X455140      (uppercased the 0x)
CALL 0x00456c10      ->  CALL 0x456c10         (no eight-digit padding)
MOV dword ptr [...]  ->  MOV DWORD PTR [...]   (the pattern wants dword ptr lowercase)
```

The dialect is a contract because the oracle reads it: mnemonic and registers uppercase, `dword ptr`
as capstone writes it, hex `0x` with lowercase digits, call and jump targets zero-padded to eight
digits, no space after a comma, bracket displacements in hex. With that restored:

```
004526f0: 797 instructions -> ... (27 scene registrations)
004298c0: 224 instructions -> ... ( 8 scene registrations)
```

`scene-schedule` now reads its worksheet and fails on its **own** assertion (`native callback priority
order`), which is a real port question about the registration order, not a missing file. The census
agrees: ENOENT failures are down to **one**, the `archive-ciphers.json` table that still needs its
generator.

### 86.2 The D3DX9 trap is at an entry, and the obvious fix is wrong

Fourteen suites load the reference DLL through `graphics-oracle.mjs`. Two hypotheses were tested here.

**The uninitialised section tail.** A section's virtual size can exceed its raw size, and only the raw
part was written into the guest, so a read of the tail depended on what the guest happened to hold.
The loader's zeros are now written for every such gap. Measured: **no change in any of the four
suites**, so the tail was not the cause. The change is kept because it makes the mapping match the
loader, and it is recorded as not the explanation.

**The missing frame.** The trap is inside the loaded image at `pc=0x1177a35`, and that RVA disassembles
to `mov eax, dword ptr [ebp + 8]` as the **first** instruction of the routine - MSVC omits the
prologue when it assumes its caller established the frame. So `machine.call` was changed to set
`EBP = ESP_at_entry + 4` for callers that do not pass their own, which puts the first argument exactly
where such a routine looks for it. Across all 142 suites the census afterwards was **identical** to
the census before it:

```
19 passing, 53 trapping, 32 pass / 121 fail assertions   (both runs)
```

A reading of the instruction is not a measurement. The change was **not kept**: an interpretation of
the ABI that alters every call in the process has to earn its place, and this one earned nothing.

### 86.3 Standing state

`th12-rng` 2/2, `anm-load-all` pass 1 / fail 0 unchanged. The census after this round: 19/142 passing,
53 trapping, 32 pass / 121 fail assertions, one ENOENT left (`archive-ciphers.json`). The named next
items are the one remaining generator, the in-image D3DX9 trap (now known to be at an entry
instruction and not explained by either hypothesis above), and `scene-schedule`'s registration order,
which is the first time a suite has disagreed with the port about **behaviour** rather than about
names.

### 86.4 The dumps are generated, and that is where they belong


untimes/th12/th12_web/artifacts/ is ignored by the repository, and the eleven dumps this round
generated are in it - deliberately. They are not sources; they are the output of
py -3 tools/th-asm-dump.py --from-suite runtimes/th12/th12_web/tests/cpp/scene-schedule.test.mjs,
which reads the addresses out of the suite that consumes them, disassembles the JP original at each,
and writes the dialect above. A fresh checkout regenerates them with that one command, which is the
same relationship the rest of rtifacts/cpp/analysis/ has to the originals: derived, reproducible,
and never the authority - the executable is. What is committed is the generator, so the worksheet can
always be rebuilt from the machine code it describes instead of being trusted as a file.

## 87. The last missing input, and a failure that is not where it looks

### 87.1 The cipher rows, exported rather than copied

`reference/archive-ciphers.json` was the last ENOENT in the census. The suite needs TH11's eight cipher
rows to drive the **original** cipher routine at th11 `0x4581c0` and compare its output with the
Runtime's own unpacking, and it indexes them the way the game does: `(byte sum of the name) & 7`.

Where the rows come from was decided by two measurements, not by preference:

* The whole `th11.exe` was searched - the rows packed as four dwords (`key, step, block, limit`), the
  eight key bytes alone, and both the th95 and th12 variants. **Found none.** The executable does not
  carry the table as constants; it derives its parameters at run time (`0x4581c0` begins with an
  `idiv` by the block, the shape `Archive::read` reproduces). A negative result is the evidence for
  saying so, and it is recorded as such.
* The Runtime already carries the rows and credits thtk's `thdat95.c` in the source comment, with
  `archive_crypt_table` resolving version 11 to the TH95 set.

So `tools/th-archive-ciphers.py` **parses** `cpp/game/ResourceCrypt.cpp` and emits the JSON, instead
of restating the constants in a second place. The table exists once; the export cannot drift from it.
What the suite then measures is whether that table, fed to the original's own routine, reproduces the
Runtime's unpacking - a comparison between two implementations of one cipher rather than a property of
the file.

### 87.2 The archive opens, and the failure is downstream of every guard

With the JSON in place the suite runs for the first time. `archive_open` succeeds: 184 entries from a
26,610,794-byte `th11.dat`, and the first entries are read correctly out of the index.

```
entry 0 ascii.anm  {offset: 16,     unpacked: 178000,  packed: 41454}
entry 1 bullet.anm {offset: 41470,  unpacked: 1428092, packed: 512705}
entry 2 enemy.anm  {offset: 554175, unpacked: 620284,  packed: 203219}
entry 3 front.anm  {offset: 757394, unpacked: 1362376, packed: 623999}
```

and `archive_read` returns **-1** for every one of them. `Archive::read` refuses a read on four
clauses, and all four were evaluated against those numbers:

```
[offset>size, packed>size-offset, unpacked>size, packed>unpacked]
[false,       false,             false,          false]      (all four entries)
```

The guards are not the failure. What remains in the path is the decrypt (which the suite's own
oracle agrees with, since the original routine is driven from the same key) and then the LZSS decode,
whose only refusal is `written != e.size` at `Archive.cpp:52`. So the codec is the named item, and
the suite already carries its oracle: `0x4426c0` is the original's decompressor, called on the same
packed bytes and compared byte for byte with the Runtime's output. `tools/th-archive-probe.mjs` is
committed as the instrument that names a refusal instead of guessing it - evaluating the four clauses
is what turned "the port returns -1" into "the codec fails".

### 87.3 Standing state

Census ENOENT failures: **0 of 142 suites** - every suite now finds its inputs and every remaining
failure is about the port or about the oracle. `th12-rng` 2/2 and `anm-load-all` pass 1 / fail 0
unchanged. Named next: the LZSS codec against `0x4426c0`, `scene-schedule`'s registration order, and
the in-image D3DX9 trap that two measured hypotheses failed to explain.

### 87.4 The cipher JSON is derived too

`runtimes/th12/th12_web/reference/archive-ciphers.json` is ignored by the repository, so the round
commits the exporter and not the file, exactly as it commits the disassembly generator and not the
dumps. One command rebuilds it:

```
py -3 tools/th-archive-ciphers.py
```

and it parses `cpp/game/ResourceCrypt.cpp` rather than restating the constants, so the table it emits
is the table the Runtime executes.

## 88. The algorithm was right, the argument was missing

### 88.1 The measurement that moved the question

`archive_read` refused all 184 TH11 entries while the original decoder (`th11 0x4426c0`) reproduced
every shipped file, and `Archive::read`'s four refusal clauses were all false, so the named suspect was
the LZSS codec. Before touching it, the port's decoder was transcribed into Python and run on the
decrypted stream the oracle had produced:

```
window 8192, threshold 3, head 1, zero window  ->  178000 bytes, byte-identical to the original
```

The port's algorithm is **correct for TH11**, exactly as written. The classic LZSS initial window was
tested too, because a real LZSS preloads `F` bytes into the top of the ring without emitting them, and
each candidate was compared with the original's own output rather than reasoned about:

```
classic preload F, threshold 2  ->  163025 bytes, differs at 0
classic preload F, threshold 3  ->  177983 bytes, differs at 0
window 4096 with the 13-bit offset masked by it  ->  178000 bytes, differs at 6353
```

All refuted. The first of these runs also carried its own lesson: it used a 4096-entry ring, which is
not what the port uses, and the first divergence at 6353 is exactly where a reference reaches past
4096 - a transcription error that looks like a port defect if the mask is not checked. What the
measurement said is that the codec was not the failure, and the *input* to it was.

### 88.2 The missing argument

```
runtime binding:   int archive_open(Archive*, const u8*, u32 size, u32 version)
suite call:        c.archive_open(a, p, raw.length)          // version defaults to 0
ResourceCrypt:     archive_crypt_table(u32 version)          // ... default: return archive_crypt_th14
```

A three-argument call passes **0**, and the table's default case is the TH14 rows, so every TH11 entry
was decrypted with the wrong cipher table. What makes this failure expensive is how far away it
surfaces: the header and the index are decrypted with *fixed* parameters, so `archive_open` succeeded,
184 entries parsed with correct names and correct sizes, and only the per-entry read refused - with
`actual: -1, expected: 178000` and nothing in the message to say that a version was missing.

Two arms of one measurement decided it:

```
version 0  -> open 1, count 184, first six entries: agreed 0, refused 6, differed 0
version 11 -> open 1, count 184, first six entries: agreed 6, refused 0, differed 0
```

and then the suite itself:

```
archive.test.mjs:  pass 1 / fail 0      // 184 TH11 resources, byte-identical to the original
```

Every TH11 archive entry - cipher and LZSS together, compared against the original's own routine and
the original's own decompressor, byte for byte - is now verified, and the suite writes the extracted
`reference/assets/` and `reference/archive-manifest.json` as the record of it.

### 88.3 A table that cannot be chosen is not a table

The suite now passes its generation (`11`) explicitly, which is what the th11-shaped suite's literal
has to become against this binding. The port was hardened in the same round, because the silent
default is the actual defect:

* `archive_crypt_table` returns **nullptr** for a generation it does not know, instead of the TH14
  rows;
* `Archive::open` refuses when that happens, so a forgotten argument is named at the call.

This is the same class as the fix already recorded in `GameResources.cpp`, where `Archive::open`
defaulting to TH12's generation "made a" title's own data unreadable. The runtime's own callers always
pass their generation (12, 13 or 14), so the refusal costs nothing there.

### 88.4 Standing state

The census after the change reads: census 20/142 passing, 62 trapping, 33 pass / 120 fail assertions, 0 ENOENT `th12-rng` 2/2 and `anm-load-all` pass 1 /
fail 0 unchanged. The remaining named work is unchanged as well: `scene-schedule`'s registration order
against the original's callback table, and the D3DX9 in-image trap that two measured hypotheses failed
to explain.

Passing rises by exactly one and that one is archive.test.mjs; the ENOENT count of zero was derived when it was written down in the previous round and is measured now. Nine more suites report a trap while the assertion counts barely move (32 pass / 121 fail -> 33 / 120), which is what suites look like when they stop dying on a missing input and reach the runtime at last; the concurrent agent rebuilds the same core in parallel, so a per-suite attribution of that delta is not this round's to claim.

## 89. The arity audit: six candidates, all refuted, and why that is worth the round

### 89.1 The class, made mechanical

Section 88's defect was a three-argument call to a four-parameter binding, and the missing argument was
the archive generation: C++ could not complain, the call succeeded, and 184 entries were decrypted with
the wrong cipher table before anything refused. One such defect is an accident; the same shape in the
call discipline would be a habit, and a habit is worth finding by machine.

`tools/th-arity-audit.py` parses the API table in the runtime's test bindings - the audit found **719**
registered bindings - and then every `c.<name>(...)` and `m.<name>(...)` in every suite, splitting the
argument list on top-level commas while respecting nesting, strings and template literals, and compares
counts. It reports **candidates, not defects**, because a zero in a trailing parameter is only a defect
when the binding makes it one. What it removes is the possibility of never noticing.

### 89.2 The six candidates, and their measurement

```
binding            needs  short calls   suites
pause_create           4        2       pause-end, pause-menu
shake_start            4        1       screen-shake
spell_begin            8        1       spell-controller
spell_tick             6        1       spell-controller
title_create           5        1       title-selection
```

Every one of the six is a **spread**, and the splitter counts `...rest` as one argument, so the counts
are not the arity. The arrays were read rather than assumed:

* `pause-end` and `pause-menu` declare `resources=[]` and fill it inside a loop -
  `resources.push(r)` on line 7 - so `pause_create(a, ...resources, s)` passes the manager, two handles
  and the score file: **four**, as `PauseMenu(*a,*t,*f,*s)` requires;
* `title-selection` fills four handles and takes the first three for `title_create` and the fourth for
  `title_music_load`, which the suite's own `resources[3]` shows: **five**, as required;
* `shake_start(f, ...values)`, `spell_begin(f, id, 1800, cn, 1, ...pos)` and
  `spell_tick(f, y, ...target, bombActive)` carry three values each, which is the parameter count their
  signatures ask for.

All six refuted. The value of a negative result is that it was reasonable to expect otherwise: after
one defect of this shape the next round could have spent its time reading call sites, and instead the
measurement says the call discipline here holds.

### 89.3 The five suites fail for other reasons, and one of them for several

Running the five candidates rather than trusting the ranking produced a different finding. They fail,
and the walls do not come from the arity:

```
pause-end          Guest memory bounds 0x1074 + 4   (and, in the same run, Unicorn code 6,
pause-menu         Guest memory bounds 0x1074 + 4    Guest memory bounds 0x0 + 1200, one wasm
title-selection    Guest memory bounds 0x1074 + 4    memory access out of bounds)
screen-shake       Unicorn.js: uc_emu_start failed with code 6
spell-controller   Guest memory bounds 0xc900d8b + 4
```

`0x1074` is **below the guest window**, which starts at `0x10000`, and the read is made by the harness
(`NativeMachine.view`), not by executing guest code - so a binding returned a pointer the suite then
read at `0x1074`, and three suites share that one signature. The same run of `pause-end` reported three
*different* faults, which means these suites carry several cases each: a suite with several walls needs
its cases separated before any fix is claimed to have flipped it, and that separation is the next
round's work rather than a conclusion for this one.

### 89.4 Standing state

`th12-rng` 2/2, `anm-load-all` pass 1 / fail 0 and `archive.test.mjs` pass 1 / fail 0 (184 TH11
resources against the original) are unchanged. The named work is the `0x1074` cluster with its
per-case separation, `scene-schedule`'s registration order, and the D3DX9 in-image trap.
## 90. An unsettled row is not a measurement

### 90.1 Where 0x1074 came from

Three suites failed with the same signature, `Guest memory bounds 0x1074 + 4`, and the read came from
the harness (`NativeMachine.view`) rather than from executing guest code, so a value had been used as a
pointer. Naming the call site gave the line:

```
pause-menu.test.mjs:9:97   m.u32(touch(0x4c3808), files[0].original)
```

`touch(0x4c3808)` returned **0x1074**. The tables explain it:

```
oracle-globals-th11-th12.json
  {"source": "th11", "sourceAddress": "0x4c3808", "references": 19, "target": "th12",
   "targetAddress": "0x00001074", "agreeingSites": 1, "ready": false,
   "candidates": [{"address": "0x00001074", "sites": 1, "of": 19},
                  {"address": "0x004cee70", "sites": 1, "of": 19}]}
```

The row says `ready: false` and its own candidates agree at **one site out of nineteen**. The translator
applied it anyway, because it read `targetAddress` and never looked at the flag that exists to
distinguish a settled pairing from a guess. That is the defect, and it is a sharper version of the one
this session keeps meeting: not a wrong number, but a number whose provenance was available and unused.

Following the candidate back explains the number itself. The tool reports it from a *twin site*:

```
th11 site 0x0040cf01  ->  th12 site 0x00407b4d run 13 -> decoded value 0x00001074
th12 0x00407b4d disassembles as     int3 / int3 / int3 / add eax,0x1074
```

The site is not an instruction start, so the emulator decoded padding and reported noise as a "decoded
value". And the value was written into an **address** field: a pair of kind errors stacked, each of
which would have been visible from a field name or an alignment check.

There is a third fact, measured while trying to settle it statically. Both globals live in a section's
**uninitialised tail**:

```
th11 .data  VA 0x4a2000  vsize 0x28e40  raw 0x6400   -> 0x4c3808 is 0x1a808 past the raw bytes
th12 .data  VA 0x4ad000  vsize 0x29460  raw 0x6a00
```

so a data-context search cannot find the counterpart - there are no bytes to compare - and the pairing
must come from reference sites. The candidate's own metadata says one site of nineteen, and that site
was padding.

### 90.2 The fix, and what it measured

`fixture-addresses.mjs` now applies a row only when it is settled (`ready === true`, or a status that is
not `candidate`/`withdrawn`/`unsettled`/`proposed`) and only when its target is a conceivable address -
if it is below the guest window's `0x10000` it cannot be a global. It keeps a trace of what it skipped
under `TH_TOUCH_TRACE`, so the next reader can see the rows that are not being used instead of
discovering them one failure at a time. The row itself is withdrawn in place with its reason and its
noise candidate removed, and it stays in the table as a candidate - deleting it would hide the work that
found the twin sites.

Six of the eleven suites that touch `0x4c3808` were measured before and after. **All six moved past the
wall**:

```
before:  Guest memory bounds 0x1074 + 4      (pause-menu, pause-end, title-selection,
                                              stage-draw, dialogue, ending)
after:   Unicorn.js: uc_emu_start failed with code 6: Invalid memory read (UC_ERR_READ_UNMAPPED)
```

The harness-bounds class is closed and these suites now reach guest execution, which is what a suite is
for. What they reach is the next honest wall: `stage-draw.test.mjs:8:85` calls the original and the
guest itself reads unmapped memory, because identity is not a substitute for a measured counterpart -
`touch` returned the fixture's own `0x4c3808`, the th12 image maps a different layout, and the read is
unmapped. So the row needs its real answer, and the tool that produced the candidate needs one check
before it may produce another.

### 90.3 Named next, now precise

* `tools/th-twin-find.py` (or the global tool that consumes it) must refuse a twin site that is not an
  instruction start. That single guard would have stopped 0x1074 at the source.
* Then the globals table can be re-measured: **25 of its 35 rows are `ready: false`**, and every one of
  them is now skipped by the translator, so settling them is the largest bounded piece of work visible
  from here.
* The code-6 guest trap that the six suites now share is the follow-on wall, and per-case separation of
  `pause-end` and `pause-menu` still precedes any claim about them.

### 90.4 The addendum the census measured

The census ran inside this round and finished after the section above was written, so its numbers are
recorded here rather than revised there.

```
21/142 passing (was 20), 85 trapping, 34 pass / 119 fail assertions, 0 ENOENT
failure shape: guest trap code 6 in 51 suites, assertion in 33, other in 58
```

The per-suite diff against the previous census is what makes the change legible, and it is **broad**:
the translator now skips 25 unsettled rows, and **93 of the 142 suites** reference at least one of those
source addresses. The net is exactly one suite:

```
flipped to passing:      enemy-commands.test.mjs, fog-interpolation.test.mjs
regressed from passing:  graphics-pipeline.test.mjs
```

and every `Guest memory bounds 0x1074 + 4` wall in the census is gone - `bomb-controller`, `dialogue`
and `ending`, to name the ones already followed - replaced by a guest trap (`unmapped@0x0 pc=0x45fbff`),
which is what reaching execution looks like.

A net of +1 over a change that touches 93 suites deserves the honest reading rather than the favourable
one: the direction is right - a target below the guest window is impossible, and an unsettled pairing
is a guess - but only **one** of the 25 rows was provably wrong, and the other 24 are now unused rather
than measured. The named next step is therefore not "keep skipping" or "restore the rows", but
**settle them**: with the twin finder refusing a non-instruction-start twin site, each row can be
re-measured and then applied with its agreement count as evidence, which is strictly better than either
a guess or the fixture's own constant. `graphics-pipeline` is part of that debt and is expected to
return with its row.
## 91. Two guards on a twin site, and a derivation that refused itself

### 91.1 The guard the previous round named

Section 90 left one instruction: the global tool's twin site `0x00407b4d` disassembled as `int3` padding,
the tool read a counterpart address out of that noise, and a row that said `ready:false` was applied
anyway. The reading of the failed candidate also pointed at the real weakness: `min_run` was **8**, and
an 8-byte window match inside padding is a coincidence, not a site.

`tools/th-twin-globals-table.py` re-measures the table with two guards, both of which are facts about the
image rather than opinions about bytes:

* **Alignment.** A reference site counts only if it lies inside a real instruction, and the twin site it
  points at must lie inside a real instruction too. Both are decided by linear disassembly from the
  enclosing function entry - the entry index is every direct call target plus padding entries, the same
  index the batch tool derives interiors from - so "inside an instruction" no longer depends on the
  bytes happening to match somewhere.
* **Shape.** The instruction at the source site and the instruction at the twin site must have the same
  text after every in-image dword is replaced, because the same engine instruction in another title
  differs only in *which* global it names. This is what the failed candidate could not satisfy:

```
0x4c3808  site 0x0040bf01 -> twin 0x004055a1
          shape differs: mov eax, dword ptr [#]  vs  mov dword ptr [eax + #], ecx
```

and a row is written as ready only when **two or more** checked sites agree on one counterpart. The old
table recorded an agreement count and nobody read it; now the count is the write condition.

### 91.2 What the guards settled, and what they left

Eight rows were settled by two or more checked sites, the largest agreement first:

```
0x4a7948 -> 0x004b2ed0   22 of 22 checked sites
0x4a8d7c -> 0x004b43dc    7 of  7
0x4c3268 -> 0x004ce8cc    4 of  4
0x4a8e94 -> 0x004b44f4    3 of  3
0x4a8e88 -> 0x004b44e8    2 of  2
0x4a8eb4 -> 0x004b4514    2 of  2
0x4c3280 -> 0x004ce8e8    2 of  2
0x4c3810 -> 0x004cee78    2 of  2
```

The table went from 10 ready rows to 18. Seventeen stay candidates, and two of them were the ones this
round most wanted: `0x4c3808` has **19 reference sites and none survives the guards**, and `0x4c2f00` has
59 with one checked site and no agreement.

### 91.3 The derivation, and why it refused

A row whose own sites yield nothing might still be reachable: the data block it lives in moved as a
whole, so if settled neighbours share one shift, the shift is measured and the address derived. The tool
implements that route and states its derivation in the row (`derivedFrom`, `derivation`) so a derived
address is never confused with a site-measured one.

It derived **nothing**, and the reason is worth more than the eight rows. The neighbours of `0x4c3808`
that are settled measure **different shifts**:

```
0x4c3268 -> 0x4ce8cc   shift +0xb664   (4 checked sites)
0x4c3280 -> 0x4ce8e8   shift +0xb668   (2 checked sites)
0x4c3810 -> 0x4cee78   shift +0xb668   (2 checked sites)
```

The two source globals are `0x18` apart and their counterparts are `0x1c` apart: the layouts are not a
rigid copy, and a shift measured 0x600 bytes away is off by four bytes already. So the "block shift" that
this session has used as a heuristic elsewhere does not hold for this block, and the honest answer for
`0x4c3808` is the one the tool produced - **unsettled**. It is worth saying plainly that the old row's
`0x4cee70` is *numerically* what one of the two competing shifts would give (`0x4c3808 + 0xb668`), which
is exactly the kind of coincidence that makes a guess look right: the value was plausible and the
evidence was padding.

### 91.4 What the eight rows measured

The census ran inside this round, so its numbers belong to this section rather than to a later one.

```
passing: 20/142   (the previous census had 21)
flipped to passing: none
regressed from passing: fog-interpolation.test.mjs
failure shape: {'guest trap': 70, 'import': 16, 'other': 25, 'assertion': 31}
```

The eight settled rows are referenced by many suites - `0x4a7948` alone has 160 reference sites - so this
is the debt of section 90 being paid rather than a new instrument being admired. Seventeen rows remain
candidates and **the constraint that matters is not their number but their evidence**: `0x4c3808`'s own
sites do not survive the guards, its settled neighbours disagree by four bytes, and the tool therefore
leaves it unsettled rather than deriving it. The remaining work is per-row measurement with the same two
guards - a bigger span or a shape comparison that tolerates a different addressing form would settle
some of them - and it is bounded: the table has 35 rows.

### 91.5 Zero flipped, one regressed, and the exclusion

The census after settling the eight rows is **20 passing against 21**, with **no suite flipped** and one
regressed (`fog-interpolation`). Both halves of that sentence have to be read rather than announced.

**The regression is not attributable to this change.** `fog-interpolation.test.mjs` line 11 writes the
*literal* `0x4a7948` into a structure field - `b.writeUInt32LE(0x4a7948,0x7c)`, used as data and never
passed through `touch` - so the globals table cannot reach it, and the suite's only `touch` call is on a
**code** address, `touch(0x4055d0)`, which this round did not touch. What fails is the port against the
native on the same input:

```
mode=0 speed=1 duration=1 frame=0
actual=0x427f20c5 expected=0x41ff20c5
```

and the two differ by exactly `0x00800000` - the sign bit of a float - so this is a sign handling
difference in the port's fog math, arriving from the runtime rather than from the table. In a workspace
where another agent edits the runtime's C++ continuously, the honest statement is that this suite's
result changed between two censuses for a cause outside this round, and the causal exclusion above is
what makes that a measurement rather than a preference.

**No suite flipped, and that is the more useful half.** The eight settled rows are correct by two
independent structural checks and they are now recorded as such - but the suites that reference those
globals fail for reasons that a correct address cannot fix. Of the 142, **70 fail inside guest code**
(`unmapped@0x... pc=...`), 31 on assertions, 16 on an import, 25 on something else; an address that is
wrong by a data-section offset changes *which* wall is hit, not whether one is. The debt of section 90 is
paid in evidence while the pass rate stays where it was, and saying so is the point: an instrument that
settles eight rows and has not yet moved a suite is worth keeping for the rows, not for a number.
## 92. The trap site as a witness

### 92.1 The largest single class, clustered

The census after round 312 left **70 of 142 suites failing inside guest code**, and clustering them by
fault turned a list into a shape:

```
pc=0x45fbff  addr=0x0          13 suites   anm-resource, bomb-controller, dialogue, ending,
                                            pause-end, pause-menu, scene-compositor,
                                            screen-deformation, spell-animations, stage-draw,
                                            stage-passes, stage-runtime, title-selection
pc=0x0       addr=0x0           5 suites   a jump through a null pointer
pc=0x454ee1  addr=0x11c         4
pc=0x4067e0  addr=0x78          3
... 45 more suites in ones and twos
```

Thirteen suites sharing one instruction and one address is not thirteen bugs. Disassembling the site
gave the whole story in two instructions:

```
0x0045fbfa  mov  eax, dword ptr [0x4ce8f0]
0x0045fbff  mov  ecx, dword ptr [eax]        <- the fault: eax is 0
```

### 92.2 The witness

`touch()` now names its misses under `TH_TOUCH_LOG`, because a miss is not an error - the documented
behaviour is to keep the fixture's own constant - but a miss *immediately before* a trap is a different
thing entirely, and this session has now needed that distinction twice. Running `bomb-controller` with it:

```
touch miss 0x4540f0 -> identity
touch miss 0x4c3288 -> identity
Invalid memory read (UC_ERR_READ_UNMAPPED)  {"address":"0x0","size":4,"pc":"0x45fbff",...}
```

The suite writes a pointer **through `touch(0x4c3288)`** precisely so that the dereference at `0x45fbff`
is legal. `0x4c3288` was an unsettled row, so the write landed at the untranslated th11 address and the
th12 code read its own `[0x4ce8f0]` - which is 0.

That is a piece of evidence the twin matcher could not produce, because it is not a similarity at all: it
is the *purpose* of the write. The tool had found one instruction-aligned, shape-matching site agreeing
on `0x4ce8f0`, below its two-site threshold, and the row stayed a candidate. Three supports now exist,
two of them measured, and they are different instruments:

* one checked site agrees on `0x4ce8f0` (`tools/th-twin-globals-table.py`);
* the behavioural proof above: the write exists so that this dereference is legal, so the two addresses
  are the same global by behaviour;
* the shift `+0xb668`, measured on its settled neighbours `0x4c3280 -> 0x4ce8e8` and
  `0x4c3810 -> 0x4cee78`.

The row is settled as `0x4c3288 -> 0x004ce8f0`, and its `evidence` field says plainly that the site count
alone did not meet the write condition. The table stands at **19 ready rows of 35**.

### 92.3 What that measured

All thirteen suites were run before and after, and the single shared wall became five different ones:

```
before (all thirteen):  read of 0x0 at pc=0x45fbff
after:  code 6 read unmapped      dialogue, pause-end, pause-menu, anm-resource,
                                  screen-deformation, title-selection
        code 7 write unmapped     stage-draw, stage-passes, stage-runtime
        code 8 fetch unmapped     bomb-controller, scene-compositor
        AssertionError            ending (ending script load failed)
                                  spell-animations (expected values to be strictly equal)
```

Two suites now fail on an **assertion** rather than on a fault, which means they execute to the point
where the port and the native can be compared - the first time this session has seen that for either of
them. The other eleven moved to later walls of three different kinds, so the cluster is not one cause
wearing thirteen faces any more; it is thirteen pieces of work, and each now has its own address to
start from.

The general lesson is worth stating as a method: **when a trap site is a global dereference, the site
names the global, and a `touch` miss in the same run names the row that should have translated it.** For
the remaining 16 candidates that is a cheaper route than any window score, and `0x4540f0` - a miss on a
**code** address just before the same trap - is the same signal pointing at the code table.

### 92.4 The census after unclustering

```
passing: 21/142   (round 312 had 20, round 311 had 21)
flipped to passing: graphics-pipeline.test.mjs
regressed from passing: none
suites still tripping the 0x45fbff null dereference: 1
failure shape: {'read unmapped': 67, 'import': 16, 'other': 26, 'assertion': 33}
```

The thirteen suites did not start passing, and expecting them to would have been the wrong test: a write
that lands in the right place lets the engine run *further*, and further is where the next wall is. What
the census can show is that the identical wall is gone - it is - and what it cannot show yet is a pass
rate, because the walls behind it are three different kinds of fault and, for two suites, a comparison.
The remaining 16 candidate rows are the same shape of work as this one row was, and the trap site plus a
`touch` miss is the cheapest way to pick them off.
## 93. The shift histogram as an audit, and what it unblocked

### 93.1 Nineteen rows, two shifts, one outlier

Section 92 settled `0x4c3288` and left sixteen candidates. The next question was whether the *derivation*
route - measure a shift on settled neighbours, apply it to the ones their own sites cannot settle - could
be used, since section 91 had to refuse it for `0x4c3808`. Writing the shifts of the nineteen settled
rows out as a histogram answers it and audits the table in the same pass:

```
+0xb660   7 rows      +0xb668   7 rows
+0xb588    1          +0xb664    1        +0xb610   1        +0xb3c8   1
+0xb8cf05  1   <- not a shift at all
```

Nineteen rows, two dominant shifts, and one absurdity:

```
0x4a8d88 -> 0x01035c8d      shift +0xb8cf05, 1 agreeing site, no evidence field
```

`0x01035c8d` is outside **every section** of the th12 image, whose window is `0x401000..0x4d8600` as
measured by the new `tools/th-image-sections.py`. The row was a legacy `ready:true` entry, and the
translator's only sanity check was `target < 0x10000000`, which admits it - so `touch(0x4a8d88)` returned
a value that cannot be an address, and every suite using it faulted **by construction**. This is section
90's class one level deeper: not a guessed row, but a row with no evidence that a numeric range check was
too weak to stop.

Two fixes came out of it:

* **The table**: the row is withdrawn, with its reason and the expected counterpart `0x004b43e8` recorded
  as a candidate (the block measures `+0xb660`).
* **The translator**: `fixture-addresses.mjs` now loads `docs/porting/oracle-image-sections.json` and
  rejects any target outside the target image's sections. That is a fact about the image, measured by
  `tools/th-image-sections.py`, not a bound chosen by hand, and it subsumes the old floor check.

### 93.2 Withdrawing one row unblocked five

The derivation route requires the settled neighbours inside a window to agree on **one** shift, and
`0x4a8d88` sat inside the `0x4a8d5c..0x4a8eb4` block with a nonsense shift of its own. It was therefore
poisoning the derivation for every unsettled row near it. With the row withdrawn, the block's seven
settled neighbours agree on `+0xb660` and the tool derived five rows in one pass:

```
0x4a8d58 -> 0x004b43b8     0x4a8d84 -> 0x004b43e4     0x4a8d88 -> 0x004b43e8
0x4a8ebc -> 0x004b451c     0x4a8ec8 -> 0x004b4528
```

`0x4a8d88` derived exactly the counterpart the withdrawal had predicted, which is the check that the two
routes are measuring the same thing rather than agreeing by construction. The table stands at **23 ready
rows of 35**, five of them derived and every derived row carrying `derivedFrom` and `derivation` so its
provenance is never mistaken for a site measurement.

### 93.3 The cluster that turned out not to be a table problem

The `pc=0x0` fetch cluster - five suites, `communication`, `player-frame`, `player-initialization`,
`player-motion`, `player-rendering` - did **not** move, and the trap payload explains why:

```
pc 0x0   address 0x0   entry 0x44acd0   calls 0
recent [{at: 'import', key: 'fixture!texture dimensions', ret: '0x46025b',
         args: ['0x2003070','0x0','0x7effe80','0x0'], pc: '0x7e00c90', drift: -168}]
regs   EAX=0x2ab0100 EBX=0 ECX=0 EDX=0 ESI=0 EDI=0x7f00000 EBP=0x0
```

The guest called the harness's import stub for *texture dimensions*, and the jump to `0x0` happens
**after that call returns**; `calls` is zero and the stack is zeros. The two `touch` misses in the run
(`0x4540f0`, a code address, and `0x4a5714`, a global) are real and remain on the list, but they are not
the proximate cause - the wall is at an import boundary. That makes this cluster a **stub ABI** question:
a four-argument `stdcall` import must return with `ret 16` and a value the caller can use, and the drift
of -168 the harness recorded is the kind of number that says the frames did not line up. It is named here
rather than guessed at, because the next round can read the stub instead of the table.

### 93.4 What the census measured

The census afterwards is **21 passing**, with **nothing** flipped and **nothing** regressed; the `0x45fbff` null
cluster stays at **1**, and the failure shapes are `{'read unmapped': 68, 'import': 16, 'assertion': 33, 'other': 25}`.

The five derived rows were measured, and the suites around them did not pass: this is the same honest
reading as section 91.4 - a correct address lets the engine run further, and further is another wall. The
value of the round is different and it is worth naming precisely: **the shift histogram found a defective
row that nineteen rows of agreement hid, and removing it unblocked five rows of derivation**. A table can
be audited by its own arithmetic, and the outliers are where the defects live.

### 93.5 The guard, proved by injection

A guard that is present but inert is worse than no guard, and the new range check had nothing left to
catch once the only offending row was withdrawn - so it was given something to catch. A synthetic
`ready:true` row, `th11 0x4a8d90 -> 0x01035c8d`, was injected into the table and the translator was asked
directly, with no test runner in the way:

```
             with the out-of-range row        without it
touch(0x4a8d90)  0x4a8d90  (identity)         0x4a8d90  (identity)
touch(0x4a8d88)  0x4b43e8  (translated)       0x4b43e8  (translated)
touch(0x4c3268)  0x4ce8cc  (translated)       0x4ce8cc  (translated)
touch(0x4a7948)  0x4b2ed0  (translated)       0x4b2ed0  (translated)
```

The injected row was refused while every legitimate row still translated, so the guard is a check that
fires rather than a comment that reads well. The table was restored afterwards and verified to hold 35
rows with 23 ready and no synthetic entry.

It is worth recording why the test runner was not used for this: the `TH_TOUCH_TRACE` summary line did not
appear in `--test` output, and instead of assuming the guard had fired because no error was raised, the
question was put to `touch()` itself. Reading the module's answer is the stronger check anyway - it names
the translation for a known address rather than reporting that some number of rows were skipped.
## 94. Two refutations at the same boundary

### 94.1 The stub ABI, measured instead of assumed

Section 93.4 named the hypothesis: the `pc=0x0` cluster looked like a calling-convention fault, because
`fixture!texture dimensions` is registered with `argc:3` and `machine.ret(value,args)` pops `4+args*4`
bytes, so if the caller pushed four arguments the callee would return with ESP four bytes low.

The caller's pushes are in the instruction stream, so the count is a measurement - provided the window
starts at an instruction boundary. The first attempt did not: the greatest entry below the return address
is `0x46022b`, and a sweep from there decodes as `mov dh, bh`, which is padding, and the candidate's
"2 pushes" was an artefact of stopping the backward walk at a `mov` that sits between two arguments. The
second attempt kept only an entry in whose sweep the return address is exactly an instruction boundary,
and printed the argument setup:

```
0x0046024e  lea   ecx, [esp + 0x18]            ; the outgoing structure
0x00460252  push  ecx                          ; argument 3
0x00460253  mov   ecx, dword ptr [edx + 0x44]  ; the fixture's texture-dimensions slot
0x00460256  push  0                            ; argument 2
0x00460258  push  eax                          ; argument 1
0x00460259  call  ecx
```

Three arguments, pushed around the vtable load exactly as a compiler emits them, and `argc:3` is
therefore **correct**. The hypothesis is refuted, and the reason the first reading looked like two is
recorded above because the same trap - a `mov` in the middle of an argument sequence - will catch the
next reader.

### 94.2 The dispatcher, instrumented and silent

The second hypothesis was mechanical: a stub is a single `ret` byte, the code hook hands the import to
`onImport`, and `helpers.mjs` answers it with `m.ret(e.handler(),e.argc)`. If a handler **throws**, the
exception leaves the dispatcher before the `m.ret`, the CPU resumes on the bare `ret`, only four bytes are
popped, and the caller's next return address is read from its own arguments - a stack misalignment
reported three frames later as a fetch at `0x0`.

That is worth guarding regardless of whether it is this cluster's cause, so the dispatcher now balances
the stack on **every** path, records each failure in `m.importFailures`, and re-raises under
`TH_IMPORT_STRICT`. Running `player-motion` with `TH_IMPORT_LOG=1`:

```
(no import failure line)
Error: Unicorn.js: Function uc_emu_start failed with code 8
{"type":21,"address":"0x0","size":1,"pc":"0x0",...}
```

The handler did not throw, so the dispatcher is not this cluster's cause either. Both hypotheses are
refuted by measurement rather than argued away, and the guard stays because the class it prevents is real
even when this instance is not it.

### 94.3 What the trail does show

The trap payload's `recent` list is the only witness that survived, and it is unambiguous:

```
import fixture!texture dimensions   ret=0x46025b   drift=-168   args=[0x2003070,0x0,0x7effe80,0x0]
import native-host!embedded texture ret=0x460221   drift=-164   args=[0x100,0x100,0x0,0x27c0ba0]
import fixture!texture dimensions   ret=0x46025b   drift=-168
import native-host!embedded texture ret=0x460221   drift=-164
import fixture!texture dimensions   ret=0x46025b   drift=-168
unmapped                            pc=0x0
```

So the guest loads textures **successfully, repeatedly** - `texture dimensions` then `embedded texture`,
three times - and then jumps to zero. `regs` at the fault are `EAX=0x2ab0100 EDI=0x7f00000` with
`EBX ECX EDX ESI EBP` all zero, and the instructions the guest would run next, from the validated sweep,
are a loop over chunks:

```
0x0046025b  xor  edx, edx
0x0046025d  lea  esi, [ebp + 0x40]        ; EBP is 0 at the fault
0x00460260  mov  dword ptr [esp + 0x84], 0
0x0046026b  cmp  dx, word ptr [ebp + 4]
0x0046023e  mov  edx, dword ptr [edi + 0x120]
0x00460244  mov  ecx, dword ptr [edx + ebx]
0x00460253  mov  ecx, dword ptr [edx + 0x44]   ; the slot that is called
```

with `ebx = [esp+0x94]` as the loop index. The call that goes to zero is one of those vtable slots, and
the register that should hold the object is zero - so the question is no longer about the harness's
imports at all, it is about a pointer the guest itself never received. The `recent` trail cannot answer
that, because it records imports and not executed addresses; the instrument the next round needs is a
bounded **executed-address ring** (the last N EIPs before a fault), which is a smaller thing to build
than another hypothesis.

### 94.4 The census


The census is **21 passing**, with **nothing** flipped and **nothing** regressed, and the same failure shapes at a glance (`read unmapped 68, import 14, assertion 34, other 26`). The counts hide the part that moved, and four suites did:

```
anm-scripts        unmapped@0x0 pc=0x0        ->  unmapped@0x78 pc=0x4067e0
frame-statistics   import@undefined           ->  AssertionError: window ...
text-raster        import@undefined           ->  unmapped@0xfffffffe pc=0x44ea56
archive            unmapped@0x0 pc=0x0        ->  passing in the census run
```

The first three are the dispatcher's doing and they are the point of it. `helpers.mjs` used to `throw` on an unimplemented import; the throw left the hook, the emulator reported `import@undefined`, and the suite's own wall was never reached. Now the stack is balanced, the failure is recorded in `m.importFailures`, and the guest continues to the place where its actual disagreement is - an assertion for `frame-statistics`, its own unmapped read for `text-raster`, its real function for `anm-scripts`. **A diagnostic that becomes the failure stops the work; one that is recorded lets it continue.** The fourth line is different in kind and is a caveat rather than a result: `archive.test.mjs` passes when it is run on its own and failed with `unmapped@0x0 pc=0x0` in the previous census run, so its result in the aggregate is **context-dependent** and should not be counted as a flip.
## 95. The executed-address ring, and the label that was called

### 95.1 The instrument section 94 asked for

Section 94 ended with a named gap: `recent` records imports, and the question had become a guest pointer
that was never handed over, so the last executed addresses are the only witness that can answer it. The
machine now keeps an **executed-address ring** - opt-in under `TH_TRACE_EIP`, because a code hook over
the whole executable range costs a hook per instruction and the ordinary census must not pay for an
instrument it does not read. Each entry carries the address and `ECX`, `EDX` and `EAX`, because at a
fault the addresses alone say which call it was and the registers alone say the call went to zero. The
ring is attached to a fault and never to a successful call.

It fell into the same trap twice on the way in, and both are worth recording because they are one class
of mistake. `PEImage` parses the section table as BigInt, so `Math.max(section.rawSize, section.virtualSize)`
threw `Cannot mix BigInt and other types` and the instrument broke the machine at `0x46ea5c` - its first
run reported a fault at the CRT bootstrap instead of at the player. Then the hook callback hands its
`address` over as a BigInt as well, which the import hook beside it already knows (`Number(address)`), and
`address>>>0` threw the same error. In both cases the symptom was a fault at an address that had nothing
to do with the question, which is the general shape of an instrument that has become the result.

### 95.2 The ring's answer

`player-motion` with `TH_TRACE_EIP=64`:

```
0x44acd0 ecx=0x0      edx=0x0 eax=0x2ab3a04
0x44acd3 ecx=0x0      edx=0x0 eax=0x2ab3a04
0x44acd8 ecx=0x0      edx=0x0 eax=0x2ab3a04
0x44acdb ecx=0x0      edx=0x0 eax=0x2ab3a04
0x44acdd ecx=0x0      edx=0x0 eax=0x2ab0100
0x44ace0 ecx=0x0      edx=0x0 eax=0x2ab0100
0x44ae98 ecx=0x0      edx=0x0 eax=0x2ab0100
0x44ae9a ... 0x44ae9b ... 0x44ae9c ... 0x44ae9d ...
```

The last executed instruction is `0x44ae9d`, and disassembling there, from a sweep that makes the address
an instruction boundary, gives the function's shared epilogue:

```
0x0044ae98  fstp st(0)
0x0044ae9a  pop  edi
0x0044ae9b  pop  esi
0x0044ae9c  pop  ebx
0x0044ae9d  ret
```

`ret` pops `[ESP]`, and `[ESP]` is not the harness's planted return address - it is one of the arguments,
which is zero. `EIP := 0` and the next fetch is at `0x0`, with `EAX` still holding the value from
`0x44acdd`. The pc=0x0 cluster is a **stack imbalance of the caller's making**, measured rather than
inferred.

### 95.3 Why the stack was imbalanced: a jump-table label was called as a function

The address the harness called is `0x44acd0`, and the function it belongs to starts at `0x44aca0`:

```
0x0044aca0  fld1
0x0044aca2  push  ebx
0x0044aca3  push  esi
0x0044aca4  mov   esi, dword ptr [0x4b4534]
0x0044acaa  dec   eax
0x0044acab  push  edi
0x0044acac  mov   edi, 1
0x0044acb1  cmp   eax, 0xb
0x0044acb4  ja    0x44ad63
0x0044acba  movzx eax, byte ptr [eax + 0x44aeb0]
0x0044acc1  jmp   dword ptr [eax*4 + 0x44aea0]
...
0x0044acd0  add   dword ptr [esi + 0x4c], edi     ; <- the label the suites call
```

`0x44acd0` is a case of the function's switch, reached through a byte table and a jump table. The suites
call it directly - `player-frame` L43, `player-motion` L25, `player-rendering` L16, `scene-compositor`
L28, and `bomb-controller` L38 - and preset `EAX`, `EDI` and `EBX` to emulate what the prologue would have
established. What no preset can supply is the **stack**: the prologue pushes `ebx`, `esi` and `edi`, the
shared epilogue pops them, and an entry past the prologue leaves those three pops to eat the caller's
frame. `ret` then reads an argument. The rule the cluster teaches is exact:

> A call into a function's interior must supply every stack slot the epilogue will pop, the x87 entry
> state the prologue would have established (`fld1` here), and any callee-saved register the prologue
> would have set (`esi` here, loaded from `0x4b4534`).

Two of the five callers are inside `m.replace(0x44acd0, ...)`, which is a different case: the replacement
hijacks the label and returns with its own argument count, so the epilogue never runs and the stack never
matters. That distinction is why the audit below is a census and not a list of failures.

### 95.4 The class, enumerated

`tools/th-interior-call-audit.py` asks the question statically for every suite: is the literal in a
`m.call(<literal>)` an entry in the image's call-target index, and if not, does the region from the label
to the end of the function pop more than it pushes? The answer for th12 is **116 literal call sites into
non-entry addresses, 54 of which pop more than they push, across 36 suite files**. The five sites above
are five of the fifty-four, and the pc=0x0 cluster is five suites that happened to reach one of them.

Two boundaries were wrong before the third was right, and both are recorded because the same trap catches
the next reader. Stopping the disassembly at the first `ret` misses a shared epilogue reached by a jump:
`0x44acd0` reaches `0x44ae98` through `jnp`, so the linear stream passes an earlier `ret` and the tool
called the site that prompted it **balanced**. Stopping at the next call target truncates a function at
one of its own interior labels, and produced a nonsense reading of 31 pops. The end of a function is its
**padding** - MSVC separates functions with `int3` runs or the `mov edi, edi` hot-patch pair - which is a
fact about the image rather than a guess about layout. The count can still over-report when a function has
several epilogues in one block; the **verdict** is the claim, not the number.

### 95.5 The census

The census is **21 passing**, with **nothing** flipped and **nothing** regressed, and **0 suites changed which wall they hit** (none). The ring is opt-in, so the census should be identical to section 94.4 and is recorded as the control that the instrument did not change the measurement.
## 96. The skipped prologue, rebuilt from the image

### 96.1 Deriving the frame instead of writing it by hand

Section 95 enumerated the class: fifty-four of th12's hundred and sixteen literal interior call sites pop
more than they push, because a suite that enters at a jump-table label skips the prologue and the shared
epilogue pops registers nobody pushed. The repair cannot be hand-written stack arithmetic in thirty-six
suites - the image already knows what the epilogue pops, so it is derived:

    py -3 tools/th-interior-calls.py --title th12 --write

which writes `docs/porting/oracle-interior-calls.json`: **81 interior call targets, 46 of them carrying
slots to supply**. The rule that produced it is the epilogue, defined as the contiguous run of `pop`s
immediately before a `ret`, taken at the **last** `ret` in the function block. The first rule was to sum
every `pop` in the block and subtract the pushes, and it reported **six** slots for `0x44acd0` where the
shared epilogue pops **three** - the extra three belong to another return in the same block that the
entered path never takes. The second rule, the first `ret` rather than the last, misses the epilogue
entirely, because `0x44acd0` reaches `0x44ae98` through `jnp`. The map's row is now
`0x44acd0 → entry 0x44aca0, slots 3, saves edi esi ebx`, which is the epilogue as disassembled.

### 96.2 The frame order, and the stack pointer as the witness

The machine rebuilds the skipped frame in `call()`: it pushes each saved register with its **current**
value, which is what the original prologue saves. The first implementation pushed those slots and then
the arguments and the return address, which puts them **above** the return address - and the epilogue pops
upward, so `ret` read a sentinel instead:

```
map off:  pc=0x0  esp=0x7efff0c  stackBase=0x7efff00   (twelve bytes ABOVE the base: three pops too many)
map on:   pc=0x0  esp=0x7efff00  stackBase=0x7efff00   (balanced, and still fetching zero)
```

`esp = stackBase` with `pc` still `0x0` is that mistake's exact signature: the frame was balanced and the
return address was on the wrong side of it. A real prologue pushes *below* the return address, so the
slots go on **after** the return address is written and the epilogue pops upward onto it. This is worth
recording because the failure looked unchanged: an instrument that is applied but ineffective is read as
"the repair did not work" unless the stack pointer is the measurement.

### 96.3 What the repair moved, measured with the map on and off

`player-motion`, same suite, same run settings, with `TH_INTERIOR_CALLS=0` as the ablation:

```
map off:  Error: Unicorn.js: Function uc_emu_start failed with code 8
          Invalid memory fetch (UC_ERR_FETCH_UNMAPPED)   type 21, address 0x0, pc 0x0
          ring tail ... 0x44ae9b, 0x44ae9c, 0x44ae9d

map on:   Error: Unicorn.js: Function uc_emu_start failed with code 6
          Invalid memory read (UC_ERR_READ_UNMAPPED)    type 19, address 0x78, size 4, pc 0x4067e0
          stack at ESP: 0x455b15, 0x56d91824, 0x7f00000, 0x294e0f0, ...
          ring tail ... 0x455b10, 0x4067e0
```

The interior call now **returns**: the planted return address `0x455b15` is on top of the stack, the
loop's frames are sane, and the guest proceeds to a read at `address 0x78` through `[eax+0x10]` with
`eax = 0x68` - a real wall of its own, one function deeper (`0x4067e0` is a genuine entry with
`mov ecx, dword ptr [eax + 0x10]`). The pc=0x0 cluster is therefore **one class removed**: the fifty-four
sites are repaired by construction, and what remains is the next disagreement.

### 96.4 Ablation, because a map that fires is not a map that helps

The map is handed to the machine by `helpers.mjs` and applied under `TH_INTERIOR_CALLS`, so the previous
census - taken before the map existed - is the control, and `m.interiorApplied` counts how often the
frame was rebuilt. The suite still fails: an interior call that returns lets the engine run further, and
further is where the next wall is. The value of the round is that the fifty-four sites are no longer a
list of failures but a derived frame with a provenance, and that the derivation's own first two rules are
recorded above so they are not re-invented.

### 96.5 The census

The census is **21 passing**, with **nothing** flipped and **nothing** regressed, and **10 suites changed which wall they hit**: ascii-text, bomb-controller, communication, damage-area, player-frame, player-initialization, player-motion, player-rendering, scene-compositor, score-popups. The map is applied by default and the control is section 95.5, which was taken before it existed: the difference between the two is the map's whole effect, and a suite that moved has a repair to thank for it while a suite that did not may be blocked by something else entirely.
## 97. Four routes to the spawn-mode rows, and four refusals

### 97.1 Where the round started: the touch misses the player suites still report

The census of section 96 left the player suites at walls that all read like the same sentence - an address
below the guest window, through a register that holds a small number. Running the two player suites with
`TH_TOUCH_LOG=1` names the reason directly:

```
touch miss 0x4540f0 -> identity
touch miss 0x4a5714 -> identity
touch miss 0x455a00 -> identity
touch miss 0x455df0 -> identity
touch miss 0x455bc0 -> identity
touch miss 0x456020 -> identity
```

Five code addresses and one global have no settled row, so `touch` returns identity and the suite calls
**th12's function at that same address**, which is a different function. This is the code-table
workstream section 94 named, and the four `spawn mode` rows are the interesting part.

### 97.2 Why the rows are withdrawn, in the table's own terms

All four rows carry the **same** candidate list, headed by `0x44bf6a`, and that candidate is five
instructions long:

```
0x455a00 spawn mode 0 (withdrawn): 0x0044bf6a run=8, 0x00414d75 run=7, 0x00414ee6 run=7, 0x0043c009 run=7
0x455bc0 spawn mode 2 (withdrawn): 0x0044bf6a run=8, 0x00414d75 run=7, 0x00414ee6 run=7, 0x0043c009 run=7
0x455df0 spawn mode 1 (withdrawn): the same four
0x456020 spawn mode 3 (withdrawn): the same four
```

`tools/th-twin-find.py` ranks by the longest run of agreeing literals, and a run of eight agreeing
literals is not a function. Withdrawing them was correct, and the question is what evidence can separate
four functions that agree that far. Disassembling the four says exactly how far: they are the same code
with different literals - the same two shared helpers, the same shape, one helper each of their own:

```
0x455a00  calls 0x4569c0, 0x456910, 0x4556e0, 0x44acd0
0x455bc0  calls 0x4569c0, 0x456910, 0x455760, 0x44acd0
0x455df0  calls 0x4569c0, 0x456910, 0x4557e0, 0x44acd0
0x456020  calls 0x4569c0, 0x456910, 0x455860, 0x44acd0
```

The distinguishing fact is the **private helper**: 0x4556e0, 0x455760, 0x4557e0, 0x455860, one per mode.
Everything else about them is shared, and that is why shape cannot decide.

### 97.3 Four routes, four refusals

Each was tried and measured, not argued away.

**A masked-shape class search.** `tools/th-shape-classes.py`, written this round, is section 91's shape
guard turned into a class search: mask every in-image dword in a window and ask which functions in the
other image equal it byte for byte. For a 48-byte window at each of the four addresses:

```
source class: 1 member (the function itself)
target class: 0 members
```

No th12 function is byte-identical to any of the four after masking, so the twins are more than operands
apart and the class method has no member to offer. (One member on the source side also corrects an
expectation the earlier round left: the four are *not* byte-identical to each other over 48 bytes, only
close enough for the run-based matcher to collapse them.)

**Derivation from call displacements.** `tools/th-twin-batch.py --derive-calls`, with the unsettled rows'
targets stripped so they join the queue, over **all 147 anchored bases** and a queue of the four spawn
functions, their four helpers, `0x456910` and `0x4540f0`:

```
queue 10 over 147 anchored bases: derived 0 from call displacements, unresolved 10
```

Not one anchored function calls into that cluster. Every caller found for those addresses
(0x40f29c, 0x41a844, 0x44bc1e, 0x44bc45, 0x455c08, ...) has an enclosing entry that is itself unanchored,
so the call graph has no foothold at all - the chain does not merely need another step, it has no first
step.

**Call-sequence matching.** Each spawn function begins `call 0x4569c0` then `call 0x456910`, which would be
a signature if both twins were known. The table settles `0x4569c0 -> 0x4621c0` and does **not** settle
`0x456910`, so the sequence cannot be anchored on both ends and the method stops at its premise.

**Settled globals as the foothold.** This was the most promising, because a global does not depend on the
caller graph: if a th11 function tests a global whose twin is settled, a th12 function testing the twin is
a candidate. The four functions carry six data references each, of which **one** is settled
(`0x4c3810 -> 0x4cee78`), and 622 th12 entries reference `0x4cee78`. One shared, widely used global
separates nothing.

### 97.4 What that leaves, stated as an instrument rather than a hope

The bijection depends on the four private helpers, so the next real step is to **make an anchor for the
helper family**: `0x4569c0 -> 0x4621c0` is the one foothold in the cluster, and the helper 0x4556e0 has
nine callers. Either one of those callers is inside a function that can be anchored by a route that does
not need this cluster (which is a search, not a guess), or the comparison has to be **behavioural**: run a
candidate th12 function under the oracle and compare what it does with what the suite expects - which is
what the method section of this plan has been building toward all along, and the first place where the
oracle is the only remaining instrument rather than the cheapest one.

### 97.5 The census, as the round's control

The census is **21 passing**, with **nothing** flipped, **nothing** regressed and **0 suites changing which wall they hit** (none). Nothing in the harness or the tables changed this round - no row was settled and no machine behaviour was touched - so the census is a control: it must read exactly as section 96.5 did, and any movement would have to be credited to the concurrent runtime edits rather than to this round.
## 98. The class-search instrument was wrong five times, and only the fifth was the question

### 98.1 An instrument must never become the result

Section 97.3 concluded "target class: 0 members" for the four `spawn mode` functions and the four private
helpers, and built the round's argument on it. The conclusion may be true; the instrument that produced it
was not, and it was wrong in a way that guaranteed that zero for **every** input. This section corrects it
one defect at a time, and ends by validating it against a row the table has held for many rounds - because
the rule in this plan's method, that a reading is not a measurement, applies to my own tools first.

### 98.2 The wildcards were computed per side

The comparison masked the source window with the source image's section ranges and the target window with
the **target** image's, so a dword that looks like an address in th11 and not in th12 produced two masked
windows compared at different byte positions. A wildcard is a claim about the *source* operand -
`pattern_and_wild` in tools/th-twin-batch.py has always worked that way - and the target must be masked at
exactly those positions.

### 98.3 The ranges were raw, not mapped

After that fix a helper window reported `0 of 96 bytes wildcarded` although its first instruction is
`mov ecx, dword ptr [0x4c3268]`. The ranges came from `raw_size`, and th11's `.data` holds references above
its raw size; with raw ranges no global was masked, and the comparison demanded th12's data live at th11's
addresses - the one thing the two titles cannot share. The ranges are now the **mapped** range,
`max(virtual_size, raw_size)`.

### 98.4 The candidate set was the wrong universe

The candidate side searched the call-target index plus int3-padded entries. That is not the universe the
method uses: tools/th-twin-batch.py scans the **whole section**, because a function reached only through an
indirect call or a jump table need not be a call target and need not be preceded by padding. The tool scans
the section and keeps only hits that section 91's alignment rule admits.

### 98.5 The rule missed the operand that moves most, and then over-corrected

With those three fixed the verdict was still zero, and the shape-equal pair showed why. Diffing the pair
tools/th-twin-batch.py reports as `paired=1.000 pairs=27/27`:

```
0x455760 -> 0x4612d0: 21/27 instructions agree after normalisation
   ** mov edx, dword ptr [0x4c3268]       | mov edx, dword ptr [0x4ce8cc]
   ** mov esi, dword ptr [edx + 0x7b562c] | mov esi, dword ptr [edx + 0x8856b8]
   ** mov dword ptr [edx + 0x7b5630], ecx | mov dword ptr [edx + 0x8856bc], ecx
   ** add dword ptr [edx + 0x7bd888], ecx | add dword ptr [edx + 0x88ed48], ecx
```

Every marked line is an operand the port is allowed to move, and the six of them are all six differences.
The byte-level rule masked only absolute in-image dwords, so a register-relative displacement was demanded
to match - while the shape-level rule counts `[edx + 0x7b562c]` and `[edx + 0x8856b8]` as the same operand
kind and says paired. The rule was extended to mask the disp32 of a MEM operand with a base or index
register, and this fix was **itself a defect**: masking every non-zero disp32 reported `23 of 48 bytes
wildcarded` for the anchored window at 0x401fd0, whose own row records 48 literal bytes - small
displacements are field offsets the method keeps as literals. The rule now masks only a displacement of
magnitude at least 0x10000, i.e. a moved address, not a field offset.

### 98.6 The fifth defect was the question

A self-check against the table turned the whole section around. The anchored row for `0x401fd0` records
`span: 48, literals: 48, run: 16`: 48 literal bytes, a longest wildcard-free stretch of 16, and - as
`literal_runs` names it - the criterion is a **longest agreeing literal run**, not byte-for-byte equality
over the window. `tools/th-shape-classes.py` demanded full-window equality, which no row in the table meets,
so its zero said nothing about any of its inputs, including the ones that are known to be right. That is
the fifth and only decisive defect: the instrument was answering a stronger question than the method asks.

### 98.7 The corrected instrument, validated on a row the table already knows

Section 91's shape guard as a class search, with the method's own criterion, over a 48-byte window:

```
0x401fd0 -> 1 boundary hit: 0x402520, agreement 48/48      (the table's anchored row)
0x455760 -> 2 boundary hits: 0x4613d0 and 0x4612d0, both 48/48
0x455860 -> 2 boundary hits: 0x4613d0 and 0x4612d0, both 48/48
0x4556e0 -> longest literal run 8, 0 hits
0x4557e0 -> longest literal run 8, 0 hits
0x455a00 -> longest literal run 14, 0 hits   (the table's withdrawn candidate 0x44bf6a does not qualify)
0x455bc0 -> longest literal run 14, 0 hits
0x455df0 -> longest literal run 14, 0 hits
0x456020 -> longest literal run 14, 0 hits
```

The instrument reproduces the row it was calibrated against, exactly and alone, and then measures the
family section 97 could not touch: the two helpers `0x455760` and `0x455860` have **two** twins, `0x4612d0`
and `0x4613d0`, full-window matches - and those two helpers are one class on the source side as well, so
the correspondence is settled **class to class**. Their private helpers are what separate the four spawn
modes from one another, so a class-level anchor in that family is the foothold section 97.4 said was
missing. `0x4556e0` and `0x4557e0` have no full-window twin, and neither do the four spawn functions, so
their rows stay withdrawn - now on the method's criterion rather than on a broken one.

### 98.8 What this round did and did not change

No fixture, no table and no machine behaviour changed: the four `spawn mode` rows are still withdrawn and
no suite can move, so the census is a control. What changed is that the tool which will be used to settle
them is now validated against a known row, and that a real foothold exists in the helper family.

### 98.9 The census, as the round's control

The census is **21 passing**, with **nothing** flipped, **nothing** regressed and **0 suites changing which wall they hit** (none). Nothing in the harness, the fixtures or the tables changed this round - every fix is inside a measurement tool the suites never load - so the census is a control and must read exactly as section 97.5 did.
## 99. The validated instrument settles a row, and a suite passes

### 99.1 The instrument, out of tools/tmp and calibrated

Section 98 ended with a class search that reproduces the table's own anchored row. It is now
`tools/th-class-search.py`, and its calibration is the first thing it prints:

```
py -3 tools/th-class-search.py --at 0x401fd0 --span 48
  0x401fd0: window 48 bytes, 24 wildcarded, longest literal run 13, 1 boundary candidate(s)
    table: 0x401fd0 -> 0x00402520 (anchored)
    0x402520  all literals agree  longest run 48/48  sub esp, 0x10
```

One candidate, every literal byte agreeing, and it is the row the table has held for many rounds. The
criterion is the method's: the wildcards come from the source window as an in-image dword, and a candidate
is admitted when every non-wildcard byte agrees and section 91's sweep makes its address an instruction
boundary.

### 99.2 The row the suites were missing, and the candidate the table had was the weaker one

`touch miss 0x4540f0 -> identity` was still in the player suites' logs, and the table held a **candidate**
row for it pointing at `0x0044f442`. The 48-byte window cannot choose between it and a second candidate:

```
0x4540f0 --span 0x30 -> 0x44f442 and 0x45fbf0, both all-literals-agree 48/48
0x4540f0 --span 0x60 -> 0x45fbf0 only, all literals agree
0x4540f0 --span 0x80 -> 0x45fbf0 only, all literals agree
0x4540f0 --span 0x100 -> no candidate whose literal bytes all agree
```

The table's candidate agrees for the first 48 bytes and diverges; `0x45fbf0` agrees over 96 and 128 bytes;
at 256 neither does, so the two sites are the same code at their entry and different afterwards. The row is
