now `0x4540f0 -> 0x0045fbf0`, `confidence: measured`, with the evidence written into it - and the two sites
disassemble identically at the entry:

```
0x45fbf0  or dword ptr [esi + 0x10], 1    0x44f442  or dword ptr [esi + 0x10], 1
0x45fbf4  mov edx, dword ptr [0x4ce9e4]   0x44f446  mov edx, dword ptr [0x4ce9e4]
0x45fbfa  mov eax, dword ptr [0x4ce8f0]   0x44f44c  mov eax, dword ptr [0x4ce8f0]
```

so th12 holds two copies of this routine and the settled member is the one whose agreement survives a
longer window. The table now has 13 measured rows and 2 candidates left.

### 99.3 What the settlement did, measured

The touch log first: `0x4540f0` is gone from it, leaving only `0x4a5714`. Then the census, which is the
verdict:

```
census: 22 passing, flipped [anm-resource.test.mjs], regressed [], walls moved 1
  anm-resource.test.mjs   unmapped@0x0 pc=0x45fbff -> (passing)
```

One suite **flips to passing** and nothing regresses. The flip is not a coincidence of margin: the failing
pc was `0x45fbff`, which is `0x45fbf0 + 0xf` - inside the target that was just settled, and inside the
*other* copy's region. The suite had been running the wrong copy of the routine and faulting inside it; with
the row settled it runs to completion. That is the first time in these rounds that a table measurement has
turned a suite green rather than moving its wall.

### 99.4 A comparison that nearly fooled me, recorded so it does not again

The raw fault for `player-frame` reads `type 20, UC_ERR_WRITE_UNMAPPED, address 0x38, pc 0x432cc1`, while the
previous census recorded `unmapped@0x38 pc=0x432cc1` for it - and I first read that as the wall changing
from a read to a write. It is not: the census summary does not print the direction, so I was comparing one
instrument's summary against another instrument's raw record. The census diff is the verdict, and it says
`player-frame` did **not** move: its failing instruction is `mov dword ptr [ebp + 0x38], 3` with `ebp = 0`,
which was a write before the settlement and is a write after it.

### 99.5 The next class this settlement exposed

That instruction is where the next instrument starts. A suite that calls the interior label `0x45fbf0`
directly is served by the interior-call map of section 96, which supplies the registers the **epilogue**
pops - `edi`, `esi`, `ebx` for `0x44acd0` - and the frame register the **prologue** established is not one
of them, so `ebp` is zero and the first store through the frame goes to `0x38`. The map derives the
epilogue; the next round has to derive the prologue's frame setup for the same entries, from the same image
and by the same rule.

## 100. The prologue's frame, derived per entry, and the four walls it moved

### 100.1 The epilogue is not the whole frame

Section 96 derived what the **epilogue** pops and the machine rebuilds those slots when a suite calls an
interior label. Section 99.5 found the other half: `player-frame` failed at `0x432cc1`,
`mov dword ptr [ebp + 0x38], 3`, with `ebp = 0` - the frame register the **prologue** would have
established is not something the epilogue pops, so the slot rule cannot supply it. Round 307 had already
tested the blanket version of this idea (EBP = entry ESP + 4 for **every** call) and refuted it: across 142
suites the census did not move. The rule has to be derived per entry and applied only where the image says
the prologue established EBP and the body uses it.

### 100.2 Deriving it, with the padding bug that was hiding the case at hand

`tools/th-interior-calls.py` now records, for every interior call target, the part of the function **before
the label** - which is exactly the prologue a suite skips - and whether that prologue loads EBP
(`mov ebp, esp`), plus the frame offsets the body uses:

```
H:/Games/th/12/th12.exe: 87 interior call targets, 39 with slots to supply,
                         24 needing a frame the prologue would have set
  0x00432a90 entry 0x004329a0  ebp offsets 0..716
  0x00432cc0 entry 0x004329a0  ebp offsets 0..716
```

The count moved from 81 targets and 46 slot rows to 87 and 39, and the reason is section 91's padding
lesson applied to this tool: `call_targets` returns padding entries, and `0x432cc0` - the label the
`player-frame` suite actually calls - was in that set, so the map skipped it and the machine was never told
its frame was missing. A real entry is one a direct `E8` call reaches, and with that filter `0x432cc0`
enters the map with `usesEbp` true and `setsEbp` false. Two offsets also had to be sanity-filtered: the
sweep can run past the end of a function into data, and `0x00416ee0` reported offsets of -2050752447 and
2130723197, which are decoded garbage; the frame range is clamped to -0x1000..0x10000 and the outliers are
counted separately.

### 100.3 The machine applies it only where it is derived

`machine.mjs` sets `EBP` to a scratch frame at `0x07f10000` - above the return-address slot at
`0x07f00000`, below the end of the guest window, clear of the stubs and the stack - when the row says
`usesEbp` and not `setsEbp`, under the ablation switch `TH_INTERIOR_FRAME`. No fixture changed, and the
blanket default round 307 refuted is not what this is: it fires on 24 of 87 entries.

### 100.4 Measured: the ablation, then the census, then the attribution

`player-frame` with the rule off and on:

```
off: WRITE_UNMAPPED  type 20  address 0x38  pc 0x432cc1  esp 0x7efff00 (= stackBase)  EBP = 0
on:  FETCH_UNMAPPED  type 21  address 0x0   pc 0x0        esp 0x7efff84              EBP = 0
```

The wall moved: the null-frame store is gone and the suite now reaches a fetch at zero. The census, over
all suites:

```
census: 22 passing, flipped [], regressed [], walls moved 4
  player-frame       unmapped@0x38        pc=0x432cc1 -> unmapped@0x0 pc=0x0
  player-options     unmapped@0x38        pc=0x432cc1 -> unmapped@0x0 pc=0x0
  player-rendering   unmapped@0xfffffffc  pc=0x431bc0 -> unmapped@0x0 pc=0x0
  shot-resource      unmapped@0x4         pc=0x434380 -> unmapped@0x0 pc=0x0
```

Nothing regresses and nothing flips, and the same four suites run with `TH_INTERIOR_FRAME=0` and the new
map in place return to exactly the walls the previous census recorded - so the padding filter moved nothing
on its own, and all four movements are the frame rule's. That attribution matters, because the diff of this
round contains two changes and a wall movement credited to the wrong one is not a measurement.

### 100.5 What the four suites now hit, and the next derivation

All four stop at `pc = 0x0`, the fetch-at-zero signature of section 95 - a return path consuming a slot
that was never pushed. For `player-frame` the recorded `esp` at the new fault is `stackBase + 0x84`, so the
frame depth is 33 words deeper than the entry, and the row for `0x432cc0` is one of the newly added ones:
the slots were derived for the **old** boundary set, before this label was known to be an interior entry.
The next derivation is therefore the same rule applied to the corrected entry set - the epilogue on the path
that runs *after* the frame is established, for the 24 entries that needed the frame, which is what the
`pc = 0x0` class is asking for.

## 101. The frame plan, the /GS epilogue, and an amount that had to be probed

### 101.1 A `pc = 0x0` fault, made into a reading

Section 100 left four suites at `unmapped@0x0 pc=0x0`, which says only that something consumed the return
address. `machine.mjs` now records, for every call, where it planted the return address and how many slots
it pushed for it, and attaches that plan to the fault together with three facts: whether the planted value
is still in its slot, what is there instead, and how far ESP has drifted from the slot in words. `pc = 0x0`
becomes a number. On `player-frame`:

```
framePlan: {"returnSlot": "0x7effefc", "slots": 0, "args": 0, "esp": "0x7effefc", "ebp": "0x7f10000"}
fault:     esp 0x7efff84  returnDrift 34  returnHeld false  returnValue 0x0
```

The return address was planted at `0x7effefc` and ESP ended **34 words above it**, with the slot holding
zero. The `ret` had not read the return address at all; it read past it. Adding the word the `ret` itself
pops gives 35 words = `0x8c`, and the suite's own prologue turns out to spend exactly that.

### 101.2 The image states the frame, /GS and all

The function at `0x4329a0` whose label `0x432cc0` the suite calls is not the textbook frame at all:

```
0x4329a0  sub  esp, 0x6c
0x4329a3  mov  eax, dword ptr [0x4ad138]     ; /GS cookie
0x4329a8  xor  eax, esp
0x4329aa  mov  dword ptr [esp + 0x68], eax
0x4329ae  push ebp
0x4329af  mov  ebp, dword ptr [esp + 0x74]   ; EBP = the first ARGUMENT, not a frame pointer
...
0x4336b9  mov  ecx, dword ptr [esp + 0x70]
0x4336bd  pop  edi
0x4336be  pop  ebp
0x4336bf  xor  ecx, esp
0x4336c1  call 0x46c932                      ; __security_check_cookie
0x4336c6  add  esp, 0x6c                     ; the frame release
0x4336c9  ret  4
```

`sub esp, 0x6c` and `add esp, 0x6c` are the frame, and the release is **108 bytes**. Two consequences for
the derivation. First, `mov ebp, dword ptr [esp + 0x74]` means EBP here is an argument pointer, so section
100's frame default and section 96's slots are about different things than the frame pointer of a textbook
prologue. Second, the pop run is **not** contiguous with the `ret`: `pop edi`, `pop ebp`, `xor ecx, esp`,
`call __security_check_cookie` and `add esp, 0x6c` all sit between the last pop and `ret 4`, which is why
this row's slots came out zero - the contiguous-run rule section 96 measured cannot see this epilogue.

### 101.3 The prefix sum is measurably the wrong amount

Reserving the prologue's whole net change, `4 * pushes + sub esp - 4 * slots`, at `0x432cc0` gives 176 -
seventeen pushes in the prefix, 108 of subtraction. It does move the wall: the return address survives
(`returnHeld` true, drift 34 -> 7) and `player-frame`, `player-options` and `shot-resource` all leave the
`pc = 0x0` class. But the census over it is the verdict:

```
census-321 -> census-322: 17 passing, flipped [], regressed
  ['enemy-commands', 'th12-aim-angle', 'th12-emitter-origin', 'th12-emitter-values', 'th12-laser-commands'],
  walls moved 16
```

Five regressions against twenty-two passing, so 176 is wrong: the prefix sum counts pushes the prefix itself
pops. The reservation is derived and carried in the map, but the machine leaves it **off** by default.

### 101.4 The amount, probed to the byte

`TH_INTERIOR_STACK_BYTES` overrides the amount, which turns the amount into a measurement instead of a
guess. Reserve nothing, 108 (the epilogue's own release), 120 or 136:

```
none: returnDrift 34  returnHeld false  returnValue 0x0      WRITE/READ past the slot
108:  returnDrift 7   returnHeld true   returnValue 0x7f00000
120:  returnDrift 4   returnHeld true   returnValue 0x7f00000
136:  no unmapped fault at all - the suite leaves this class
```

The drift falls by one word per four bytes, and at **136** it is zero. 136 is `0x6c` (108, the release the
image states) plus 28 bytes, i.e. **7 words** of pushed registers whose pops the entered path executes but
whose pushes it skipped. So the model is confirmed to the byte and only the derivation is missing: the
quantity is the ESP balance **at the label**, which is a property of the path that reaches it, not a sum
over the prefix, and the probe is evidence, not a fix.

### 101.5 What is kept

The plan instrument, the frame rule of section 100, and the derivation of the amount, with the amount off.
The next derivation is the balance at the label - the pops the entered path will execute whose pushes it
skipped, which for this entry is seven words - and the `pc = 0x0` class in the four suites is what it is
for.

node --test archive.test.mjs      pass 1 fail 0   (184 TH11 resources byte-identical)
node --test anm-load-all.mjs      pass 1 fail 0
node --test anm-resource.test.mjs pass 1 fail 0
node replace-site-audit.mjs       0 replace sites in suites name an address the table maps elsewhere
```
## 102. Three static quantities, refuted by measurement, and what is left

### 102.1 The prediction the probe made possible

Section 101 probed the amount `0x432cc0` needs at **136** bytes: drift 7 at 108 (the epilogue's own release,
which the image states), 4 at 120, and zero at 136. That number is a prediction a derivation can be tested
against, and three candidates were computed and compared with it.

```
                        prefix sum   balance at label   forward to ret   probed
0x00432cc0                 176            124               56            136
0x00432a90                 128            124              120            -
0x00434480->0x434380       268            104              104            -
0x0044acd0                   0            -12              -12            -
0x00431bc0                   4             -4                4            -
```

**None of the three is 136.** The prefix sum was already refuted by the census in section 101 (17 passing
against 22, five regressions, because it counts pushes the prefix itself pops). The balance at the label -
the ESP offset where the label starts running, walked from the entry and stopped at the dispatch - says 124,
and the forward walk from the label to the first `ret` says 56. The three quantities disagree with each
other as well as with the probe, which is itself the finding: the two halves of a path are not additive here
because the walks do not follow the path. The label's body branches among thirteen returns, and a linear
sweep either runs into a branch it does not take or stops at a `ret` the path does not reach.

### 102.2 What that rules out

The requirement is not a static prefix quantity, not a static suffix quantity, and not their sum. What the
machine must pre-apply is the ESP the *executed* path leaves in place when the label starts, and for a
jump-table label reached through a chain of conditional exits the executed path is not the byte range. Three
independent static readings of the same image land on three different numbers, so the next instrument cannot
be a better sweep; it has to observe the path.

### 102.3 The instrument that is left, and its acceptance test

The machine already records the executed `pc` sequence for a fault, and the frame plan of section 101 says
where the return address was planted and how far ESP drifted from it. Those two together are a measurement
of the requirement that does not need a static derivation at all: run the interior call once with the
reservation at zero, read `returnDrift` at the fault or at the return, then apply exactly that drift and
require it to be zero. The acceptance test is not the drift - a number the machine tuned to itself is not
evidence - it is that the **return address is still in its slot and the register slots still balance**, and
above all that the **census** moves. That is the next round: a self-calibrating interior frame with a
drift-zero and return-address-held acceptance test, measured against the census like every other change.

### 102.4 Kept, in the final state

The plan instrument, the section 100 frame rule, the derivation of all three quantities with their
provenance recorded in the map (`atLabel`, `prefix`, `forward`, `sub`, `pushes`), and the reservation off by
default. Nothing in this round changes behaviour: the re-census confirms it.

## 103. The return-site repair, a ReferenceError that swallowed it, and what the ring showed

### 103.1 The instrument, and the first measurement that said nothing

Sections 101 and 102 left the requirement as an executed-path property: three static derivations (176, 124, 56)
were refuted by the probed 136, so the machine cannot sweep it. What the machine does know, because it
plants the return address itself, is the invariant the path has to end on: when a `ret` executes, ESP must be
the slot that was planted. The tool now records every `ret` address of the function a label belongs to (there
are thirteen in this one, because its body branches among returns), and `machine.mjs` installs a hook on each
of them for the duration of the call. The hook restores ESP **only when it is not already the slot**, so a
path that is already correct is untouched, and nothing is run twice.

The first measurement of it was **zero**: on and off, `player-frame` failed identically, `returnDrift` 34,
`returnHeld` false. The repair was never firing. The cause was mine: `u`, the Unicorn module namespace, is a
`const` local to `init()`, and `call()` used `u.HOOK_CODE`, which threw a ReferenceError that an empty
`catch{}` swallowed - an instrument that fails silently, which is the same mistake section 296 recorded for
an unguarded diagnostic. The namespace is on the instance as `this.uc`, and a failed hook install is now
recorded in `recent` as `ret-hook-failed` instead of eaten.

### 103.2 The repair fires, and the ring says what is really broken

With the scope fixed, the difference is measurable: `returnDrift` falls from 34 to 2 and ESP from
`0x7efff84` to `0x7efff04`. But the suite still ends at `pc = 0x0`, so the ring was read (`TH_TRACE_EIP`):

```
... 0x46e92b, 0x46e92c, 0x4336c6, 0x4336c9
```

`0x4336c6` is the instruction after `call 0x46c932` (__security_check_cookie) and `0x4336c9` is the `ret 4` -
so the path **did** reach the hooked return. And the slot told the rest: at the fault the word at the planted
slot `0x7effefc` was `0x4336c6`, not the machine's own return address. Under the wrong ESP, that inner call
had written its return address **over** the planted one. Restoring ESP is half the repair; the slot has to be
re-planted, and the machine knows the value.

### 103.3 Re-planting the slot, and what it moved

With both halves restored - the slot and then ESP, only when either is wrong - the class dissolves for
`0x432cc0`: the call returns, and the next fault is an unrelated entry at `0x431070` with `returnDrift` 0.
Measured across the suites that carried this wall:

```
player-frame      0x432cc1 [ebp+0x38] with EBP=0  ->  returns, next wall 0x431070 returnDrift 0
player-options    0x432cc1                        ->  no unmapped fault at all
shot-resource     0x434380                        ->  no unmapped fault at all
player-rendering  0x431bc0 [ebp-4]                ->  0x431c01, and EBP is now a real frame 0x7effef0
enemy-frame       0x454d25                        ->  0x454d25 with EDI = the machine's return address
```

The census over the change is the verdict, and it is in section 103.4.

## 104. The resets that were inside a comment, and an ablation that says the slots are no longer what moves

### 104.1 Four statements in a comment

While reading the machine for this round's ablation, the per-call reset turned out not to exist:

```
// reading of the instruction.this.fault=null;this.recent.length=0;if(this.eipRing)this.eipRing.length=0;++this.calls;
```

Four statements had been appended to the end of a prose comment - probably when the comment above them was
extended - so `fault` was never cleared, `recent` accumulated across every call in the process, and `calls`
was **never incremented**. That is why every fault payload in the last four rounds reported `calls: 0`: the
instrument was printing a counter it never incremented. The statements now have their own line. Nothing about
passing or failing changed, which is what a diagnostics-only defect should look like, and it is recorded
because a reader of those payloads had no way to know.

### 104.2 The repair gets its own list

Section 103's repair pushed its records into `recent`, which is the list the census summarises a wall from -
and one suite's wall was reported as `ret-repair@undefined`. An instrument must not crowd out the reading it
exists to support, so repairs now go to `this.repairs`, are attached to the fault as `fault.repairs`, and
`recent` carries imports again.

### 104.3 Does the return-site repair make section 96's slots redundant?

Section 103 made the interior call end on the planted return address, and `enemy-frame` showed the machine's
own return address (`0x7f00000`) popped into `EDI` - so the slots and the repair overlap, and the question
worth measuring is whether the slots are still doing anything. `TH_INTERIOR_SLOTS=0` ablates exactly that,
leaving the frame rule and the repair in place.

On the eight suites that carried the walls, the ablation changed **almost nothing**: the same entries, the
same addresses (`0x4cecdc0d` at `0x431070`, `0x548be8dd` at `0x45568c`, `0xcb20eae8` at `0x431c01`), the
same three suites with no unmapped fault at all. Over the whole census, the first diff taken against section 103's census reported twelve walls moved and
five suites degrading from a guest-level import reading to a host-level `RuntimeError: memory access out of
bounds`. That attribution was **wrong**, and in the way section 321's lesson warns about: the comparison
crossed the diagnostics fix of section 104.1, so nine of those twelve movements and all five degradeations
belong to the fix and not to the ablation. Taken on the same side of the fix - census-325 (slots on) against
census-325-noslots (slots off) - the ablation moves **three** walls and no pass:

```
slots off:  22 passing, flipped [], regressed [], walls moved 3
  ascii-text        unmapped@0x223f13e0 pc=0x454d25 -> import@undefined pc=0x7e00ce0
  score-popups      unmapped@0x223f13e0 pc=0x454d25 -> import@undefined pc=0x7e00ce0
  player-rendering  unmapped@0xcb20eae0 pc=0x431c01 -> unmapped@0xcb20eae8 pc=0x431c01
```

Both readings in the first two rows are guest-level, and the one with the slots on names the instruction that
faulted, so it is the more useful of the two; the third differs only by eight bytes of the address it reads.
The larger finding is the one the correction exposed: the nine walls the **fix** moved mean section 103's
census was, for those nine suites, reporting a stale reading - `recent` had accumulated across calls in the
process and `fault` was never cleared, so the wall those suites were recorded as hitting was not always the
one they hit. With no pass to gain either way, the default stays on, and the switch is kept so the question
can be asked again rather than assumed.

## 105. The epilogue is not a contiguous run of pops, and the sentinel stopped leaking

### 105.1 The defect the reading showed

`enemy-frame` failed at `0x454d25` with `EDI = 0x7f00000` - the value the machine plants as a return address.
A guest register holding the harness's own sentinel is a 1:1 fidelity defect, not a wall: the real prologue
would have pushed that register with its own value, so the value the epilogue pops back must be the guest's,
never the harness's. Section 101.2 had already read the reason off the image, in the /GS epilogue:

```
0x4336b9  mov  ecx, dword ptr [esp + 0x70]
0x4336bd  pop  edi
0x4336be  pop  ebp
0x4336bf  xor  ecx, esp
0x4336c1  call 0x46c932                      ; __security_check_cookie
0x4336c6  add  esp, 0x6c
0x4336c9  ret  4
```

The pops are **not** contiguous with the return - the cookie check and the frame release sit between them -
so section 96's rule, which counted the contiguous run immediately before the `ret`, reported **zero slots**
for this row. With too few slots pushed, the epilogue popped the machine's planted return address instead.

### 105.2 The rule, corrected to walk the epilogue

`epilogue_pops` walks **back** from the last `ret`, collecting pops and skipping the instructions that belong
to the epilogue without touching the register stack - the frame release (`add`/`sub`/`lea esp`), the cookie
check (`call`, `xor`, `mov`, `cmp`) - and stopping at anything that ends the path: a `push`, another `ret`, or
a branch, because a function's earlier returns belong to paths this label does not take. The old count is kept
in the map as `contiguous`, so the difference is visible rather than asserted: **45 of 87** rows changed, for
example

```
0x00407220  contiguous 1 -> 4   edi esi ebp ebx
0x00408d00  contiguous 0 -> 4   edi esi ebp ebx
0x00409700  contiguous 0 -> 6   ecx edi esi ecx edi esi
0x0040ae90  contiguous 1 -> 5   edi esi ebp ebx ebp
```

### 105.3 Measured

Three suites shared the `0x454d25` wall, and two of them stopped hitting memory faults altogether:

```
enemy-frame     unmapped@0x454d25 with EDI=0x7f00000  ->  unmapped@0x130 pc=0x4615cc with EDI=0x0
ascii-text      unmapped@0x223f13e0 pc=0x454d25       ->  no unmapped fault at all
score-popups    unmapped@0x223f13e0 pc=0x454d25       ->  no unmapped fault at all
```

`enemy-frame` no longer shows the harness value in a guest register, and the two suites that shared the site
leave the class. The census over the whole rule is the verdict:

```
census-325 -> census-326: 22 passing, flipped [], regressed [], walls moved 4
  ascii-text.test.mjs    unmapped@0x223f13e0 pc=0x454d25 -> import@undefined pc=0x7e00ce0
  enemy-frame.test.mjs   unmapped@0x0 pc=0x454d25 -> unmapped@0x130 pc=0x4615cc
  enemy-movement.test.mjs unmapped@0xdc pc=0x4615dd -> unmapped@0x130 pc=0x4615cc
  score-popups.test.mjs  unmapped@0x223f13e0 pc=0x454d25 -> import@undefined pc=0x7e00ce0
```

## 106. The sentinel leak as a metric, and a metric that can be gamed

### 106.1 From a story to a check

Section 105 fixed a case where an epilogue popped the machine's planted return address into a guest
register, because too few slots had been pushed. That is one instance of a property the 1:1 claim needs as a
**check** rather than as a story: a register left holding the harness's sentinel means the guest was handed a
value the original never had. `scanSentinel` now runs at the end of every call and at every fault, and reports
which registers hold `0x7f00000` and at which `pc`. A leak in the **stack** is not one - the machine planted
the value there on purpose - so only the guest's registers are scanned. Under `TH_SENTINEL_REPORT` the
machine prints a per-process line at teardown:

```
sentinel-leaks <count> interior-applied <n> framed <n> repaired <n> samples <pc register> | ...
```

Measured on three suites:

```
player-frame      sentinel-leaks 5  interior-applied 2  framed 1  repaired 3   samples 0x7f00000 EDI | 0x7f00000 ESI EBP | 0x431070 ESI EBP
player-rendering  sentinel-leaks 1  interior-applied 2  framed 1  repaired 3   samples 0x7f00000 EDI
enemy-frame       sentinel-leaks 0  interior-applied 1  framed 1  repaired 0
```

### 106.2 The walk correction, and the count that went the wrong way

Section 105's walk gave `0x432cc0` the saves `esi ebx edi ebp esi ebx edi ebp` - the same four registers
twice, because the walk skipped every `ret` and so crossed into the pops of a **second** return path. The
walk now stops at the second `ret`, and the row becomes four slots instead of eight. The five rows that still
carry a duplicate pair are recorded in the map's `saves` rather than hidden, and they are the next thing to
look at.

The leak count then went **up**, not down: three before the correction, five after. That is worth stating
plainly, because it is evidence about the instrument and not about the fix. With eight slots pushed, the
epilogue's pops read words **above** the region where the sentinel sits, so the sentinel stops appearing in a
register - while the values the guest receives are still wrong, because the machine only ever had the current
registers to push. **A larger slot count can lower the leak count without improving fidelity.** The metric is
a floor on the defect, not a measure of correctness, and it must be read next to the census.

```

## 107. Attributing the leak, and refusing to hand the sentinel on

### 107.1 The leak now names its call

Section 106's metric said three registers in `player-frame` held the sentinel but not which call put them
there. `scanSentinel` now records the calling address as well - `this.currentCall` is set on entry to `call` -
and the samples read `call-register-pair`:

```
player-frame      0x44acd0->0x7f00000 EDI | 0x432cc0->0x7f00000 ESI EBP | 0x431070->0x431070 ESI EBP
player-motion     0x44acd0->0x7f00000 EDI | 0x455a00->0x45568c EDI
player-rendering  0x44acd0->0x7f00000 EDI
```

The first entry is the same in all three suites: **`0x44acd0` leaves EDI holding the sentinel**. That is the
origin, and the rest are downstream of it.

### 107.2 Why the origin is not a slot miscount, and why slots cannot fix it

`0x44acd0`'s row is `slots=3` (`edi esi ebx`), `contiguous=3`, entry `0x44aca0`, and the function holds **six**
returns. Its tail reads

```
0x44ae89  fstp dword ptr [esp]
0x44ae8c  push ecx
0x44ae8d  push 0xd
0x44ae8f  call 0x4273f0
0x44ae94  pop edi
0x44ae95  pop esi
0x44ae96  pop ebx
0x44ae97  ret
```

The three slots the machine pushes match the last `ret`'s path, but which of the six returns the entry takes
is a property of the **executed path**, which sections 101-103 already established cannot be read off the
image. So the machine cannot supply the register's true value here - what it can do is stop handing the guest
the harness's value.

### 107.3 Containment, and its measurement

`slotValue` refuses that substitution: a register equal to the planted return address is pushed as **zero**
instead - a guest's absence rather than a harness address - and every scrub is counted and printed as
`scrubbed N`, so the substitution is visible rather than silent. The slots are pushed with the registers'
current values, so without this the sentinel travels down the call chain and one origin leak becomes many:

```
                       before   after
player-frame           5        3        scrubbed 1
player-rendering       1        1        scrubbed 0
player-motion          2        2        scrubbed 0
enemy-frame            0        0        scrubbed 0
```

The propagation is gone (`player-frame`'s ESI entry disappeared) and the origin remains, correctly attributed.

```

## 108. The register half of the return-site repair

### 108.1 From containment to repair

Section 107 could only refuse to hand the sentinel on: `slotValue` substitutes zero, which stops the leak
travelling but does not give the guest the value it should have had. The machine does know that value,
though. The slots it pushes are the registers' own values at the call - the caller's values - and a correct
pop of that slot produces exactly that value. So when a hook fires at a `ret` and a register is found holding
the **sentinel**, the register is restored to the value this call supplied for it. The sentinel is never a
legitimate guest value, so the write is targeted: a register the path changed to anything else is left alone,
and the value used is the one already in the supplied slot rather than a substitute.

This is the same repair as section 103's, one register wider: section 103 restores ESP and the planted slot,
because under the wrong ESP the path writes over the slot; section 108 restores the registers, because under
the wrong ESP the pops read the sentinel. Both come from the same fact - which of a function's returns the
entry takes is an executed property that sections 101-103 showed cannot be read off the image.

### 108.2 Measured

```
                       leaks before   leaks after   restored   repaired
player-frame           3              0             2          3
player-rendering       1              0             1          3
player-motion          2              0             1          2
enemy-frame            0              0             0          0
```

Every leak attributed in section 107 is gone, including the origin `0x44acd0 -> EDI` that appeared in three
suites, and `scrubbed 0` on all four: the values used are the slots' own, not the zero substitute of section
107, which is why the containment still exists but is no longer needed on these paths.

### 109.1 The report was discarded, not absent

Section 106's per-process line is printed by the machine's `close`, and running a few suites by hand showed it
working. A census with `TH_SENTINEL_REPORT` set reported **nothing**, which looked like an environment
problem and was not: the census runner captures each suite's stdout with `spawnSync` and only parsed the
`pass`/`fail` counts, so the line was read and thrown away. The runner now takes `--leaks`, asks the machine
for the line per suite with the environment it sets itself, and aggregates what it captures. An instrument
whose output is discarded looks exactly like an instrument with nothing to say, and that is worth the sentence
it takes to record.

## 110. The verdict table is a committed artifact that a filtered run cannot take over

### 110.1 The overwrite that was not noticed

The census writes a JSON table - every suite, its pass/fail counts, and the wall it stopped at - and that
table is what a round's verdict is read from. It was written into `tools/tmp/`, which is gitignored, and it
had a single output path. So when this round began by running the census with `--filter game-resources` to
check the promoted runner, that one-row run **replaced the whole corpus table**, and the next reader of the
file would have been reading a verdict about one suite while believing it was the corpus. Nothing failed and
nothing warned: the file was there, it parsed, and it was wrong.

The output path now follows what ran. A full run writes `docs/porting/census-th12.json`, which is **committed**;
a filtered or limited run writes `docs/porting/census-th12-filtered.json`; `--out` names a file explicitly.
A verdict that cannot be reproduced from the repository is not evidence, and a verdict a subroutine can
silently narrow is worse than one that does not exist, because it looks like one.

## 111. The walls classified, so the next target is chosen by evidence

### 111.1 What the committed table says

The verdict table committed in section 110 carries, for every trapping suite, where it stopped, the address it
touched and the pc of the instruction. `tools/th-wall-classes.py` reads that table and groups those addresses,
because the class of an address is a next step and a suite name is not:

```
null-base      47 suites   an unmapped read at a small absolute address: a zero base plus a struct offset
garbage-base   14 suites   an unmapped access at an address that is not a plausible offset, so a register
                           holds something that is not a pointer at all
import-stub     6 suites   the suite reached an unimplemented host import
```

Two thirds of the walls are one class. The four most frequent sites are shared:

```
null-base   pc=0x454ee1 x4   bullet-manager, enemy-callbacks-bullet, laser-infinite, laser-line
null-base   pc=0x4067e0 x3   anm-scripts, shot-damage, shot-manager
null-base   pc=0x4615cc x3   enemy-frame, enemy-movement, hud-text
null-base   pc=0x405032 x3   stage-draw, stage-passes, stage-runtime
garbage     pc=0x45568c x2   anm-geometry, player-motion
import      pc=0x7e00ce0 x3  ascii-text, enemy-animations, score-popups
```

### 111.2 The shared site read directly

`0x454ee1` was taken as the largest shared site and the machine's payload read for `bullet-manager`:

```
address 0x11c   pc 0x454ee1   ECX 0x0   EBP 0x2d93400   EDI 0xffffffff
entry 0x40a250  calls 18   returnDrift -10   returnHeld true
framePlan {slots 0, args 5, ebp 0x0}
```

A null base plus `0x11c`, with the entry's row supplying no slots and no frame, and a **ten word** drift at the
wall: this is the executed-path class of sections 101-103 again - the entry takes a path the row's slots do not
describe - rather than a defect that can be repaired from the address alone. It is recorded as the class it
is, and it is why the null-base class is worth reading site by site rather than counted.

### 111.3 An instrument gap this exposed, recorded rather than worked around

The classifier's `entry` and `calls` columns are **`None` for every row**. The census runner reads them from
`trap.target.entry`, and the trap payloads no longer nest them there, so two columns of the verdict have been
empty since the payload shape changed. The classification above does not depend on them, which is why it could
be finished; the columns themselves are a wrong reading that the next round has to repair or remove.

## 112. The verdict's two stale columns get a source that exists

### 112.1 What the trap artifact actually holds

Section 111.3 recorded that `entry` and `calls` were `None` for every row of the verdict, and that the runner
read them from `trap.target.entry`. Reading one artifact directly shows why that could never work:

```
top-level keys   target, error, errorFields, trap, recent, apiMisses, stubStats
target           game, version, language, executable, sha256, size, imageBase, evidence, ...
trap             (no keys at all)
recent[-1]       at, type, address, size, pc
```

`target` is the **title metadata**, `trap` is empty, and a `recent` entry carries the wall and nothing else -
so those two columns had no source in that file at any point after the payload shape changed. The repair is
therefore a reading of something that exists: the wrapper prints a payload that does carry both, the runner
already captures that output, and it simply never looked at it.

### 112.2 The repair, and that it reads what section 111 read by hand

Both columns are parsed from the captured payload, and are `null` when a suite never reaches a call, rather
than zero. On `bullet-manager`:

```
entry 0x40a250   calls 18
```

which is exactly what section 111.2 read by hand out of the same payload. The columns are not a new
instrument: they are the same reading, taken where it is written instead of where it is not.

## 113. A gap that was my own reading, and the audit that refuted it

### 113.1 The claim

Section 112's repaired `entry` column made it possible to rank targets by the entry a suite reaches, and the
first thing done with it was a scratch script that compared those entries against the oracle map. It reported
**27 of 60 entries called but not in the map**, with `0x455a00` (four suites) at the top, which reads as a gap
in the interior machinery worth one round of work.

### 113.2 Why that number was wrong

The scratch script built its set of mapped addresses like this:

```
{key.lower().replace('0x00', '0x') for key in oracle}
```

`0x00401670`.replace(`0x00`, `0x`) is `0x401670` - **seven** hex digits - while the verdict writes `0x00401670`
with eight, so the two sets never intersect and every mapped row was counted as missing. The claim was an
artifact of one line of my own string handling, and it is recorded because the number was plausible, was
quoted, and would have sent a round after something that does not exist.

### 113.3 The audit that asks the tool's own criteria

`tools/th-interior-calls.py --audit` answers the question where the answer exists: against the row set the
tool itself writes, and using the two filters it already applies - an address that is a **direct-call target**
is a real entry (entering it runs its own prologue, so no row is needed), and an address **below every known
entry** cannot be given one. Everything else is a row that should exist and does not.

```
suite-called addresses:                     89
covered by a row:                           87
real entries (no row needed):                2      0x00428270 (laser-probe-cancel), 0x004489e0 (screen-fade, screen-shake)
below every known entry (no row possible):   0
SHOULD have a row and does not:              0
```

**The map has no gap.** The addresses the first script called missing are covered rows; the two that are not
covered are real entries, which is the correct state for them.

### 113.4 The keepers

```

node --test archive.test.mjs      pass 1 fail 0   (184 TH11 resources byte-identical)
node --test anm-load-all.mjs      pass 1 fail 0
node --test anm-resource.test.mjs pass 1 fail 0
node replace-site-audit.mjs       0 replace sites in suites name an address the table maps elsewhere
py -3 tools/th-interior-calls.py --audit    the coverage above
```

The census did not run: no machine behaviour and no row changed, so section 112's verdict stands.
## 114. The round that produced no record, and why

### 114.1 The truncation

Round 335 was to be a check of the evidence chain. Its script ended like this:

```
io.open(PLAN, 'wb').write(plan.rstrip(b'\r\n') + b'\n' + SECTION.rstrip(b'\n').encode('utf-8'))
```

`SECTION` is a **str**, so `.rstrip(b'\n')` raised `TypeError` - but evaluation order is not left to right
across the whole expression: `io.open(PLAN, 'wb')` runs **first**, and opening for write **truncates**. So the
plan was emptied, the write never happened, and the script died with a traceback that pointed at a string
method. The check that followed printed `plan: 0 bytes, sections 0`.

### 114.2 The recovery, and what it shows

The content was committed at HEAD, so nothing was lost:

```
before restore   0 bytes
after  restore   443838 bytes, CRLF 303, 113 sections, byte-identical to HEAD
```

`git restore --source=HEAD -- docs/porting/porting-plan.md` restored it, and the comparison in 114.3 confirms
the file is exactly what section 113 committed. The lesson is about how a record is written, not about what it
said: **build the bytes first, then open the file**, because a `write()` whose argument can raise is a file
that can be destroyed by an error that has nothing to do with the file. This script does that now, and prints
the size after the write rather than assuming it.

### 114.3 The state the incident left

```
HEAD                        8573242   (section 113, unchanged by round 335)
porting-plan.md             443838 bytes, CRLF 303, 113 sections
census-th12.json            ran 142, passing 22, trapping 67, leaks {"reported": 107, "total": 0, "scrubbed": 0}
tracked instruments         committed, no pending edits
```

### 114.4 A field that was misread in the round that was not recorded

The unrecorded round also intended to claim that `verifiedAtHead` named a stale commit. It does not name a
commit at all: the field is the **browser probe snapshot** taken when the record was last verified, holding
`error`, `framesThisRun`, `pageErrors`, `phase`, `stage` and `th12`. The claim would have been false, which is
why it is worth one paragraph now instead of a silent correction later.

  garbage-base 14, import-stub 6 (section 111).

  class: a null base plus `0x11c`, `framePlan` with slots 0 and args 5, and a ten word drift at the wall. The
  next target is a null-base site whose entry row is **short**, read the same way - payload first, then the row

- The interior map needs no repair (section 113): 89 suite-called addresses, 87 covered, 2 real entries.
- `GameResources::read`, the port-side gap behind the `ascii ANM` assertions, lives in `cpp/game/`, which the

## 115. The null-base shortlist, and the short row at the top of it

### 115.1 Why a shortlist rather than a site

Section 114.5 named the next target as a null-base site whose entry row is **short** - "slots = the epilogue
pops", so a row with too few of them describes a path the entry may not take. `tools/th-null-base-targets.py`
builds that list by joining the committed verdict's trapping rows to the oracle map on the address the suite
reached, and it does two things the earlier scratch script did not:

- it compares addresses as **integers**, never as strings, because section 113's false gap of 27 was one
  normalization of `0x00401670` against another;
- it quotes the row's `slots`, `reserve` and `saves` from the map instead of remembering them, so a short row
  is visible before a round is spent on it.

## 116. The short row read at the site, and a drift number that had to be read carefully

### 116.1 The payload

Section 115.2 named `pc=0x415518` at `addr=0x4` over two suites, reached through entry `0x004154d0` with a row
that supplies **no slots** and a prologue reserve of 32 bytes. Both suites were run and their payloads are
identical:

```
type 19 read unmapped    address 0x4    pc 0x415518
entry 0x4154d0           calls 7         returnDrift -202    returnHeld true
regs  EAX 0x7effeec  EBX 0x200404c  ECX 0x200404c  EDX 0x0  ESI 0x0  EDI 0x0  EBP 0x7effef8
framePlan  returnSlot 0x7effefc  slots 0  args 0  esp 0x7effefc  ebp 0x0
```

The read is four bytes of `[reg+4]` with `reg` zero, and the zero registers are `EDX`, `ESI` and `EDI`
(`EAX` and `EBP` hold stack addresses, `EBX`/`ECX` a heap address). The machine supplied **no arguments and no
slots**: `args 0` is what the suite passed, `slots 0` is what the row says.

### 116.2 The drift that is not evidence of a mis-supplied frame

`returnDrift -202` reads like a catastrophic stack error and is not one. It is measured against **this call's**
return slot, while the guest is deep inside its own nested calls - guest `call`s push their own frames - so a
large negative drift at an interior site is expected and says nothing about the row. Reading it as damage would
have repeated section 111.2's mistake in the other direction: the number has to be read with the call depth it
was taken at, exactly as the sentinel figure had to be read with its substitution count.

### 116.3 What the row leaves unapplied

The row knows the entry's prologue changes ESP by `reserve 32`, and the machine does not apply it: the
reservation machinery is **off by default**, because round 322 measured that turning it on for every row
regressed the census (the prefix-sum reading of 176 slots) and the switch was left off. So at this label the
entered code runs with ESP 32 bytes away from where the real path would have it, and any `[esp+disp]` the body
reads is shifted by eight words. Whether that is what makes `EDX`/`ESI`/`EDI` zero here is **not** established
by this payload; what is established is that the two candidates worth measuring are the missing argument frame
and this unapplied reserve, and that a selective switch - reserve where a row has `reserve>0` and `slots==0` -
can be measured against the census instead of against a reading.

### 116.4 The keepers

```

node --test archive.test.mjs      pass 1 fail 0   (184 TH11 resources byte-identical)
node --test anm-load-all.mjs      pass 1 fail 0
node --test anm-resource.test.mjs pass 1 fail 0
node replace-site-audit.mjs       0 replace sites in suites name an address the table maps elsewhere
```

The census did not run: no machine behaviour and no row changed, so section 112's verdict stands at
22 of 142 passing, 67 trapping, leaks {"reported": 107, "total": 0, "scrubbed": 0}.
## 117. The selective reserve, measured and refuted

### 117.1 The change

Section 116.3 named the experiment: reserve the prologue's net ESP where a row has a positive `reserve` and
supplies **no slots**, because such a row reconstructs no frame at all. It was implemented in `machine.mjs` as
the default for that selector, with `TH_INTERIOR_STACK=0` still killing the whole mechanism and
`TH_INTERIOR_STACK_BYTES` still probing an amount. This is a **different selector** from the one section 322
refuted - that was the reserve ON for every row - so it had to be measured rather than assumed.

### 117.2 It reached the code path, which had to be shown

At `pc=0x415518` the row's plan moved as the arithmetic predicts:

```
framePlan.esp  0x7effefc -> 0x7effedc   (-32, exactly the row's reserve)
returnDrift    -202      -> -210        (-8 words, consistent)
```

An instrument that reports nothing is indistinguishable from one that does nothing, so this is the part that
had to be checked before the census meant anything: the switch reached the site.

### 117.3 The site did not move

The wall at `0x415518` is **unchanged**: same unmapped read of `[reg+4]` at address `0x4`, same zero
registers `EDX`, `ESI`, `EDI`. So the unapplied reserve is **not** what makes the base register null there.
That is one of section 116.3's two candidates refuted by measurement, and it was the cheap one to refute.

### 117.4 The census refuted the selector

Full corpus run with the selector on, against the committed baseline:

```
                     baseline (HEAD)     selector on
ran                  142                 142
passing              22                  17          <- five regressed
trapping             67                  73
sentinel leaks       0 over 107 procs    2 over 106 procs
walls moved                              anm-resource   none -> 0x415518
                                         archive        none -> 0x415518
                                         enemy-animations 0x7e00ce0 -> 0x3f800000
regressed     enemy-commands, th12-aim-angle, th12-emitter-origin, th12-emitter-values, th12-laser-commands
```

Two suites that had **no wall at all** trap at `0x415518` under the selector, and the sentinel leak count
rises from 0 to 2 while one process stops reporting. Section 322's conclusion therefore holds for a **second,
narrower selector**: the prologue's net ESP is not the frame the entered path needs, in this shape either.

### 117.5 Reverted, and kept

The change is reverted: `machine.mjs` is restored byte-identical to HEAD, `TH_INTERIOR_STACK` is off by
default again, and the canonical verdict `docs/porting/census-th12.json` is restored to the committed run at
22 passing / 67 trapping / 0 leaks. The experimental run is **committed** as
`docs/porting/census-th12-reserve-selector.json`, so the refutation is checkable by the next reader rather
than narrated by this one.

### 117.6 What is left of the site

Of section 116.3's two candidates, the reserve is refuted here; the remaining one is the **absent argument
frame** - the payload shows `args 0`, which is what the suite passed, while the label's body reads
`[reg+4]` with `reg` null. So the next question is not about the machine's arithmetic but about the **call**:
whether an interior label of that shape is a place a caller can legitimately enter with no frame, and what the
original path has in the register at `pc=0x415518`. That is a question the image can answer at the call site,
and the next round should read `0x4154d0` to `0x415518` in the original rather than change the machine again.

### 117.7 The keepers

```

node --test archive.test.mjs      pass 1 fail 0   (184 TH11 resources byte-identical)
node --test anm-load-all.mjs      pass 1 fail 0
node --test anm-resource.test.mjs pass 1 fail 0
node replace-site-audit.mjs       0 replace sites in suites name an address the table maps elsewhere
```
## 118. The label is a function, and the wall is a register argument

### 118.1 The image at the label

Section 117.6 said the next question was the **call**, not the arithmetic, and that the image should be read
before the machine was changed again. It was:

```
0x004154d0  push ebp          mov ebp, esp        and esp, 0xfffffff8
            push -1           push 0x4976ce       mov eax, fs:[0]      push eax
            sub esp, 0x308    mov eax, [0x4ad138] xor eax, esp        mov [esp+0x300], eax
            push ebx          push esi            push edi
0x00415518  mov eax, [esi + 4]            <- ESI = 0 gives address 0x4, the wall
0x0041551b  mov edi, [eax + 4]
0x0041551e  movzx eax, word ptr [edi + 4]
```

`0x004154d0` is a **function start**, not an interior label: SEH frame, `/GS` cookie, the standard
`push ebp / mov ebp,esp / and esp,-8`, then `push ebx / push esi / push edi`. The wall is
`mov eax, [esi+4]` with `ESI` zero.

### 118.2 This corrects a claim section 113 made

Section 113 reported the interior map had **no gap** because 87 of 89 suite-called addresses were *covered by a
row* and the other 2 were real entries. That was a statement about the tool's two filters, and the filters
cannot see this case: `0x004154d0` has a **row in the map**, while the image says it is a function. The row
exists because the tool's rule for "real entry" is *a direct `E8` target*, and this entry is reached
**indirectly** - by a call through a pointer or table - so it is neither a direct-call target nor below every
known entry, and the tool classified it as interior. Its row's facts come from the **wrong enclosing entry**
(the `reserve 32` is the neighbouring function's prologue, while this one subtracts `0x308`).

**So "covered" is not "correct".** Section 113's audit answered the question it asked - is any row missing -
and the answer to *that* still stands. It does not establish that every address with a row is an interior
label, and for this address it is not.

### 118.3 What the machine can and cannot supply

`machine.mjs` line 118:

```
call(address, {ecx = 0, edx = 0, args = [], limit = 10_000_000} = {})
```

Arguments can be passed in `ECX`, `EDX` and on the stack. They **cannot** be passed in `ESI` (or `EDI`,
`EBX`), and the interior-entry machinery has no notion of a register argument at all - section 108 supplies a
**return** value for a register at a hooked `ret`, which is a different thing from supplying an argument on the
way in. Both suites call only `touch(0x412e30)` with `{ecx: q}`; neither calls `0x4154d0`, so the machine
reached it from inside the guest, and there `ESI` was zero.

### 118.4 What that leaves

The missing quantity is the **caller's register state at the entry**, which is a property of the path taken to
the call, not of the address - the same distinction sections 101 to 103 drew for the stack. So the next step is
still a read, not an edit: find the **indirect call site** that reaches `0x004154d0` in the image (a
`call [table+n]` or a jump table entry), and read what it loads into `ESI` before the call. Only then can a
register supply be added to `call()` with a defensible value instead of a guess - and the shape of that
addition is already known to be safe when it is optional, because `ecx` and `edx` default to 0 today.

### 118.5 The keepers

```
node --test th12-rng.test.mjs     pass 2 fail 0
node --test archive.test.mjs      pass 1 fail 0   (184 TH11 resources byte-identical)
node --test anm-load-all.mjs      pass 1 fail 0
node --test anm-resource.test.mjs pass 1 fail 0
node replace-site-audit.mjs       0 replace sites in suites name an address the table maps elsewhere
```

The census did not run: no machine behaviour and no row changed, so section 112's verdict stands at 22 of 142
passing, 67 trapping, 0 sentinel leaks.
## 119. A dispatcher with no reference in the image, and register arguments that are provably inert

### 119.1 The thunk, from the shipped file

```
0x004154c0  add ecx, 0x1040
0x004154c6  jmp 0x4154d0
0x004154cb  int3    int3    int3    int3    int3
0x004154d0  push ebp          <- the dispatcher's own SEH + /GS prologue
```

The `int3` run is the compiler's own padding between two functions, so `0x004154c0` is a **thunk** and
`0x004154d0` is a **separate function**: EnemyInf's slot 0 dispatcher. The thunk states the convention the
dispatcher's body depends on - it adds `0x1040` to `ECX` and jumps - and the body reads its object from
**`ESI`** (`mov eax,[esi+4]` at `0x415518`).

### 119.2 The address appears nowhere in the image

Scanned three ways over the whole file:

```
little-endian dword 0x004154d0 anywhere       0 occurrences
immediate operand equal to 0x004154d0 in .text 0 instructions
relative jmp landing on 0x4154c0 or 0x4154d0   0 sites
```

So neither the dispatcher nor its thunk is called or jumped to by anything in the shipped binary. Section 118
had already found this the other way round, by the tool's filters; this is the direct reading, and it agrees
with the finding round 150 recorded at runtime - that `0x4154c0` and `0x4154d0` have **zero direct callers** -
which means the address is reached only through a **pointer computed at runtime** (a vtable or a checkpoint
table), not through any constant the file contains.

### 119.3 What the payload's entry field is

Section 112 warned that the runner's `entry` column had been read from `trap.target.entry`, which is title
metadata. The payload's own field is not that:

```
machine.mjs:246    this.fault.calls=this.calls; this.fault.entry=hex(address); ...
```

`entry` there is the **address passed to `call()`**. So a call with the target `0x004154d0` really happened -
and since the shipped image contains no such call, the target came from **outside the image**, which is the
harness's checkpoint tables. That is where the next read belongs, and it is why no suite's text names the
address: the pointer is built rather than written.

### 119.4 The capability added

```
call(address, {ecx = 0, edx = 0, esi = null, edi = null, ebx = null, args = [], limit = ...} = {})
```

`ESI`, `EDI` and `EBX` can now be supplied as arguments, and each is written **only when supplied**, so no
existing caller can change behaviour: the registers are callee-saved in the image and the emulated function's
own pushes and pops restore them. The dispatcher reads its object from `ESI`, so a suite that has to enter it
the way the real caller does needs exactly this.

### 119.5 Inertness, shown twice

At `pc=0x415518` in both suites the payload is **byte-identical** to section 116's reading - same `[esi+4]`,
same `ESI=0`, `returnDrift -202`, `framePlan.esp 0x7effefc`.

And the full corpus, against the committed baseline:

```
                baseline (HEAD)      with register arguments
ran             142                  142
passing         22                   22          <- 0 flipped
trapping        67                   67          <- 0 regressed
sentinel leaks  0 over 107 procs     0 over 107 procs
walls moved     0
```

**Liveness is not yet shown.** The inertness proof says the supply cannot change anything that does not ask
for it; it does not say that supplying `esi` reaches the code and moves the wall. That demonstration is one
suite call away - pass the enemy pointer in `esi` on the `0x4154d0` path and read the wall again - and it is
named here as the next step rather than implied by the code.

### 119.6 The keepers

```

node --test archive.test.mjs      pass 1 fail 0   (184 TH11 resources byte-identical)
node --test anm-load-all.mjs      pass 1 fail 0
node --test anm-resource.test.mjs pass 1 fail 0
node replace-site-audit.mjs       0 replace sites in suites name an address the table maps elsewhere
```
## 120. The ring was dead, and the caller of the dispatcher is the harness

### 120.1 An instrument that recorded nothing

Section 118.4 asked for the indirect call site that reaches `0x004154d0`, and the trace existed all along - it
is recorded at every executed instruction into `this.eipRing` and attached to the fault. Two things stopped it
from ever being read:

- it is reset to length 0 at the start of **every** call (`if(this.eipRing)this.eipRing.length=0`), so it only
  ever holds the instructions of the call being executed;
- the artifact the suites write carried `recent`, `trap` and `errorFields`, and **not** the fault, so the ring
  was dropped on every trap. `errorFields` was empty because it serialises the fields of the thrown error
  object, which are primitives - nothing.

The second is the one that mattered: an instrument whose output is discarded is indistinguishable from one
with nothing to say, and this one had been discarded since it was written. `helpers.mjs` now writes `fault`
and `eipRing` into `trap-*.json`.

### 120.2 The switch, and my own two mistakes

The ring is populated only when `ringSize > 0`, from `TH_TRACE_EIP`. Two of my own errors are recorded here
because both produced a plausible-looking "no evidence" answer:

- I set **`TH_EIP_RING`**, which nothing reads, and read the empty ring as absence;
- my one-liner printed `absent` for a present-but-empty list, because an empty list is falsy in Python. The
  second mistake turned "the ring is empty" into "the field is missing", which is a different finding.

With `TH_TRACE_EIP=400` and the artifact carrying the ring, the trace appears - and it is 22 entries long
whatever the requested size, which is 120.1's first fact showing up as a measurement.

### 120.3 What the trace says

```
0x4154d0 ecx=0x200404c edx=0x0 eax=0x0     <- first instruction of the faulting call
0x4154d1 ... 0x4154fa                       <- the dispatcher's own SEH + /GS prologue
0x415500 eax=0xbb40e64e
0x415502 eax=0xbcaf1d96
0x41550a eax=0x7effeec
0x415512 eax=0x7effeec
0x415518                                     <- the wall
```

The ring is reset per call, so its **first entry is the address the machine was called at**. That address is
`0x4154d0`. If the guest had reached the dispatcher by jumping into it from the thunk - which is how the image
says the game reaches it - the ring would begin with the enclosing function's instructions and contain the
jump. It does not. **The call came from outside the image: the harness.** The state it arrived with is
`ECX=0x200404c`, `EDX=0`, and `ESI=0` (the ring records ECX, EDX and EAX only; ESI is in the payload), while
the dispatcher's body reads its object from `ESI`.

### 120.4 What follows

The image states the convention - the thunk `0x4154c0` is `add ecx,0x1040 ; jmp 0x4154d0`, and the body reads
`[esi+4]` - and section 119 added optional `ESI`, `EDI` and `EBX` arguments for exactly this. The next step is
the one section 119.5 named and did not yet do: **supply the enemy pointer in `esi` where the harness calls
`0x4154d0` and read the wall again.** The trace now makes the effect visible instead of inferred, because the
artifact carries the ring.

### 120.5 Inertness of the instrument changes

```
census with the artifact fields and the env-gated prints: ran 142, passing 22, trapping 67,
                                                         0 sentinel leaks over 107 reporting processes
```

The machine changes are env-gated console output on the fault path and in `close()`; the fault-path print did
**not** fire in the path observed here (the fault object is built elsewhere), so it is recorded as unproven
rather than as working. The artifact change adds two fields and alters no assertion.

### 120.6 The keepers

```
node --test th12-rng.test.mjs     pass 2 fail 0
node --test archive.test.mjs      pass 1 fail 0   (184 TH11 resources byte-identical)
node --test anm-load-all.mjs      pass 1 fail 0
node --test anm-resource.test.mjs pass 1 fail 0
node replace-site-audit.mjs       0 replace sites in suites name an address the table maps elsewhere
```
## 121. The caller named, and ESI derived from ECX

### 121.1 The call trace

Section 120.3 concluded from the instruction ring that the call to `0x004154d0` came "from outside the image:
the harness". That was half right and its reasoning was wrong: the ring is reset per call and its first entry
names the **target**, which cannot distinguish a caller. A JavaScript stack can, and `TH_CALL_TRACE` now prints
it for every call:

```
CALLTRACE 0x46ea5c <- machine.mjs:124 <- helpers.mjs:200 <- oracle
CALLTRACE 0x47562a <- ...            <- oracle
CALLTRACE 0x47b31d <- ...            <- oracle
CALLTRACE 0x47b07b <- ...            <- oracle
CALLTRACE 0x47af44 <- ...            <- oracle
CALLTRACE 0x472d44 <- ...            <- oracle
CALLTRACE 0x4154d0 <- machine.mjs:124 <- helpers.mjs:200 <- TestContext.<anonymous>
```

The seventh call is the one at the wall, and its caller is the **test itself**. `touch()` translates a **th11**
fixture address into the **th12** address of the counterpart function, and the th11 command dispatcher's
counterpart in th12 is `0x004154d0`. So the address was never written in the image because it is **computed by
the translation tables** - which is what section 119.2 measured and this explains.

### 121.2 The image derives ESI, it does not receive it

```
0x00415510  mov ebx, ecx                 <- EBX := ECX, the caller's argument
0x00415512  mov esi, [ebx + 0x174c]      <- ESI := [ECX + 0x174c]
0x00415518  mov eax, [esi + 4]           <- the wall
0x0041551b  mov edi, [eax + 4]
```

**ESI is not an argument.** It is loaded from the caller's object at `+0x174c`, exactly as the thunk's
`add ecx, 0x1040` implies a structured base. Section 118's statement that "the dispatcher reads its object
from ESI" was true of the **instruction** and wrong about the **convention**, and section 119 added optional
`ESI`, `EDI`, `EBX` arguments on that reading. Those arguments are inert and harmless - the census before and
after adding them was identical - but they are **not** the fix for this site: the machine overwrites `ESI` two
instructions into the body.

### 121.3 The mechanism, measured

The suite passes `{ecx: q}` where `q = n + 0x103c`, and the dispatcher reads `[q + 0x174c]`, which is far
outside `n`'s `0x2678` allocation, so `ESI` is zero and the read is at `0x4`.

Two edits turn that into a measurement:

```
m.u32(n + 0x174c, manager)          the field the body reads
m.call(touch(0x412e30), {ecx: n})   the base the body expects
```

The wall **moves at once**:

```
before   address 0x4           pc 0x415518
after    address 0x7de64de0    pc 0x415518
```

Same instruction, same pc, a different address: the value read from `[ecx+0x174c]` reached `ESI`, and the fault
is now `[esi+4]` with `ESI` holding what was written. That is the mechanism established by measurement rather
than by the reading that proposed it - and it is the first movement of this site in the session.

### 121.4 What is left, and what it generalises to

The suite still fails: the pointer written is a **th11-shaped** value, and the body walks a th12-shaped chain
(`[ecx+0x174c]` then `[+4]` then `[+4]`). So the next step is to build the object graph the th12 dispatcher
walks, not to change the machine.

The general point is larger than the site: `touch()` translates **addresses** between the th11 fixture and the
th12 runtime, and it does not translate **structure offsets**. Every th11-derived suite that passes an object
through a translated address is therefore walking a th11 layout against th12 code. That is a class worth
auditing across the corpus - how many suites pass a translated address where the callee indexes a field - and
it is named here as the next round's first question.

### 121.5 The keepers

```
node --test th12-rng.test.mjs     pass 2 fail 0
node --test archive.test.mjs      pass 1 fail 0   (184 TH11 resources byte-identical)
node --test anm-load-all.mjs      pass 1 fail 0
node --test anm-resource.test.mjs pass 1 fail 0
node replace-site-audit.mjs       0 replace sites in suites name an address the table maps elsewhere
```

The census is run with the test edits in place; section 112's verdict is the baseline it is compared to.
## 122. The derived-argument class, measured - by a tool that had to be tested first

### 122.1 What the audit asks

Section 121.4 named the class: `touch()` translates **addresses** between the th11 fixture and the th12 runtime
and does not translate **structure offsets**, so a suite that hands a th11-shaped object to a th12 function
walks a th11 layout against th12 code. `tools/th-derived-args.py` measures it. It reads the translation tables,
finds every `m.call(touch(<th11 address>), {...})` site in the suites, and disassembles the th12 target to see
whether its first instructions load a pointer **out of** a register the call supplied - through copies, because
section 121's shape is `mov ebx, ecx` followed by `mov esi, [ebx+0x174c]`.

### 122.2 The result

```
translation rows: 178;   call sites through touch(): 81 targets, 139 sites
targets whose body DERIVES a pointer from a supplied register: 14
    0x0040f790  menu-cursor                  ECX,EDX   mov eax, [edx + 8]
    0x00412050  enemy-phase                  ECX       mov eax, [ecx + 0xc]
    0x004154d0  bullet-manager, cancellation-integration  ECX   mov esi, [ebx + 0x174c]
    0x004287c0  laser-line                   ECX,STACK mov ax, [ebx + 0x478]
    0x0042ab80  laser-infinite               ECX,STACK mov ax, [ebx + 0x4a4]
    0x004526e0  screen-shake                 ECX       mov eax, [edi + 0x1c]
    0x0045dcd0  anm-geometry                 ECX       mov ebp, [edx + 0x478]
    0x0045df36  anm-renderer-effects         ECX       mov ecx, [eax + 0x478]
    0x00468e20  ecl-context                  EDX,STACK mov esi, [edx + 4]
    0x00468f70  ecl-context                  ECX,STACK mov edx, [ecx + 0x100c]
    0x004690b0  ecl-context                  ECX,EDX   mov eax, [edx + 4]
    0x004692e0  ecl-control, ecl-resource    ECX,STACK mov eax, [esi + 4]
    ... 67 more targets with no such derivation in their first 40 instructions
```

Fourteen of eighty-one. That is a **measurable** class rather than a suspicion, and it names the suites.

### 122.3 The tool was tested on the known case first, and failed twice

The proof that section 121 is right is `0x004154d0`, so the tool was pointed at it before any of its numbers
were believed. It reported **0 of 81**, and each of the three defects was its own:

1. **RVA vs VA.** It disassembled from `entry - section.virtualAddress`, but suite addresses are **virtual**
   addresses and a section header holds an **RVA**, so the slice was empty and every disassembly produced no
   instructions. It reported "0 of 81" - the failure mode the audit exists to catch, committed by the audit
   itself. Fixed by adding the PE image base.
2. **A window that decided the answer.** While the immediate operand was missing, the detector looked only at
   the first **10** instructions; `mov ebx, ecx` is the **20th** at `0x4154d0`. Widened to 40 and stated in the
   report, because a window is a measurement choice, not a fact.
3. **A crash that hid the rest.** `insn.reg_name(right.mem.base)` returns `None` for absolute addressing, which
   aborted the run rather than skipping the operand.

All three are recorded because the first two each produced a **plausible negative** - "no target derives
anything" - which is the most dangerous kind of wrong answer an audit can give.

### 122.4 What the flags mean, and what they do not

The alias analysis follows register copies **inside the 40-instruction window only**. A body that loads the
base from the stack, or through a call, is not resolved, so some flags are conservative and some
`[eax + disp]` cases are false positives. The flags are a **queue**, not a verdict:

- the strongest case is one where the derived register is **never supplied** by the call - `screen-shake`
  reads `[edi + 0x1c]` while the site passes `ECX` alone;
- `0x4154d0` is the case already confirmed by measurement in section 121.3, and it is flagged correctly.

The next step is to work that queue: for each flagged target, read the derivation and decide whether the call
site supplies the register the body actually dereferences, and whether the object it points at is th12-shaped.

### 122.5 The keepers

```
