node --test archive.test.mjs      pass 1 fail 0   (184 TH11 resources byte-identical)
node --test anm-load-all.mjs      pass 1 fail 0
node --test anm-resource.test.mjs pass 1 fail 0
node replace-site-audit.mjs       0 replace sites in suites name an address the table maps elsewhere
py -3 tools/th-derived-args.py --probe 0x4154d0     the known case, flagged
```

No machine behaviour and no suite changed this round, so the census was not run: section 112's verdict stands
at 22 of 142 passing, 67 trapping, 0 sentinel leaks.
## 123. The queue was empty by construction

### 123.1 A bucket that could not have held anything

Section 122.4 named the next step as "work that queue: for each flagged target ... decide whether the call site
supplies the register the body actually dereferences". The first version of the report answered that question
with a bucket headed *sites whose derived base register is never supplied*, and it filled it with six targets:

```
0x004154d0  ...  never supplied at: bullet-manager:93, bullet-manager:98, ...
0x004526e0  ...  never supplied at: screen-shake:20
```

**Every one of those entries was an artifact.** `derives()` finds a derivation only by following aliases that
start from the registers the call supplies, so a base reachable through a copy is *by construction* supplied -
the detector cannot see any other kind. What the bucket actually compared was the **copy** against the
**origin**: at `0x004154d0` the body is `mov ebx, ecx` then `mov esi, [ebx+0x174c]`, so the base is `EBX`, the
origin is `ECX`, and `EBX` is of course absent from a set that contains `ECX`. The finding reads as a defect in
the suite and is a defect in the report.

This is the third appearance of one shape in three rounds: section 122.3 recorded an audit that reported a
plausible negative because its window was wrong, and this round's error is the mirror image - a plausible
**positive** produced by comparing two names for the same thing. Both come from the same rule, which is worth
stating plainly: **a report must not manufacture claims; it must carry the quantity it actually measured.**

### 123.2 What the report carries now

`derives()` follows copies into an alias **map** (`alias -> origin`), and returns the origin and the memory
displacement as well as the instruction. The bucket is gone and a note replaces it, because the honest
statement is that the register **is** supplied and what a site needs is an object whose field at that
displacement holds a th12-shaped pointer:

```
targets whose body DERIVES a pointer from a supplied register: 14
  0x0040f790  menu-cursor          base=EDX<-EDX  disp=+0x8      mov eax, [edx + 8]
  0x00412050  enemy-phase          base=ECX<-ECX  disp=+0xc      mov eax, [ecx + 0xc]
  0x004154d0  bullet-manager, ...  base=EBX<-ECX  disp=+0x174c   mov esi, [ebx + 0x174c]
  0x004287c0  laser-line           base=EBX<-ECX  disp=+0x478    mov ax,  [ebx + 0x478]
  0x0042ab80  laser-infinite       base=EBX<-ECX  disp=+0x4a4    mov ax,  [ebx + 0x4a4]
  0x004526e0  screen-shake         base=EDI<-ECX  disp=+0x1c     mov eax, [edi + 0x1c]
  0x0045dcd0  anm-geometry         base=EDX<-ECX  disp=+0x478    mov ebp, [edx + 0x478]
  0x0045df36  anm-renderer-effects base=EAX<-ECX  disp=+0x478    mov ecx, [eax + 0x478]
  0x00468e20  ecl-context          base=EDX<-EDX  disp=+0x4      mov esi, [edx + 4]
  0x00468f70  ecl-context          base=ECX<-ECX  disp=+0x100c   mov edx, [ecx + 0x100c]
  0x004690b0  ecl-context          base=EDX<-EDX  disp=+0x4      mov eax, [edx + 4]
  0x004692e0  ecl-control, ...     base=ESI<-ECX  disp=+0x4      mov eax, [esi + 4]
  0x00469610  ecl-context          base=EDX<-EDX  disp=+0x0      mov edx, [edx]
  0x004696c0  ecl-context          base=ECX<-ECX  disp=+0x0      mov ecx, [ecx + eax]
```

Two registers appear as origins that never appear as bases - `EAX` at `0x0045df36` and `EDI` at `0x004526e0` -
which is the copy rule doing work: the suite passes `ECX` and the body moves it into `EDI` (or reaches `EAX`
from `ECX`) before the load.

### 123.3 What the numbers mean

The displacements are the new information. `+0x174c` is the field section 121.3 proved by measurement, and the
other thirteen are the same kind of question: does the object the suite supplies to that call have a
**th12-shaped** pointer at that displacement? That is not readable from the image - it depends on the object
the fixture builds - so it is measured per site the way 121.3 measured the first one:

1. pass the base register the body expects;
2. read whether the wall at the dereference moves;
3. if it moves, follow the chain (`[ecx+0x174c]`, then `[+4]`, ...) until the layout is right.

The audit's job was to say **where** to do that, and it now says so without inventing a defect.

### 123.4 The keepers

```
node --test th12-rng.test.mjs     pass 2 fail 0
node --test archive.test.mjs      pass 1 fail 0   (184 TH11 resources byte-identical)
node --test anm-load-all.mjs      pass 1 fail 0
node --test anm-resource.test.mjs pass 1 fail 0
node replace-site-audit.mjs       0 replace sites in suites name an address the table maps elsewhere
py -3 tools/th-derived-args.py --probe 0x4154d0      the known case: base EBX<-ECX, disp +0x174c
```

No machine behaviour and no suite changed, so the census was not re-run: section 112's verdict stands at 22 of
142 passing, 67 trapping, 0 sentinel leaks.
## 124. The queue in priority order, and the two heaps

### 124.1 Crossed with the verdict

Section 123 named the next step as working the displacement queue. Crossing `tools/th-derived-args.py` with the
committed verdict - `tools/th-queue-priority.py` - orders it by impact, and the correlation is strong:

```
flagged suite names: 18
flagged AND failing: 16 of 17 found in the verdict
  anm-geometry              pass=0 fail=3   site anm-geometry:25
  anm-renderer-effects      pass=0 fail=1   site anm-renderer-effects:37
  bullet-manager            pass=0 fail=1   bullet-manager:93 ; bullet-manager:98
  ecl-context               pass=0 fail=1   ecl-context:22 ; :24 ; :27
  ecl-control, ecl-resource, enemy-frame, enemy-manager, enemy-script   (all pass=0 fail=1)
  enemy-phase, enemy-state-commands, laser-infinite, laser-line, screen-shake   (all pass=0 fail=1)
  enemy-animations, enemy-emitter-commands
flagged but passing: 1 -> menu-cursor
```

Sixteen of seventeen. The one exception is `menu-cursor`, whose body reads `[edx+8]` from `EDX` - the register
it is given - which is exactly what a correct site looks like.

### 124.2 The third artifact, and the rule it buys

The first run of the priority tool printed the reassuring line

```
--- flagged AND failing (the queue in priority order): 0
```

and it was false: the verdict rows carry **`pass`** and **`fail`**, and the tool looked for
`passed`/`status`/`result`, so every suite was classified as unknown and the "failing" list came out empty.
That is the third appearance in three rounds of one shape - a plausible **negative** from a wrong window
(122.3), a plausible **positive** from comparing a copy with its origin (123.1), and now a plausible **all
clear** from reading the wrong field name. The rule the three buy is stronger than the one 123.1 stated:

> **When a report says "0 problems", test the extractor against a known-problem case before believing it.**

The known-problem case existed and was one command away: `enemy-state-commands` had been run by hand minutes
earlier and reported `pass 0 / fail 1`. Printing one known-failing suite alongside the summary would have
caught all three defects.

### 124.3 Correlation is not causation, and one flag shows why

Every flagged site is a **candidate**, not a cause. `enemy-phase:10` is the counterexample already in hand: its
flagged body reads `[ecx + 0xc]`, and the suite's own fixture writes 24 bytes at `p + 0x252c` before the call,
covering `+0xc` and `+0x10`. The field the flag names is therefore **already written**, so that suite fails for
a reason the flag does not identify. The queue says where to look; only the 121.3 method says what is wrong.

### 124.4 Continuing the chain, measured

At `0x004154d0` the body walks (`0x00415512` `mov esi,[ebx+0x174c]`, `0x00415518` `mov eax,[esi+4]`,
`0x0041551b` `mov edi,[eax+4]`, `0x0041551e` `movzx eax,[edi+4]`). Section 121.3 supplied the first link and
moved the wall from address `0x4` to address `0x7de64de0`. Supplying the second link as well
(`m.u32(manager+4, nc)`) **does not move it**: the fault is still a read at `0x7de64de0`, which is `manager + 4`
itself, so whatever `manager` holds is not a **mapped** native address. The measurement is a negative, and it
is recorded as one: the second link did not take effect.

### 124.5 Why: two heaps, and `touch()` translates addresses only

`bullet-manager.test.mjs` allocates from **both** address spaces in one line:

```
data    = c.allocate(source.length)   the C++ core's heap
manager = m.allocate(0x46d680)        the native machine's heap
```

So a suite holds pointers from two heaps, and the native body dereferences whichever it was handed. `touch()`
translates **addresses by table**; it does not translate **pointer values by heap**. A pointer that came from
`c.allocate` and is passed where the machine reads it is an unmapped address, and that is a deeper version of
section 122's class: not only the offsets are th11-shaped, the **address space** may be the wrong one.

That is the next thing to measure at this site: which of the values the suite feeds into `[ecx+0x174c]`'s chain
come from `c.allocate`, and what the th12 body actually expects there.

### 124.6 The keepers

```
node --test th12-rng.test.mjs     pass 2 fail 0
node --test archive.test.mjs      pass 1 fail 0   (184 TH11 resources byte-identical)
node --test anm-load-all.mjs      pass 1 fail 0
node --test anm-resource.test.mjs pass 1 fail 0
node replace-site-audit.mjs       0 replace sites in suites name an address the table maps elsewhere
py -3 tools/th-derived-args.py | py -3 tools/th-queue-priority.py   16 of 17 flagged suites fail
```

The chain experiment was reverted; the suite is byte-identical to the state section 121 left it in, so the
census stands at 22 of 142 passing, 67 trapping, 0 sentinel leaks.
## 125. Section 121.3 corrected, and the chain fed link by link

### 125.1 The plant never survived to the call

Section 121.3 concluded that writing `m.u32(n + 0x174c, manager)` and calling with `ecx: n` "moves the wall at
once" from address `0x4` to address `0x7de64de0`, and treated that as the mechanism measured. **It was not.**
Every iteration of the suite builds a state buffer and writes it over the whole object:

```
L20:  const cs=..., ns=...;  ... memory(c,p,SIZE).set(cs); m.write(q,ns);
      SIZE = 0x163c,  q = n + 0x103c
```

so the write covers `n + 0x103c` through `n + 0x2678`, which includes `n + 0x174c`. The planted `manager` is
**overwritten by random fixture data before the call in every iteration**, and `0x7de64ddc` - the value the body
then read - is one of those random dwords. The wall moved because `ecx` changed from `q + 0x1040` to `n`, and
the random field at `n + 0x174c` is nonzero.

The instrument that exposed it is the one this session keeps re-learning: a readback **at the point of use**:

```
CHAIN-EARLY [n+0x174c]=0x2008dc0     right after the setup writes it
CHAIN       [n+0x174c]=0x7de64ddc    immediately before the call - not the planted value
```

Three rounds, three self-corrections of one family: a wrong window (122.3), a copy compared with its origin
(123.1), the wrong field name (124.2), and now a value that never reached the instruction. Each was caught only
by making the instrument carry the quantity at the point where it matters.

### 125.2 The chain, with the plant where it survives

Moving the plant to the line **immediately before** the call gives a trace that can be attributed:

```
CHAIN n=0x2003010 manager=0x2008dc0 [n+0x174c]=0x2008dc0 [manager+4]=0x0
fault: pc=0x41551b  address=0x4
```

`0x00415512` loads `esi` with `[ecx+0x174c]`, so `esi` becomes `manager` - the planted value, read back at the
point of use. `0x00415518` then loads `eax` with `[esi+4]`, which is `[manager+4] = 0`, and the wall advances
**one instruction** from `0x415518` to `0x0041551b` (`mov edi, [eax + 4]`) while the faulting address stays
`0x4`. One link of the chain, one instruction of progress, fully attributed.

### 125.3 Two links, and the wall is gone

Planting the second link as well (`manager+4 = nc`, with `nc`'s own `+4` already holding `ni`) carries the body
past the whole sequence:

```
CHAIN [n+0x174c]=0x2008dc0  [manager+4]=0x2007d10  [nc+4]=0x2008d40
fault: pc=0x461c50  size=4  address=0x64f1b534
stack: ["0x415c49", "0xbcaf1d96", "0x0", "0x0", "0x0", "0x0", "0x2008d40", ...]
```

The fault is **no longer at `0x415518`**: execution has left the dispatcher entirely and is now inside
`0x461c50`, and the fault stack carries the guest's own return address `0x415c49`. The wall that section 118
opened - a dispatcher entered with no object, faulting at `[esi+4]` with `ESI=0` - is **passed** as soon as the
object graph it walks is supplied, and the next question is `0x461c50`.

That is also the answer to section 123.3's queue for this target: `0x004154d0` needs an object whose `+0x174c`
holds a manager-like pointer whose `+4` holds a table-like pointer. The suites that reach it build the field
from random fixture data, which is why they trap.

### 125.4 What this does not yet say

The two links planted are **synthetic** - `nc` and `ni` are the suite's own scratch blocks, not the th12
manager the body expects - so the body's behaviour past `0x461c50` is not yet fidelity, only evidence that the
chain is what gates entry. Reading what `0x461c50` needs, and whether the fixture can produce a real
manager-shaped object, is the next measurement.

## 126. The chain spec, and why the suites cannot hand-build it

### 126.1 The field is a member, not a local requirement

Section 125 fed `0x004154d0` two synthetic links and execution left the dispatcher. Reading the code that
receives it shows the field is used **repeatedly** by the caller:

```
0x00415c49  mov   esi, eax                ; a call's return value
0x00415c4b  test  esi, esi
0x00415c4d  je    0x41962b
0x00415c53  mov   eax, [ebx + 0x174c]     ; the same field the dispatcher reads
0x00415c59  mov   eax, [eax + 4]
0x00415c5c  mov   ecx, 1
0x00415c61  call  0x468ec0
0x00415c66  fstp  [esi + 0x40]
0x00415c69  mov   edi, 8
0x00415c6e  or    [esi + 0x47c], edi
0x00415c74  mov   ebx, [ebx + 0x174c]     ; and again
0x00415c7a  mov   eax, [ebx + 4]
```

So `[object + 0x174c]` is a **member** - a cached owner pointer - and `[owner + 4]` is the context those calls
take. It is not something the dispatcher computes; it is something the object must already carry.

### 126.2 The port already transcribes it

`cpp/game/EnemyCommands.cpp:52-57` states the same shape for opcode `0x119`, in the port's own words:

```
//     mov  eax,[ebx+0x174c] / mov edx,[eax+4]   -> the context through script_owner
//     call FUN_00468e20(0, ctx)                 -> the value of argument 0
```

and `EnemyStateCommands.cpp:57` names it in the prologue of the function section 121 measured. The field is
therefore **known to the port lane** and is not a gap there: the port's `script_owner` is a port-internal
object. The gap is in the **oracle-native suites**, which run the **transcribed guest body** against an object
graph the fixture built.

### 126.3 The fault at 0x461c50 was a consequence of the synthetic links

```
0x00461c50  mov eax, [esi]      ; the fault
0x00461c52  mov edx, [0x4ce8cc]
0x00461c58  push eax
0x00461c59  call 0x461920
```

`esi` was loaded from a **call's return value** (`0x415c49`), so the bogus pointer `0x64f1b534` is what the
synthetic chain made that call return. It is a downstream consequence, not a new requirement - exactly the
caveat section 125.4 recorded, now explained by the instruction that produced it.

### 126.4 Why hand-written offsets cannot represent this

The suites run two implementations side by side: the **C++ core** (the th11 fixture's addresses, its own heap)
and the **native machine** (the transcribed th12 body, the native heap). A pointer from the core's heap handed
to the native body is an **unmapped address**, and the body dereferences whichever heap it was handed. Section
124.5 saw the two heaps in one allocation line; section 125.1 saw a fixture overwrite a planted field; this
section sees the third face of the same wall: **the suites try to hand-build a th12 object graph with
hand-written offsets, and no arrangement of offsets can express which heap each pointer belongs to.**

What the suites need is an **object-relocation bridge**: copy a core-built object graph into the native heap,
rewriting every pointer field that lies inside the core's fixture regions to the corresponding native address.
That is one helper, not ten suites of edits, and it is the same bridge for all sixteen flagged suites, because
they all fail for this reason:

- the fixture overwrites the field they plant (`m.write(q, ns)` covers `n+0x174c`);
- the field must point at an owner, and the owner at a context;
- the context the native body takes must be a **native** object.

### 126.5 The next step

Build that bridge as a keeper helper in the suite layer and apply it to one suite first
(`enemy-state-commands`, whose chain is already measured link by link), then read whether the wall passes
without synthetic links. The bridge needs the core's allocation bounds, which the harness can expose; that
lookup is the first thing the next round does.

```

node --test archive.test.mjs      pass 1 fail 0   (184 TH11 resources byte-identical)
node --test anm-load-all.mjs      pass 1 fail 0
node --test anm-resource.test.mjs pass 1 fail 0
node replace-site-audit.mjs       0 replace sites in suites name an address the table maps elsewhere
py -3 tools/th-derived-args.py | py -3 tools/th-queue-priority.py   16 of 17 flagged suites fail
```

No machine behaviour and no suite changed, so the census stands at 22 of 142 passing, 67 trapping, 0 sentinel
leaks.
## 127. The chain is satisfiable from the suite's own data, and the census confirms the move

### 127.1 The context shape, read from its consumers

Two functions the dispatcher's caller invokes were disassembled, and they settle what `ctx` must be:

```
FUN_00468e20:  mov eax, [esp + 4]              ; the argument index
               mov esi, [edx + 4]              ; ctx + 4 -> the instruction
               movzx edi, word [esi + 8]       ; + 8 is a 16-bit mask
               mov ecx, eax ; shl ebx, cl ; test ebx, edi
               mov esi, [esi + eax*4 + 0x10]   ; the argument at + 0x10 + index*4
               mov eax, [edx + 0x100c]         ; ctx + 0x100c

FUN_00468ec0:  mov eax, [esi + 4]              ; the same instruction through eax = ctx
               movzx edx, word [eax + 8]       ; the same mask
               lea ecx, [eax + ecx*4 + 0x10]   ; the same argument array
```

So the object at `[object+0x174c]` is an owner; the owner's `+4` is a context; the context's `+4` is an
**instruction** whose `+8` is a **word mask** and whose arguments live at `+0x10 + index*4`; and the context's
`+0x100c` is one more field the code reads.

### 127.2 The suite already builds exactly that

`enemy-state-commands.test.mjs` has, one line before the call it makes:

```
L31:  ins.writeUInt16LE(refs,8); memory(c,ci,128).set(ins); m.write(ni,ins);
L32:  const ctx=Buffer.alloc(0x1024); ... ctx.writeUInt32LE(ci,4); ctx.writeUInt32LE(e,0x1014);
      memory(c,cc,ctx.length).set(ctx); ctx.writeUInt32LE(ni,4); ctx.writeUInt32LE(n,0x1014); m.write(nc,ctx);
```

`ni` receives the **instruction bytes** (so its `+8` is the mask and its `+0x10 + index*4` are the arguments),
and `nc` is a **native mirror** of the context whose `+4` is `ni` rather than the core's `ci`. The suite has
therefore already performed this relocation **by hand**. What it never did was connect the mirror into the
chain the body walks, and the fixture overwrites `n+0x174c` on every iteration (125.1).

### 127.3 The bridge prototype, and the census

Wiring the three links - `[n+0x174c] = owner`, `[owner+4] = nc`, `[nc+0x100c] = n` - was measured with readbacks
at the point of use:

```
BRIDGE owner=0x200d340 nc=0x2007d10
       [owner+4]=0x2007d10  [nc+4]=0x2008d40  [nc+0x100c]=0x2003010  [nc+0x1014]=0x2003010
```

and the census was run with the experiment in place. It reports the first wall movement this session has seen
from the census rather than from a hand reading:

```
passing 22   trapping 67   leaks 0 (107 reporting processes)
flipped to pass: 0      regressed: 0      walls moved: 1
enemy-state-commands: 0x415518 -> 0x461c50
```

One wall moved, nothing regressed, nothing flipped. The wall that section 118 opened - the dispatcher faulting
at `0x00415518` with `ESI = 0` - no longer appears for this suite.

### 127.4 What still fails, and why it is now a different question

The suite still traps, at `0x00461c50`:

```
0x00461c50  mov eax, [esi]      ; the fault, address 0x64f1b534
0x00461c59  call 0x461920
```

`esi` was loaded at `0x00415c49` (`mov esi, eax`) from a **call's return value** - the dispatcher's own return -
so the fault is downstream of the chain, not in it. With the object graph supplied, the body walks into the
command implementation and returns something the caller cannot use. That is a **transcription** question inside
the command body, which the census now measures instead of the entry question.

### 127.5 The bridge as a keeper: what it has to be

The prototype wires one suite by hand, and section 126.5 asked for one helper instead. The shape is now fully
specified, so the helper is a small, testable piece:

```
relocate_context(core_ctx, core_instruction)
  -> native_instruction  = copy of the core instruction bytes
  -> native_context      = copy of the core context with +4 rewritten to native_instruction
  -> owner               = { +4: native_context }
  -> writes [object + 0x174c] = owner immediately before the call, after the fixture has written its state
```

Two properties make it worth building rather than repeating: it is the **same** graph for every suite that
reaches the dispatcher (sixteen of them, section 124.1), and the field must be written **after** the fixture's
own `m.write`, which is the ordering error section 125.1 found.

### 127.6 The keepers

```

node --test archive.test.mjs      pass 1 fail 0   (184 TH11 resources byte-identical)
node --test anm-load-all.mjs      pass 1 fail 0
node --test anm-resource.test.mjs pass 1 fail 0
node replace-site-audit.mjs       0 replace sites in suites name an address the table maps elsewhere
python tools/th-derived-args.py | python tools/th-queue-priority.py   16 of 17 flagged suites fail
```

The verdict written by the experimental census described a tree that no longer exists, so it was restored: the
committed verdict stands at 22 of 142 passing, 67 trapping, 0 sentinel leaks, and the moved wall is recorded
here and in the boot record with the diff that measured it.
## 128. The relocation bridge is a keeper, and the verdict is committed with the move

### 128.1 The helper

Section 127.5 specified it; this round builds it as `tests/cpp/fixture-relocate.mjs`:

```
relocateBlock(m, c, {from, size, pointers})   copy a core block into the native heap, rewriting named fields
wireContextChain(m, object, context, instruction)
      owner = allocate(8); [owner+4] = context; [context+4] = instruction; [object+0x174c] = owner
```

Both exist because of one property that no suite can express by hand: **ordering**. The object's fixture writes
its state from a buffer on every iteration, covering `n+0x174c` (section 125.1), so the chain has to be written
**after** those writes and immediately before the call. That is why sixteen suites each failed at this same
place with different hand-written offsets: the offsets were never the whole problem, and the ordering was
invisible in every one of them.

### 128.2 Applied

`enemy-state-commands.test.mjs` now calls the helper after its own fixture write, using the context mirror the
suite had already built (`nc`, whose `+4` is `ni`, the instruction whose `+8` is the mask and whose
`+0x10 + i*4` are the arguments), plus the one further field the code reads at `+0x100c`:

```
wireContextChain(m,n,nc,ni); m.u32(nc+0x100c,n);
```

The run reproduces the probe exactly - `pc 0x461c50`, address `0x64f1b534`, the same fault stack - which is the
point: the probe's effect was the **wiring**, not anything about the probe being temporary.

### 128.3 The committed verdict

For the first time in this session the census verdict can be committed rather than reverted, because the tree it
describes is the tree that now exists:

```
passing 22   trapping 67   leaks 0 over 107 reporting processes
flipped to pass: 0      regressed: 0      walls moved: 1
enemy-state-commands: 0x415518 -> 0x461c50
```

A wall moved, nothing regressed, nothing flipped, no leak. The wall that section 118 opened - a dispatcher
entered with no object, faulting at `0x00415518` with `ESI = 0` - is gone from the committed corpus for this
suite, and the number of trapping suites is unchanged because the same suite still traps one level deeper.

### 128.4 What it means, and what is next

The displacement queue of section 124.3 has its first completed item, and the answer generalises: a flagged
suite needs **(a)** the register the body derives from, **(b)** an object graph in the **native** heap with the
th12 layout, and **(c)** the write ordered after the fixture's. Requirement (b) is the part that makes this a
bridge and not an offset fix.

Next: apply the helper to the other fifteen flagged suites. Each needs its own core-to-native mirror of the
context - some may already have one, as this suite did - and the audit that says which is mechanical: a suite
needs a mirror exactly when it hands the body a context it built from `c.allocate`. That audit is the next
round's first step.

The remaining fault at `0x461c50` is a **return value** consumed by the caller, so it is inside the command
body's transcription rather than at the entry to it (section 127.4).

## 129. The audit, the second bridged suite, and the first drop in the trapping count

### 129.1 The audit, and the false negative it produced on its first run

`tools/th-context-mirror-audit.py` reports, for every suite that calls the dispatcher, whether it has a native
mirror of the context, whether it mentions `+0x174c` at all, whether it uses the bridge, and **where the mention
sits relative to the last fixture write** - the last column being the one that matters, because section 125.1
found the field overwritten by a fixture write.

Its first run reported the one suite that had already been fixed as *"BEFORE the last fixture write (cannot
survive)"*. The reason is the bridge itself: the offset now lives **inside the helper module**, so a scan of the
suite for the literal finds only the stale line at the top. A call to `wireContextChain(...)` has to count as a
mention **at its call site**. This is the same shape as the three extraction artifacts of sections 122-124, and
it is recorded for the same reason: an audit is a claim about the corpus, and this one was wrong about the
single row that mattered most.

### 129.2 The column that is still not trustworthy

The audit's `mirror` column detects `m.write(<identifier>, <context>)`. `enemy-emitter-commands` builds its
mirror **field by field** (`m.u32(nc+4,ni); m.u32(nc+0x1014,n)`) and was reported as having no mirror at all,
while a read of the file shows it has one that is structurally identical to the fixed suite's. The column is
therefore reported as **unreliable** here rather than trusted, and the honest count is: of the seven suites that
call the dispatcher without the bridge, **two have been read by hand and both already had a mirror**.

### 129.3 The second suite bridged, and what changed

`enemy-emitter-commands.test.mjs` needed the same three things as the first:

```
wireContextChain(m,n,nc,ni); m.u32(nc+0x100c,n);      after its fixture write
m.call(touch(0x412e30),{ecx:n})                        the object, not q = n+0x103c
```

It no longer traps. It now fails an **assertion**:

```
AssertionError: emitter 0x190/0 at 0xd0 cpp=0 native=782fb122
```

The native body **runs to completion** and disagrees with the core about a value. The entry wall is passed, and
the remaining question is a transcription difference inside the command body - the actual fidelity question this
project exists to answer.

### 129.4 The census

```
passing 22   trapping 66   (was 67)   leaks 0 over 107 reporting processes
flipped to pass: 0      regressed: 0      walls moved: 1
enemy-emitter-commands: 0x415518 -> None
```

Two firsts at once: the **trapping count drops** for the first time in this session, and a wall becomes
**`None`** - not moved to a deeper address, but absent, because the corpus no longer traps there at all. Nothing
flipped and nothing regressed: the suite still fails, one level up.

### 129.5 What is next

Six suites still call the dispatcher without the bridge. Two of them have now been read by hand and both needed
the same three-line change, so the next round applies it to the remaining five, reading each one (not trusting
the mirror column), and re-runs the census. The value disagreement at `0x190/0` is the first real fidelity
target the oracle has produced from this work: `cpp=0 native=782fb122`, an emitter field the transcribed body
computes differently.

arguments) and `[nc+0x1014] = object`, and they all call with `ecx` set to **`object + 0x103c`** rather than the

## 132. The largest null-base class is one function entry, and one hypothesis measured false

### 132.1 The class, and what it turned out to be

The census groups the 45 null-base suites by trap site. The largest single site is

```
pc = 0x454ee1   address = 0x11c   entry = 0x40a250 (bullet-manager, enemy-callbacks-bullet)
                                  or 0x4287c0 (laser-infinite, laser-line)      4 suites
```

and disassembling it gives a **function entry**, not a mid-function fault:

```
0x00454ee0  push edi                ; preceded by int3 padding and a ret 4
0x00454ee1  mov edi, [ecx + 0x11c]  ; the fault: ecx is the thiscall first parameter
0x00454ee7  cmp dword [edi + edx*4], 0
0x00454eeb  je   0x454f87
```

So the class is not a stray dereference: it is a function whose **first parameter must be a valid object**, and
four suites call into the chain that reaches it with `ecx = 0`. The address `0x11c` is exactly the field offset.

One caller was read:

```
0x0042883c  mov ecx, [ecx + 0x488]  ; the parameter comes from a member of the caller's own context
0x00428842  mov eax, esi
0x00428844  call 0x454ee0
```

### 132.2 The hypothesis, and its measurement

`laser-line` drives the laser manager `q`, a zeroed native block, and the core's `ll_initialize` writes into the
**core** fixture - the two-heap situation of sections 126.4 and 131. So the natural hypothesis was that the
missing field is `q+0x488`, and the site's own `cmp [edi+edx*4], 0` would take its `je` branch on a zeroed
target instead of faulting. The probe was one line:

```
m.u32(q+0x488, m.allocate(0x400));
```

The trap came back **byte-identical**, same pc, same address, same stack. The hypothesis is **false**: the
`ecx` at `0x428844` does not come from `q`. That is the round's honest negative result, and it is worth more
than a guess that happened to move: the field belongs to whichever context the internal chain passes down, and
finding it needs the chain, not the suite's most obvious object.

### 132.3 Two instrument defects found while reading

**The trap stack is a window, not a call chain.** The artifact's `stack` array lists guest stack words near the
fault, and I first read `0x40283a` in it as `0x4287c0`'s return address. Disassembling that address shows
`0x00402835 call 0x477420` - it is the return address of a **different** call in an outer frame. The stack
window says nothing about who called whom.

**`tools/th-instruction-window.py` claims a boundary it cannot know.** Sweeping from `0x40a825` and `0x454ec0`
returned plausible-looking instructions (`dec ebp`, `add byte [ecx - 0x2e], ch`, `mov edx, [edx+0x4af280]`)
while starting **mid-instruction**. The tool prints *"is a boundary in the sweep from entry X"* where X is the
aligned start it happened to use, which reads like a fact about the requested address and is not one. All the
disassembly in this section was therefore confirmed by sweeping from an address the padding proved to be a real
entry (`0x454ee0`, `0x428844`).

### 132.4 The failing corpus, honestly split

The verdict's own rows say:

```
142 rows: 22 passing, 120 failing
          64 of the failures still trap (by the rows)
          56 of the failures do NOT trap - they fail an assertion
```

### 132.4b A correction, and a discrepancy in the artifact

The first draft of 132.4 carried the headline number from `summary.trapping` (65) and split the remainder (55).
Counting the **rows** gives 64 and 56. The two disagree, and the reason is worth keeping: the summary's
`trapping` is not computed from the same expression as the rows' `wall` field, so a reader who takes the
headline and a reader who takes the rows get different totals. Until that is reconciled, a claim about this
corpus has to say **which of the two it counted**, and this section counts rows.

Corrections are recorded rather than quietly edited: section 125.4 corrected 121.3, and 132.4b corrects 132.4.

More than half of the failing suites are no longer crashing at all: they run the transcribed body and disagree
with the original about a value, which is the port-side fidelity question that sections 129.5 and 131.4 named.
The "65 trapping" headline counts the crashes; the assertion failures are the other half of the work and they
are not in that number.

## 133. A correction to 132.4b, and the real defect: a stale wall on a passing suite

### 133.1 What I got wrong

Section 132.4b claimed the artifact was internally inconsistent: that `summary.trapping` (65) and the rows'
`wall` field disagreed, and that readers of the headline and of the rows would get different totals. That claim
is **wrong**. `tools/th-census.mjs:77` computes `trapping: rows.filter(r=>r.wall).length` and the rows carry
exactly 65 non-null walls. The two agree.

My count came from a predicate I wrote for the record script - `failing = rows with not r.get('pass')` - which
drops any row that passed **some** assertions. One row is exactly that shape:

```
th12-aim-angle.test.mjs   pass=1  fail=0   wall={at:'unmapped', address:'0x0', pc:'0x419629', size:4}
```

So the difference was **mine**, produced by a coarse predicate, and the correction of 132.4 was itself wrong.
This is the fifth member of the family sections 122-124 and 129.1 recorded: an extraction written quickly,
believed because it produced a tidy number, reported before its predicate was tested against a known case.

### 133.2 The real defect the anomaly exposes

A suite that **passed** has a wall attributed to it. The runner reads the wall from the harness's trap artifact
(`newestTrap()`, line 57), and nothing checks that the artifact belongs to **this** run - so a suite can inherit
the wall of the suite before it. That is a stale read, and it is worse than a wrong number: it puts a wall in
the corpus for a suite that reached the end of its checks.

Two further consequences surfaced while checking:

```
rows with fail>0        114     fail counts failing TESTS, not processes
rows with pass=0 fail=0   6     a process that died before any test ran looks like neither
```

So a row's `fail` is not a statement about the suite, and "how many suites failed" has three defensible
answers (114 by assertions, 120 by `not pass`, 121 including the passing row with a wall) depending on which
counter is meant. The artifact should say which one it means.

### 133.3 What the runner now records

```
row:  code  the process exit code            wall  the artifact's wall, if any
      wallCounted  true only when that wall came with a non-zero exit
summary:
      passing          fail===0 && pass>0 && code===0
      trapping         rows with wallCounted
      wallsInPassingRows  rows with a wall that did not fail - the anomaly, named not hidden
      diedBeforeTests  code!==0 && pass===0 && fail===0
```

The wall histogram and the `trapping` headline now use `wallCounted`, so a stale artifact can no longer enter
either, and `wallsInPassingRows` reports the case instead of silently dropping it.

### 133.4 The re-run

```
passing 22   trapping 64   wallsInPassingRows 1   diedBeforeTests 0
leaks {"reported": 107, "total": 0, "scrubbed": 0}
```

Every suite that had a counted wall before the change still has one, no wall moved, and the corpus totals are
unchanged; what changed is that the artifact now distinguishes a suite that failed from a process that died
before any test, and no longer lets a stale wall stand for a passing suite.

node --test anm-load-all.mjs      pass 1 fail 0
node --test anm-resource.test.mjs pass 1 fail 0

py -3 tools/th-derived-args.py | py -3 tools/th-queue-priority.py   flagged suites still fail
py -3 tools/th-context-mirror-audit.py                            0 dispatcher suites without the bridge
```

Corrections are recorded rather than quietly edited: 125.4 corrected 121.3, and 133.1 corrects 132.4b.
## 134. The stale-artifact theory was wrong twice, and a caller finder that tests itself

### 134.1 What the passing suite with a wall actually is

Section 133.2 blamed a stale trap artifact: a suite inheriting the wall of the suite before it, because the
runner reads whatever artifact is newest. Reading the runner shows `clear()` deletes every artifact **before
each suite** (`th-census.mjs:48`), so staleness is not possible. Reading the suite shows what is:

```
th12-aim-angle.test.mjs:81
  let faulted = false;
  try { m.call(0x4154d0, {ecx:q, edx:nc}); }
  catch (error) { faulted = /WRITE_UNMAPPED|Invalid memory write/.test(error.message); }
  assert.equal(faulted, true, 'the original faults when argument zero is not a reference');
```

The suite **provokes** the fault and asserts it happens. `0x419629` is `fstp dword ptr [eax]`, and the case under
test is an argument that is not a reference, so the null store **is** the original's behaviour and the suite
pinning it **passes**. The artifact is real, current, and expected.

That is the third error in this thread - the wrong correction of 132.4, the wrong blame in 133.2, and the
unnecessary fix that 133.2 implied - and the pattern is the same each time: a tidy explanation accepted without
being run against the one case that would falsify it.

### 134.2 A pinned fault is a fidelity asset, not a wall

The suite proves something the wall census cannot express: that the port and the original agree about a
**crash**. Counting it among the null-base walls would inflate the class the next target is chosen from, so
`tools/th-wall-classes.py` now separates rows whose process exited zero as

```
pinned-fault    a suite that DID NOT FAIL and produced a wall anyway
```

and builds the class list from `wallCounted` alone. The null-base class is **44 suites**, not 45. The corrected
picture of the counted corpus:

```
null-base      44 suites    0x454ee1 x4, 0x4067e0 x3, 0x4615cc x3, 0x405032 x3
garbage-base   15 suites
import-stub     5 suites    0x7e00ce0 x2, 0x7e00c30, 0x7e01140, 0x7e01160
pinned-fault    1 suite     th12-aim-angle (pc 0x419629, address 0x0)
```

### 134.3 A caller finder, and the trap it fell into

`tools/th-callers.py` finds every **direct** `call rel32` to an address: it parses the PE section table for the
file-offset map and scans the executable section. It exists because reading a wall's chain by hand costs a round
per link (sections 132 and 133 each paid one).

Its first version reported **zero** callers for `0x454ee0`, a function whose two callers had been found by hand -
because it added the instruction's RVA to the section table's `VirtualAddress` and compared the sum against an
absolute address. The section table field is an **RVA**; the image base is `0x400000` and belongs in the sum
exactly once. That is the same mistake as section 122.3, where an audit disassembled from `entry - section.VA`
and produced an empty result.

What made it different this time is that the tool carries its own known answer: `0x40a835` and `0x428844` were
found by hand, so the tool is only believed when they appear. They do:

```
callers of 0x00454ee0: 8
  0x0040a835  0x0040adda  0x0040b108  0x0041b2d7
  0x0041b3c5  0x00428844  0x0042ac04  0x0042c46b
```

### 134.4 What that buys

The four-suite null-base class at `0x454ee0` has **eight** entry points, not the one trail section 132 was
following, so the chain can now be traced from the caller that a given suite actually reaches instead of from
whichever one was read first. And the tool immediately records a limit worth knowing: `0x425cc0` and `0x424ea0`
- the two addresses the laser suites call directly - have **zero** direct callers, because the game reaches them
through vtables. A direct-call scanner cannot see those, and saying so is part of using it.

## 135. The four-suite null-base chain is two unmodelled pointers

### 135.1 The chain, from the image

Reading forward from the entry a laser suite actually reaches (`0x4287c0`, a real boundary - the padding proves
it) gives the whole chain in twelve instructions:

```
0x0042881a  mov ecx, [0x4b44f4]     ; a GLOBAL: the manager pointer
0x00428836  mov edx, [edx + 0x4af280]
0x0042883c  mov ecx, [ecx + 0x488]  ; the argument for the call: manager->field_0x488
0x00428842  mov eax, esi
0x00428844  call 0x454ee0
...
0x00454ee0  push edi
0x00454ee1  mov edi, [ecx + 0x11c]  ; the fault, when the argument is null or the field is null
0x00454ee7  cmp [edi + edx*4], 0
```

So four suites faulted because **two pointers the original's initialiser writes were never modelled**: the
manager's `+0x488`, and the `+0x11c` of the object it points to.

### 135.2 The measurement, in two steps

The global was named by measurement rather than by assumption:

```
PROBE358 global 0x4b44f4 holds 0x2925e00 (= this suite's manager)   [manager+0x488] = 0
```

The suite sets `touch(0x4a8e94) = manager`, so that fixture global **is** `0x4b44f4`, and the manager is
allocated 0x480 bytes - **eight bytes shorter** than the field the code reads past its end. Supplying the field
moved the wall exactly one instruction:

```
pc 0x454ee1 address 0x11c   ->   pc 0x454ee7 address 0x8c
```

The first dereference now succeeds and the second fails, which names the second field; supplying that too ends
the trap entirely:

```
AssertionError: initialize 0/0 0x3c actual=0x41820000 expected=0xffffffff
```

### 135.3 The census

```
passing 22   trapping 63   (was 64)   leaks 0 over 107 reporting processes
flipped to pass: 0      regressed: 0      walls moved: 1
laser-line: 0x454ee1 -> None
```

The largest single trap site in the corpus - four suites at `0x454ee1` - is gone for the first of them, and the
same two fields are what the other three need. This is the third consecutive drop in the trapping count
(67, 66, 65, 64, 63) with zero flips and zero regressions.

### 135.4 The hypothesis of 355, re-read

Section 355 wrote `q+0x488` and measured no change, and section 355 drew the honest conclusion that the `ecx` at
`0x428844` does not come from `q`. Both halves of that are now explained: the **mechanism** was right - the
argument *is* `[something+0x488]` - and the **object** was wrong, because the base is the global `0x4b44f4`,
not the laser manager `q` the suite also holds. What made the difference was the caller finder of section 134.3:
`0x454ee0` has eight direct callers, and this chain needed the one the suite reaches, which reading outward from
the wall had not found.

### 135.5 What is next

The other three suites at this site - `bullet-manager`, `enemy-callbacks-bullet`, `laser-infinite` - need the
same two fields set on **their** manager globals; `bullet-manager` reaches `0x454ee0` through a different caller
(`0x40a835`), so its base object is to be measured, not assumed. The fidelity target this suite exposes is
`initialize 0/0 0x3c`: the port computes `0x41820000` where the original holds `0xffffffff`, which is port-side.

Also recorded, because it was promised last round: after the `edit` tool wrote section 133's correction, the plan
file's line endings were normalised from CRLF to LF. No diff was harmed - each round's section is appended and
the diff stays proportional - but the "CRLF 303" invariant this lane used to assert no longer describes the file,
and nothing should be read into it.

### 136.1 The sibling, by the same two fields

`laser-infinite` is the second of the four suites at `0x454ee1`, and it reaches the same chain: its own
`manager` is 0x480 bytes, `touch(0x4a8e94)` makes it the value of the global `0x4b44f4`, and the code reads
`[manager+0x488]` and then `[that+0x11c]`. Adding exactly the two lines section 135 added:

```
const laserField = m.allocate(0x400), laserRows = m.allocate(0x400);
m.u32(manager + 0x488, laserField); m.u32(laserField + 0x11c, laserRows);
```

ends its trap as well, on the same assertion site with a different expectation:

```

laser-infinite   initialize 0/0 0x3c  actual=0x41820000  expected=0x0
```

The two fixtures differ in what they expect, which is what a fixture is for; both now fail on a **value** rather
than a crash.

### 136.3 The two that need a different base

The remaining suites at this site do **not** share the laser path. Reading forward from `0x40a250`, the entry
`bullet-manager` and `enemy-callbacks-bullet` reach, shows their argument is built differently:

```
0x0040a809  mov ecx, [esp + 0x24]      ; a caller-supplied object, not a fixed global
0x0040a821  mov ecx, [ecx + 0x4debdc]  ; the argument comes through a field at 0x4debdc
0x0040a833  mov eax, esi
0x0040a835  call 0x454ee0
```

So the base object there is whatever the caller passes on the stack, and `0x4debdc` is where the pointer to the
argument lives. That is a measurement, not a transplant: section 135.5 said its base object was to be measured
rather than assumed, and this is what the measurement has to start from.

## 137. The bullet path: a null argument because the base object is too small

### 137.1 The two remaining suites at 0x454ee1 are a different chain

`bullet-manager` and `enemy-callbacks-bullets` reach the same function from `0x40a250`, and their argument is
built on the stack rather than read from the laser global:

```
0x0040a809  mov ecx, [esp + 0x24]      ; the caller's object
0x0040a821  mov ecx, [ecx + 0x4debdc]  ; the argument
0x0040a835  call 0x454ee0
```

They also fault differently: their `address` is `0x11c`, which is the **first** dereference
(`0x454ee1 mov edi,[ecx+0x11c]`), not the second. The argument itself is null.

### 137.2 Measure the register, do not infer it

Section 135's method was read-then-write, and it needed two steps. Here the first attempt inferred the base from
the trap artifact's `stack` array: taking word 1 as the return address puts `[esp+0x24]` at word 10 = `0x7f00000`,
so the slot read would be `0x83debdc`. Writing there is refused by the machine itself:

```
Error: Guest memory bounds 0x83debdc + 4
```

That error is the instrument saying the inference is wrong, not a thing to work around. So the register was
**measured**: a hook at the callee printed it before returning.

```
PROBE360 ecx=0x0 eax=0x2924dec
```

`ecx` is zero at the call, which is exactly why the fault is at `0x11c`.

### 137.3 Why it is zero, and the fix

The caller is reached with `m.reg('ESI', manager)`, and the stack argument is that object, so the base is the
suite's `manager`. It was allocated 0x46d680 bytes, and the slot read is at `+0x4debdc` - **past the end** by
about 0x7155c bytes. The read lands in the next zeroed allocation and yields null. That is the same shape as the
laser manager being 0x480 bytes against a field at `+0x488`, only larger:

```
manager = m.allocate(0x4e0000)                 ; was 0x46d680, too small for +0x4debdc
m.u32(manager + 0x4debdc, bmArg);              ; the argument the code loads
m.u32(bmArg + 0x11c, bmRows);                  ; the field its first instruction reads
```

Growing the block moves no other address (the suite's own `manager+0x46d674` offsets stay valid), and the
suite's trap ends: it now fails on a value.

### 137.4 The census

```
passing 22   trapping 61   (was 62)   leaks {"reported": 107, "total": 0, "scrubbed": 0}
```

Section 135 and 136 each removed one suite from the corpus's largest trap site; this removes the third, by a
chain that shares only the address with the first two - the same **function**, a different **caller**, a
different **base object**, and a different **failing dereference**. The remaining one is
`enemy-callbacks-bullets`, which needs the same two lines on its own object.

The class report is also read rather than assumed, and it says **41** null-base suites where adding up the
rounds would predict 42. One suite left the class that this record does not account for, so the discrepancy is
named here instead of being smoothed over, and the next round starts by diffing the two verdicts' wall sets to
find it.

### 137.5 What this leaves

Three suites that used to trap now measure a value, which is the point of the instrument:

```
laser-line         initialize 0/0 0x3c  port 0x41820000 vs original 0xffffffff
laser-infinite     initialize 0/0 0x3c  port 0x41820000 vs original 0x0
bullet-manager     spawn 0/0 bullet 0 offset 0xc  port 8 vs original 0
```

All three are port-side, and all three are now reachable without a crash, which is what makes them reportable.

**not** close is the figure in section 135's own report, which says 44 null-base suites where its committed
verdict says 43. The mechanism is not established here, and the honest step is to name it rather than choose an
explanation: it is the sixth member of the family sections 122-124, 129.1, 132.4b and 133.2 recorded, and this
time the instrument that caught it was a **diff of two committed verdicts** rather than a re-reading.

### 138.4 What five suites at one address taught

One address, `0x454ee0`, held four suites and three distinct causes:

```
laser-line, laser-infinite   the argument comes from the global 0x4b44f4, and its field +0x488 was
                             past the end of a 0x480-byte manager
bullet-manager, enemy-...    the argument comes from [base+0x4debdc] with base = the suite's manager,
                             and +0x4debdc was past the end of a 0x46d680-byte manager
both                         the callee's first instruction then reads [argument+0x11c]
```

Three of the four lessons are the same lesson: a fixture whose object is a few bytes too short reads a zero and
hands the callee a null. The difference is only which object and which offset, and both were found the same way -
by moving the wall exactly one instruction and reading what the new address names. Nothing was fixed by reading
the C++ or by guessing a value; every step was a measurement whose effect the census then confirmed.

## 139. The next three-suite site: the null base is edi, and a boundary claim refuted before use

### 139.1 The site

`0x4067e0` holds three suites - `anm-scripts`, `shot-damage`, `shot-manager` - all faulting at
`address=0x78 pc=0x4067e0`, and it is not a leaf: the caller finder of section 134.3 lists **97** direct
callers. Its first instructions:

```
0x004067e0  mov ecx, [eax + 0x10]   ; the fault, at address 0x78
0x004067e3  mov edx, [esp + 4]
0x004067e7  test cl, 1
```

A read at `0x78` with the fault on `[eax+0x10]` means `eax` held `0x68`.

### 139.2 Measure the register, not the address

`eax = 0x68` is a value, not a cause: it is the first operand of a `lea`, and the base it adds to is what is
null. Hooking the callee and printing the frame gave the cause and the caller at once:

```
PROBE362 eax=0x68 ret=0x455b15 ebp=0x0
```

The return address names the call site, and reading forward to it shows the load:

```
0x00455b09  mov ecx, [esi + 0x14]
0x00455b0c  push ecx
0x00455b0d  lea eax, [edi + 0x68]   ; so edi = 0, and eax = 0x68
0x00455b10  call 0x4067e0
```

So the null base is **`edi`**, not `eax`, and `0x78 = 0x68 + 0x10` is exactly the address the artifact reported.
Reading the address alone would have sent the next round looking for a bad `eax`.

### 139.3 edi is a parameter, and it is never set

Scanning the ninety instructions from `0x455a00` for `edi` finds it used ten times and **loaded zero times**:

```
0x00455a27 mov ecx, edi     0x00455a3e mov ecx, edi     0x00455a5c mov eax, edi
0x00455a74 mov eax, edi     0x00455a9c mov ecx, edi     0x00455ab3 mov ecx, edi
0x00455ace mov eax, edi     0x00455ae6 mov eax, edi     0x00455b0d lea eax,[edi+0x68]
0x00455b15 mov edx, [edi + 0x3ec]
```

It is a parameter of this body, so whoever enters the body sets it - and the artifact's `entry=0x455a00` says the
suite called that address. The next step is to find the address the game itself enters this body at, by listing
the direct call targets in `[0x455800, 0x455a00]`, and then to call that instead or to set `edi` as it does.

### 139.4 A boundary claim refuted before it was written down

The instruction window tool answers with `0x4559d0 is a boundary in the sweep from entry 0x4559d0` when asked
about `0x4559d0`. That sentence is **self-referential** for whichever address is passed: it reports that the tool
started its sweep there, not that anything else refers there. Its content confirms it - `xor eax,0xf6000001`,
`or byte ptr [ebx+ecx+0x51], dh` - which is what misaligned decoding looks like.

Section 129.1 records the same tool producing a real finding from exactly this text, and section 134.3 records
`0x455a00` and `0x425cc0` being called directly by suites. So the claim "`0x4559d0` is the entry" was **not**
written into this plan: the tool's self-referential sentence was refuted before it became a section, which is the
first time in this lane that the §122-129 family's lesson was applied before the error rather than after it.

The probe was removed and `anm-scripts.test.mjs` is byte-identical to its committed state, so no suite and no
machine file changed and the census was **not** re-run. The committed verdict therefore still reads:

```

```

## 140. The true entry is found by who is called, and edi is a null argument

### 140.1 The caller finder learned to list targets

Section 135's tool answers "who calls this address"; the question here is the mirror - **which functions are
called from this range**. `tools/th-callers.py --targets LO HI` lists every direct call whose site lies in a
range, and it carries a known answer like the rest of the tool: the call at `0x40a835` to `0x454ee0`, found by
hand in section 132, must appear when the range contains it.

```
py -3 tools/th-callers.py IMAGE --targets 0x40a800 0x40a900
  0x0040a804 -> 0x00402520
  0x0040a835 -> 0x00454ee0        <- the known one
```

### 140.2 The entry, found by evidence rather than by a tool sentence

Section 139 refused to call `0x4559d0` the entry, because the only thing saying so was the window tool's
sentence about its own sweep start. The targets in `[0x455000, 0x455a00)` are a different kind of answer:

```
0x00454dba -> 0x00455630    0x00454eaa -> 0x00455630
0x00454f75 -> 0x00455630    0x004550a9 -> 0x00455630
0x004556db -> 0x00455580    0x004556ec -> 0x004553f0    then 16 more inside the body
```

Only two addresses in that whole range are ever called, `0x455630` and `0x455580`, and the second one is itself
called from inside the first. So the body containing `0x455a00` is entered at `0x455630`, and reading its head
confirms it:

```
0x0045563e  push edi
0x0045563f  mov edi, [ebp + 8]   ; edi is the function's first stack argument
0x0045564f  mov eax, [edi + 0x47c]
0x004556b5  lea eax, [edi + 0x68]   ; the same shape as 0x455b0d
0x004556bd  mov edx, [edi + 0x3ec]  ; and as 0x455b15
```

This is the evidence section 139 said was missing, and it also settles what `edi` is: not a field the caller
forgot to set, but the function's **first argument**.

### 140.3 What that means for the three suites

`edi` is null because whoever called `0x455630` passed null. The three suites - `anm-scripts`, `shot-damage`,
`shot-manager` - never call into that range at all, and none of them sets `EDI`; the wall is reached from inside
one of their own calls, most plausibly `m.call(touch(0x406100))`, which two of them use for shot timers. So the
next round follows that call to the site that reaches `0x455630` and reads what it passes, rather than guessing a
value for `edi`. The defect is on the **calling** path, which is a different kind of finding from sections 135-137,
where the object existed and was too small.

### 140.4 What changed

`tools/th-callers.py` gained the `--targets` mode and its self-test; no suite and no machine file changed, so the
census was not re-run and the committed verdict stands:

```

## 141. The anm wall is a null first argument, propagated through two functions

### 141.1 Where the wall is called from

Section 140 left off before the site that reaches `0x455630`. Reading forward from the function it belongs to
shows the argument, four times over, and it is always the same register:

```
0x00454db9  push esi
0x00454dba  call 0x455630
0x00454ea9  push esi
0x00454eaa  call 0x455630
```

So the null that becomes `edi` in `0x455630` is a null `esi` at the call site.

### 141.2 Finding the entry when nobody calls it

The function holding those sites is not called anywhere in `[0x454b30, 0x454dba)`, so the earlier "the entry is
what is called nearby" method has nothing to work with. The padding does: a run of `int3` ends a function, so the
last one before the sites names the next entry.

```
int3 padding at 0x454d0f, so the next function starts at 0x454d10
bytes at 0x454d10: 55 8b ec 83 e4 f8 51 53 8b 5d 0c 56
```

`push ebp; mov ebp, esp; and esp, -8; push ecx; push ebx; mov ebx, [ebp+0xc]; push esi` - a prologue, and the
head settles the question:

```
0x00454d10  push ebp
0x00454d11  mov ebp, esp
0x00454d18  mov ebx, [ebp + 0xc]
0x00454d1d  mov edi, ecx
0x00454d1f  mov eax, [edi + 0x11c]     ; the same shape as 0x454ee1
0x00454d25  cmp [eax + ebx*4], 0       ; and as 0x454ee7
0x00454d3c  mov esi, [ebp + 8]         ; esi IS the function's first argument
0x00454d46  mov [esi + 0x3ea], bx
```

So `esi` is `[ebp+8]`, the same argument that becomes `edi` in `0x455630`, which is pushed unchanged into the
call. The null is not created anywhere in this path; it arrives with the entry. The chain is:

```
0x454d10 (arg1 = 0) -> push esi -> 0x455630 (edi = arg1) -> lea eax,[edi+0x68] -> [eax+0x10] = address 0x78
```

### 141.3 The tool learned to reject its own false positives

The range mode of section 140 produced two kinds of wrong answer in its first listing, and both are now filtered
and documented: a target computed outside the image (`0x454b38 -> 0x-17ba67cf`) and a "call" into the `ret`/int3
padding that ends a function (`0x45487e -> 0x454b00`, whose first byte is `ret`). A target is kept only if it
lies inside a section and does not begin with int3, and the self-test - the call at `0x40a835` to `0x454ee0` -
still passes. The listing for `[0x454b30, 0x454dba)` is now empty, which is the honest answer: nothing calls that
function directly, and that is why the padding method was needed.

### 141.4 What that leaves for the three suites

The wall is the same in `anm-scripts`, `shot-damage` and `shot-manager`: a body reached with a null first
argument. The next step is on the calling path again - find the indirect call that enters `0x454d10` from the
suite's own call (`m.call(touch(0x406100))` is the likely one, used by two of the three for shot timers) and read
what it should have passed. No suite and no machine file changed this round, so the census was not re-run:

```
passing 22   trapping 60   leaks {"reported": 107, "total": 0, "scrubbed": 0}
```

## 142. The two suites do not share a path, and what an oracle hook returns to

### 142.1 A generalisation that was not measured

Section 141 ended by saying "the wall is the same in `anm-scripts`, `shot-damage` and `shot-manager`". Only
`anm-scripts` had been measured. Measuring `shot-manager` the same way - hook `0x454d10` and print the frame -
produces **nothing**: the hook never fires, and the emulator then faults as before.

So the claim was an over-generalisation, and the honest correction is that one suite was measured and the other
was assumed. What `shot-manager` actually reaches is measured next, by hooking the wall function itself:

```
PROBE365 eax=0x68 ecx=0x56d91824 ret=0x455b15
```

It reaches the **same call site** as `anm-scripts` - `ret=0x455b15` - without passing through `0x454d10`.

### 142.2 What is still true about 0x454d10, and what is not

Section 141.2 inferred "the entry is `0x454d10`" from a run of `int3`. Read out byte by byte, that run is real:

```
0x454d0b: cc   0x454d0c: cc   0x454d0d: cc   0x454d0e: cc   0x454d0f: cc   0x454d10: 55
```

Five bytes of padding followed by `push ebp`, so `0x454d10` **is** a padded function boundary and that part of
the inference survives. What does not survive is calling it the entry the suites use: the body containing both
`0x454dba` (which pushes `esi` into `0x455630`) and `0x455b15` (which is where the wall's frame returns) is
entered some **other** way, because `shot-manager` reaches it without executing `0x454d10`.

That other way is invisible to the instrument used: `--targets` lists **direct** calls only, and it is empty for
`[0x454b30, 0x454dba)`. The same limit was recorded in section 134.4 for `0x425cc0` and `0x424ea0`, which have no
direct callers either. So the next step is to find the indirect entry - a vtable slot or a function pointer - and
the place to look is what the suite's own call (`m.call(touch(0x406100))`) reaches.

### 142.3 A measured fact about the oracle's hooks

The same hook run shows its first line before the wall:

```
PROBE365 eax=0x2951540 ecx=0x0 ret=0x7f00000
```

A return address of `0x7f00000` is the value section 137 saw in a trap artifact's `stack` array and could not
explain, and the machine then refused `0x83debdc` as out of bounds. Put together: `0x7f00000` is where a replaced
function returns to, so a `m.replace` hook appears in a stack window as a return address. Section 137's reading of
that array was wrong; this is the missing half of why.

### 142.4 What changed

The probe was removed, `shot-manager.test.mjs` is byte-identical to its committed state, and no machine file
changed, so the census was not re-run:

```

```

## 143. A directly called guest entry needs its registers set, not only its arguments

### 143.1 The measurement that corrected the chain's owner

`shot-manager` calls `m.call(touch(0x406100), {args:[0]})`, and printing the mapping answers where that goes:

```
PROBE366 touch(0x406100) = 0x4067e0   np = 0x2950c10
```

It calls the **wall function itself**. So the `0x455630` / `0x454d10` body that sections 141 and 142 traced
belongs to **`anm-scripts`**, not to this suite; the shared call site `0x455b15` seen in section 142 is a
different path through the same code. That is the second over-attribution in two rounds and the same kind: a
chain measured in one suite was described as the suite class's chain. This time it was caught by printing one
address rather than by a later probe failing.

### 143.2 The fix, and what it shows about calling a guest entry

Before this round the suite set `EAX` and left `EDI` alone. The callee's first instruction uses `EAX`
(`mov ecx, [eax+0x10]`), so `EDI` looked irrelevant - and the wall moved the moment it was set:

```
m.reg('EAX', np + 0x930);
m.reg('EDI', np);                 <- added
m.call(touch(0x406100), {args:[0]});
```

```
shot-manager: 0x4067e0 -> 0x45568c
```

The lesson generalises past this suite: when a fixture calls a guest function **directly**, the machine plants
a return address and starts there, so every register the function's reachable path reads is the fixture's
responsibility - not only the arguments it passes. A callee whose first instruction uses one register can still
depend on another three calls down.

flipped to pass: 0      regressed: 0      walls moved: 1
shot-manager: 0x4067e0 -> 0x45568c
```

The count does not change, and the record says so: the trap **moved** rather than disappeared. What did change
is the composition of the site - `0x4067e0` held three suites and holds two - and where this suite traps next:

### 143.4 The new wall is in a known class

`0x45568c` is one of the garbage-base sites the class report already listed, with `anm-geometry` and
`player-motion`:

```

```

So `shot-manager` has moved out of the null-base class and into the garbage-base one, which is a next target
with two other suites behind it, and the same treatment - read the instruction, measure the register, then
complete the fixture - applies there.

## 144. The entry map of the region, and a padding rule that needs a run rather than a byte

### 144.1 What the shot-damage probe found instead

Section 143's rule was applied to the second suite at `0x4067e0` by setting `EDI` before the same
`m.call(touch(0x406100), ...)` that carries `shot-manager`'s fix. Nothing happened: the probe never printed and
the wall stayed at `0x4067e0` with `address=0x78`. The artifact explains why:

```
stack: ["0x455b15", "0x56d91824", "0x7f00000", ...]   entry: 0x455a00
```

`shot-damage` traps with `0x455b15` on its stack and `0x455a00` as its entry, so it does **not** call
`0x4067e0` directly at all - it takes the `0x455a00` path that section 142 measured for `anm-scripts`. The line
the fix was written on is not on its wall's path. The edit was reverted and the file is byte-identical to its
committed state.

This is the third time in this thread that a fix aimed at the right address landed on the wrong **path**, and
the pattern that catches it is the same each time: print the mapping, or hook the site, before editing.

### 144.2 The entry map of 0x454dba-0x455a00

Reading every run of `int3` in that region gives the boundaries, and two of them are real function entries:

```
0x454ed4-0x454edf (12 bytes) -> 0x454ee0   57 8b b9 1c 01 00 00      push edi; mov edi,[ecx+0x11c]
0x455624-0x45562f (12 bytes) -> 0x455630   55 8b ec 83 e4 f8 81 ec d4 00 00 00 53 56
                                            push ebp; mov ebp,esp; and esp,-8; sub esp,0xd4; push ebx; push esi
```

and the region between `0x455630` and `0x455a00` contains **no** boundary at all, so

```
0x455630  <  0x455a00  <  0x455b15
```

`0x455a00` is **inside** the function that starts at `0x455630`. The artifact's `entry=0x455a00` is therefore
not a function entry but an address inside one, which is consistent with section 140's finding that this body
takes its object from `[ebp+8]`: entered at `0x455a00`, the prologue at `0x455630` never ran, so `ebp` is stale
and the argument slot it reads holds whatever the machine left there.

It also places `shot-manager`'s new wall: `0x45568c` is inside the same function as `0x455a00`, so that suite did
not leave this body, it moved to a different instruction in it.

### 144.3 The padding rule, corrected

Section 141.2 and section 142.2 both leaned on "a run of int3 ends a function". The run has to be a **run**: this
region contains many single `0xCC` bytes inside code - `0x454dc0`, `0x454def`, `0x454f7b`, `0x4550af`, `0x455172`,
`0x455193`, `0x4557a4`, `0x4557f6` - and the bytes after several of them are ordinary instructions, not
prologues. Only the multi-byte runs are padding:

```
0x454ed4-0x454edf  0x454f99-0x454f9f  0x4550bd-0x4550bf  0x4551a2-0x4551af
0x4553e8-0x4553ef  0x4554c3-0x4554cf  0x455572-0x45557f  0x4555e8-0x4555ef
0x455624-0x45562f
```

so the corrected rule is: a function entry is where a **run** of at least two `int3` bytes ends, and even then
the first instruction should look like a prologue before it is believed.

### 144.4 What is next

The chain is now: this body's object arrives in `[ebp+8]`, the caller that supplies it is the one reaching
`0x454d10` (four direct sites, all inside another body), and that body's own `esi` came from the same slot. The
next step climbs one level with the tools already built - list call targets around the four sites' containing
run of code, and read what each site pushes - rather than editing a suite line that a stack frame says is not on
the path.

No suite and no machine file changed this round, so the census was not re-run:

## 145. What the artifact's entry really is, and a call site that never runs

### 145.1 The measurement that failed to fire

Sections 142 and 144 both rested on an artifact line: `shot-damage` traps with `0x455b15` on its stack and
`entry=0x455a00`, which was read as "this suite takes the `0x455a00` path". Hooking `0x455630` **and** `0x454d10`
in that suite produces neither line:

```
(no PROBE368 output; the emulator faults as before)
```

So neither address is executed by `shot-damage`, and `0x455b15` is a value sitting in stack memory, not a live
return address. The same reasoning that section 144 applied to `0x454d10` applies to its own evidence: presence
in a stack window is not proof that the frame is live.

The two probes were removed by restoring the file from `HEAD`, so `shot-damage.test.mjs` is byte-identical to
its committed state.

### 145.2 What `entry` actually records

Read from the machine rather than inferred, `machine.mjs` line 266 sets it in the trap builder:

```js
this.fault.calls=this.calls; this.fault.entry=hex(address); this.fault.stubs=this.stubSummary();
```

`entry` is the **address the JavaScript side asked `m.call` to enter** - not a function boundary, not the
deepest frame, and not a return address. So an artifact's `entry` names one of the fixture's own calls, and a
value like `0x455a00` has to be found among the calls the fixtures make. `shot-damage`'s own `touch` addresses
all map elsewhere:

```
th11 0x406100 -> th12 0x4067e0
th11 0x4a5714 -> th12 0x4a5714
th11 0x4a8eb4 -> th12 0x4b4514
```

and `anm-scripts` contains no `touch(0x...)` call at all. So the call that enters `0x455a00` is made by shared
fixture code - the anm oracle wrapper is the obvious candidate - not by the suite under test, which is why
editing a suite line could not move this wall.

### 145.3 Three rounds of the same mistake, now with the rule written down

The pattern is worth stating plainly, because it has cost four corrections:

- section 142 read an `entry` value as proof of a path and was wrong about which suite owned it;
- section 143 set `EDI` on a line that looked right and was not on the wall's path;
- section 144 read `0x455a00` as an address inside a function and drew a conclusion about which entry the
  fixture used;
- this section shows that the address is not executed at all by that suite.

The rule that would have caught all four is one sentence: **before asserting a path, hook the address and see
the line print.** Everything else - the entry map, the call list, the stack window - is consistent with a path
that is not taken.

### 145.4 What is next

Find the `m.call` that passes `0x455a00`: it is in the shared fixture code (`anm-oracle.mjs` or a helper it
imports), and when the target is an interior address the fix is to call the function's entry instead. That is
also the shape of section 144's entry map - `0x455630` is the entry of the function containing `0x455a00` - but
the map should be used to **choose a hook**, not to conclude a path.

## 146. The trail ends at a named fixture line, and a mapping divergence behind it

### 146.1 The call that enters 0x455a00

Section 145 ended with "find the `m.call` that passes `0x455a00`". It is in the shared anm oracle, and reading
it gives the whole convention at once:

```js
spawn(resource, script, layer, mode = 0) {
  m.reg('ESI', handle);
  m.call([touch(0x455a00), touch(0x455df0), touch(0x455bc0), touch(0x456020)][mode],
         {args: [resource, script, layer]});
  return m.u32(handle);
}
```

with `handle = m.allocate(4)` further up. So the fixture pushes three stack arguments - which is exactly right
for a function with a standard prologue, since `[ebp+8]` would then be `resource` - and reads the result from the
four-electron slot `ESI` points at.

### 146.2 The hypothesis, and one line of evidence for it

If the only defect were the target address, calling the function's real entry instead should fix it. One line was
changed - `touch(0x455a00)` to the raw `0x455630` - and three suites were run:

```
anm-scripts:   wall 0x45568c          (was 0x4067e0)
shot-damage:   assertion, actual 0, expected 1     (no emulator trap)
shot-manager:  assertion, actual 0, expected 1     (no emulator trap)
```

It is half right. `anm-scripts` moves to `0x45568c` - the **same** wall `shot-manager` reached in section 366,
which is convergence rather than coincidence - but the other two stop trapping and start failing the handle
contract, because the real th12 entry does not write the result through `ESI` the way the th11 body did.

So this is not a one-line fix and the change was **reverted**; `anm-oracle.mjs` is byte-identical to its
committed state and the census was not re-run. What the experiment measured is worth keeping:

### 146.3 The divergence it exposes

`touch(0x455a00)` returns `0x455a00` - the mapping is the identity - and the fixture reads that as "the th11
anm spawn function also starts at this th12 address". Section 144 says otherwise: in the th12 image `0x455a00`
is **inside** the function that starts at `0x455630`, so entering there runs code from the middle of another
function, with no prologue and with `ebp` left at whatever the machine plants.

That makes this the first point in the whole trail that ends at a **named, fixable port-side object**: the
oracle's address mapping for this entry. The fix is two-part and belongs together:

1. `fixture-addresses.mjs`: map the th11 anm spawn entry to th12's real entry `0x455630` rather than to an
   identity;
2. `anm-oracle.mjs`: adapt the call convention to the entry's actual signature (its first argument in
   `[ebp+8]`, and its result not in the `ESI` slot) instead of the th11 shape.

Doing only the second, or only the first, is what produced two assertion failures and a moved wall - which is
the evidence that both halves are needed.

## 147. Two candidate entries measured and excluded, with the numbers

### 147.1 What the assertion actually compares

Section 146 read the two assertion failures as "the handle contract broke". Reading the suite line instead says
what it is really comparing:

```js
const option = c.anm_manager_spawn(manager, a, 0, 22, 0), id = read(option);
assert.equal(o.spawn(original, 0, 22), id);          // shot-manager.test.mjs:34
```

This is a **1:1 comparison**: the oracle's `spawn` result against the C++ core's handle. So `actual 0, expected
1` means the oracle returned zero where the core returned a real pointer - a fidelity miss, which is a stronger
statement than "the fixture broke".

### 147.2 The arguments are right at 0x455630

Retargeting the fixture to the real entry and hooking it prints the whole frame:

```
PROBE370 args=0x294e0f0,0x0,0x16 ret=0x7f00000 ecx=0x0 eax=0x2951540 esi=0x27c1060 ebp=0x0
```

`resource`, `script` and `layer` arrive exactly as the fixture pushed them, `ESI` holds the handle slot, and the
machine has planted `0x7f00000` as the return. With a proper prologue `[ebp+8]` is therefore `resource` - the
object the function expects. The arguments are not the problem.

### 147.3 What the function returns, and what it does not

Removing the hook so the body runs, and reading every place the result could be:

```
PROBE370B slot=0x0 eax=0x0 callReturn=0
```

The `ESI` slot is not written, `EAX` is zero, and the machine's return is zero. Setting `ECX` to the manager
before the call - the thiscall shape the fixture's other methods use - changes none of it:

```
PROBE370B slot=0x0 eax=0x0 callReturn=0
```

So `0x455630` accepts the arguments and produces no handle, which excludes it as the spawn entry the fixture
needs, and the same measurement excludes `touch(0x455a00)` for the opposite reason: entered there, the machine
traps at `0x4067e0`. Two candidates, two different failures, both recorded with their numbers rather than
described.

The oracle's spawn has to return the same pointer the core's `anm_manager_spawn` returns. Neither address does
that, so the th12 entry is still unidentified, and the useful next instrument is not another guessed address but
the core's own behaviour: the suite already has `id = read(option)`, so a temporary print of that value names
