## 233. The frame mapping, corrected - and the block cleared

### 233.1 Withdrawal: section 232.2's conclusion

Section 232.2 reported a measurement and then drew the wrong conclusion from it. The measurement was right: placing
values at `base+0xc` and `base+0x10` put them at stack indices six and seven, and a second run showed the block
reading **index seven**, since the fault register took that value. But the pair placed was `{ pointer, count }`
while the pair the function stores is `{ count, pointer }` in the other direction, and the conclusion then moved in
the wrong direction as well.

**Withdrawn: section 232.2's "`[esp+0x18]` is `base+0x14` and `[esp+0x1c]` is `base+0x18`".** The measured mapping
is

```
base+0xc  -> stack index 6
base+0x10 -> stack index 7  = [esp+0x18] at the block   <- the pointer
base+0x14 -> stack index 8  = [esp+0x1c]                <- the count
```

so the two stores are `base+0x10` for the pointer and `base+0x14` for the count. This is a **twenty-sixth named
failure mode**: *reading back a swapped pair as a mapping* - two values written in one order, measured in the
other, and the index inferred from the wrong member of the pair, which then displaces the conclusion by one slot.

### 233.2 The block now runs to its end

With the corrected offsets, the fault leaves the block entirely:

```
{"address": "0x130", "size": 4, "pc": "0x4615cc", "regs": "EAX=0x17 EBX=0x17 ECX=0x0 EDX=0x2ff8518 ESI=0x2ff8564 EDI=0x0 EBP=0x0"}
```

The register holds the pointer the block loaded, and the stack shows `0x43a118`, the return address of the call at
`0x43a113`, so execution ran the whole block - the divisibility test, the state byte, the handle resolve, the float,
the release by id, the handle cleared, the second state-byte test - and reached the call at the end of it.

### 233.3 The wall class again

The new fault is at `0x4615cc`, which is already in the wall-class list as `null-base 0x4615cc x3`. That is the
third time in this chain - after the handle accessor and the same function's earlier wall - that a recorded wall
class turns out to be the same missing fixture pattern the title screen is walking into.

## 234. The entity creation call, and a trap deep in the render path

### 234.1 The function the block calls

```
0x004615a0  sub esp, 0xc
0x004615a3  test dword ptr [0x4cee78], 0x8000
0x004615ad  push ebx / ebp
0x004615af  mov ebp, dword ptr [esp+0x18]   ; -> [ebp+4] at entry = the FIRST STACK ARGUMENT
0x004615b3  push esi / edi
0x004615b5  mov ebx, eax                     ; a category
0x004615b7  mov edi, ecx
0x004615b9  je 0x4615cc
0x004615bb  push 0x4cf1d0 ; call [0x498088] ; inc byte [0x4cf221]   ; a scope timer, skipped normally
0x004615cc  inc dword ptr [ebp+0x130]        ; <- the trap: a counter in the argument
0x004615d2  call 0x4621c0                    ; create a record
0x004615d7  mov esi, eax
0x004615d9  test ebx, ebx ; jl
0x004615dd  mov dword ptr [esi+0x20], ebx
0x004615e0  or dword ptr [esi+0x480], 1
```

So it increments a counter in the structure it is given, creates a record, writes the category into it and flags
it. A hundred and forty-two call sites use it.

### 234.2 Why the argument was zero

The block's call sequence pushes four words before this call:

```
0x43a0f3  push 0
0x43a102  push eax            ; eax = 5
0x43a10a  push ecx            ; ecx = lea [esp+0x28]
0x43a10b  push eax            ; eax = [edx+0x10], and edx is obj+0xa58
0x43a113  call 0x4615a0
```

The first stack argument is the **last** pushed, `[obj+0xa58+0x10]` - which is `obj+0xa68`, a field the
constructor clears. The fixture's object had it zero, so the counter increment dereferenced zero. Supplying a
zeroed sub-structure there moves the fault out of this function entirely.

### 234.3 The measured result

```
{"address": "0x14", "size": 4, "pc": "0x454d25", "regs": "EAX=0x0 EBX=0x5 ECX=0x3004260 EDX=0x0 ESI=0x3889b30 EDI=0x3004260 EBP=0x7effebc"}
```

The fault is now far from the block, in the render path, with a return address from the entity-creation function
above it on the stack. The chain has gone from a state byte, through a handle resolve and release, through an
entity creation, and into drawing.

### 234.4 The same shape, a third time

Three times now the missing piece has been **a pointer the original always has and the fixture leaves zero**: the
state pointer at `obj+0xacc`, the handle at `obj+0xa70+0x34`, and now the sub-structure at `obj+0xa68`. The
recurring form is worth naming: *an object field that the original's start-up populates and the fixture's zeroed
block does not*, which is exactly the open question of section 227.3, now seen from a third direction.

## 235. A per-category array, and the question moving up a level

### 235.1 The instruction that traps

```
0x00454d10  push ebp ; mov ebp,esp ; and esp,0xfffffff8
0x00454d18  mov ebx, dword ptr [ebp+0xc]   ; a category - the second stack argument
0x00454d1d  mov edi, ecx                   ; this - the record
0x00454d1f  mov eax, dword ptr [edi+0x11c]  ; a field of the record
0x00454d25  cmp dword ptr [eax + ebx*4], 0  ; <- the trap: the field is zero
```

`[record+0x11c]` is a **pointer to an array indexed by category**, and it is zero, so the indexed read addresses a
small offset and faults. The category is the function's second argument and the record is its `this`.

### 235.2 Why this instance is different

The previous three instances of the same shape were fields of the title object - an object the fixture had zeroed
itself. This one is a field of a record that **the original's own create call produced** a few instructions earlier:

```
0x43a113  call 0x4615a0     ; the entity creation call
0x4615d2  call 0x4621c0     ; which creates the record
```

So the fixture did not leave this field zero; the original's create function did. Which means the create function
itself is working from something the fixture has not supplied - a template, table or manager - and **the question
has moved up one level**, from "which beacon the title object did not have" to "what the record factory needs".

That is a better question than the previous three, because the record factory is called from a hundred and forty-two
sites, so whatever it needs is needed by the whole engine and not by the title screen alone.

## 236. The record factory is a pool over the manager

### 236.1 The factory

```
0x004621c3  mov edi, dword ptr [0x4ce8cc]     ; the manager - the SAME global as the handle lookup
0x004621c9  mov eax, dword ptr [edi+0x4b50bc] ; a free-slot cursor
0x004621d1  imul ecx, eax, 0x4b4              ; record size is 0x4b4
0x004621d7  cmp byte ptr [eax+edi+0x4b40bc], 0 ; an in-use flag per slot
0x004621df  lea ebp, [ecx + edi + 0xbc]       ; record = manager + 0xbc + slot*0x4b4
0x004621ff  mov dword ptr [edi+0x4b50bc], eax ; advance the cursor, wrapping
0x00462205  cmp byte ptr [eax+edi+0x4b40bc], 0
0x00462214  je 0x462246                       ; a free slot: reuse it
0x00462216  push 0x4b4 ; call 0x46c9ea        ; exhausted: operator new(0x4b4)
0x00462229  call 0x4027e0                     ; construct
```

So the factory is a **fixed-size pool inside the manager object**: a cursor, an in-use byte per slot, and slot
storage of `0x4b4` bytes each starting `0xbc` into the manager.

### 236.2 The fake manager is the cause

The fixture pointed `0x4ce8cc` at a zeroed block. That block was large enough that nothing faulted, which is why
this went unnoticed: the cursor read zero, the in-use byte read zero - meaning "free" - and the record was taken
straight out of the zeroed storage. So the record was **all zeros**, and its per-category array was zero, and the
trap of section 235 followed.

**This resolves the "same shape a fourth time".** The missing thing is not four separate fields; it is **the real
manager object**. And that makes section 227.3's open question concrete and answerable: the manager at `[0x4ce8cc]`
is constructed by something at start-up, and every one of the factory's hundred and forty-two call sites and the
handle lookup both depend on it. Getting it right serves the engine, not one screen.

### 236.3 Other readers and writers of the field

Thirty-six instructions address `[reg+0x11c]`. The writers are `0x40156f`, `0x404d07`, `0x404d31` (two clears),
`0x40ea80`, `0x40f2b3`, `0x43e42f` and `0x43ebdd` - the last two inside the title region, which makes them
candidates for the initialisation pass this section is looking for.

## 237. The manager has one writer, and two negatives about using it

### 237.1 The single writer

Searching the section for stores to `0x4ce8cc` finds **exactly one**, the same shape as the player object's:

```
0x0044f762  push 0x88ed54
0x0044f767  call 0x46c9ea                  ; operator new(0x88ed54)
0x0044f771  cmp eax, ebx ; je
0x0044f775  push eax
0x0044f776  call 0x45dfa0                  ; the manager's constructor
0x0044f77d  xor eax, eax
0x0044f77f  mov dword ptr [0x4ce8cc], eax
0x0044f784  cmp dword ptr [0x4ce9fc], ebx
```

So the manager is `0x88ed54` bytes and is built by `0x45dfa0`. The global has four hundred and twenty-three
references. **The fixture's fake manager was `0x8856c4` bytes - smaller than the real object** - which is a defect
of the fake in its own right, on top of the pool problem of section 236.

### 237.2 Negative: the global is not populated at the fixture's setup point

Using whatever `0x4ce8cc` already held, instead of pointing it at a fake:

```
pc 0x454d25   address 0x14   (identical to the fake-manager run, same stack)
```

The fault did not move, so at the point the fixture assembles its state the global is not a working manager. The
host harness does not run the original's start-up, which the whole chain has been assuming in effect.

### 237.3 Negative: the constructor is not self-contained

Calling the original's own constructor on a correctly sized zeroed block, exactly as the original does:

```
entry 0x45dfa0
pc 0x4623c1   address 0x18   trap inside the constructor
UC_ERR ... uc_emu_start failed with code 6
```

The constructor faults inside its own subtree, so it cannot be run standalone either: it depends on state that
earlier start-up would have built.

### 237.4 What this means, recorded rather than worked around

Put the two negatives together and the method reaches its limit. Building the engine's start-up forward, one
measured field at a time, has taken the chain a long way - from a state byte through a handle resolve and release,
an entity creation, a record pool and into the render path - but the point at which it stops working is now
identifiable: **the fixture needs the original's real initialisation order, not more hand-built fields.** That is a
different kind of change from every round since section 226, and it is the honest conclusion rather than a
workaround.

Nothing: both experiments of this round were undone and the test file is back at the committed state, whose fault
is the furthest verified progress (section 235's `0x454d25`). The census was not re-run:

```

## 238. Outward from the manager to the start-up region

### 238.1 The image

```
.text   0x401000  0x96c00
.rdata  0x498000  0x15000
.data   0x4ad000   0x6a00
.rsrc   0x4d7000   0x1600
AddressOfEntryPoint = RVA 0x6e81d  ->  VA 0x46e81d
```

A units slip worth recording: the first report of this round printed the entry as an RVA and read it as a virtual
address, which put it outside the section and looked like a non-standard entry. It is an ordinary one - the RVA has
to be added to the image base like any other.

### 238.2 The functions around the manager

The region's callers, found by collecting every relative call whose target falls in it:

```
0x44f0a0  <- 0x44ef80, 0x44efa3
0x44f180  <- 0x46ca3b
0x44f200  <- 0x44fb7f, 0x44fdb1
0x44f2c0  <- 0x44fd1b
0x44f370  <- 0x44f994, 0x450373, 0x4505a4, 0x4507a7
0x44f400  <- 0x44f9c4, 0x45038a, 0x4505bb, 0x4507be
0x44f4b0  <- 0x450825
0x44f560  <- 0x46e7ad          <- the entry region
```

The manager is created inside the function entered at `0x44f560`, whose only caller is `0x46e7ad` - and `0x46e...`
is the region the process entry point `0x46e81d` sits in. So the upward chain from the manager reaches the
original's start-up directly, which is what section 237.6 needed.

A note on method: a backwards scan to a `CC` boundary put this function's entry in the middle of an instruction and
reported no callers. Collecting call targets instead is the reliable direction here, and it is the same lesson as
section 223's five-bytes-early label, from the other side.

### 238.3 The manager is a set of subsystems

One of the neighbouring functions writes nothing but reads the manager heavily:

```
0x44f375  mov edi, [0x4ce8cc]
0x44f37b  add edi, 0x4b50c0
0x44f390  mov eax, [edi]
0x44f398  cmp dword ptr [eax+0x10c], ebp
0x44f3a2  mov ecx, [eax+0x120]
0x44f3aa  test byte ptr [ecx+0x10], bl
```

A slot table with counts and liveness bytes, inside the manager, at yet another offset. The manager is not one
structure but a set of subsystems hung off fixed offsets - which is why a hand-built stand-in cannot work and why a
zeroed one produces zeroed records.

## 239. The entry chain, winmain's initialisation, and the decision

### 239.1 The chain

```
0x0046e81d  call 0x47b369                ; CRT entry
0x0046e822  jmp 0x46e69f                  ; mainCRTStartup
...
0x0046e7a8  push 0x400000                 ; the image base = hInstance
0x0046e7ad  call 0x44f560                 ; WinMain
```

`0x44f560` has exactly one caller, and it is this one. The manager is created inside it. So the start-up chain is
entry -> CRT -> `WinMain` -> manager, and the question of section 237.6 is now about one function.

### 239.2 WinMain's initialisation

```
0x0044f560  push ebp ; mov ebp,esp ; and esp,0xfffffff8 ; sub esp,0x12c
0x0044f56c  mov eax,[0x4ad138] ; xor eax,esp ; mov [esp+0x128],eax   ; the SEH cookie
0x0044f57a  mov eax,[ebp+8]                                          ; hInstance
0x0044f58c  mov [0x4cf3f8],eax
0x0044f591  call [0x498294]                                          ; an OS/CRT call
0x0044f597  push 4 ; call 0x46c9ea                                   ; operator new(4)
0x0044f5ab  or dword ptr [0x4cee78],0x8000                           ; a global flag
0x0044f5b5  mov [0x4ce898],eax
0x0044f5ba  mov edi,0x4cf0f8 ; mov esi,0xc
0x0044f5c4  push edi ; call [0x498090] ; add edi,0x18 ; sub esi,1 ; jne   ; twelve 0x18-byte objects
0x0044f5d3  push 0x4a24cc ; mov ecx,0x4b0ec8 ; call 0x464220              ; a global object's constructor
0x0044f5e5  push 0x4a2974 ; push 1 ; push ebx ; call [0x4980e8]
0x0044f5f3  mov [0x4d4ea8],eax
0x0044f5f8  call [0x4980e4] ; cmp eax,0xb7 ; jne 0x44f61c
0x0044f61c  call 0x451530 ; cmp eax,-1 ; je 0x44fb99                ; failure path
```

**A cross-confirmation worth recording**: the flag `0x44f5ab` sets - `or dword ptr [0x4cee78],0x8000` - is exactly the
flag the entity-creation function of section 234 tests to decide whether to take its scope-timer branch. Two
independent readings of the image have landed on the same global, which is the kind of agreement that makes an
interpretation worth trusting.

### 239.3 The decision

Section 237.6 asked whether to run the original's real start-up in the fixture instead of synthesising its results.
With the chain above, the answer is yes, and it is now concrete: run `WinMain`, let it perform its initialisation,
and stop it before the main loop. The stop has a natural mechanism - the oracle can replace one address, so stubbing
the loop call makes `WinMain` return with everything initialised.

The alternative - continuing to hand-build the manager's contents - is now known to be hopeless in principle: the
manager is a set of subsystems at fixed offsets, and section 237 showed a hand-built stand-in produces silently
zeroed records.

## 240. WinMain runs in the fixture, and stops one function from the manager

### 240.1 The probe

Section 239 decided to run the original's real start-up rather than synthesise it. That decision was tested with a
standalone probe - not a keeper suite - that loads the oracle, reads the manager global, calls `WinMain` exactly as
the CRT start-up does, and reads the global again:

```
[0x4ce8cc] before: 0x0
m.call(0x44f560, {args:[0x400000, 0, 0, 1]})
```

### 240.2 What was measured

```
before: [0x4ce8cc]=0x0
threw:  Unicorn.js: uc_emu_start failed with code 8 (UC_ERR_FETCH_UNMAPPED)
fault:  pc=0x0  address=0x0  type=21
regs:   EAX=0x0 EBX=0x0 ECX=0x1 EDX=0x7effb84 ESI=0x105 EDI=0x7effb84 EBP=0x7effee8
stack:  0xbcaf1d76, 0x44f621, 0x0, 0x1, 0x4a2974, ...
after:  [0x4ce8cc]=0x0
```

Two facts, both measured rather than inferred. First, **the manager was still not created**: execution never
reached `0x44f762`. Second, and more important, **everything before that point ran**. The CRT entry, the OS call,
`operator new(4)`, the `0x8000` flag store, the twelve-object loop, the global object's constructor and the Win32
calls all completed, because the next instruction to fault is inside the call at `0x44f61c`, whose return address
`0x44f621` is sitting on the stack exactly where it belongs.

So the failure is an indirect transfer to address zero inside `0x451530`'s subtree - `EAX=0` at the fault - which is
the classic signature of a table entry that was never filled.

### 240.3 Why this is the round's result

Section 239's decision was made from reading; this section is its measurement, and the measurement supports it. The
wall has moved from "the fixture has no engine" to **"the engine's own initialisation, one function away from the
manager"**. That is a different kind of obstacle from every one the chain has hit so far: the previous walls were
fields the fixture had not supplied, and this one is a table the original fills during its own start-up.

### 240.4 What changed

No source file changed this round; the probe is a temporary instrument. The keeper suites were not touched and the

## 241. The start-up function works out the game directory

### 241.1 What 0x451530 does

```
0x0045153d  mov dword ptr [esp+0x260], eax          ; the SEH cookie again
0x00451546  push 0x40
0x0045154c  push 0
0x0045154e  push eax
0x0045154f  mov dword ptr [esp+0x18], 0x44
0x00451557  call 0x477420
0x0045155f  push 0x105                              ; 261 = MAX_PATH
0x00451564  lea ecx, [esp+0x160]
0x0045156b  push ecx
0x0045156c  push 0
0x0045156e  call dword ptr [0x4980b4]                ; GetModuleFileNameA(NULL, buf, 261)
0x00451574  push 0x105
0x00451579  lea edx, [esp+0x58]
0x0045157d  push edx
0x0045157e  call dword ptr [0x4980d8]                ; a second 261-byte path call
0x00451584  lea eax, [esp+0xc]
0x00451588  push eax
0x00451589  call dword ptr [0x4981bc]                ; a third call returning a pointer
0x0045158f  mov eax, dword ptr [esp+0x18]
0x00451593  test eax, eax ; je 0x45165e
0x0045159e  call 0x46d260                            ; with 0x2e pushed: a strchr-style scan for '.'
0x004515ad  call 0x463df0
0x004515c8  call 0x46e3f8                            ; with 0x4a299c: a strcmp-style compare
0x0045164e  mov byte ptr [0x4cf418], 1               ; a flag, on one of the paths
```

Two `push 0x105` calls with a null first argument, a third returning a pointer, then scanning for a dot and
comparing against a string constant: this is the function that works out **where the executable is and what it is
called** - the game's own directory resolution. It is the first thing in the original that has to succeed before
the manager exists, and it is why a bare fixture cannot get past it: it asks the operating system a question.

### 241.2 The fault is one of three IAT reads

All three indirect calls read their target from `.rdata` - an import address table slot, not a game table:

```
0x4980b4, 0x4980d8, 0x4981bc
```

One of them transferred to zero, and `EAX=0` at the fault is consistent with that. So in the fixture, **at least one
of these slots was never bound**.

**The paradox worth recording**: `WinMain` got past its own early OS calls, including a successful
`call dword ptr [0x4980e8]` at `0x44f5f1`. So some slots are bound and others are not, which rules out the simple
reading that the loader bound nothing. What is left is specific: these three names are missing from whatever binds
the import surface.

`ESI=0x105` at the fault is consistent with the code having just pushed `0x105` - the MAX_PATH constant - two
instructions before.

## 242. The slots are bound, and the inference is withdrawn

### 242.1 Negative

Section 241.2 inferred, from a transfer to zero at an indirect call, that at least one import address table slot had
never been bound. Dumping the slots refutes it:

```
slot 0x4980b4 = 0x7e00370   KERNEL32.dll!GetModuleFileNameA
slot 0x4980d8 = 0x7e00400   KERNEL32.dll!GetConsoleTitleA
slot 0x4981bc = 0x7e00790   KERNEL32.dll!GetStartupInfoA
slot 0x4980e8 = 0x7e00440   KERNEL32.dll!CreateMutexA
slot 0x4980e4 = 0x7e00430   KERNEL32.dll!GetLastError
slot 0x498240 = 0x7e00990   USER32.dll!ShowCursor
slot 0x498294 = 0x7e00160   WINMM.dll!timeBeginPeriod
```

Every one is bound, and every one points into the stub region the harness registers. So the inference was wrong, and
it is withdrawn here rather than left standing.

### 242.2 What the refutation points at instead

The transfer to zero was not a missing binding. It was a **stack imbalance around a bound stub** - and that failure
mode is already documented in this harness, in the comment beside its import table: a stdcall stub registered with
the wrong argument count leaves the callee's stack bytes behind, and the caller's next return pops a stale word.

That is consistent with everything measured. The three calls at `0x45156e`, `0x45157e` and `0x451589` are stdcall
calls to `GetModuleFileNameA` (three arguments), `GetConsoleTitleA` (two) and `GetStartupInfoA` (one), and the fault
arrived with `EAX=0` and a return address on the stack - the signature of a returned call followed by a wrong pop
rather than of a call through a null pointer.

### 242.3 The named failure mode

The twenty-seventh: **inferring a missing binding from a null transfer, when the binding existed and the argument
count was wrong.** The evidence for the wrong inference was a fault address; the evidence against it was four
bytes of table. The habit this adds is to read the table before naming its absence.

## 243. The binding mechanism, an arity repair, and a second refutation

### 243.1 The mechanism

```
machine.mjs:52   for(const entry of this.image.imports) this.u32(entry.address, this.registerImport(entry));
machine.mjs:89   registerImport(entry){ ... const existing=this.stubByKey?.get(key); ... }
machine.mjs:99   replace(address,name,handler,argc=0){ ... if(importMap.has(target)) importMap.set(target,{...,argc}); ... }
```

The load-time binding pass hands `registerImport` the image's import record, which carries a dll, a name and an
address and **no argument count** - as the note beside the harness's table already says. So every import bound at
load gets the default of zero arguments. The imbalance is therefore **systematic, not local to the three calls that
presented it**. `replace` updates the argument count of an existing stub in place, which gives the repair a home.

### 243.2 The repair

`helpers.mjs` now re-registers the three names start-up calls with their real arities - `GetModuleFileNameA` three,
`GetConsoleTitleA` two, `GetStartupInfoA` one - by finding their already-bound stub and calling `replace` on it. The
stub's address does not change, so a second binding would have been pointless.

The repair stays, because it is right by the documented contract of the harness's own import table and it makes the

## 244. The witness names the cause: a cookie check, and a stub that returned

### 244.1 The recording

The trap artifact's ordered trace, read oldest first, ends like this:

```
import  kernel32.dll!GetModuleFileNameA   ret=0x451574
import  kernel32.dll!GetConsoleTitleA     ret=0x451584
import  kernel32.dll!GetStartupInfoA      ret=0x45158f
import  kernel32.dll!IsDebuggerPresent    ret=0x46e8e8
import  kernel32.dll!SetUnhandledExceptionFilter  ret=0x46e8fd
import  kernel32.dll!UnhandledExceptionFilter     ret=0x46e908  args=["0x49cd68", ...]
import  kernel32.dll!GetCurrentProcess            ret=0x46e924
import  kernel32.dll!TerminateProcess             ret=0x46e92b  args=["0xffffffff", "0xc0000409", ...]
unmapped  type=21  address=0x0  size=1  pc=0x0     code: "Guest memory bounds 0x0 + 16"
```

### 244.2 What it says

`0xc0000409` is `STATUS_STACK_BUFFER_OVERRUN`, and the sequence around it - a debugger query, a filter
installation, the filter itself, the current process, and a terminate with that code - is the CRT's fixed
`__report_gsfailure` path. So the cause is a **security cookie check that failed**, and the run was already in the
CRT's abort path before the address-zero fetch.

**And the address-zero fetch is a consequence, not the cause.** `TerminateProcess` is stubbed in this harness and the
stub returns; a function that never returns in reality therefore fell through into its own unreachable tail and
fetched whatever the next bytes decoded as. The `pc=0` that two rounds were spent reasoning about is this.

### 244.3 Two corrections

First, the premise of sections 241 and 242 was wrong in a smaller way than either withdrawal said. The three path
calls at `0x451530` did not fail: their return addresses are on the recorded stack and the trace shows all three
returning normally, with `GetStartupInfoA` the last of them. There was never a transfer to zero inside that
function.

Second, a general lesson worth naming: **a stubbed terminating API that returns lets its caller run into code that
is unreachable in reality.** The correct host behaviour for `TerminateProcess` is to end the run, not to return zero.

### 244.4 What this leaves

The cookie mismatch itself is the next question, and it is now a small one: `0x451530` stores the cookie from
`0x4ad138` into its frame and checks it later, and `__security_init_cookie` ran during the same call (the trace
shows the CRT region `0x46e8..` as the return addresses of those imports). Whether the cookie changed between store
and check, or the check compares against a slot the fixture disturbed, is one reading of one function away - and it
is a question about the fixture's stack, not about the game.

```

## 246. The stub mechanism, read rather than inferred

### 246.1 The implementation, verbatim

```
L90   const key=(entry.dll||'')+'!'+(entry.name||'');
L93   const existing=this.stubByKey?.get(key);
L94   if(existing!==undefined){this.importMap.set(existing,entry);return existing;}
L95   const address=this.stubAddress;this.stubAddress+=16;
L96   if(this.stubByKey)this.stubByKey.set(key,address);
L97   this.importMap.set(address,entry);this.cpu.mem_write(address,[0xc3]);return address;
L99   replace(address,name,handler,argc=0){
L102    const old=Buffer.from(this.bytes(address,5)),target=old[0]===0xe9?(address+5+old.readInt32LE(1))>>>0:0;
L103    if(this.importMap.has(target)){this.importMap.set(target,{dll:'native-host',name,handler,argc});return;}
L104    const dest=this.registerImport({dll:'native-host',name,handler,argc}); ... this.write(address,jump);
```

Three facts fall out of this and they explain every measurement of the last three rounds:

- a stub registered fresh is **a single `RET` byte** (`0xc3`), because the machine traps execution landing in the
  stub region and dispatches in JavaScript;
- re-registering under an existing key **updates the map entry and returns the same address**;
- `replace` **computes the jump destination first** - if the first byte is `e9` it follows the relative jump - and
  then updates the entry at *that* destination.

### 246.2 Why the measurements read as they did

```
IAT stub 0x7e00880 bytes:  e9 cb 03 00 00      -> jmp 0x7e00c50
importMap.get(0x7e00880) : {dll:'kernel32.dll', name:'TerminateProcess', handler: undefined}
before replace: u32@stub+1 = 0x3cb   after replace: 0x3cb   (bytes and entry unchanged)
```

The IAT stub had already been converted into a jump by some earlier `replace` - that is what the `e9` means - so the
entry carrying the handler is at **the jump's destination**, not at the stub. Every probe so far read
`importMap.get(stub)`, found `handler: undefined`, and concluded that the repair had not taken effect. The entry it
should have read is `importMap.get(0x7e00c50)`, which the measurement never printed.

So three rounds of "the edit did not take effect" have a single, ordinary explanation, and it is a reading error of
the same family as section 245's: **reading a table at the address that was handed in, when the code says the entry
is at the address jumped to.**

### 246.3 What changed

Nothing: the three repair attempts made in this and the previous two rounds are reverted, and the shared harness is
back at its committed state. They were not left in the tree, because an edit whose effect cannot be shown should not
accumulate in a file that every suite loads. The census was not re-run:

```
passing 23   trapping 59   leaks {"reported": 0, "total": 0, "scrubbed": 0}
```

re-registration. Two lines, and whichever of the two repair routes moves that entry is the one the harness supports.
Then the terminate handler can be installed for real and the cookie question of section 244 can be asked again.

## 247. The dispatch hook, both routes measured, and the instrument's own flaw

### 247.1 The dispatch, read verbatim

```
L53   this.hooks.push(c.hook_add(u.HOOK_CODE,(cpu,address)=>{
L54     const entry=this.importMap.get(Number(address));if(!entry)return;
L62   },null,0x07e00000,0x07e0ffff));
```

A code hook covers the whole stub region and looks the import table up at **the address execution has landed on**,
skipping the lookup when there is no entry. So dispatch is by landing address, and a stub that has been converted
into a jump has **two** addresses in the picture: the stub itself and the jump's destination.

### 247.2 Both repair routes, measured

```
before          stub.entry={n:TerminateProcess, h:undefined}          target.entry={n:TerminateProcess, argc:2, h:function}
after replace   stub.entry unchanged                                  target.entry={n:'probe-replace', argc:2, h:function}
after re-reg    stub.entry={n:TerminateProcess, argc:2, h:function}    target.entry unchanged
```

Both routes work, and they work on **different entries**: `replace` on the stub updates the entry at the jump's
destination; re-registering under the same dll and name updates the entry at the stub. That settles the question of
section 246.4 - the two mechanisms are not alternatives that one of which is broken, they are two different places.

### 247.3 The thrower did not fire, and the instrument cannot tell why

A throwing handler installed through `replace` on the stub did not fire; the run faulted exactly as before. The
reason is **not established**, and the round's own instrument is why:

> **the probe checked the handler's type - `h:function` - and a type does not identify which function.**

So the output cannot say whether `replace` installed the new handler or left the previous one in place, and no
conclusion can be drawn from it either way. The twenty-ninth named failure mode: **checking the type of a handler
instead of its identity** - the same family as reading the wrong table address, one step further in.

## 248. The dispatch is onImport, not the entry handler

### 248.1 The hook body, verbatim

```
L54   const entry=this.importMap.get(Number(address));if(!entry)return;
L55   const key=(entry.dll||'')+'!'+(entry.name||''),stat=this.stubStats.get(key)??{registered:0,calls:0};
L56   stat.calls++;this.stubStats.set(key,stat);censusHit(key);
L59   try{ ... this.recent.push({at:'import',key,esp,drift,ret,args,pc,ebp,back}); }catch{}
L61   if(this.onImport)this.onImport(entry);else throw new Error('Unimplemented import '+entry.dll+'!'+entry.name+' return '+hex(this.u32(this.reg('ESP'))));
```

**The hook never calls `entry.handler`.** It records statistics and forensics, and then hands the entry to
`this.onImport`, or throws "unimplemented" if there is no such callback. So the `handler` field on an import entry is
consulted only by whatever implementation of `onImport` chooses to consult it.

### 248.2 Where the behaviour actually lives

```
machine.mjs:61      if(this.onImport) this.onImport(entry); else throw ...
helpers.mjs:147     m.onImport=e=>{ ... }        <- the real dispatch
th12-oracle.mjs:54  m.onImport = e => { ... }
world-oracle.mjs:45 const baseImports=m.onImport;m.onImport=e=>{ ... }
```

### 248.3 The withdrawal, stated plainly

Every repair of the last four rounds wrote to an import entry's `handler`:

- section 243 gave three names their argument counts through `replace` on the bound stub;
- sections 244 and 245 installed a throwing handler for the terminating APIs;
- section 246 established which of two entries each route writes.

**None of those can have had any effect**, because the dispatch path never reads that field. The bit-identical
outcomes were not evidence about the mechanism at all; they were the correct reading of an inert edit, which is what
section 245's own named failure mode said and what sections 246 and 247 then failed to apply.

The thirtieth named failure mode: **editing a data field that the dispatch path never reads** - and the habit it
adds: before repairing a mechanism, find the line that consumes the thing being written.

## 249. The real dispatch, two harness defects, and the trap moving at last

### 249.1 The dispatch, verbatim

```
L144   TerminateProcess:[()=>{throw Error('th12 called TerminateProcess');},2],
L145   ExitProcess:[()=>{throw Error('th12 called ExitProcess');},1],
L156    if(e.handler){m.ret(e.handler(),e.argc);return;}
L157    const stub=e.dll==='kernel32.dll'?kernel32[e.name]:undefined;
L158    if(stub&&stub[1]!==undefined){m.ret(stub[0](),stub[1]);return;}
L160    m.ret(0,e.argc??0);
L162   }catch(error){
L164    importFailures.push({dll:e.dll,name:e.name,argc:e.argc,message:error.message});
L165    m.ret(0,e.argc??0);
L166    if(process.env.TH_IMPORT_STRICT)throw error;
```

So `handler` **is** consulted, first - but a load-time IAT binding has none, so those imports fall to the table
below it, which is keyed by dll and name and carries a real arity. And the two terminating imports are answered by
handlers that **throw on purpose**, because a process that ends cannot be answered with a value.

### 249.2 The two defects

1. **The catch popped the wrong number of bytes.** `e.argc` is undefined for every import the image binds
   directly, so `m.ret(0, e.argc ?? 0)` popped **zero** bytes for `TerminateProcess` - which had been given two
   arguments. The process was told to end, the throw was swallowed, and the caller's next return read its own
   arguments as a return address. That is the fetch at 0x0 this chain has been chasing since section 241.
2. **A terminating import was resumed.** Even with the right arity, swallowing the throw and returning would
   continue a process that is over.

Section 243 suspected the argument count and could not make it matter, because it wrote to the entry's `handler`
field, which section 248 showed the dispatch does read - but only for entries that have one, and the load-time
bindings do not. The suspicion was right and the location was wrong: the arity that matters is the one the **catch**
pops with.

### 249.3 The fix, and the trap moving for the first time in five rounds

`helpers.mjs` now resolves the pop arity from the import's own table entry and lets the two terminator errors
through. The measurement:

```
before the fix:  pc=0x0  address=0x0  FETCH_UNMAPPED   (five rounds, every probe)
after the fix:   Error: th12 called TerminateProcess
                 pc=0x7e00880
                 stack: 0x46e92b, 0xffffffff, 0xc0000409, 0xbb40e64e, 0x44bf19b1, ...
```

The trap moved off address zero and now says what is actually happening: the guest asked to end the process. The
abort path no longer masquerades as a memory fault, and the stack is intact. **This was a harness defect, not a game
or fixture defect**, and it is the root cause of the whole address-zero chain.

### 249.4 What remains, now on an honest footing

The abort itself is still real: the CRT's fail-fast sequence with `0xc0000409` means a security cookie check failed
during start-up. That is section 244's question, and it can now be asked without a spurious fault in front of it.

suites are run in this round's commit so the shared harness change is verified. The census was not re-run:

```

## 250. The cookie measured, and initialising it is not enough

With the abort path finally reporting itself (section 249), the question of section 244 can be asked directly.
The stack of the abort held `0xbb40e64e`, which is the sentinel value MSVC's cookie has before it is initialised,
and the cookie global reads exactly that:

```
cookie at 0x4ad138 = 0xbb40e64e        (the uninitialised sentinel)
```

So the cookie had never been set. The function that sets it was identified by its own immediate rather than by a
guess: the only `0xbb40e64e` in `.text` sits at `0x47b381`, and the `55 8b ec` prologue above it is `0x47b36b`.
Calling that function changes the cookie:

```
0x47b36b: cookie 0xbb40e64e -> 0x7effef8
```

### 250.1 It is not sufficient

Running the start-up again with the cookie initialised still aborts:

```
WinMain: Error: th12 called TerminateProcess
cookie now = 0x7effef8   manager = 0x0
```

So the failing check is not simply a cookie that was never written. Initialising it moves nothing.

### 250.2 The reporter, and the global it reads

The address on the abort's stack, `0x46e92b`, is a `leave; ret` at the end of a function that begins `0x46e62f`
and whose first instructions are:

```
0x46e62f: 8b ff 55 8b ec 83 3d d8 38 4b 00 01 75 05 e8 1c 4b 00 00 ...
                            cmp dword [0x4b38d8], 1
```

That global is zero both before and after the cookie is initialised, so the branch it tests is not being taken
either way. Two globals now have to be read together: the cookie at `0x4ad138` and this flag at `0x4b38d8`.

### 250.3 What the abort path consists of

```
recent tail: IsDebuggerPresent, SetUnhandledExceptionFilter, UnhandledExceptionFilter,
             GetCurrentProcess, TerminateProcess
```

That is the CRT's fail-fast sequence, and it is the same one section 244 named by its exit code `0xc0000409`.

### 250.4 The stub census names two suspects

```
kernel32!EncodePointer=48   kernel32!DecodePointer=34   kernel32!IsProcessorFeaturePresent=1
kernel32!GetProcAddress=101  kernel32!GetModuleHandleW=90  kernel32!TlsGetValue=88
native-host!malloc=2  native-host!free=11  kernel32!FlsAlloc/FlsGetValue/FlsSetValue
```

The start-up walks the CRT's pointer-encoding path many times. A stub that encodes or decodes a pointer to a wrong
value defeats exactly the mechanism the fail-fast is protecting, so those two are the next thing to read - and they
are read the same way the dispatch was: open the stubs and see what they return, rather than guessing.

## 251. The initialiser proven by disassembly, and the second global

The previous round identified the cookie's initialiser by the immediate `0xbb40e64e` above a prologue. Disassembly
proves it, and the proof is worth more than the guess was:

```
0x47b371  a138d14a00        mov eax, dword ptr [0x4ad138]      ; read the cookie
0x47b380  bf4ee640bb        mov edi, 0xbb40e64e                ; the sentinel
0x47b385  bb0000ffff        mov ebx, 0xffff0000
0x47b38a  3bc7              cmp eax, edi
0x47b38c  740d              je  0x47b39b                       ; cookie is the sentinel: initialise it
0x47b392  f7d0              not eax
0x47b394  a33cd14a00        mov dword ptr [0x4ad13c], eax      ; <-- the COMPLEMENT global
0x47b39b  lea eax, [ebp-8] ; push eax ; call [0x4981dc]       ; GetSystemTimeAsFileTime(&ft)
0x47b3a6  mov esi, [ebp-4] ; xor esi, [ebp-8] ; call [0x49810c]
```

So the cookie has **two** globals, the value at `0x4ad138` and its complement at `0x4ad13c`, and the checker is
expected to compare a stored word against both. The search for writes to `0x4ad138` found none because the write on
the already-valid path is to `0x4ad13c` - one address over.

### 251.1 The pointer-encoding lead is closed, in the negative

```
helpers.mjs:69  EncodePointer:[()=>m.u32(m.reg('ESP')+4),1],DecodePointer:[()=>m.u32(m.reg('ESP')+4),1],
```

Both return their own argument. For a host that does not need pointer obfuscation, identity is the correct
behaviour, so the most promising suspect of section 250 is **not** a defect. Recorded as a negative.

### 251.2 A correction to this round's own method

The previous round took `0x46e62f` to be the function containing the abort's return address, using "the nearest
preceding call target at or below the address" as a containment test. Disassembly shows that function ends with
`ret` at `0x46e657`:

```
0x46e62f  8bff 55 8bec  833dd8384b0001 7505  e81c4b0000   ff7508 e843490000  68ff000000 e80d460000 ...
0x46e64a  push 0xff ; call 0x472c61 ; pop ecx ; pop ecx ; pop ebp ; ret    ; ends at 0x46e657
```

`0x46e92b` is not in it. The address on the stack is real, but the containment was inferred from a call target rather
than read from the function, so the label attached to it was wrong. **Thirty-first named failure mode: using "the
nearest preceding call target" as a containment test** - after section 238's warning that a back-scan desynchronises
into mid-instruction bytes, this is the same habit applied to call targets instead of `int3` padding.

## 252. The pair is consistent, the frame is an SEH frame, and a pattern of my own was wrong

### 252.1 The cookie pair, measured

```
before init: cookie[0x4ad138]=0xbb40e64e  complement[0x4ad13c]=0x44bf19b1  isComplement=true
after  init: cookie[0x4ad138]=0x7effef8   complement[0x4ad13c]=0xf8100107  isComplement=true
```

The pair is consistent before and after initialisation, and `0x44bf19b1` - the value that appeared on the abort's
stack - is exactly the complement of the uninitialised sentinel. So the mechanism the fail-fast protects is intact in
both states, and **the cookie pair is not the cause**. That is the second candidate closed in the negative.

### 252.2 The frame at the abort is an SEH frame

Resynchronising on the `8b ff 55 8b ec` prologue inside a window that contains the abort's return address finds the
function that really contains it:

```
prologue 0x46e827:
  0x46e827  8bff            mov edi, edi
  0x46e829  55              push ebp
  0x46e82a  8bec            mov ebp, esp
  0x46e82c  81ec28030000    sub esp, 0x328
  0x46e832  a3e8394b00      mov dword ptr [0x4b39e8], eax
  0x46e837  890de4394b00    mov dword ptr [0x4b39e4], ecx
  ...                       edx, ebx, esi, edi
  0x46e855  668c15003a4b00  mov word ptr [0x4b3a00], ss
  0x46e85c  668c0df4394b00  mov word ptr [0x4b39f4], cs
  ...                       ds, es, fs, gs
```

Saving all six segment registers is the MSVC exception handler, so `0x46e92b`'s `leave; ret` ends an SEH handler
frame rather than a security check. The previous round's label was wrong and this is the read replacement for it.

### 252.3 A pattern of my own was wrong

The cookie global is `0x4ad138`, whose little-endian image is `38 d1 4a 00`. The earlier searches used
`38 c1 4a 00`, which is `0x4ac138` - **one digit transposed**. So "no instruction references the cookie" was not a
fact about the binary; it was a typo in the needle. With the correct image, the cookie is read from roughly 180
places, including the initialiser at `0x47b371` and the game-directory function at `0x451536`.

**Thirty-second named failure mode: searching for an address with a wrongly transcribed byte image.** A negative
result from a pattern search is only as good as the pattern, and this one had not been re-derived from the address it
was supposed to encode before the negative was recorded.

## 253. The fail-fast reporter, read end to end, and it has no direct caller

Forward disassembly from the function's own prologue reads the whole abort:

```
0x46e902  ff15cc814900        call dword ptr [0x4981cc]
0x46e908  833d30394b0000      cmp dword ptr [0x4b3930], 0
0x46e90f  7508                jne 0x46e919
0x46e911  6a01                push 1
0x46e913  e8e7ca0000          call 0x47b3ff            ; the cookie initialiser one address over
0x46e918  59                  pop ecx
0x46e919  68090400c0          push 0xc0000409          ; STATUS_STACK_BUFFER_OVERRUN
0x46e91e  ff15fc814900        call dword ptr [0x4981fc] ; GetCurrentProcess
0x46e924  50                  push eax
0x46e925  ff15f8814900        call dword ptr [0x4981f8] ; TerminateProcess
0x46e92b  c9                  leave
0x46e92c  c3                  ret
```

So `0x46e827` is the fail-fast reporter: it makes sure the cookie is initialised, pushes `0xc0000409`, and
terminates the process with it. **`0x46e92b` - the address the previous two rounds treated as a frame - is this
reporter's own `leave; ret`.** Nothing about it belonged to a caller.

### 253.1 No direct caller

Scanning every relative `E8` in `.text` for a target of `0x46e827` returns nothing:

```
direct callers of 0x46e827 (__report_gsfailure): (none)
```

It is therefore entered **indirectly**, through a pointer, which is exactly what the abort's own trace shows one layer
up - `SetUnhandledExceptionFilter` followed by `UnhandledExceptionFilter`. The fail-fast is reached as an unhandled
exception, not as a call, so no call-site scan will ever name the check that failed.

### 253.2 A table next to the cookie

Immediately after the reporter is another function, and its first instructions show a table that starts four bytes
past the cookie's complement:

```
0x46e937  3b04cd40d14a00   cmp eax, dword ptr [ecx*8 + 0x4ad140]
0x46e941  83f92d           cmp ecx, 0x2d
0x46e953  8b04cd44d14a00   mov eax, dword ptr [ecx*8 + 0x4ad144]
```

Forty-five eight-byte entries holding a code and a value, beginning at `0x4ad140` - the CRT's own exception-code
table, laid out directly behind the cookie pair.

## 254. The recorder names the site, and the site is the cookie check's tail

The recorder installed at the reporter fires, and it names the caller that no static scan could:

```
esp=0x7effb2c   ret=0x451681   ebp=0x7effee8
stack: 0x451681, 0x4cf218, 0x0, 0x0, 0x44, ...
regs:  eax=0xffffffff  ecx=0x7effb34  edx=0x7effb84  ebx=0x0  esi=0x105  edi=0x7effb84
```

`0x451681` is inside `0x451530` - the function whose three Win32 calls this chain watched succeed in section 240 - so
the fail-fast is reached from the end of the game-directory function, and `eax` is `0xffffffff` when it is.

### 254.1 That tail, read

```
0x451665  a1a84e4d00        mov eax, dword ptr [0x4d4ea8]
0x45166a  8b8c2468020000    mov ecx, dword ptr [esp + 0x268]
0x451671  f7d8              neg eax
0x451673  1bc0              sbb eax, eax
0x451675  5f                pop edi
0x451676  f7d8              neg eax
0x451678  5e                pop esi
0x451679  33cc              xor ecx, esp
0x45167b  48                dec eax
0x45167c  e8b1b20100        call 0x46c932
0x451681  81c464020000      add esp, 0x264
0x451687  c3                ret
```

The function's last act is to call `0x46c932` with two values prepared: `ecx`, which is the stack-stored cookie
exclusive-or'd with the frame pointer, and `eax`, which the `neg / sbb / neg / dec` sequence reduces to a boolean:

- `[0x4d4ea8] != 0` gives `eax = 0`;
- `[0x4d4ea8] == 0` gives `eax = 0xffffffff`.

**The recorder measured `eax = 0xffffffff`, so `[0x4d4ea8]` is zero** - and that is the state in which the check is
being performed. The site, the argument and the flag are now all named by measurement rather than by inference, which
is the whole of what the previous rounds' instruments were trying to reach.

## 255. The checker is a plain comparison, and this round did not verify its own install

### 255.1 The checker, five bytes of it

```
0x46c932  3b0d38d14a00   cmp ecx, dword ptr [0x4ad138]
0x46c938  7502           jne 0x46c93c
0x46c93a  f3c3           repz ret
0x46c93c  e9e61e0000     jmp 0x46e827
```

It is a plain comparison of `ecx` against the cookie, with an early return when they are equal and a jump into the
fail-fast reporter when they are not. **There is no frame hashing, no complement, and `eax` is never read.** So the
`neg / sbb / neg / dec` arithmetic the caller performs to build `eax` is a red herring, and so is the flag it comes
from.

### 255.2 The flag, for completeness

```
[0x4d4ea8] = 0x0
refs to 0x4d4ea8 (2): 0x44f5f4 (inside WinMain)   0x451666 (the read in 0x451530)
```

Two references in the whole text: one inside `WinMain`, one at the read this chain followed. It is zero, and the only
consumer of the value derived from it is a register the checker ignores.

### 255.3 What that leaves

The caller passes

```
ecx = [esp + 0x268] xor esp
```

and the checker requires `ecx == [0x4ad138]`. So the check passes **if and only if** `[esp+0x268] == cookie xor esp`.
Either the store wrote the frame-hashed value into that slot, in which case the convention is self-consistent and the
failure is elsewhere, or it wrote the raw cookie, in which case the comparison can never succeed while `esp` is
non-zero. One measurement decides it: read both slots at the check.

### 255.4 The instrument that did not fire, and why that matters

A recorder was installed at `0x46c932` and the run went straight to the terminating import without it ever firing:

```
run: Error: th12 called TerminateProcess
```

The install was not verified - the bytes at the target were not read back, and neither was the table entry - so this
round cannot say whether the mechanism failed or the recorder was never reachable. **Thirty-third named failure mode:
installing without checking the install** - the same habit section 245 named, in its third appearance: a result that
looks like a mechanism's answer, produced by an edit whose effect was never confirmed.

### 255.5 What changed

No source file changed this round. The census was not re-run:

```
passing 23   trapping 59   leaks {"reported": 0, "total": 0, "scrubbed": 0}
```

## 257. The ring, the reporter reached, and stale translation measured

### 257.1 The executed-address ring

```
ring length: 1   ->  0x46e925
```

With the machine's opt-in executed-address ring switched on, the last executed address before the terminating
import is `0x46e925` - inside the reporter, at the `push eax` before its `call` to the terminating import. That
matches the reporter's disassembly instruction for instruction, and it says the reporter's own body runs, so
whatever entered it did so through its entry.

### 257.2 The reporter fires, and the return address is the one from before

```
installed; bytes at 0x46e827 now: e9 44 24 99 07
run WITHOUT flush: hits=1
run AFTER  flush: hits=1   first esp=0x7effb2c ret=0x451681
has ctl_flush_tb? undefined
```

A recorder at the reporter's entry fires, once, and the word on the stack is `0x451681` - the instruction after the
`call 0x46c932` at `0x45167c`. The path is now fully accounted for: `0x451530` calls the checker, the checker's
comparison fails, and it **tail-jumps** into the reporter, so the reporter sees the original return address still on
the stack.

So section 254's conclusion was right by measurement after all, and section 256's withdrawal of it was itself
premature: the reason a recorder at the checker did not fire was not that the checker is never reached.

### 257.3 Why the checker's recorder did not fire: stale translation

The install at the checker was verified at the byte level through both channels, and the call does happen. The
difference between the two sites is when each was first executed:

```
0x46c932  executed during the harness bootstrap (the CRT performs GS checks)   -> recorder never fired
0x46e827  not executed during the harness bootstrap                            -> recorder fired, once
```

The machine's own binding comment says the mechanism: **a bounded Unicorn build can retain a translated jump after
its immediate destination is rewritten.** A write to a byte range the translator has already compiled is therefore
invisible to the CPU, and reading the bytes back - even through the CPU's own memory interface - cannot see that,
because the bytes really are changed. It is the *translation* that is stale.

That is why `replace`'s first branch exists: when the target already begins with a jump, it updates the entry at the
jump's destination rather than rewriting the jump's bytes. For a plain code address there is no such route.

**Thirty-fifth named failure mode: verifying a code patch by reading the bytes back instead of by seeing it execute.**
A memory read proves a write; only execution proves a patch.

## 260. The prologue is a textbook frame-hash, and the measurement contradicts it

### 260.1 The store

```
0x451530  81ec64020000     sub esp, 0x264
0x451536  a138d14a00       mov eax, dword ptr [0x4ad138]
0x45153b  33c4             xor eax, esp
0x45153d  89842460020000   mov dword ptr [esp + 0x260], eax
```

There is no `push ebp` and no frame pointer: `esp` itself is the frame base. The prologue loads the raw cookie,
exclusive-ors it with `esp`, and stores the result in the frame. That is the frame-hash convention, and it means the
epilogue's `xor ecx, esp` is correct **by construction**, not a bug - the two halves are meant to cancel.

### 260.2 The slot arithmetic, done with each pointer

Writing `S` for `esp` right after the `sub`, and `E` for `esp` at the `xor`:

```
store:   [esp+0x260] with esp = S           -> S + 0x260
read:    [esp+0x268] at 0x45166a, before the two pops, esp = S - 8
                                            -> S - 8 + 0x268 = S + 0x260   (same slot)
check:   0x451675 pop edi, 0x451678 pop esi, so esp = S at 0x451679
         ecx = (cookie ^ S) ^ S = cookie                                       (passes)
```

So the guest code is self-consistent, and it passes on its own terms.

### 260.3 What was measured instead

```
E = 0x7effb2c    ecx = 0x7effb34 = E + 8
slot should hold cookie ^ S = 0xbb40e64e ^ 0x7effb2c = 0xc5bf1d62
slot appears to hold        E + 8    = 0x7effb34
```

The check is handed a value eight bytes above the stack pointer - a pointer into the caller's frame - where the
prologue's hashed cookie should be. Either the slot was overwritten between the store and the read, or the `esp` at
one of those two instructions is not the one the code's own arithmetic assumes.

### 260.4 The suspect the machine already names

The machine carries fields for exactly this: `interiorCalls`, `interiorApplied`, `interiorFramed`, `interiorReserved`,
`interiorRetRepaired`, `slotScrubbed`, `interiorRegRestored`. Its frame repair for interior calls exists because an
entry at a label inside a function skips the prologue and the shared epilogue then pops what was never pushed. An
eight-byte delta is exactly a two-push frame.

**Thirty-eighth named failure mode: reading a stack delta as a statement about the guest's code when the harness
rewrites frames.** The arithmetic in 260.2 is right about the code and says nothing about the run, because the run's
frames are not only the code's.

## 261. The frame-repair suspect refuted, and the epilogue read verbatim

### 261.1 The counters are all zero

```
FAILING CHECK #1
  E(esp at check) = 0x7effb2c   ecx = 0x7effb34   cookie = 0xbb40e64e
  [E+0x260] = 0x46ca09   <- the prologue's store slot
  [E+0x270] = 0x44f621   <- the slot the read address lands on
  [E+0x268] = 0x0        [E+0x264] = 0x4
  counters: interiorApplied=0 interiorFramed=0 interiorReserved=0 interiorRetRepaired=0
            slotScrubbed=0 interiorRegRestored=0 calls=7 sentinelLeaks=0
  interiorCalls entry for 0x451530 = absent
```

The harness did not rewrite this frame. Section 260.4's suspect is withdrawn by measurement, not by argument: every
counter that would have shown a repair is zero, and the interior-call map has no entry for the function at all.

But the slots say something else as well: neither `E+0x260` nor `E+0x270` holds `ecx`. So `ecx` was not read from a
slot near `E`, and the model of which slot the epilogue reads - or of which `esp` it reads it with - is wrong.

### 261.2 The tail, read verbatim

```
0x451650  18f4                 sbb ah, dh          <- misaligned: 0x451650 is not an instruction boundary
0x451655  832578ee4c00bf       and dword ptr [0x4cee78], 0xffffffbf
0x45165c  eb07                 jmp 0x451665
0x45165e  830d78ee4c0040       or dword ptr [0x4cee78], 0x40
0x451665  a1a84e4d00           mov eax, dword ptr [0x4d4ea8]
0x45166a  8b8c2468020000       mov ecx, dword ptr [esp + 0x268]
0x451671  f7d8                 neg eax
0x451673  1bc0                 sbb eax, eax
0x451675  5f                   pop edi
0x451676  f7d8                 neg eax
```

Two facts, one confirming and one correcting. `mov ecx, [esp+0x268]` at `0x45166a` is confirmed. But the `pop edi`
at `0x451675` is followed by `neg eax`, not by a second pop - and the bytes before `0x451655` do not decode from
`0x451650` at all.

So section 259's model - that the read and the exclusive-or straddle two adjacent pops, which is how the slot was
said to be eight bytes off - is built on a decoding that straddles an instruction boundary. The delta still has to be
explained, but not that way.

**Thirty-ninth named failure mode: modelling a stack delta from a disassembly that straddles an instruction
boundary.**

## 262. The true epilogue, the call's own return address, and the value four

### 262.1 The epilogue from a true instruction boundary

```
0x451671  f7d8           neg eax
0x451673  1bc0           sbb eax, eax
0x451675  5f             pop edi
0x451676  f7d8           neg eax
0x451678  5e             pop esi
0x451679  33cc           xor ecx, esp
0x45167b  48             dec eax
0x45167c  e8b1b20100     call 0x46c932        ; pushes 0x451681
0x451681  81c464020000   add esp, 0x264
0x451686  c3             ret
```

There are two pops after the read, exactly as section 259 said. Section 261 was right that the bytes before
`0x451655` do not decode, and right that the pop at `0x451675` is followed by another `neg` - but the conclusion it
drew from that, that the two-pop model was wrong, does not follow: the second pop is at `0x451678`, three
instructions later. The correction is itself corrected here.

### 262.2 The link that was missing

A `call` pushes its return address, so `esp` at the checker is not the caller's `esp` at the exclusive-or - it is
four bytes below it.

```
E = 0x7effb30            (esp at 0x451679, where the xor runs)
esp at the checker = E - 4 = 0x7effb2c      (what the recorder saw)
read address = esp_at_read + 0x268 = (E + 8) + 0x268 = E + 0x270
slot value   = ecx ^ E = 0x7effb34 ^ 0x7effb30 = 0x4
```

**The failing check is handed four.** And section 261's own probe had already printed it, one row away, labelled by
the uncorrected pointer: `[E+0x264] = 0x4`.

**Fortieth named failure mode: comparing a callee's stack pointer with its caller's.** The arithmetic was off by
exactly the return address the call instruction pushes.

### 262.3 What that means for the defect

The prologue stores the hashed cookie at `S+0x260`, and the epilogue reads `S+0x260` too, once the read's `esp` is
accounted for. So the slot is the right one, and at the check it holds four - a small integer, not a stack cookie.
Either the prologue's store was overwritten by a later write to that local, or the prologue's store is not what runs
for this frame.

## 263. The hook route fails, and the check now closes exactly

### 263.1 The hook that would not install

```
UC_HOOK_CODE = undefined  (typeof hook_add = function)
hook_add(2, ...) -> threw: undefined
```

The constants object has no hook-type constant, and the wrapper's `hook_add` does not accept the engine's own
hook-type number. So the store cannot be watched with a code hook, and the instrument that would answer 262.5's
question directly is not available on this wrapper. Recorded as a negative.

**Forty-first named failure mode: retrying an interface with a guessed constant instead of reading its contract.**
The constant was guessed twice - once by name from the constants object, once by number from the engine's
documentation - and the second failure reported nothing but `undefined`, because the thrown value had no message.
The contract is in the wrapper's own source and can be read.

### 263.2 The check closes exactly

Read at the failing check, with the stack pointer the checker itself sees:

```
esp at checker = 0x7effb2c           E = esp + 4 = 0x7effb30
store slot, [esp + 0x264] = [E + 0x260] = 0x4
read  slot, [esp + 0x270] = [E + 0x268 + 8] = 0x44f621
4 ^ E = 0x4 ^ 0x7effb30 = 0x7effb34  = ecx    exactly
```

The epilogue reads the very slot the prologue wrote: the exclusive-or of that slot's contents with `E` is the value
the checker is handed, to the byte. **The code is not at fault.**

### 263.3 What the slot's contents rule out

If the prologue's store had taken effect, the slot would hold `cookie ^ esp_store`. For that to equal four:

```
esp_store = cookie ^ 4 = 0xbb40e64e ^ 0x4 = 0xbb40e64a
```

which is not a stack address, and cannot be the `esp` the prologue had. So the four in the slot is not the value the
store wrote. Either something overwrote the slot between the two, or the store never ran for this frame and four was
already there.

## 265. The hook is live, and a BigInt comparison silenced it

### 265.1 The hook fires

The hook is installed and called - once, before my own callback threw.

### 265.2 Why it threw, and what that means for the store watch

The engine hands the callback a **BigInt** address. My callback did `address >>> 0` and compared
`address === 0x45153d` - a BigInt against a number - so the first call threw, the exception crossed into
`uc_emu_start`, and the bootstrap died at its first call. And in the previous round's store watch, the filter was the
same strict comparison, which for a BigInt against a number is **always false**.

**So the store watch was live and never matched. Section 264's conclusion - that the prologue's store does not run -
is withdrawn.** Its hook was not silent because the guest skipped the store, but because a type made the test
unsatisfiable.

**Forty-third named failure mode: strict-comparing a BigInt address from an engine callback with a numeric
literal.** The instrument reported absence, and the absence was its own.

The same run also shows a second hazard in the same family: a throwing hook does not merely fail - it propagates
into the emulator and produces a *fault*, complete with an artifact naming a guest address. A broken instrument can
wear the guest's clothes.

## 266. The prologue runs and writes; the read lands eight bytes low

### 266.1 The hook is live, and the answer is the opposite of the last two rounds

```
total hook fires = 32941
ENTRY esp=0x7effd9c   S = esp - 0x264 = 0x7effb38
STORE esp=0x7effb38   eax=0xbcaf1d76   slotBefore=0x0    eax == cookie ^ esp?  TRUE
AFTER esp=0x7effb38   slotAfter=0xbcaf1d76               == cookie ^ esp?      TRUE
READ  esp=0x7effb28   [esp+0x268]=0x4
CHECK esp=0x7effb2c   ecx=0x7effb34   slot=0x4
```

The hook fires thirty-three thousand times. The prologue runs. Its store executes, and it writes exactly the hashed
cookie - the value in the slot immediately after is `cookie ^ esp`, true to the byte. So the store is not missing,
and the slot is not unwritten.

### 266.2 The two addresses

```
store address = S + 0x260 = 0x7effd98
read  address = 0x7effb28 + 0x268 = 0x7effd90 = S + 0x258
```

Eight bytes apart. The epilogue reads one slot **below** the one the prologue filled, so the hashed cookie sits
undisturbed where it was written while the check is handed whatever is eight bytes lower.

### 266.3 Why they differ

The store used `esp = S`. The read used `esp = S - 0x10`. The code's own arithmetic - store at `[esp+0x260]` with
the pointer `S`, read at `[esp+0x268]` with the pointer `S-8` - matches only if the pointer at the read is eight
below `S`. It is sixteen below. **The function body's net stack motion is eight bytes more than the code expects.**

A body's stack motion is decided in part by calls: each import the harness services is completed with an
argument-count pop, and a count that disagrees with what the caller pushed moves the stack by the difference. This is
the same family as the arity repair of section 249, on the other side of the call.

**Forty-fourth named failure mode: reading a frame's stack mismatch as the guest's arithmetic when the harness
decides how many arguments an import pops.**

## 269. One missing table entry, and the chain it explains

### 269.1 The measurement that named it

Reading the stack pointer either side of each import the function dispatches:

```
before the fix
  GetModuleFileNameA  0x7effb20 -> 0x7effb30   d=16   (4 + 3*4: correct)
  GetConsoleTitleA   0x7effb24 -> 0x7effb28   d=4    (4 + 0:   two arguments left on the stack)
  GetStartupInfoA    0x7effb20 -> 0x7effb28   d=8    (4 + 1*4: correct)
```

`GetModuleFileNameA` and `GetStartupInfoA` pop exactly what their callers pushed. `GetConsoleTitleA` pops nothing
but the return address, so the two arguments its caller pushed stay on the stack, and the function's frame ends eight
bytes below where its own arithmetic puts it.

### 269.2 The cause, and a false positive on the way

`GetConsoleTitleA` was absent from the table the harness consults - `kernel32`, starting at `helpers.mjs:67`. Its only
occurrences in the file were a registration loop two hundred lines further down, from the th11 era:

```
helpers.mjs:204  for(const [name,argc] of [['GetModuleFileNameA',3],['GetConsoleTitleA',2],['GetStartupInfoA',1]]){
```

The lookup failed, the argument count defaulted to zero, and nothing else in the file noticed.

The first attempt to add the entry reported "already present", because it asked the **file** rather than the **table**.
Same shape as the round's own second failure: an existence check that does not ask where.

**Forty-sixth named failure mode: checking that a name exists somewhere, rather than in the table that is
consulted.**

### 269.3 The fix, and its verification

```
after the fix
  GetConsoleTitleA   0x7effb24 -> 0x7effb30   d=12   (4 + 2*4: correct)
  ENTRY esp=0x7effd9c      READ esp=0x7effb30        (was 0x7effb28)
  checks recorded = 4      passing = 4                (was 3 passing)
  run: FETCH_UNMAPPED, and no longer th12 called TerminateProcess
```

The frame now sits where the code's own arithmetic expects it, the stack-cookie check passes all four times, and the
fail-fast reporter is not reached. The run ends instead at the mapping fetch that was always there behind it.

So the chain that five rounds of measurement walked - the checker, the cookie slots, the frame-hash convention, the
reporter's stack word, the harness frame repair, the headless CRT - was touched off by a missing entry in a
function-name table. Every step could be measured, and none of them said so.

### 269.4 What changed

`helpers.mjs`: the `kernel32` table gains `GetConsoleTitleA:[()=>0,2]`, with the reason in a comment. The body
returns zero and writes no title; a title-writing body is a separate fidelity question and is not claimed here.

The census was not re-run:

```
passing 23   trapping 59   leaks {"reported": 0, "total": 0, "scrubbed": 0}
```

### 269.5 Next instrument

Re-run the census, which has not been re-run in many rounds, and see what the drift's removal moves: the fail-fast is
gone and the remaining wall is the mapping fetch behind it.

## 272. The promoted trace, and what the suite's route is not

### 272.1 The keeper's lead, examined first

```
refs to 0x432cc0 in .text: 0
head bytes at 0x432cc0: 07 c7 45 38 03 00 00 00 8b 95 ec 01 00 00 52 bb 01 00 00 00 ...
```

Nothing branches to `0x432cc0`, and the bytes there begin mid-instruction. So the wall-class keeper's `entry=` field is a
recorded address, not a call target - it is not a function's start. The field means what its producer makes it mean,
and here the producer is a call recorder that names an address it saw, not an entry point. The label was read as a
contract it does not have.

### 272.2 The instrument, promoted where it belongs

Section 268 hand-rolled a wrapper around `onImport` to read the stack pointer either side of every import. This round
moved it into the harness, gated on an environment variable, installed **after** the handler the helper assigns - so that
it wraps the one that is in force rather than being replaced by it (the mistake of section 267):

```
helpers.mjs  (before the first bootstrap call)
  if(process.env.TH_IMPORT_TRACE){
   const inner=m.onImport;
   m.onImport=e=>{const b=m.reg('ESP');const r=inner(e);const a=m.reg('ESP');
    console.log('IMPORT '+e.dll+'!'+e.name+' d='+(a-b)+' ret=0x'+(m.u32(b)>>>0).toString(16));return r;};
  }
```

It works for every suite, not only for the one that prompted it, which is the difference between an experiment and an
instrument.

```

IMPORT fixture!texture dimensions      d=16 ret=0x46025b

IMPORT kernel32.dll!SetUnhandledExceptionFilter d=8  ret=0x46e8fd
IMPORT kernel32.dll!UnhandledExceptionFilter    d=8  ret=0x46e908
IMPORT kernel32.dll!GetCurrentProcess           d=4  ret=0x46e924
```

Not one import in the whole run has a delta that is not `4 + 4n`: the value fetched beside each argument count is the
value that was pushed. The defect of section 269 does not repeat here. The suite reaches the terminating stub through
the CRT's own filter chain - a terminal event - and the cause of the abort is elsewhere.

`TerminateProcess` prints no line of its own, though it is the import that decides the run. The wrapper logs the
delta **after** the handler returns, and this handler throws; the throw unwinds past the log.

**Forty-ninth named failure mode: an instrument that records after the call cannot record the call that throws.** The
absence sits at the instrument, and reading it as the guest's silence is the same mistake in a new place.

## 273. The exit code names the check, and the machinery is not inert

### 273.1 The existing instrument, and the numbers it already carried

The trap artifact has carried these fields all along: `target`, `error`, `errorFields`, `trap`, `recent`, `fault`,
`eipRing`, `apiMisses`, `stubStats`. Running the suite with `TH_TRACE_EIP=96` fills the ring and the sentinel report,
and the artifact answers the question section 272 asked:

```
stack:  ["0x46e92b","0xffffffff","0xc0000409","0xbb40e64e","0x44bf19b1","0x0", ...]
recent: kernel32.dll!TerminateProcess
        args=["0xffffffff","0xc0000409","0xbb40e64e","0x44bf19b1"]
exit code = 0xc0000409
```

`0xc0000409` is `STATUS_STACK_BUFFER_OVERRUN`: the CRT's fail-fast after a failed stack-cookie check. So this suite
dies of the same check as the winmain chain of section 269 - but in a **different function**, and with no argument-count
drift anywhere in the run (section 272 measured zero bad deltas). Sameness of symptom, difference of cause.

### 273.2 The machinery, on the same run

```
sentinel: interior-applied 2  framed 1  restored 1  repaired 2 samples
back=["0x7f00000","0x4336c6"]
framePlan ${"{"returnSlot":"0x7effefc","slots":4,"args":0,"esp":"0x7effeec","ebp":"0x7f10000"}"}
esp=0x7effbc4  stackBase=0x7efff00
```

The interior-call machinery - frame planning, restoration, return repair - is **active in this suite**: two applications,
one frame, one restoration, two repairs. The chain passes through its trampoline page `0x7f00000`, and the frame plan
is built from an `ebp` of `0x7f10000`, which is **outside the real stack**, whose base is `0x7efff00`.

Section 261 measured the same counters as zero, and drew a conclusion about the machinery; it was a measurement at
one site, and this run shows the machinery acting elsewhere. A zero at one site is a fact about that site.

**Fiftieth named failure mode: reading a single site's zero as a property of the machinery.**

Nothing but this record and the boot state. The run in this round used the instrument as it already exists.

```
bytes=off
  returnHeld=False   returnDrift=-206   returnValue=0x4336c6
  stack[0..3]: 0x46e92b 0xffffffff 0xc0000409 0xbb40e64e
  esp=0x7effbc4      stackBase=0x7efff00    framePlan.ebp=0x7f10000    EBP=0x7f00000

bytes=136
  returnHeld=True    returnDrift=-38    returnValue=0x7f00000
  atStack=0x7f10000
  code=07c74538030000008b95ec01000052bb
  esp=0x7effe64      framePlan.ebp=0x7f10000    EBP=0x0
```

Without the reservation the run dies in the CRT's fail-fast - `TerminateProcess(-1, 0xc0000409)`,
`STATUS_STACK_BUFFER_OVERRUN`, the cookie check of section 269 in another function. With 136 the planted slot holds
the planted value and the run reaches a new place: the trap's code bytes are those of the interior label `0x432cc0`
itself, executed at the scratch frame page. The suite still fails, but it fails further on, and the wall it used to
die at is behind it.

So 136 is what this entry's path needs, and - with the census note above - not what every entry needs. A property of
the path, applied as a constant, regresses elsewhere.

### 274.3 A measurement of the table, read as a measurement of the guest

The first sweep printed a `returnHeld` column and the column was empty for every row. The field exists in the
sentinel line the machine prints, and not in the trap artifact the sweep was reading from. An empty cell in a table
is a measurement of the table.

**Fifty-first named failure mode: reading an empty column as a measurement.**

### 274.4 What changed

Nothing but this record and the boot state. The sweep used the probe switch that already existed,
`TH_INTERIOR_STACK_BYTES`.

### 274.5 Next instrument

Derive the reservation for one entry from the executed path instead of guessing it: bracket the smallest value at which
`returnHeld` turns true for the entry under test, and compare it against the entry's own interpreter-derived slot
count. If the bracket and the derivation agree for this entry, the derivation can be applied per entry, which is the
shape the note asks for; and the census over the change is then a measurement and not a guess.
