## 314. The row for 302, and the defect its own bits exposed

### 314.1 The table already named the body, so the row is a lookup, not a transcription

```
AnmOpcodes.hpp: { 302, 67, 0, "native" },  // five-bit draw mode
the title-16 block carried rows for 6, 102, 306, 423, 429, 430 and nothing for 302, while this
  title's own 302 at 0x4623dc shifts the argument by 0x19 into a five-bit field at 25..29 -
  the same five bits the older tables call the draw mode.
row added: {302, 67, 40, "native"}, witnesses 40 - the measured votes of section 314.2.
```

### 314.2 The rule read in this port's own bits, and the twelve cases that named the defect

```
the rule in the original's terms (field bits 25..29 by the resolved argument):  4 of 40
the rule in this port's own bits: ((argument & 15) << 22) | ((argument & 16) << 25):  28 of 40
the twelve, printed case by case:
  value 18: observed 0x00800000   want 0x20800000
  value 19: observed 0x00c00000   want 0x20c00000
  value 255: observed 0x03c00000  want 0x23c00000
  (and the same two variants of each, always with the argument's fifth bit set)
```

The observed values were the low four bits and no more: the port's `set_drawing_mode` wrote the fifth
bit of the mode only for titles 13 and 14 (`if constexpr`), so under title 16 it was written by
nobody - while this title's own update reads it back out of `flags` (`flags&0x20000000`). The original
keeps all five bits of the mode in one field.

### 314.3 The fix, and its verdict

```
AnmVm.hpp, set_drawing_mode:  title 16 writes flags bit 29 from (mode & 16) << 25
AnmVm.hpp, drawing_mode:      title 16 reads that fifth bit back, instead of returning zero for it
the rule in this port's own bits after the fix:  40 of 40, advanced 40 of 40
```

The two halves are the pair the port needed to be self-consistent, and the rule that measures them is
the one read off 0x4623dc. The checker stays green through the change: statuses empty, pairs 12 to 12
in 4124 cases and 16 to 16 in 40, no mismatching opcode, derived mapping unchanged at 0x1c -> word+0x408,
0x28 -> delta, 0x4ac -> word+0x3b4, 0x4b0 -> word+0x3b8 and 0x544 -> word+0x5c, comparisons 22900
with zero differing, unmapped slots 85.

### 314.4 The reading that stays open

```
the same pair under other titles: 13 and 14 write th13_native_flags bit 25; title 12's fifth bit
  was not touched here, and whether this title's own tables need it is the next title's measurement.
```
## 315. One pipeline, and the rows it settles

### 315.1 The pipeline, written once

The method that earned the row for 302 is now a tool (tools/th16-rule-select.mjs): for an opcode, take
the corpus's record of the offsets it writes and the values it writes there, then walk every canonical
command of the title-16 build across the fixture's fifteen named quantities and ask which command makes
one of those quantities move by the measured amount in every writing case, with the pointer advancing by
the stored length. The older titles' own rows are printed beside the answer, so the measurement and the
inherited table can be compared instead of trusted.

### 315.2 The lesson the walk taught about comparison

```
first criterion: the port's post value equals the measured post value in every case
  op 306: only 306 matched          op 310: 733 commands matched
the writing cases are not all interesting: a case whose measured word is unchanged (or changes by one
  bit under any body that adds one) lets a body that writes nothing - or writes anything - match.
second criterion: the measured delta equals the measured delta, in the cases whose measured delta is
  nonzero (a vote is a case where the original writes something):
  op 306: 306 only, 32 of 32 votes      op 305: 74 only, 32 of 32      op 311: 73 only, 32 of 32
  op 310: still 733 (all 32 writing cases carry the one same delta of one bit)
  op 313: none      op 314: none
```

### 315.3 What the three settled rows are

```
306: the command resolves through the table to 0x7003, whose own comment is "raw flags bit 15" -
     exactly the bit the corpus shows written (0x530: 0 to 0x8000), on the port's own title flags
     word, in 32 of 32 writing cases. The existing row's odd literal is replaced by that name.
305: resolves to 74 (0x4a), member flags, 32 of 32 - while the older titles' row for 305 says 73
     and carries no witnesses at all. Under this title's bytes, 73 is the answer for 311.
311: resolves to 73 (0x49), member flags, 32 of 32 - while title 13 names 89 and title 14 names
     anm_th14_rgb for 311. The number is not portable; the effect is what was measured here.
```

All three rows now carry measured witnesses (32) instead of the eight-vote grid or none at all.

### 315.4 The readings left open, named

```
310: 733 commands satisfy a one-bit delta; the older titles say 72, and the walk cannot separate it
  without a criterion that reads the argument, not the delta.
313, 314: the quantity these handlers write lands outside the fixture's fifteen names, so the walk says
  none and does not guess.
```
## 316. The walk over every word of the port's own VM, and the criterion that is still too thin

### 316.1 The instrument grew a third step

```
step one, named quantities: eleven readings, two of which (the pointer's presence and the timer)
  move for every body, so a one-bit write matched hundreds of candidates (section 315.2)
step two, every aligned word of the VM: the fixture already exposed slot(byteOffset) and size(), so
  the walk compares all 269 words of the port's own structure instead of eleven readings
step three, a fixed shift per slot: the port may keep a measured field at another bit position, as
  the draw mode showed in section 314, so a slot matches when one shift maps it to the measurement
```

The first step of every run is measured too: a slot is called a frame quantity when its delta is
identical for every body in a case the original writes (185 of the 269 words qualify), and those words
are excluded rather than trusted to say something about a command.

### 316.2 The slot map the run measured, agreeing with the checker's own derivation

```
flags 0x404        flags2 0x408        layer 0x20
color 0x374        secondary color 0x378        integers[1] 0x3b8
the checker, from measured value sequences and knowing nothing of layout, wrote: 0x1c -> word+0x408
  and 0x4b0 -> word+0x3b8 and 0x544 -> word+0x5c. Two independent routes, the same two slots.
```

### 316.3 Why the criterion is still too thin

```
with the plain slot criterion:  303, 304, 307, 313, 314 matched no command at all
with the shifted criterion:     all of them matched 733 commands - and 733 is what one body per
  command column of a frame quantity looks like: a slot in the VM's header row moves every frame by an
  amount the case sets, with the same shift in every case, so it matches with no help from the body.
```

The measurement that would separate them is named, not guessed: for one command, the forty cases
include writing ones and cases the original leaves alone, and the winning slot must move exactly in the
writing ones. That is the general form of the at-least-two-changes rule this arc wrote for the native.

### 316.4 One regression of my own, caught by the walk

```
first run of step two reported "every op writes 0x28 at delta 0xc" - the original's position slot,
  which the walk had stopped excluding when the slots replaced the hand-written offsets. Restoring the
  exclusion restored the real targets: 0x530, 0x18 and 0x534.
```
## 317. The paired-case criterion, and the ceiling it measured for the slot route

### 317.1 The two holes the walk found in its own criterion

```
hole one: the second side of the measurement was missing. A slot that moves in the cases the
  original leaves alone is moving for the frame's reasons; the walk now requires the winning slot to
  move exactly in the writing cases. Implementation: still = the cases with no context change at all.
hole two: the shift was chosen per body, so a phenomenon that has nothing to do with the command
  could pass on each body with a different shift. It is now calibrated once, on a body that is not
  the answer (body 0), and applies to every body unchanged.
```

### 317.2 What the walk then measured

```
op 303: 34 writing cases write 0x530 (4 distinct deltas), 6 cases write nothing - 733 commands match
op 307: 32 writing cases write 0x534 (1 distinct delta),    8 cases write nothing - 733 commands match
op 310: 32 writing cases write 0x530 (1 distinct delta),    8 cases write nothing - 733 commands match
op 313: 34 writing cases write 0x534 (4 distinct deltas),  6 cases write nothing - 733 commands match
op 314: 32 writing cases write 0x534 (1 distinct delta),   8 cases write nothing - 733 commands match
the matching slots are the same header row every time - layer 0x20, and the words at 0x28, 0x2c,
0x34, 0x38 and 0x3c - and their deltas are identical FOR EVERY BODY in every case.
```

So for these five commands the movement of every candidate word belongs to the case, not to the
command: the case sets it, the frame carries it, and no body has to do anything for the word to move
by the measured amount. This is the ceiling of the route that compares one step's deltas: it can
attribute an effect to a body only when the port applies that effect on the body's own path.

### 317.3 What the route is still good for, and what goes around its ceiling

```
it named three rows at 32 votes each (section 315): 306 -> 0x7003, 305 -> 74, 311 -> 73, because
  for those the port's own words - flags and the title flags - move only when the right body runs.
the four-digit corpus - 4684 unfaulted cases over 141 opcodes - is the place where a body-independent
  movement cannot hide, because a whole-corpus sequence has to match shape as well as value. The
  checker's derivation already works that way for five slots, and its answers agree with this run's
  measured slot map on both of the slots the two routes can see.
```

### 317.4 The next measurement, named

```
extend the checker's derivation from value equality to (value, change-shape) equality over the whole
corpus, for every offset of the original's context and every aligned word of the port's VM. The shape
half is what this round measured to be missing from the one-step route; the corpus half is where the
values of a frame-driven word can still be seen to come from one command and not from another.
```
## 318. The body-sensitive pass: five words, and the fourth way a comparison can be too thin

### 318.1 The criterion the ceiling asked for

Section 317 named the missing half: a word says something about a command only if the command can move
it. The walk now runs eight sampled bodies on every writing case and keeps a word only when at least two
of them move it by different amounts. The slots collapse from a whole header row to five words of 269.

### 318.2 What those five words are, body by body, in one measured case

```
sensitive 0x5c  -> 0:0x1 1:0x0 7:0x1 73:0x1 74:0x1 302:0x1 760:0x1
sensitive 0x60  -> 0:0x1 1:0x0 7:0x1 73:0x1 74:0x1 302:0x1 760:0x1
sensitive 0x64  -> 0:0x3f800000 1:0x0 ... (the same for every body but the one)
sensitive 0x3a8 -> 0:0x11da8 1:0x0 ... (the same for every body but the one)
sensitive 0x404 -> 0:0x0 1:0xffffffff 7:0x0 73:0x800 74:0x2000 302:0xc00000 760:0x0
```

Four of the five move by one and the same amount for every body but body 1 - frame quantities, still.
The fifth is the port's own flags at 0x404, and it is the one word in the whole VM whose movement
differentiates one command from another:

```
body 73  writes flags bit 11 - one bit
body 74  writes flags bit 13 - the same shape, two bits along
body 302 writes 0xc00000 - bits 22 and 23, the low half of the five-bit draw-mode field that
  section 314 measured at the original's 25..29, and that section 314's defect repair made
  self-consistent for this title
body 1   writes 0xffffffff - the reset-shaped body
```

### 318.3 The fourth way a comparison can be too thin

```
with the shift calibrated once and the sensitivity filter in place, the walk still reports 711 of
771 commands for four of the five opcodes, and the reason is arithmetic:
  the first measured delta of 307 is 0x400, the calibrated shift is 22, and 0x400 << 22 in
  thirty-two bits is ZERO. Every body whose flags word does not move matches on the strength of the
  wrap, and most of them do not move it.
the repair is named: the shifted value must be nonzero, and a shift that annihilates the
  measurement is not a relation between the port and the original.
```

### 318.4 What is solid and what is named

```
solid: 269 words reduced to five measured as body-sensitive; the port's own response to three
  distinct bodies' commands read off (bits 11, 13, and the draw-mode pair 22 with 23), with the
  306, 305 and 311 rows already carrying 32 votes each.
named: (1) require a nonzero shifted delta, (2) use the opcodes whose measured deltas take several
  distinct values (303 with four, 304 with six, 313 with four), because a single repeated delta
  cannot separate one body from another however the criterion is drawn.
```
## 319. Nonzero shifts, calibration by the writing body, and the one operand shape that resolves

### 319.1 The two repairs 318 named, both made

The shift search now requires a nonzero shifted value, and the shift is calibrated on the first writing
case from the body under test, because the word the command writes is zero until that body moves it.
The first repair takes the walk from 711 matches to none on all six opcodes, which proves the 711 were
the wrap; the second gives the pattern below.

### 319.2 The measured operand shapes of the six opcodes, from the original's own bytes

```
303 -> 0x60 0x20 0x40 0x1e0                 = v << 5         with v in 3 1 2 15   (bits 5..8)
304 -> 0xbffffff9 0x3fff6ff9 0xbffffffa 0x3fff6ffa 0xc00000f8 0x3fff70f8
307 -> 0x400                                 = 1 << 10        (bit 10)
310 -> 0x1                                   = 1 << 0         (bit 0)
313 -> 0x300000 0x100000 0x200000 0x700000  = v << 20        with v in 1 2 3 7    (bits 20..22)
314 -> 0x800000                              = 1 << 23        (bit 23)
writing cases and cases that write nothing: 303 34/6, 304 10/0, 307 32/8, 310 32/8, 313 34/6, 314 32/8
```

### 319.3 The answer, per opcode, and the one that is resolved

```
303 (four distinct deltas) -> 0 bodies     304 (six distinct deltas) -> 0 bodies
307 (one delta)            -> 7 bodies, all on 0x404 flags: shifts +1 +3 +17 +18 +19
310 (one delta)            -> 7 bodies, all on 0x404 flags: shifts +11 +13 +27 +28 +29
313 (four distinct deltas) -> ONE body: 0x42, shift -16, on 0x404 flags
314 (one delta)            -> 7 bodies, all on 0x404 flags: shifts -12 -10 +4 +5 +6
```

313 is the first opcode in this arc whose measured delta takes several distinct values and whose
reading lands on exactly one body. Read out, the reading is arithmetic and complete:

```
0x300000 >>> 16 = 0x30 = bits 4 and 5      0x100000 >>> 16 = 0x10 = bit 4
0x200000 >>> 16 = 0x20 = bit 5             0x700000 >>> 16 = 0x70 = bits 4 5 and 6
so: the original's field at bits 20 21 and 22 is the port's own flags bits 4 5 and 6, a shift of
sixteen between the field origins - the rewrite of a field into the port's own bits that section 314
asked of the judgement, now measured on one body with four distinct operand values behind it.
```

The two disagreements are the next questions and they are different in kind. A single repeated delta
cannot name one body among the seven (318.4 said so before this run), so 307, 310 and 314 need a
second criterion, and the port's own bit owners are the place to read it. 303 and 304 name no body
at all, so for them the sensitive-word filter may itself be too narrow; the slice-bitmap measurement
of section 316 is the instrument for that, and it is named below.

### 319.4 Named next

```
(1) name the port's own owners of flags bits 4 5 and 6, print the older tables' rows for 313 beside
    the answer, and award the row with the four distinct measured operands as witnesses;
(2) make the seven-body answers exclusive with the port's own bit owners, since one operand value
    cannot separate bodies;
(3) for 303 and 304, re-open the candidate set with the slice-bitmap probe instead of the sensitivity
    filter: the port may write a command's operand into a word that the filter removed.
```
## 320. The port owns bits 4-6 of its flag word, and opcode 313 of title 16 is now that writer

### 320.1 Who writes which bits

The port switch says plainly which case writes which field: `case 66` writes
`field(0x70,4,arg)`, so the port keeps the blend value in flags bits 4, 5 and 6. Cases 73, 74,
82, 85 and 86 write one-bit fields at bits 11, 13, 27, 28 and 29. `anm_th14_blend` is the
same three bits plus a fourth operand bit in the title flag word; `anm_th14_resolution` writes
flags2 bits 19, 20 and 21 and `anm_th14_flag22` writes flags2 bit 22. The seven bodies that
answered for 307 and 314 are exactly the six one-bit writers, so one measured bit cannot pick
between them.

### 320.2 The older rows for 313, printed beside the answer

```
title 13: {313, 0,                    0, "native-default"}  canonical 0, no witness
title 14: {313, anm_th14_resolution,  0, "native"}       claims flags2 bits 19..21, no witness
title 16: absent                                        kept its raw value; the switch has no
                                                        case 313, so nothing was written
```

Both older rows carry zero witnesses, so under section 315 neither is evidence. For title 14 the
number meant resolution. For title 16 it meant nothing, which is the defect the measurement
found: four distinct operands were written by the original and by nothing on the port side.

### 320.3 The awarded row, and the read-back that proves it

```
title 16: {313, 66, 34, "native"}    canonical 66 writes field(0x70,4,arg)
read back through the fixture: canonical(313)=66, canonical(66)=66, canonical(314)=314
opcode 313 flags deltas for the four measured operands:
  arg=1 -> 0x10   arg=2 -> 0x20   arg=3 -> 0x30   arg=7 -> 0x70    (status 0 in all four)
the original wrote v<<20:  0x100000 0x200000 0x300000 0x700000
v<<20 >>> 16:             0x10     0x20     0x30     0x70
the referee after the row: differing comparisons 0, unmapped slots 85, both unchanged
```

### 320.4 What is open, and with which instrument

307, 310 and 314 each leave seven one-bit writers as candidates; one operand value cannot
separate them, so each needs a second distinct operand from the grid. 303 and 304 name no body
under the sensitivity filter, so they go to the slice-bitmap probe of section 316. The rows
standing on their own witnesses - 306, 305, 311, 302 and now 313 - need nothing further.

## 323. The flag family has a home in the port, and its bit index is one below the slot bit

### 323.1 The homes, read from the switch

```
anm_th13_flag6  and 7 and 8 : flags2 bits 6, 7, 8, from the byte argument or integer
anm_th13_flag15            : the title flag word, bit 15
anm_th14_flag22            : flags2 bit 22, from one bit of integer(0)
anm_th14_flag24            : flags2 bit 24, from the byte argument
anm_th14_visual_rng        : flags bit 30 plus flags2 bit 9
anm_th14_rgb               : flags bit 31 plus flags2 bit 10
```

The first two lines were already in the tables with names. The last two show that the named
handlers carry a second, numbered copy of the flag in flags2, one index below the run bit, and
that copy is what makes the name of the run member checkable rather than asserted.

### 323.2 The relation in slot 0x534, carried by five names

```
op 424 writes bit 7  and the tables name it flag6      -> bit = N + 1
op 431 writes bit 8  and the tables name it flag7      -> bit = N + 1
op 432 writes bit 9  and the tables name it flag8      -> bit = N + 1
op 314 writes bit 23 and the tables name it flag22     -> bit = N + 1
op 315 writes bit 25 and the tables name it flag24     -> bit = N + 1
and the run pair the port mirrors into flags2 bit 9 and bit 10 is 307 and 311 at bits 10 and
11, the same one-apart reading.
```

So a single bit in this slot is not a rename problem: the corpus gives the ANM flag index, and
the port keeps a named handler for that index. The measurement in this title then only has to
agree on the shape, and it does: 314 and 315 write one bit from the argument in 32 of 40
cases each, arg&1 predicting 40 of 40 for both.

310 writes mask 0x1, and the vocabulary has one writer with that mask: case 72

Both sibling tables name 72 for this number with the note visibility, and the port clears bit

## 326. The two named holes are closed, and the matcher proves it case by case

### 326.1 A criterion that can fail

```
A candidate body must reproduce the native XOR delta of the slot in EVERY case of that op,
through ONE fixed shift, in either flag word - 40 cases usually, and the shift must be the
same for all of them. Two requirements make it able to fail:
  the shift must map the union mask of the native deltas onto the union mask of the port
    deltas exactly, which removes the zero-annihilating shifts of section 319 (k = -31 used
    to shrink every delta to zero and let an idle body fit), and
  the candidate must also write nothing in every case where the native writes nothing.
```

### 326.2 Opcode 303: the port had no body at all

```
measured: 40 cases, 34 write slot 0x530, 6 write nothing, and the writes have four
  distinct deltas, 0x20 0x40 0x60 0x1e0. They are the operand low nibble placed at bits
  5 to 8, and the last one is the whole field.
verdict of the matcher over the existing vocabulary: no candidate body. No body held mask
  0x1e0 at shift 5 for all cases. This is a measured gap, not a missing table row.
the title-14 table names this number blend with no witness, so the name is this number own.
fix: anm_th16_blend = 0x7111 writes field(0x1e0,5,argument) and keeps the numbered copy
  in flags2 bits 5 to 8. Row: {303, anm_th16_blend, 34, native}.
after the fix, the same matcher over the same space: 303(28945, flags, k=0, mask=0x1e0)
  and 303(28945, flags2, k=0, mask=0x1e0). Read back by hand: code 303 with argument 3
  moves flags by 0x60, one of the four deltas the corpus measured.
```

### 326.3 Opcode 305: the flags half was right, the numbered copy was missing

```
measured: the matcher confirms case 74 with shift 0 and mask 0x2000 exactly, so the row
  that stood was right. Nothing wrote the numbered copy, flags2 bit 13.
fix: anm_th16_flag13 = 0x7110 holds that same write and adds flags2 bit 13. After the fix
  the matcher reports 305(28944, flags, k=0, mask=0x2000) and 305(28944, flags2, k=0,
  mask=0x2000): both words, every case, one shift.
read back: canonical(303)=28945 (0x7111), canonical(305)=28944 (0x7110); code 303 with
  argument 3 moves 0x60, code 305 with argument 1 moves 0x2000, in both words.
```

### 326.4 State and the next step

```
referee: unmapped slots 86, differing comparisons 0, unchanged by the two new bodies and
  rows, so neither write landed on a slot the comparison reads.
keepers: title 13 PASS on 694 state and 250 random-polar cases; geometry pass 3 fail 0.
next: run the matcher over every op of the corpus and print the ops with no candidate body
  at all. Those are the port vocabulary gaps for this title, listed by measurement; the two
  closed here are the ones the coverage matrix had already named. The same table then goes
  to the second slot of this title and to the other five titles.
```
## 327. The whole title in one scan: fifty-seven writes, one vocabulary gap left

### 327.1 The scan

```
tools/th16-op-gaps.mjs runs the matcher of section 326 for every op of the corpus at the two
flag slots, so the answer is a count and not a search:
  first run:  57 op-and-slot pairs with a write; 54 had a fitting body; 3 did not,
              op 302 at 0x530, op 304 at 0x534 and op 312 at 0x530.
  after this: 56 have a fitting body and one does not, op 304.
```

### 327.2 Opcode 302: a five-bit field where the row wrote two bits

```
measured: 40 cases, 36 write, seven distinct deltas; (argument&31)<<25 predicts all 40 of
  them, including argument 63, where 0x3e000000 is the widest one. So the original
  writes five bits at slot 0x530 bits 25 to 29.
the row that stood, case 67, writes only bits 22 and 23, two bits of the same value at a
  shift of three; the all-case matcher rejected it, because five bits cannot fit two.
fix: anm_th16_field25 = 0x7112 writes the five bits and keeps the numbered copy in flags2
  bits 25 to 29. Row: {302, anm_th16_field25, 40, native}.
after the fix the scan reports 302(28946, flags, k=0, mask=0x3e000000) and the same in
  flags2; by hand, argument 63 moves 0x3e000000 in both words.
```

### 327.3 Opcode 312: the second argument, and the rng and rgb selectors together

```
measured on before and context: the slot ends at (argument2&3)<<30 in all 40 cases -
  argument2 1 gives 0x40000000, 2 gives 0x80000000, 3 gives 0xc0000000, and the two
  cases that did not move have argument2&3 zero. The channel is the second argument: the
  first-argument reading predicts only 20 of 40.
this title had no row for 312, so the number ran its raw body, which is the default body
  and writes nothing here: it agreed in 2 of 40 cases, the ones in which the original also
  wrote nothing.
fix: anm_th16_visual_pair = 0x7113 writes (argument2&3) at bits 30 and 31 and mirrors the
  same two bits to flags2 bits 9 and 10, the two homes the rng and rgb bodies keep.
after the fix the scan reports 312(28947, flags2, k=-21, mask=0x600) and the values agree
  in every case. The flag word itself is not where the fit is reported: the fixture seeds
  flags with bit 30 set while the original state had the bit clear, so a correct write of
  zero to that bit shows as 0x40000000 there. That is the preset blindness of section 322
  read from the other side, and the numbered copy, whose bits start clear, is the arm that
  reads out clean. By hand: argument2 16 moves the flag word by 0x40000000 and the copy by 0.
```

### 327.4 The gap that is left, named with its numbers

```
op 304 at 0x534: 40 cases, 30 write one constant bit, 0x40000 = bit 18, and 10 write
  nothing. The silent cases are the unpaired rows with argument 0, 1, 255, 256 and -1; the
  paired rows, where the same value arrives with argument 3, all write.
rivals scored against the 30 writing cases: argument&1 30 of 40, argument>=2 36 of 40,
  argument!=1 32 of 40, value nonzero 30 of 40. None of them is the rule, so the condition
  is not a function of one operand, and the next round reads it out of the paired rows.
this is the one op of the title whose original write no body in the vocabulary reproduces.
```

read back: canonical(302)=28946 (0x7112), canonical(312)=28947 (0x7113), both used, since

referee: unmapped slots 86, differing comparisons 0, unchanged by the two new bodies and the

## 328. The last gap: a branch, and the title scans clean

### 328.1 What opcode 304 does, read from the whole state

```
diffing every byte of before against context for the 40 cases, the op touches three places:
  two of its own objects, one at 0x18 and one at 0x28, in every case, and
  slot 0x534 in 30 of the 40, by one constant bit, 0x40000 = bit 18.
the split is the argument low byte, and nothing else:
  0x00, 0x01 and 0xff stay quiet; 0x03, 0x10, 0x11, 0x12, 0x13 write.
the corpus pairs many rows with argument 3, and those all write; the unpaired rows carry
  the grid values. That is why the first reading looked like a pair effect and why no
  single-operand rival could fit: the rival has to look at the low byte of the argument,
  not at the whole value. Scores: low byte in 2..254 40 of 40; low byte at least 3 and
  not 0xff 40 of 40; argument at least 2 36 of 40; argument&1 30 of 40.
```

### 328.2 The two boundaries the corpus does not decide

```
no case carries low byte 2, so at least two and at least three are the same statement on
  this corpus, and the body takes at least two with the reading on record.
the slot starts clear in all 40 cases, so a clear and a no-write look alike, and the body
  writes only in the writing branch.
both are open questions with a named case to build, not assumptions of the moment.
```

### 328.3 The fix and the verdict

```
body: anm_th16_layer = 0x7114 writes the constant bit when the argument low byte is at
  least two and not 0xff, and keeps the numbered copy at flags2 bit 17, which is the index
  the one-below relation of section 324 gives for slot bit 18. Row: {304, anm_th16_layer,
  30, native}.
scan: 57 op-and-slot pairs write a flag slot; with a fitting body, 57; without, 0. The gap
  list is empty and the tool prints the number in one line.
read back: canonical(304)=28948 (0x7114), used. By hand, low bytes 0 and 1 move nothing,
  2, 3, 19 and 254 move flags by 0x40000, and 255 moves nothing, which is the table the
  corpus measured.
the matcher reports the row as 304(28948, flags, k=0, 0x40000): the mask is exactly the
  one the original moves, in every case, with the quiet cases quiet.
referee: unmapped slots 86, differing comparisons 0. keepers: title 13 PASS, geometry
  pass 3 fail 0.
```

### 328.4 What the scan should cover next

```
the scan as it stands asks one question of the two flag slots: 57 of the title flag-slot
  writers, all named. The same machinery asks it of the whole state: for every op, for
  every byte the native moves, is there a body whose write matches case by case. The bound
  is then a number for the title as a whole rather than for the two slots, and the same
  number for the other five titles is the campaign measure of how much vocabulary is left.
```

## 330. The oracles of the two newest titles, and the map that did not transfer

### 330.1 One finder, checked against the title whose anchors are known

```
tools/th-anm-native-newer.py reads the three anchors out of the executable instead of
  carrying them: the loop is the jump at the default handler tail, the position slot and the
  register that holds the virtual machine come from the same tail, and the cookie is the
  compare-against-a-global site with the most call sites in the code, replaced with a return.
the check is the known title first. On 16 the finder returns loop 0x45fb9a, position slot
  0x28, register ebx, float constant 0x494720 and cookie 0x47499b with 308 call sites,
  which is exactly the block section 307 wrote by hand; the runner up has 0 call sites, so
  the criterion separates a real check site from a look-alike rather than accepting the first
  match. After that the finder can name the same five on a title nobody has anchored.
```

### 330.2 Title 17

```
anchors measured: loop 0x467015, position slot 0x28, virtual machine register esi, no float
  constant in the tail, cookie 0x47b23f with 283 call sites against a runner up at 0.
corpus: 1000 cases over 25 measured handlers plus the defaults, 0 faulted, written to
  artifacts/th17/anm-native.json. The handlers move the position slot in every case, and the
  two flag words at 0x530 (352 writes, 26 distinct deltas) and 0x534 (422 writes, 22).
  Those are the offsets of title 16, on a different executable, which is the first
  cross-title evidence for the flag pair itself.
the run of the three names is the second: 424 leaves only 0x80, 431 only 0x100 and 432
  only 0x200, the same three masks title 16 gives for the same three names. The relation
  between a name and the flag it writes is therefore a property of the engine family and not
  of one binary.
```

### 330.3 Title 18, where the offsets moved

```
anchors measured: loop 0x4786e8, position slot 0x2c, register ebx, float constant
  0x4b9418, cookie 0x48dc60 with 296 call sites against a runner up at 0.
the position slot is four bytes past the one title 17 uses, and the flag pair sits at 0x534
  and 0x538 where 17 has 0x530 and 0x534. Assuming the family offsets would have written

and the name-to-bit map moved with them: 424 writes 0x200, 431 0x400, 432 0x800, 307

the seed offsets of title 18: the position slot moved by four, so the input fields the

the row table of title 18 for the two names that changed words, 307 and 311;

and the port comparator for 17 and 18, which is the first part of the method the two

## 331. The same rows read twice: off the code and out of the corpus

### 331.1 The idiom, and what reading it buys

```
every handler that writes one flag bit uses the same shape: load the argument byte at the
  instruction + 8, shift it by the bit, exclusive-or it against the flag word, mask it to
  1 << bit, and write back. So the pair (slot, bit) can be read off the code and the
  argument decides the value. tools/anm-newer-flag-rows.py disassembles each real handler of
  each of the three newer titles, takes the first such shape it finds, and writes the rows
  to docs/porting/anm-flag-rows-16-18.json.
that is a second instrument for the same fact the corpora measure: one reads the code,
  the other runs it. Agreement between them is worth more than either alone.
```

### 331.2 Title 17 reads exactly like title 16

```
seven handlers carry the shape in each title, and on those seven names title 17 differs
  from title 16 in no bit and in no slot: the difference is zero in all seven, twice.
the corpus said the same the round before, from the other side. A code read and a run
  read agreeing on seven names is the cross-title claim with two witnesses.
```

### 331.3 Title 18 moves the slot always, and the bit per name

```
the slot: title 18 is four bytes past title 16 in all seven, without exception. The flag
  pair of that family therefore shifts as a pair, and a reader may derive it.
the bit: five of the seven shift by two, 424 from 7 to 9, 431 from 8 to 10, 438 from
  18 to 20, 307 from 10 to 12 and 315 from 25 to 27; 421 shifts by one, 21 to 22, and
  423 does not shift at all, 17 to 17. So the tempting rule - title 18 equals title 16
  with one constant pair added - is true of the slot and false of the bit, and a table
  per name is what the title needs.
the masks agree with the shifts: with the bit at 9 the mask is 0x200, at 12 it is 0x1000,
  at 20 it is 0x100000. Where the mask covers two bits (0x600000, 0xc0000) the bits are
  adjacent, which is the same shape one column wide and a different value.
```

### 331.4 The two instruments check each other

```
asked the fail-able way: of the 21 rows read from code (seven names in three titles), in
  how many does the corpus show every bit of that mask. Answer: 21 of 21. And in how many
  does the corpus show the mask itself as a delta, the strongest of the two: 21 of 21.
nothing was excused. A reader that took the first shape it met, on three binaries, would
  have been caught here if it had taken a shape that the handlers do not execute.
the partialness is named in the tool: the shape covers 7 of the 134 real handlers of
  title 16, so the rest of the flag writes use other shapes and are the next extension.
```

### 331.5 The corpora, and which one carries what

```
the cross-check reads artifacts/th16/anm-native-all.json for title 16, because the smaller
  artifacts/th16/anm-native.json keeps named fields and has no context snapshot; the two newer
  corpora keep the snapshot. That is a difference of the corpora and not of the titles, and
  it is why the reference title is read from the all-corpus here.
```
## 332. The flag writers of the whole population, and a list that names its own blind spots

### 332.1 What the population counts say

```
the census of section 329 counted flag writers inside the corpus sample; the reader of this
  round walks all 134 real handlers of title 16, all 134 of 17 and all 136 of 18, and
  records every write to a title flag word on the straight path:
    title 16: 42 of 134 write a flag word, 92 do not; per slot 0x530 thirty handlers,
              0x534 twelve.
    title 17: 42 of 134; per slot thirty and twelve, the same distribution.
    title 18: 43 of 136; per slot 0x534 thirty and 0x538 thirteen, which mirrors
              title 16 as the four byte shift of section 330 predicts: 30 against 30 and
              13 against 12.
so the four byte claim is not only true of the seven names that shift the argument; it is
  true of the shape of the whole population. And title 17 and 16 agree here twice over,
  which is the third witness for that pair.
```

### 332.2 The shapes, and which source they read

```
the writes are made by and, or, xor and mov. In title 16: 4, 4, 27 and 26 instructions;
  where the source is nameable, six carry an immediate and the argument byte appears in a
  handful of shifted forms (bit 21 three times, bits 10 and 17 twice). The rest carry a
  register whose source the reader does not yet name, which is why the shift shape of
  section 331 covers seven of these 42 and no more.
reading the register back to its definition is the next step of this reader and the reason
  it is written down here: the number is 43 unnamed sources in title 16, not "a few".
```

### 332.3 The two readers disagree, and both lists are named

```
title 16: the corpus moves a flag slot for 48 handlers, the code read finds 42, they share
  31. The corpus shows writes at 304, 312, 401, 402, 410 and 411 that this reader does
  not attribute, because it walks a bounded straight path and those handlers leave it; those
  six are the extension of this reader, named.
the code finds writes for -1, 1, 3, 4, 301 and 317 where the corpus moves nothing: those
  are the seeded cases, and section 327 showed that a correct write onto a preset bit
  leaves no delta. That list is a property of the fixture, not of the port.
titles 17 and 18 repeat the same picture inside their smaller corpora: 20 shared, and the
  corpus names 304 and 312 again. A disagreement that is listed is a measure; the list was
  not produced by the code reader alone or the corpus alone, which is the point.
```

### 332.4 What the campaign takes from this

```
the flag words of the newer family are now known in three ways: which handlers write them
  (this section, full population), which bit by name (sections 330 and 331) and which
  change by case (the corpora, and the port scan of 325 to 328). The same three readers
  apply to titles 13 and 14, whose tables predate this work and whose corpora exist.
the port side of 17 and 18 is still the missing first part of the method: their corpora
  can be compared case by case only after a fixture binds the port's fields to those
  snapshots, and the anchor shifts measured in section 330 say that binding is title specific.
```
## 333. The reader closes its own list: every flag writer the corpus saw, title 16

### 333.1 The three steps the reader needed

```
one: a straight line stops at the first jump, and the first jump of these handlers is
  often into the shared tail or past a conditional branch, so the write is never seen.
two: following the jumps without a stop follows the dispatch loop itself and credits every
  later handler to this one; 133 of 134 handlers "wrote" a flag word, which is the
  signature of a walk that never ends. Stopping where a handler stops, at the jump back
  to the dispatch loop, brought that to 58 of 134.
three: a write inside a called helper belongs to the caller. Following call targets to a
  depth of two brought the count to 70 of 134, and it is that step which closes the list.
```

### 333.2 The list closes, and the closed list is the measure

```
title 16: the corpus moves a flag word for 48 handlers; the reader now explains all 48,
  with nothing left over: corpus only, empty. The reader also finds 22 more, whose write
  the corpus cannot see because the fixture presets the bits (section 327), and those are
  listed by name: -1, 1, 3, 4, 7, 200 and the rest.
title 17: 21 of 22 shared, one name left, 304.
title 18: 21 of 22 shared, the same name left, 304.
a walk that had closed the list by widening its claims would not have been a walk worth
  keeping; this one closes it while the corpus keeps naming its misses, and the one name
  still missing is one name.
```

### 333.3 The population, and the shift again

```
writers: title 16 has 70 of 134, title 17 has 70 of 134, title 18 has 71 of 136.
by slot, counting distinct handlers: title 16 reaches 0x530 from 52 handlers and 0x534
  from 31; title 17 from 53 and 28; title 18 from 52 and 29, at 0x534 and 0x538.
the pair of numbers for title 18 is the pair for title 16 with the slot shifted: 52
  against 52 and 29 against 31. The four byte shift is therefore visible in the
  handler level distribution of the whole population, one round after it was visible on
  the seven names and two rounds after it was visible in the corpus.
```

### 333.4 What is left, and it is small

```
one name in the two newest titles, 304, whose write the walk still does not reach;
the register sources, 43 of the writes in title 16 by the earlier count, are still named
  only as registers, so the argument path and the register path are not separated yet;
and the same three reads on titles 13 and 14, which have tables and corpora of their own.
the instrument is worth more than the number it prints: the corpus names what the reader
  misses, which is what makes the reader trustworthy.
```
## 334. The last blind spot of the reader, and the name that closed it

### 334.1 Why name 304 was invisible

```
the handler of 304 in the two newest titles does not name the flag word in a memory
  operand at all. It calls a helper, and the helper takes the address of the word:
    th17  call 0x406530, and inside:  lea edi, dword ptr [ecx + 0x534]
    th18  call 0x4066b0, and inside:  lea edi, dword ptr [ecx + 0x538]
so the write reaches the word through a register. Every reader before this one looked
  for the paired form, displacement and register together, and a form of an address in
  a register is by construction invisible to it. That is one blind spot, named.
the fix is the narrow one: remember a register that a lea has set to the address of a
  flag word, and count a later write through that register as a write of that word, with
  the pointer named in the note that is kept with the row.
```

### 334.2 The lists close, in all three titles

```
title 16: the corpus moves a flag word for 48 handlers, the reader explains 48, nothing
  left over.
title 17: 22 and 22; title 18: 22 and 22. Corpus only, empty, three times.
the writers the reader finds beyond the corpus are still listed, and they are still the
  preset invisibility of section 327: a case is seeded with bits already set, so a write
  that agrees with the preset moves nothing.
```

### 334.3 The same shift, in a fourth place

```
the corpus for 304 records what the write does, before any reading of the code:
  title 17 moves 0x534 by 0x40000, which is bit 18;
  title 18 moves 0x538 by 0x100000, which is bit 20.
that is the slot shift of four and the bit shift of two, on a name that is not one of
  the seven of section 331 and that no earlier reader could see. And the code says the
  same thing in its own way: the displacement baked into each helper is the title's own
  slot, 0x534 in one binary and 0x538 in the other, so the shift is inside the code
  of each title and not a parameter. The port needs both, on a per-title row.
```

### 334.4 The instrument, at the end of this thread

```
readers: the shift shape of 331, the four writes of 332, the control flow of 333 and the
  pointer of 334; and against all of them the corpora, which name what a reader misses.
the numbers a reader prints are: how many handlers write a flag word, 70, 71 and 72 of a
  hundred and thirty four, a hundred and thirty four and a hundred and thirty six; how
  many of them the corpus can show, 48, 22 and 22, and every one of those is explained.
the remainder of the work on this family is small and on record: the register sources
  that are still registers in the output, and titles 13 and 14, whose tables and corpora
  predate this instrument and to which its three reads have not yet been pointed.
```
## 335. Titles 13 and 14 keep their flags where the newer three do not

### 335.1 A slot reader for any title, checked on the title whose slots are known

```
tools/anm-flag-slots.py walks a title's handlers and counts store instructions by
  displacement. Two rankings come out, and title 16 decides between them because there
  the answer is on the record:
    by frequency of writing: 0x538 110 handlers, 0x530 103, 0x540 81, 0x534 60. The
      known pair is second and fourth, so frequency alone does not find a flag word, and
      that is a measurement and not an opinion.
    by the shape of the mask: a flag word is written with a bit field, at most two
      bits set or two cleared. That ranking gives 0x530 with 15 handlers and 0x534 with
      12, then a drop to 2. On the title with an answer, the shape finds the pair and
      the frequency does not.
the same walk carries the lessons of sections 333 and 334: it follows basic blocks, stops
  at the dispatch loop, enters called helpers two deep and follows a register a lea set to
  the address of a field.
```

## 338. The reader with a single base register breaks, and the measured table closes it

### 338.1 A field profiler, checked on a field whose shape is known

```
tools/anm-field-profile.py answers what a word at an offset is: the handlers the write
  reader finds there with their masks, and from the widest corpus the deltas and the
  question that names a field - is the delta a function of the argument the case carries,
  of the variant, or of the handler alone?
checked on 0x18 of title 13, a word whose shape is known: the run side answers as it
  should, op 302 writing 0x2000000 for the argument 1, 0x6000000 for 3 and 0x3e000000
  for 255 or -1, which is a shifted field of the argument and nothing else.
the same self-check found a defect in the code side: the write reader matched the
  displacement against any base, and 0x18 is also the displacement of the stack slot
  [esp + 0x18]. Rows of the form `mov edx, dword ptr [esp + 0x18]` were being counted
  as writes of a flag word.
```

### 338.2 The restriction, and what it costs

```
restricting the match to the register measured for the title - ebx in 13, edi in 14,
  ebx in 16, esi in 17, ebx in 18 - removes the collision and takes three handlers in
  title 16 and one in each of 17 and 18 out of the reader's coverage. Corpus only stops
  being empty: [304, 413, 414] in title 16, [304] in 17 and [304] in 18.
a criterion that never fails proves nothing, so this is the shape of the work: the
  loosest reader was believed by accident, the strictest broke, and the measurement
  decides the reader to keep.
```

### 338.3 The bases are measured, not chosen

```
tools/anm-base-registers.py walks every real handler with no base restriction and tallies
  the register each write to a flag slot is addressed through. Per title, the counts for
  the pair:
    title 13  0x18 ebx 197, esp 125, ecx 36, eax 18, esi 3, edi 2; 0x1c ebx 80, esp 6
    title 14  0x18 edi 123, ecx 23, esi 18, eax 13, ebx 2; 0x1c edi 116, esi 25
    title 16  0x530 ebx 97, esi 11, edi 8, ecx 4; 0x534 ebx 84, esi 31, ecx 13, edi 8
    title 17  0x530 esi 139, edi 6, ecx 4; 0x534 esi 119, edi 16, ebx 5
    title 18  0x534 ebx 122, esi 34, edi 6; 0x538 ebx 77, esi 34, edi 16
the 125 writes through esp in title 13 are the collision, counted rather than argued.
the handlers the restriction dropped use the registers the tally already names: op 304
  writes through ecx, 413 through edi and 414 through ecx in title 16; and in 17 and 18
  op 304 writes through a pointer the lea set, whose own base is outside the single
  register.
and the measured set is a set, not a register:
the table the reader now carries is the measured set per title with the stack and frame
  pointers left out, since at a small displacement they address a stack slot of the same
  shape: ebx, ecx, eax, edi and esi for 13; edi, ecx, esi, eax, ebx and edx for 14;
  ebx, edi, esi, ecx and edx for 16 and 18; esi, edi, ecx, ebx and edx for 17.

## 339. The second word read from the code, and the second reader defect it named

### 339.1 The address of the word goes into a shared routine

```
asking the code what writes the second word answers the question in the handler itself:

    title 13, op 200 at 0x462542:  lea eax, [ebx + 0x538]
                                   call 0x4016c0
    title 14, op 200 at 0x4700d1:  lea ecx, [edi + 0x548]
                                   call 0x408b00

the routine is a reset: it receives the address and stores the block

    mov dword ptr [eax], 0xfff0bdc1        the first word, a colour
    mov dword ptr [eax + 4], 0
    mov dword ptr [eax + 0xc], 0x4c0a28    the address of the float 1.0
    mov dword ptr [eax + 0x10], ecx        a guard bit, read and written back

so the word at 0x538 in title 13 and at 0x548 in title 14 is the first word of a
  0x14-byte block - the colour and geometry of a thing the handler draws - and every
  handler of the contiguous family 200 to 213 passes its address to one reset routine
  rather than writing through it. The seed of the earlier named work put the pointer
  0x4c0a28 at 0x544 of title 13, and the block says the same thing at +0xc: the two
  instruments agree on the structure.
```

### 339.2 What that exposed: a store through a pointer whose source is an immediate

```
the reader had a branch for a store through a register a lea set to the address of a
  field, but it asked for the memory operand at the end of the operand list, which is
  what `mov dword ptr [ecx], edi` looks like. The reset writes `mov dword ptr [eax],
  0xfff0bdc1`, where the immediate comes last, and every such store was invisible.
the corpus named the loss before the code did: of the 15 handlers that move the word,
  the reader found 10 in title 13 and 10 in title 14, and the 12 and 13 missing ones
  were exactly the family the address is passed from.
the branch now takes the destination operand and asks whether it is a bare memory
  operand, which covers the immediate and the register form alike. One handler: op 200
  went from 0 rows at the word to 3, the immediate and the two register stores.
```

### 339.3 With the fix the second word closes as well

```
title 13: the code now finds 20 handlers writing 0x538, the corpus moves it for 15, the
  intersection is all 15 and corpus only is empty. Title 14: 25 and 15, intersection
  15, empty.
the five handlers and the ten the code has and the corpus does not write the value the
  seed already holds, which is the preset invisibility the pair shows too.
and the pair itself is unchanged by all of this, which is the regression line: corpus
  only empty at 32 of 32 in 13, 37 of 37 in 14, 48 of 48 in 16, 22 of 22 in 17 and in
  18, with the same code-only families named before.
```

### 339.4 Two defects in one instrument, two rounds apart, both found by the corpus

```
the base register of the reader was a guess until the stack collision at 0x18 named it;
  and the form of a store through a pointer was a guess until the family that writes the
  second word showed that the guess had a hole of exactly its shape.
in both cases the corpus named the misses, and in both cases naming them was enough to
  read the answer off the code: ecx, edi and the two pointer bases in the first case,
  and a single immediate in the second.
```

```
the colour block is the first structure the work has named in these two titles rather than
  only located; the words the corpus found at 0x53c and 0x540 of title 13 and 0x54c and
  0x550 of title 14, and their reset routine, are the same kind of reading two offsets

title 12 remains the one title of the six with no oracle at all.
```

The line of section 293.3 - build the checker for TH16, TH17 and TH18 after the shape
the other titles carry - is one title short of done and now two titles shorter than it was:

### 340.2 The derivation is a claim the port can fail, and all three do - for one reason

```
The checker declares no mapping. It asks which port word carries, across every case, the
same sequence of values as a given native slot, and then asserts equality through the
mapping. A native slot with no candidate is a failure in the open.
  title  comparisons  differing  cases  opcodes  port words matched
  16     18216        0          5640   141      4
  17     4000         0          1000   25       4
  18     3000         0          1000   25       4
Zero differing comparisons in all three is the strongest line this instrument can print:
where the port exposes the same structure, it exposes the same value, case for case.
```

### 340.3 The gap, named per slot

```
the four port words that match in every title are the position delta and the integer
slots. What no port word matches is the newer flag word: in title 16 the native 0x530
carries 36 distinct values across the cases and 0x534 carries 25; in 17 and 18 the
same pair carries on the order of ten; and no single port word carries that sequence.
that is not a missing value but an arrangement: the port keeps the newer titles flags in
bits of its own word, and the native word is a permutation of them. A derivation by
equality of whole words cannot see through a permutation, and the checker says so by
naming the slot and the count of cases in which the nearest named member differs -
1126 of 4684 for 0x530 in title 16, 36 of 1000 and 40 of 1000 for parts of the pair
in 17 and 18.
so the remaining work is port work with a target now: give the newer titles a channel
that carries the native arrangement of the flag word, from the measured row tables of
sections 331 to 339 - the shifts and the slots per name are already written down - after
which the derivation has a candidate and the checker has a chance to differ.
```

    title 18  0x534 union 0x7fceb9e9 and 0x538 union 0xbf43e7f, the same

## 342. The arrangement, solved one opcode at a time, and the port work it names

### 342.1 Co-change is not attribution, and one opcode at a time settles it

```
the case pool of a whole corpus cannot answer where a native bit comes from: every case
  changes some port word, so every native bit co-changes with the same few port bits,
  and the first table of this work said bits 0 to 2 of the port word at +0x5c for
  every one of the 23 varying native bits of 0x530.
the exact question is which XOR of port bits reproduces the native bit in every case,
  solved over GF(2). Pooled over the corpus it has no answer either, for the reason
  the per-opcode pass gives away: title 16, opcode 307, 40 cases, native 0x534 bit
  10 comes back as flags2 bit 9, exactly; and the same 0x534 bit 10 is written by
  other opcodes from other port bits, so the pooled system is overdetermined and
  inconsistent. The arrangement is per name, which is what the row tables of section
  331 always said - they record one shift per name.
```

### 342.2 Five names, solved, against the five code rows

```
title 16, the port bit each measured name moves the native bit from, and the row the
  code side recorded for that name:
    name  solved from the values             the code row (anm-flag-rows-16-18)
    307   flags2 bit 9   -> 0x534 bit 10      slot 0x534 shift 10   agrees
    315   flags2 bit 24  -> 0x534 bit 25      slot 0x534 shift 25   agrees
    424   flags2 bit 6   -> 0x534 bit 7       slot 0x534 shift 7    agrees
    431   flags2 bit 7   -> 0x534 bit 8       slot 0x534 shift 8    agrees
    423   title flags bits 17 and 18 -> 0x530 bits 17 and 18       shift 17, mask
          0x60000, and the port holds that pair as one field
five names, two instruments, and the regression between them is the one-below rule of
  section 324: the port keeps each of these at one below the native bit, and the two
  rows were measured by reading handlers and by running the port against the original.
```

### 342.3 The pair rows, which are the shape of the work left

```
two of the seven names do not come back as a single port bit: 421 writes bits 21 and
  22 of 0x530 and 438 writes bits 18 and 19 of 0x534, and neither is any XOR of up
  to three of the port bits in those cases. That is the same shape the code rows
  describe for them, a mask over an adjacent pair, and the pair lives in the port as
  a field rather than as a bit - so the channel for a pair row is the field, and the
  probe names exactly which ones.
```

### 342.4 Titles 17 and 18: the native side confirmed, the port side absent

```
the same four single-bit names, solved per opcode on the other two corpora:
    title 17   bits 10, 25, 7 and 8 - identical to title 16, which is the
               cross-title finding of the row tables measured again from the values
    title 18   bits 12, 27, 9 and 10 - each exactly two above title 16, which is the
               +2 the row tables recorded for five of the seven names
and on both, the port side has no combination at all: compiled as PORT_TITLE 17 and
  18 it changes no port bit in step with the native bit for these names, because those
  titles take the generic path in the port where title 16 takes the branch that
  carries the shift. So the port work is named and has acceptance rows: for each of
  the seven names of title 17 the same rows as title 16, and for title 18 those
  rows at +2 bits and the +4 slot pair the values already show.
```

## 343. The port carries the shift for titles 17 and 18, and the values say so

### 343.1 One branch, and the two measurements behind it

```
the port maps a title's own opcodes to the bodies that carry the newer semantics, and
  until now only title 16 had that mapping: `anm_canonical_opcode` returned the raw
  number for 17 and 18, so the newer bodies never ran and no port bit moved with the
  native bit - which is exactly what section 342 measured as "no exact combination".
the branch now takes 16, 17 and 18 on the same rows. Two independent measurements
  say it should:
    docs/porting/anm-flag-rows-16-18.json shares seven names across all three titles,
      records for 17 zero bit and zero slot differences against 16, and for 18 the
      same seven at +2 bits and +4 on the slot
    tools/anm-arrangement-search.mjs read the native side from the values and got bits
      10, 25, 7 and 8 for 17 - identical to 16 - and 12, 27, 9 and 10 for 18, each
      exactly two higher
the other rows of the table are measured for 16 alone and a number with no measured
  row still keeps its raw value, so the change adds a path and removes none.
```

```
the test is the per-opcode solve of section 342 on the four single-bit names, and it
  can fail; it did fail before the change:

    17 op 315 NO EXACT COMBINATION        flags2 bit 24 -> 0x534 bit 25  native = port + 1
    17 op 424 NO EXACT COMBINATION        flags2 bit 6  -> 0x534 bit 7   native = port + 1

    18 op 424 NO EXACT COMBINATION        flags2 bit 6  -> 0x538 bit 9   native = port + 3

## 344. The arrangement is a table per name, and the tables are here

### 344.1 Two rules tried and refused

```
a shift of one port channel, taken as the native word itself, fails because the native
  word carries the corpus's own seed and the port's seed differs: title 16, 0x530,
  union 0xffe6b9ff, and no channel at any of the 32 shifts equals it in eight cases
  of ten. Taken over the case CHANGES, where the seed cancels, the same shape was
  tried with two channels and every pair of shifts: for 0x534 of title 16 the flag
  channel moved left by 26 to 30 reaches 4070 of 4684 cases and 734 differing bits,
  and for 17, 18 and the other slot no two-source rule reaches two wrong cases in a
  hundred. The reason is the one the per-name solve gave: one native bit of the pair
  is written, over the corpus, by several different names from different port bits, so
  no fixed rule of one or two sources can be the whole word.
```

### 344.2 The values-side table for title 17, one row per name

```
the tool now walks the corpus's own opcodes and solves each against the port, which is
  the only complete description of a per-name arrangement. Title 17: 18 names, 31 of
  the 43 changing native bits with a port row. The structure in it:
    pair slots   0x530 and 0x534, the measured pair, and title 423 lands on the
                 first of the pair with the identity - title flags bits 17 and 18 to
                 bits 17 and 18, on every one of the three titles
    the mirrors  names 302, 303, 304, 305 and 306 write the native word at the
                 position the port already uses: flags bit 25 to 0x530 bit 25, flags
                 bits 5 to 8 to bits 5 to 8, flags bit 18 to 0x534 bit 18, flags bit
                 13 to bit 13, title flags bit 15 to bit 15
    one below    names 307, 311, 314, 315, 424, 431 and 432 are the flags2 family:
                 flags2 bit 9 to bit 10, bit 24 to bit 25, bit 6 to bit 7, bit 7
                 to bit 8, bit 8 to bit 9, bit 22 to bit 23, bit 10 to bit 11
    a field      name 313 moves port bits 4 to 6 of flags to 0x534 bits 20 to 22,
                 which is the port's blend_mode(), the three-bit field the handler
                 names
```

### 344.3 Title 18, the same table at the measured displacement

```
    pair slots   0x534 and 0x538 - the +4 the row tables recorded, from the values
    the mirrors  303, 305, 306 and 423 keep their identity; 302 moves one higher
                 (flags 25 to 29 to bits 26 to 30)
    the third    307, 311, 314, 315, 424, 431 and 432 are flags2 at it + 3: bit 9

### 346.2 The clock sources, and the filter that names them

```
two of the channels change for reasons of their own. `live` says the VM still has
  an instruction, and a handler that ends its instruction changes it in exactly the
  cases a row asks about; the timer's fractional part changes in most cases for no
  reason related to the flags at all. Both were satisfying the per-case equality and
  taking rows they should not: with a preference that tries `live` last, title 16
  still sources 13 of its 36 rows to the timer's fractional part and 1 to live,
  title 17 sources 3 and 1.
the filter that answers it is a clash: two native bits cannot come from one port bit
  of the same opcode. A row whose source bit is claimed by more than one native bit
  of its own opcode is a coincidence by that test, and the census now reports the
  counts apart.

## 347. The th12 oracle plan, measured off the image and confirmed live

### 347.1 What title 12 already had, and the one thing it did not

```
the campaign has native ANM oracles for 13, 14, 16, 17 and 18, and title 12 - the
  title the goal starts from - has none: its two artifacts are the browser proof and
  the stage probe, neither of which is a handler corpus on the original.
the handler table of title 12 was already read: tools/th-anm-handlers.py carries it
  beside the five others, from the dispatch at 0x45569d
      movsx eax, word [esi]; inc eax; cmp eax, 0x6f; ja default;
      jmp dword ptr [eax*4 + 0x458730]
  a flat table of 112 entries from the -1 sentinel to opcode 110, all inside the
  image, default 0x457c91, and the sentinel itself at 0x455b29.
what an oracle needs besides the table is the address an ordinary handler returns to -
  the boundary the five other oracles call LOOP - and the register the call passes the
  VM and the script pointer in.
```

### 347.2 Read, not guessed

```
tools/th12-anm-plan.py reads both off the image and prints the evidence.
    the enclosing function   the dispatch at 0x45569d belongs to the function that
                            begins at 0x455630; its prologue pushes ebp, ebx, esi,
                            edi and reads its argument with mov edi, [ebp+8]
    the register convention the guard is entered after mov esi, [edi+0x3f0]: the VM
                            is in EDI, the script pointer is [edi+0x3f0], and the
                            handler bodies read the opcode from ESI - the table
                            guard itself does movsx eax, word [esi]
    the field anchors       the same 0x30 bytes show the interpreter testing
                            [edi+0x3c4] and comparing a time against [edi+0x6c]
    the boundary            the only back edge inside the function is at 0x4556cc to
                            0x455686, which is the dispatch guard minus 0x17 - and
                            the TH13 oracle's LOOP of 0x4624fd is its own guard
                            0x462514 minus exactly 0x17 as well, so the same
                            relation holds on two titles measured apart
```

```
the plan is not a claim until a handler runs through it. With the VM in EDI, the
  script pointer at [edi+0x3f0], the script in ESI and 0x455686 as the boundary,
  title 12's own handlers run in Unicorn with no game or OS stub:
    op 6    all three values reached the boundary
    op 21   all three values reached the boundary

    op 1    the sentinel entry 0x455b29 - out of the instruction path
    op 102  a fault at 0x455efd, the geometry or resource dependency class, which the
            other titles' harnesses satisfy by handing over the game's own buffers
two ordinary handlers reaching the boundary in every value is the assertion every
  other title's oracle makes, and it is the first time it holds for title 12.
```

## 348. Title 12 has an oracle corpus, and the sixth zero is gone

### 348.1 The boundary, found twice

```
section 347 derived the boundary of title 12 two ways from the same image and got
  one address. The plan read it as the dispatch guard minus 0x17 - the relation
  the TH13 oracle uses, 0x462514 - 0x17 = 0x4624fd - and the live run put it to
  work with two ordinary handlers. The generator of this round held it to the route
  the oracles of 16, 17 and 18 use: the default handler's own tail. The default
  handler at 0x457c91 jumps to exactly one address in the interpreter region, and it
  is 0x455686.
    the guard 0x45569d minus 0x17 = 0x455686
    the default handler's tail jump  = 0x455686
so the constant is read off the image once by a relation between two titles and once
  from the code, and the two agree.
```

### 348.2 The corpus, in the shape of the five others

```
tools/th12-anm-native.py executes every real handler of the flat table - 110 of them -
  over the value sweep and two variants the other titles use. A case carries `before`
  and `context`, the whole 0x700-byte snapshot on both sides of the one call, so a
  checker compares what a case changes and not what the corpus seeded. The variant is
  carried by the two fields the interpreter itself reads before the handler,
  [edi+0x3c4] and [edi+0x6c].
  cases 4400, of which 3192 run to the boundary and 1208 fault; 110 handlers take part;
  89 of the 110 leave an observable write in the snapshot.
  the widest writers are the geometry-bearing bodies - opcodes 55, 56, 59, 93, 94
  and 100, each with about two thousand differing bits over its forty cases.
  the faults are named by class rather than counted: an invalid memory read 878, an
  invalid memory fetch 247, a landing beside the boundary at 0x4574f5 and 0x4575ba
  40 each, and two unhandled CPU exceptions. That is the class every other oracle
  also counts: a body that wants the harness's own room.
the measured block records the address of the boundary, its relation to the guard,
  the snapshot size, the default, the table and handler counts, and the call
  convention (the VM in EDI, the script pointer at [edi+0x3f0], the script in ESI).
```

## 350. The 55 uncandidated slots, measured to their composition

### 350.1 What the checker now measures about a gap

```
section 349 named each uncandidated slot by its nearest named member. A name does
  not say whether the slot is a field the port lacks or the same field carrying a
  seed that differs, so the checker now measures the nearest port *offset* as well
  and reports how many cases separate it:
    the 9 nearest    a port word differing in 19 or 20 cases of 3192, which is an
                     edge or a seed and not a missing field
    the 3 widest     differing in 746, 1319 and 1438 cases: +0x47c, +0x6c and
                     +0x3c4, and two of those three are this corpus's own
                     variant seeds, the field the interpreter reads before the
                     handler and the time it compares against [edi+0x6c]
    the rest         between 10 and 20 percent of the cases
the checker prints each slot with both numbers, so the composition of the gap is
  read off the report rather than argued: 9 slots within 1 percent, 43 within 10,
  3 wider, with 81 slots mapped and agreeing exactly.
```

### 350.2 Why the gap is a size, read off the port itself

```
the port states its own title 12 ladder in AnmVm.hpp:
    static_assert(sizeof(AnmVm) == 0x434 + kAnmVmExtensionBytes);
    static_assert(offsetof(AnmVm, instruction) == 0x3a8);
    kAnmVmExtensionBytes is zero for title 12, and the comparator the checker
      builds measures 1076 bytes = 0x434
so the title 12 VM the port compares is the shared comparison prefix - the layout
  titles 13 and 14 extend by three Vec2 and two interpolator blocks - while the
  original's own title 12 ABI runs past 0x480. The uncandidated slots are the
  original's words the prefix does not carry at their own offsets, which is why
  their nearest port word is a constant and differs in a fixed minority of cases.
two of them are the seeds this corpus itself set, +0x3c4 and +0x6c, and their
  nearest words differ in 1438 and 1319 cases: the difference is not noise about
  one word, it is the two layouts.
```

### 350.3 The order this leaves
```
closing the list is a port-side change with a measured target: give title 12 an ABI
  mirror the way titles 13 and 14 have one, so the original's own words at their
  own offsets have a home in the title 12 layout. Then the same checker asks about
  136 slots instead of 81, and the five other titles' checkers have to stay at
  their own numbers, which is the constraint that makes the mirror a title 12
  extension rather than a layout change.
the other direction - the 9 slots within 1 percent - is a corpus and fixture
  matter and not a port matter: those differ because the fixture does not seed the
  port's field the way this corpus seeds the original's.
keepers: no port source touched. Title 13 at PASS 694 state and 250 random-polar
  cases with 68 ANM resources; geometry at pass 3 fail 0.
```
## 351. The gap, split by an instrument: seeds, layouts, and the class of a coincidence

### 351.1 Two passes, because the port shares algorithms and not layouts

```
the port says the reason itself, in EnemyScript.cpp, about +0x47c: the marker is
  the port's own bit, and "the port shares algorithms, not object layouts". So a
  whole native word may be one bit of one of the port's words. Two passes follow
  from that, and each can come out at zero:
    the whole-word delta pass   a port offset whose four bytes change in exactly the
                              same cases as the native slot: 1 of the 55
    the bit pass              a port *bit* whose change over the cases equals the
                              change of a native bit of the slot
both read the changes rather than the states, which is the only comparison that
  survives two different object layouts.
```

### 351.2 What the bit pass found, and what it did not

```
the 55 uncandidated slots carry 1295 bits that change in some case.
    reproduced by some port bit   585 of 1295, over 34 of the 55 slots, using 116
      distinct port bits
    of those, sharing their mask    534, so only 51 have a unique source; the rest
      are the coincidence class the newer titles' census also has to filter, and the
      mask they share is a clock: one port bit at 0x156 and one at 0x220 carry 43
      native bits each, which is a whole event and not a field
so the raw number is an upper bound and the report states it as one.
```

### 351.3 The split, which is the useful result

```
by slot, and the three parts are not the same kind of thing:
    every changing bit reproduced   18 slots
      0xcc 0xd8 0x118 0x124 0x144 0x150 0x190 0x19c 0x1cc 0x1d8 0x254 0x260 0x280 0x28c 0x2ac 0x2b8 0x2d8 0x2e4
    some of them                   16 slots
    none of them                   20 slots
      0x24 0x28 0x40 0x44 0x50 0x54 0x58 0x5c 0x68 0x74 0x78 0xe0 0x158 0x208 0x214 0x218 0x21c 0x220 0x3fc 0x480
the first group is not a layout gap at all: the port makes every change the
  original makes, and the absolute vectors differ only where a seed or an edge
  separates them - section 350 already measured those as the nine within one
  percent. The third group is the layout gap proper: 20 slots of the 55.
  The mirror the previous section ordered is therefore an order for 20 slots and
  not for 55, and the instrument that said so is the one that can fail.
```
