  replay.test.mjs, and the browser boots above.


## 367. The record rows were the generation's, and two walls moved

The wall last round left was `stage battle initialization failed: initial player stage reset (110)`
on TH16 and TH17. That number is `PlayerFrame::rebuild_options` (100 + the option rebuild's own
code), and the code inside is one division: `count = power / power_step`, rejected when it lands
past the eight formation levels the two option tables have. A fresh stage's power is a small
number, so the wall said the load had put something else in there.

**The pair.** A record stores the stage's start, and in every attract demo of every title that is
the pair (0, 51200) - 1/128 turns the second into the 400 pixels a stage puts the player at. So
the question "where does this title keep it" is answerable from the title's own demos: look for
exactly that pair inside the record's fixed part and require the *same* offset in every demo a
title ships. The two rows whose place was already read out of machine code are the control, and
both come out right - TH12 at +0x30 (`th12.exe`) with no other offset, TH13 at +0xC
(`lea ecx,[edi+0xc]` at 0x048feb, restoring through 0x47850) with no other offset:


| title | the pair sits at | demos it holds on | what the port read there before |
| ----- | ---------------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------- |
| th12 | +0x30 | 4 | the pair (the row the port carried) |
| th13 | +0xC | 4 | -1, 0 |
| th14 | +0xC | 3 | -1, 0 |
| th16 | +0xC | 4 | that demo's character (1, 3, 0, 2), 0 |
| th17 | +0xC | 3 | that demo's character (0, 1, 2), 0 |
| th18 | +0xC | 4 | 0x38123B0E, 0x16C0F8BB in all four |


So the pair belongs to the generation, TH12 is the outlier for the third time (its container, its
selection words, now its pair), and the scalars stay TH12's alone: the shared restore hands the
pair over and leaves the live economy to the game. The last column is the same measurement's
other half - TH16's +0x30 holds that demo's character, TH18's holds two constants - so the
"power" the port divided was not a power. Both titles moved:

**The ECL shape.** TH16 and TH17 then stopped one instruction later, in the stage script:
`[ecl] handler trap EnemyEmitterCommands.cpp:81 command=0x1f6`. The port already knew this opcode
from TH13 - one parameter where TH12's record has three, and a parameter past the eight emitters
TH12's body indexes - and had made it a documented no-op for TH13 alone. The other three titles
answer for themselves: in all 22 of TH16's stage scripts, all 138 of its 0x1f6 records are
length 20 with one parameter (arguments 0x20, 0xc, 0x10, 0x4c, 0x120, 0x20d among them);
TH17's 99 and TH18's 110 are the same shape, and TH12's are 28/3. The gate now covers the
generation rather than one title, and the two runs say where it left them: th16 34 s, 10487 frames, stage 0 / phase 1 stopping at
`stage battle initialization failed: stage main: ECL opcode 23`, th17 34 s, 10487 frames, stage 0 / phase 1 at `stage battle initialization failed: stage main: ECL opcode 23` - the main stage script's own next unhandled opcode, which is the piece
after this one.

**The next wall, already measured.** TH14 did not go the same way. Its run is
`35 s, 374638 frames, stage 0 / phase 0` with `original demo resource missing`, and the source of that error is
`GameSession.cpp:182`: after 1800 idle frames on the title screen the port plays an *original
attract demo*, and the name it builds is TH12's - `demo3.rpy` first, then 2, 1, 0. The titles
ship their own sets:


| title | its own attract demos | what the port asks for |
| ----- | --------------------- | --------------------- |
| th12 | demo0..demo3 | all four present - the naming the port carries |
| th13 | demo0..demo3 | all four present |
| th14 | demo0..demo2 | demo3.rpy missing |
| th16 | demo1..demo4 | demo0.rpy missing (the first miss is demo0) |
| th17 | demo1..demo3 | demo0.rpy missing |
| th18 | demo1..demo4 | demo0.rpy missing |


Two things are per title in that one line: the generation numbers its demos from 1 while TH12 and
TH13 start at 0 (and TH14 has three where TH16 and TH18 have four), and the order the original
plays them in is the title's too, which is the next piece. The set alone is measured from each title's own
archive (`artifacts/th12/rpy-dump/th<title>`).

| title | the run | the error now |
| ----- | ------- | ------------- |
| th14 | 35 s, 374638 frames, stage 0 / phase 0 | `original demo resource missing` |
| th16 | 34 s, 10487 frames, stage 0 / phase 1 | `stage battle initialization failed: stage main: ECL opcode 23` |
| th17 | 34 s, 10487 frames, stage 0 / phase 1 | `stage battle initialization failed: stage main: ECL opcode 23` |

`tools/th-replay-entry-scan.py` and `tools/th-ecl-instructions.py` are the two scans behind this
(the second, run over a whole stage set, is where the counts above come from).

keepers: the offline walk over every demo of all six titles (tools/th-replay-parse.py), the
  container and geometry controls (tools/th-replay-container.py, tools/th-replay-geometry.py), the
  selection search (tools/th-replay-selection.py), the entry-pair scan with its two machine-code
  controls (tools/th-replay-entry-scan.py on 12/13/14/16/17/18) and the browser boots above.


## 368. The wait's number moved for the whole generation, and the stage script went on

The wall this round opened on was `stage main: ECL opcode 23` - the bytecode 0x17 - raised from
`spawn_root` on TH16 and TH17. The port's interpreter switches on TH12's numbers, where the
frames-counted wait is 0x53, and the title's own number reaches it through `ecl_vm_opcode`. That
function had the row for TH13 and, inside TH14's measured table, for TH14, and nothing for the
three newer titles.

Each of them answers from its own scripts, and by three instruments of different kinds:

* the census of the whole ECL set (`tools/th-ecl-wait-census.py`, walking each title's staged
  `.ecl` files with the layout the walk validates). The wait is one number in each title, and no
  title uses both:


| title | its own scripts use 0x17 (23) | and 0x53 (83) | file(s) / words walked |
| ----- | ---------------------------- | -------------- | --------------------- |
| th12 | 0 | **1890** | 9 / 28409 |
| th13 | **1468** | 0 | 21 / 21899 |
| th14 | **1609** | 0 | 24 / 24798 |
| th16 | **1591** | 0 | 22 / 24302 |
| th17 | **1514** | 0 | 22 / 24655 |
| th18 | **1510** | 0 | 22 / 22721 |


  So the row is a plain one-to-one: 0x17 is the wait wherever TH12 spells it 0x53, six titles of
  six, and it is measured directly from the bytes the titles ship rather than inferred from the
  number's neighbours.

* by corpus fingerprint (`tools/th-ecl-opcode-map.py`): pairing every TH16 number against every
  TH12 number by the multiset of records it occurs with, TH16's 0x17 pairs with TH12's 0x53 in
  981 of its 1591 records, against 556 (35%) for the next candidate.

* by alignment inside one stage (`tools/th-ecl-script-align.py th16:st01.ecl th12:stage01.ecl`),
  which pairs records positionally and reads the two opcodes off each pair: 0x017 -> 0x053 in 10
  aligned pairs, the same pairing again.

The row is landed for the whole generation, and it moved both runs. What the census also says is
where the *next* command is likely to come from: the modern five use 0x53 (0x35) 141/142/186/88/59
times where TH12 uses it 503 times, and use 0x16 55/201/207 and 0x54 8..23 times, numbers TH12
never spells - so the bytecode block around the wait was renumbered as a block, and each of those
numbers needs its own row before the scripts run end to end. Both runs also went much further: TH16
nearly doubled (8474 -> 19832 frames) and reached a *running battle*, where it stopped at a number
the port already refuses on purpose, 321 (it is in `kTh12CollidingOpcodes` - a number the two
titles spell differently, so it waits for its own evidence), and TH17 reached 17464 frames and
stopped in the emitter family's own gate (`EnemyEmitterCommands.cpp:86`, command 0x20c). The runs:

| title | the run | the error now |
| ----- | ------- | ------------- |
| th16 | 35 s, 19832 frames, stage 0 / phase 1 | `battle update failed: -1001 ECL opcode 321 at time 0.000000` |
| th17 | 36 s, 17464 frames, stage 0 / phase 1 | `[ecl] handler trap EnemyEmitterCommands.cpp:86 command=0x20c` |

keepers: the offline walk over every demo of all six titles (tools/th-replay-parse.py), the entry-pair
  scan with its controls (tools/th-replay-entry-scan.py), the six-title wait census
  (tools/th-ecl-wait-census.py) and the browser boots above.

## 369. The named spawn's number belongs to the generation too, and the next wall is an index

The wall was `battle update failed: ECL opcode 321` on TH16 - the bytecode 0x141, reached inside a
running battle (the title's own attract demo had begun). 321 is one of the three numbers
`kTh12CollidingOpcodes` carries, and that list exists because a number whose TH12 body is not
decoded must not be given a TH12 body in a title that spells something else with it. TH13's escape
was already measured (its 0x141 is TH12's named spawn byte for byte); the question was what TH16's
0x141 records are.

They are the same record. In its own staged data, TH16's `st06bs.ecl` holds 0x141 eight times,
every one length 52 with six parameters and the arguments
`0xc "MapleEnemy3" 0 0 0x64 0x3e8 0`, and its `st07.ecl` holds it twice with `MapleEnemy` and
`MapleEnemy2` - the name a stage chooses, then the same four numbers. TH13's `st06.ecl` 0x141 and
TH12's 0x118 are that same record (`tools/th-ecl-instructions.py`). The census over each title's
whole ECL set is the second reading, and it reads one number per title:


| title | 0x118 (the named spawn over TH12) | 0x141 (the generation's) | 0x116 | 0x119 |
| ----- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ----- | ----- |
| th12 | 4 | 1 | 1 | 40 |
| th13 | 0 | 7 | 0 | 0 |
| th14 | 0 | 7 | 0 | 0 |
| th16 | 0 | 16 | 0 | 0 |
| th17 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| th18 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |


(the collision list's other two numbers are TH12-only as well - 0x116 appears once, in TH12, and
0x119 forty times, nowhere else - so the generation inherits nothing from them either). The row
`ecl_named_spawn_relative` now covers the generation, and through it `colliding()` stops refusing
0x141 there.

**The next wall.** With the row, TH16 goes past 321 and lands on the *same* wall TH17 already
had: the emitter family's gate (`EnemyEmitterCommands.cpp:86`, which reads the record's first
argument as an index into the eight emitters TH12's layout has and traps past it), on command
0x20c. The records say the modern command is not TH12's:


| title | 0x20c records | shape (length, params) | first argument |
| ----- | ------------- | ----------------------- | -------------- |
| th12 | 53 | 24, 2 | 0..2, all inside the eight slots |
| th13 | 75 | 20, 1 | 0..7, all inside |
| th16 | 71 | 20, 1 | up to 81 (21 of 71 inside 0..7) |
| th17 | 75 | 20, 1 | up to 81 (19 of 75 inside) |
| th18 | 78 | 20, 1 | up to 81 (20 of 78 inside) |


So TH12's 0x20c is a two-parameter, 24-byte record whose index never leaves the eight slots,
while TH13's and the three newer titles' are one-parameter 20-byte records whose first argument
reaches 81 - 0x51. Either the modern command indexes a larger emitter table, or 0x20c means
something else there; the corpus fingerprints leave it ambiguous (TH17's 0x20c has seven
signatures and no TH12 counterpart above 26%), which is exactly the case the machine code has to
settle: the modern titles' own body for it, not a TH12 body inherited by number.

| title | the run | the error now |
| ----- | ------- | ------------- |
| th16 | 34 s, 17502 frames, stage 0 / phase 1 | `[ecl] handler trap EnemyEmitterCommands.cpp:86 command=0x20c` |
| th17 | 36 s, 17464 frames, stage 0 / phase 1 | `[ecl] handler trap EnemyEmitterCommands.cpp:86 command=0x20c` |

keepers: the offline walk over every demo of all six titles (tools/th-replay-parse.py), the entry-pair
  scan with its controls (tools/th-replay-entry-scan.py), the six-title wait census with the command
  words it now also prints (tools/th-ecl-wait-census.py --words 278,280,281,321) and the boots above.


## 370. The modern 0x20c is not TH12's: its own group, its own case, its own value

Both boots stopped at the emitter family's gate on 0x20c (`EnemyEmitterCommands.cpp:86`, the first
argument read as a slot index and refused past the eight TH12's layout has). The instrument order
mattered: the record alone says the modern one is different, and the dispatcher and the title's own
routine say what it is.

**The record.** Counting the shapes of every 0x20c record in each title's whole ECL set
(`tools/th-ecl-wait-census.py` and the shape walk in round 369) separates the two commands before
any code is read:


| title | 0x20c records | shape (length, params) | first argument |
| ----- | ------------- | ----------------------- | -------------- |
| th12 | 53 | 24, 2 | 0..2, inside the eight slots |
| th13 | 75 | 20, 1 | 0..7, inside |
| th16 | 71 | 20, 1 | up to 81 (21 of 71 inside 0..7) |
| th17 | 75 | 20, 1 | up to 81 (19 of 75 inside) |
| th18 | 78 | 20, 1 | up to 81 (20 of 78 inside) |


**The dispatch.** Over the whole extended domain (0x12c..0x2bc, one line per opcode from
`tools/th-ecl-dispatch.py`) TH16, TH17 and TH18 each resolve 0x20c through group 69, and in each of
the three that group holds exactly one opcode, 0x20c itself, while the neighbouring opcodes share
theirs (0x210 and 0x21a both land in group 67). So for once the group handler is the case, and no
second-level branch has to be traced: TH16 0x4222bf, TH17 0x425d00, TH18 0x435b23 - the three
titles' own bodies.

**The body.** `tools/th-code-window.py`, at TH17's own address (RVA 0x25d00):

    0x025d00  push 0 / mov ecx, edi / call 0x28cc0   ; read the record's one argument
    0x025d09  mov ecx, [0x4b76b0] / push esi / call 0x29b10
    0x025d17  mov [edi + 0x4548], esi                ; store the value
    0x025d1d  mov [edi + 0x454c], 0                  ; and zero its neighbour
and the routine it calls (RVA 0x29b10): `mov [0x4b59e4], ecx ; mov [eax + 0x24], ecx` with
`eax = [0x4b76b0]`. Four memories of one value, and not a slot index anywhere.

**Why the argument reaches 81.** Each title's own reset routine walks its emitter table once, and the
decrementing register is the slot count - the number the port's gate had guessed as 8 from TH12:


| title | the title's own clear loop | slots | stride | base |
| ----- | -------------------------- | ----- | ------ | ---- |
| th12 | RVA 0x123fe, `lea ebx, [ebp+9]` with ebp = -2 | 8 | 0x214 | +0x48c |
| th16 | RVA 0x1a798, `mov edi, 0x10` | 16 | 0x380 | +0x598 |
| th17 | RVA 0x1ea4d, `mov ebx, 0x10` | 16 | 0x380 | +0x598 |
| th18 | RVA 0x2e12d, `mov ebx, 0x10` | 16 | 0x488 | +0x598 |
| th13 | its own loop not found by this pattern yet | ? | 0x5a4, 0x5bc, 0x5cc seen as scales | ? |
| th14 | same | ? | 0x5cc seen as a scale | ? |


So the modern slots number 16, and the records' arguments reach 0x51 (81): the value is handed to
a routine, not used as an index at all. TH13's and TH14's own loop has not been found by this
pattern yet, and the section says so rather than filling the row with the neighbours' number.

The port now handles the generation's 0x20c before the slot index is read, keeping one mirror per
destination the original writes, and TH12 keeps its own case (the emitter radius, the two-parameter
record). Both boots went past the gate and much further:

| title | the run | the error now |
| ----- | ------- | ------------- |
| th16 | 34 s, 19915 frames, stage 0 / phase 1 | `battle update failed: -1001 ECL opcode 630 at time 0.000000` |
| th17 | 35 s, 19838 frames, stage 0 / phase 1 | `battle update failed: -1001 ECL opcode 630 at time 0.000000` |

The next wall is measured the same way and is a clean one: opcode 630 (0x276) in a running
battle, which TH12 spells **zero** times and the other five spell 4, 28, 35, 34 and 33 times
(`py -3 tools/th-ecl-wait-census.py --words 630`) - a number that belongs to the generation alone,
like the wait and the named spawn before it.

keepers: the offline walk over every demo of all six titles (tools/th-replay-parse.py), the dispatch
  resolver over the modern domain (tools/th-ecl-dispatch.py, one line per opcode), the six-title
  command census (tools/th-ecl-wait-census.py --words ...), the new durable clear-loop reader and
  code window (tools/th-emitter-count.py, tools/th-code-window.py, both reproducing the TH12 control:
  8 slots of stride 0x214 at +0x48c) and the boots above.

## 371. The next wall is the generation's numeric script selection, and it is measured

Both boots stopped on the same opcode 630 (0x276) inside a running battle, and the census says why
TH12 had never needed it:


| title | 0x276 (630) | the shape of its records | the ids it selects |
| ----- | ----------- | ------------------------ | ------------------ |
| th12 | 0 | - | - |
| th13 | 4 | 20 bytes, one parameter | 1 |
| th14 | 28 | 20 bytes, one parameter | 1, 2, 4 |
| th16 | 35 | 20 bytes, one parameter | 1, 2, 5 |
| th17 | 34 | 20 bytes, one parameter | 1, 2, 5 |
| th18 | 33 | 20 bytes, one parameter | 1, 2, 5 |


A number used by five titles and by none of TH12 is not a renumbering to guess at - it is a command
the older title does not have, so it needs its own reading, and the order was the same as for the
0x20c row: record shape, group, body, and what the stream does afterwards.

**The shape** is one parameter of 20 bytes, with the identifiers 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6.

**The group.** Over the whole extended domain (0x12c..0x2bc, one line per opcode,
tools/th-ecl-dispatch.py) 0x276 lands in a group that holds only itself - group 141 in TH16 and
TH17, 143 in TH18, where the neighbouring numbers share theirs. So the routine the resolver returns
is the case: TH17's is at 0x42627d.

**The body.** TH17's own reads the record's single argument and hands it to a walk (RVA 0xc580)
over the records tagged 0x10 - which is the tag every `ECLH` block header in these files carries,
`word [+4] == 0x10` - comparing the argument against the record's dword at +8, and then stores the
found entry's byte offset into the owner's pair at +0x20/+0x1c. A lookup that answers with the
block it found, not with an index into an emitter or a bullet table.

**The stream.** What follows a 0x276 continues in place rather than jumping to the selected block:
st06bs.ecl's 0x276 at record 333 is followed by `0x1f8`, then by two `0x00b` records carrying the
name - a spawn - and the ones in the same file stand right after a manager call with the same
argument (records 548..549 are `0x21c 4` and `0x276 4`). So the command selects what comes next.

The port has the same model already, under a name: `EclProgram` keeps the file's `ECLH` blocks as
`definitions`, (file, index) pairs, and the owner selects one through `select_subroutine(const
char*)` - the name-carrying form. What the port lacked was a row for the numeric form, which is
where both boots fell through. The row now keeps the id the original resolved and reports success,
and says plainly what it has not consumed yet: which block that id selects, and through what
numbering, since the port resolves blocks by their names today.

The records also show why the low numbers of the generation need no rows: the scripts of the three
newer titles use 0x00b, 0x00c and 0x00d in the stream - the port's own 11, 12 and 13, Call, Jump
and JumpIfZero - and run them; only the block the wait sits in was renumbered.

| title | the run | the error now |
| ----- | ------- | ------------- |
| th16 | 35 s, 19896 frames, stage 2 / phase 1 | `battle update failed: -1001 ECL opcode 518 at time 10.000000` |
| th17 | 34 s, 19816 frames, stage 0 / phase 1 | `battle update failed: -1001 ECL opcode 518 at time 10.000000` |

Both went past the selection and reached 19896 and 19816 frames - and TH16's own record now shows
stage 2 rather than 0, so it is walking the demos' stages. The next wall is 518 (0x206) at ten
seconds in, and it arrives with a measured row half-written already: 0x206/0x207 are the dialogue
pair TH13 spells 0x1a2/0x1a3, and `ecl_state_opcode` carries that translation gated to TH13 alone,
while the census shows the pair belongs to the whole generation - 518 and 519 are 0 in TH12's whole
ECL set and 50/59, 49/69, 56/68, 55/59 and 58/92 in the other five
(`py -3 tools/th-ecl-wait-census.py --words 518,519`). What the row still needs before it is widened
is what it was measured with in the first place, run on each title's own records: the alignment and
the two bodies that named 0x206 as the dialogue starter.

Keepers: the offline walk over every demo of all six titles (tools/th-replay-parse.py), the dispatch
resolver over the modern domain (tools/th-ecl-dispatch.py, one line per opcode), the six-title
command census (tools/th-ecl-wait-census.py --words ...), the clear-loop reader
(tools/th-emitter-count.py) and the code window (tools/th-code-window.py).

## 372. The generation's dialogue pair: a row that was measured for one title and belonged to five

Both boots stopped ten seconds in on 518 and tried to route `0x206` to a handler while the title's
own machine code sends it somewhere else. The pair was not new work: an earlier round had measured
0x206 and 0x207 as the dialogue starter and its wait for TH13, written the row and the reasoning
into `EclRoutes.hpp`, and left it gated to TH13 - because TH13 was the title that had been read.
What the gate needed was the same reading done on each title that spells it, which is what the
census said the whole generation does: 518 and 519 are 0 in TH12's whole ECL set and appear
50/59, 49/69, 56/68, 55/59 and 58/92 times in TH13/14/16/17/18.
The reverse census agrees from the other side: the spelling the row replaces is 48 and 75 records in TH12's whole set and 0 or 0 in each of the five newer titles (`--words 418,419`).

Three measurements, of the three kinds this port has been using for a renumbering:

**The records.** In each of TH13/16/17/18 the pair is 20 bytes with one parameter (0x206) and 16
with none (0x207) - the shape TH12 spells 0x1a2 and 0x1a3 - and the ones in a stage's opening
carry the same clock values and the same single argument across the titles
(tools/th-ecl-instructions.py).

**The alignment.** The instrument that named the pair for TH13 (which ignores opcode words and
matches record sequences) reproduces it on its control title - 0x206 with 0x1a2 three times, 0x207
with 0x1a3 four - and pairs TH16's 0x207 with 0x1a3 three times
(tools/th-ecl-script-align.py).

**The bodies.** Each title resolves the pair to handlers of its own, and the addresses are of a
different kind than the ones the older row cites: 13 0x41e3da/0x41e407, 14 0x428819/0x428847,
16 0x4216b3/0x4216e0, 17 0x42506e/0x4250af, 18 0x434dbf/0x434e2b
(tools/th-ecl-dispatch.py). The 0x207 side of each is TH13's own three steps: read the manager,
test its field and leave through the shared tail when the dialogue is not done, else answer minus
one. TH16's reads `mov eax,[0x4a6dcc]; mov eax,[eax+0x1c8]; test eax,eax; je 0x22a9b; cmp dword
ptr [eax+0x18c],0; jne 0x22a9b; or eax,-1` - the same tail its other cases leave through
(tools/th-code-window.py). The starter side resolves argument 0 through the title's own accessor and
hands it to the title's dialogue manager - the shape the TH13 body behind the original row has.

The whole difference was the gate, and the port's state handler already owned 0x1a2 and 0x1a3.

| title | the run | the error now |
| ----- | ------- | ------------- |
| th16 | 34 s, 19090 frames, stage 0 / phase 1 | `battle update failed: -1001 dialogue animation creation` |
| th17 | 35 s, 19018 frames, stage 0 / phase 1 | `battle update failed: -1001 dialogue animation creation` |

The row did its job - 518 is gone and both boots now reach the dialogue at ten seconds in - and it
exposed the next wall underneath, of the same family one layer down: `dialogue animation creation
failed`. The dialogue builds its animation through the port's own TH12 spelling (`Dialogue.cpp`:
`create(8, logo, 2, 27)` for the logo dialogue and `create(0, text, scripts[stage], 27)` for the
stage one), i.e. script 2 of the logo animation file and the per-stage script out of a seven-entry
table, both of them numbers the generation authors for itself. The three instrument classes that
have been resolving numbers like these apply directly: the title's own 0x206 starter body calls its
dialogue manager, so the manager's animation arguments are reachable in that title's machine code;
the animation resource of the opening dialogue can be listed for its script count and for which ids
the title uses; and the port's own load path shows which file id indexes what. Which of the two
numbers fails here is the first thing the next round reads out of its own candidate.

Keepers: the six-title command census (tools/th-ecl-wait-census.py --words 418,419,518,519), the
dispatch resolver over the modern domain (tools/th-ecl-dispatch.py), the aligner
(tools/th-ecl-script-align.py), the code window (tools/th-code-window.py) and the offline replay walk
over all six titles demos (tools/th-replay-parse.py).

## 373. The dialogue wall, measured down to its ANM opcode

With 518 routed, both boots reached the dialogue ten seconds in and stopped inside its first creation.
The port's message was `dialogue animation creation`, with nothing in it, while the port's own title
screen already says `title animation creation failed: 83 (ANM opcode 0)`. Three boots of that one
message turned the wall into four numbers, which is the whole of this round's port work.

**`AnmManager::create` has more than one way to return null** (`AnmManager.cpp:30-53`): a negative
script, a script at or past the resource's script count, a creation nested past 128 - and, behind
them, a VM whose first update failed, where the manager records the offending ANM opcode in
`last_error` before destroying the VM. A message that names the slot, the script, the resource's
script count, the file id, the depth and that opcode separates the four.

The boots read, in order:

| the reported fields | what they rule out |
| ------------------- | ------------------ |
| `slot 3, script 0 of 74 (file 0)` | a script that does not exist in a resource that is too small |
| the same message with `depth 0` | a creation nested past the manager limit |
| the same message with `ANM opcode 0` | everything except a failing first update of the VM |

The first answer - slot 3, script 0 of a 74-script resource, file 0, depth 0 - rules out the three
front checks, and the second names the real one: ANM opcode 0. Both titles report exactly the same
number, and the title screen of TH18 has been reporting it too; one opcode family is behind three
walls.

That the resource really holds the slot is worth a reading of its own, and the port's loader keeps
two counts next to each other that are easy to swap - the u16 at +4 counts **sprites**, whose
four-byte offsets fill the first table, while the u16 at +6 counts the **scripts**, whose eight-byte
records start at `64 + ns*4` and end at the first instruction with opcode -1. The promotion of
`tools/th-anm-script-slots.py` was settled by running it against the durable dumper
(`tools/th-anm-script-dump.py`), which walks the same two tables: TH12's ascii.anm comes out at 21
script slots, and the dumper reads slot 20 without complaint; TH12's and the generation's own
st05logo.anm come out at 7 slots each, so the dialogue's `create(8, logo, 2, 27)` has its script.
The failing resource reports 74, and its slot 0 is the one that would not interpret.

**What the two text animations look like**, out of the title's own archive
(`tools/th-archive-dump.mjs <title> <version> ascii.anm`, then slot 0):

    th12 ascii.anm slot 0 (284 bytes):  op=3   len=12 time=0    (then 65, 63, 64, 52, 4, 64)
    th16 ascii.anm slot 0 (320 bytes):  op=300 len=12 time=-1   (then 421, 304, 313, 403, 400,
                                          402, 412, op=0 len=8 time=30, then the small band)

The generation's own scripts open with a band (300, 4xx) that TH12's opening does not have, at
frame -1, and fall back to TH12's numbers afterwards - so the newer titles extend their ANM command
space rather than renumber it, and the opcode that stops the port has to be resolved in each title's
own table (`tools/th-anm-opcode-resolve.py`, `tools/th-anm-script-dump.py`), the same way the ECL
numbers in the sections before it were.

| title | the run | the error now |
| ----- | ------- | ------------- |
| th16 | 34 s, 21735 frames, stage 0 / phase 1 | `battle update failed: -1001 dialogue animation creation: slot 3 , script 0 of 74 (file 0, depth 0 , ANM opcode 0)` |
| th17 | 34 s, 21659 frames, stage 0 / phase 1 | `battle update failed: -1001 dialogue animation creation: slot 3 , script 0 of 74 (file 0, depth 0 , ANM opcode 0)` |

Keepers: the ANM slot reader (tools/th-anm-script-slots.py, with its two controls), the ANM script
dumper (tools/th-anm-script-dump.py), the archive dumper through the port's own decoder
(tools/th-archive-dump.mjs), the ECL pair census (tools/th-ecl-wait-census.py --words 418,419,518,519)
and the offline replay walk over all six titles demos (tools/th-replay-parse.py).

## 374. The label marker is spelled differently in the generation, and the wall moved

Section 373 ended on ANM opcode 0 with nothing further in it, and a zero opcode has two readings:
a command the port does not dispatch, or a reader that left the instruction stream and landed on a
zero word. The manager now records the failing instruction's byte offset next to its opcode, and the
first of the two readings went away in one boot: the offset is **+0x0005**, inside the first
twelve-byte instruction, where a word of length zero cannot be a command. So the interpreter
*jumped* into the middle of the stream before it failed.

The script's own bytes make the pair that produced it easy to find. The generation's text.anm slot 0
begins

    +0x000 op=300 len=12    +0x018 op=400 len=20    +0x038 op=313 len=12    +0x050 op=4 len=8
    +0x00c op=421 len=12    +0x02c op=304 len=12    +0x044 op=403 len=12    +0x058 op=5 len=12

and of those, every number the generation's own measured table knows (304, 313, 4) is harmless,
while the raw 5 at +0x058 was the one with a TH12 meaning attached: TH12's canonical 5 is
`counter -= 1; if(counter > 0) jump` (`AnmInterpreter.cpp:254`). The generation writes 5 as the
**label marker** - the number TH12 spells 64, which is what the interrupt scan walks for
(`AnmInterpreter.cpp:27`) and which TH13 and TH14 both move raw 5 onto in their own tables.

The census of the titles' own files is two-sided, and it is the row's evidence
(tools/th-anm-marker-census.py was promoted with TH12's own files as its control):

| file | scripts | raw 5 (with an id) | raw 7 | raw 64 |
| ---- | ------- | ------------------- | ----- | ------ |
| th12 text.anm | 86 | 0 | 0 | 176 |
| th12 ascii.anm | 21 | 0 | 0 | 22 |
| th16 text.anm | 74 | 207 (207) | 6 | 0 |
| th16 ascii.anm | 20 | 26 (26) | 8 | 0 |
| th17 st05enm.anm | 22 | 50 (50) | 11 | 0 |

Zero overlap in either direction: the generation has no raw 64 anywhere and TH12 has no raw 5. The
pinned dispatchers agree from the machine-code side - tools/th-anm-handlers.py reads raw 5 as the
default body in all three generation titles (0x4629c8 for 16, 0x46a141 for 17, 0x47b6f3 for 18),
which is exactly the no-op a label has, and is why TH13's own table calls this row `native-label`.

So the shared table for 16, 17 and 18 gained the one row, and the wall moved by measurement:

| boot | slot / script | the reported position |
| ---- | ------------- | -------------------- |
| before the row | slot 3, script 0 of 74 | `ANM opcode 0 at +0x0005` |
| after the row | slot 3, script 0 of 74 | `ANM opcode 0 at +0x002f` |

Both boots stop at the same creation (slot 3, script 0 of the 74-script text resource), so what
changed is only how far the interpreter got inside that script: +0x0005 was mid-instruction with a
length of zero, and +0x002f is a real walk that now reaches the command at +0x02c (the generation's
raw 304, one of the rows the value matcher measured). The next reading is the same instrument one
instruction earlier: the offset is three bytes into that twelve-byte command, so whatever moved the
pointer there is the next body to measure.

The record is in docs/porting/browser-th13-boot.json (dialogueAnmLabelMarker_374), the census tool is
tools/th-anm-marker-census.py, and the offset is recorded by AnmManager (last_error_offset) and
printed by Dialogue.cpp, both kept so the next wall is read as a byte position rather than a guess.

## 375. The command at the failing position, read from the path that reached it

Section 374 moved the dialogue wall to +0x002f and left the question of *how* the interpreter got
three bytes into a twelve-byte command. The answer needed the path, not the position, so the
interpreter now keeps a sixteen-entry ring of the commands it dispatches - the byte offset inside the
script and the number that ran, which is already in this port's numbering because the loader
translates on the way in (`AnmResource.cpp:87-99`). The manager copies the ring at the failure, and
Dialogue.cpp prints the tail of it; a position that repeats without moving would fill the ring with
itself, so a push that repeats the previous entry is dropped.

The first boot showed the ring working but shouting: the zero-length word at +0x002f was dispatched
over and over, and the tail was eight copies of `002f:0`. With repeats dropped, the path is nine
distinct positions and reads like a diagnosis by itself:

    path 000c:421,0018:400,002c:28948,0038:66,0044:403,0050:4,0040:64990,002f:0

`002c:28948` is the layer row the value matcher measured last time (0x7114), `0038:66` is raw
313's native row, and everything to that point walks linearly. Then `0050:4`. The generation's
table has no row for raw 4, so it stayed 4, and TH12's canonical 4 is `jump(argument(0))`
(`AnmInterpreter.cpp:253`) - a jump whose argument is not its own: the command is eight bytes long
and has no argument field, so `argument<u32>(0)` read the *next* instruction's header word,
`05 00 0c 00` = 0x000c0005. The interpreter jumped 786437 bytes past the script, read a garbage
command, and wandered back to +0x002f, where a zero word of length zero stopped it.

Raw 4 is the second half of the pair whose first half was already ported. The generation writes
its commands in two shapes, and the shapes decide the row: in their own text.anm, raw 4 appears 29
times, every one of them in the eight-byte, argument-less form, and raw 3 appears 122 times in
that same form; TH12 writes those two shapes as 69 (32) and 63 (98), and its own raw 4 is a
single long-form command. Counted per title (the parenthesis is the count in the eight-byte form):

| file | 3 | 4 | 5 | 7 | 63 | 64 | 69 |
| ---- | - | - | - | - | -- | -- | -- |
| th12 text.anm | 86 (0) | 1 (0) | 0 (0) | 0 (0) | 98 (98) | 176 (0) | 32 (32) |
| th12 ascii.anm | 19 (0) | 7 (0) | 0 (0) | 0 (0) | 16 (16) | 22 (0) | 0 (0) |
| th16 text.anm | 122 (122) | 29 (29) | 207 (0) | 6 (6) | 0 (0) | 0 (0) | 0 (0) |
| th16 ascii.anm | 14 (14) | 0 (0) | 26 (0) | 8 (8) | 0 (0) | 0 (0) | 0 (0) |

TH13's table measures 4 -> 69 over 48 witnesses and TH14 carries the row as native, and the
generation's own dispatchers read 5 as the no-op a label has. The shared table for 16, 17 and 18
gained its second row, {4, 69, 0, "native"}, and one more boot measured the effect: the text
lines create in **both** titles now, and the chain reaches the portrait, MSG opcode 1.

| title | the run | the error now |
| ----- | ------- | ------------- |
| th16 | 35 s, 23390 frames, stage 2 / phase 1 | `battle update failed: -1007 dialogue animation creation: slot 0 , script 31 of 27 (file 7, depth 0 , ANM opcode 0 at +0x0000) MSG opcode 1` |
| th17 | 34 s, 26474 frames, stage 0 / phase 1 | `battle update failed: -1007 dialogue animation creation: slot 0 , script 31 of 41 (file 7, depth 0 , ANM opcode 101 at +0x0134 path008c:119,00a0:415,00b4:117,00c8:117,00dc:117,00f0:117,0104:420,0134:101) MSG opcode 1` |

The two walls are different from each other, and their difference is the point: TH12's portrait
read (`Dialogue.cpp:71-88`, `mov eax,[0x4b0c90] ; mov ecx,[eax*4+0x4b2f84]` -> 31/30/28) is a
table of TH12's own, and the generation has its own table and its own player files - the same
script index 31 is out of range for title 16's 27-slot player file and in range for title 17's 41,
where the creation then interprets and stops on canonical 101 with a path to +0x0134. Those are the
next two readings: the portrait table out of each generation title's own machine code (the address
and the entries, as the comment does it for TH12 and TH13), and canonical 101 for title 17.

One honesty fix went in with them: `AnmManager::create` now clears the failure fields on entry, so a
range or depth failure cannot report the opcode, position and path of an earlier failure. The boot
before the fix showed exactly that - `ANM opcode 0 at +0x0000` on a script index of 31 out of 27.

Keepers: the dispatch ring (`AnmTrace.hpp`, pushed by `AnmVm::update`, copied by `AnmManager`), the
byte-position report (Dialogue.cpp), the marker census (tools/th-anm-marker-census.py, now with the
pair's numbers) and the offline replay walk over all six titles' demos (tools/th-replay-parse.py).

## 376. The portrait index is a table per title, and the run says which wall follows

Sections 374 and 375 got the text lines drawing. The first thing behind them was the portrait
(MSG opcode 1), and it named its own evidence: with TH12's table, title 16 asked its 27-slot
player file for script 31, and title 17 asked its 41-slot file for the same 31. TH12's read is
already in the port as a comment (`Dialogue.cpp`, `0x0042013f mov eax,[0x4b0c90]`,
`0x00420144 mov ecx,[eax*4+0x4b2f84]`), so the question is whether each generation title has the
same shape of site - and whether its table can be checked from a second side.

`tools/th-portrait-table.py` scans an image for the two instructions and reads the table the site
indexes. Its controls are the two tables the port already carries: TH12's must come out at
0x4b2f84 with 31 30 28, and TH13's at 0x4c0aa0 with 29 34 30 28. Both do, and the second side
of the control is the exported files: those entries are exactly the last script index of each
title's player files in order (32 31 29 and 30 35 31 29 - counted by the promoted slot reader).

The scan then reads the generation:

| title | the site | its table | entries | the title's own player slots |
| ----- | -------- | --------- | ------- | --------------------------- |
| th16 | 0x4443a1 | 0x492c00 | 8 7 11 11 | 27 17 23 36 (order pl00 pl02 pl03 pl01) |
| th17 | 0x42e153 | 0x4a1760 | 40 46 33 | 41 47 34 |
| th18 | 0x43f7b2 | 0x4b6620 | 40 46 29 28 | 41 47 30 29 |
| th14 | 0x432ba0 | 0x4d9c7c | 27 37 25 | (not exported here) |

TH17's and TH18's entries are exactly their own player files' last script index, the rule TH12 and
TH13 satisfy, so image and files agree on those two. TH16's do not satisfy it (8 7 11 11), and
that is not a reason to prefer the rule: its site is the portrait shape by disassembly, instruction
for instruction with TH17's - the read goes to a created object's own setter
(`call 0x46f600` then `push value; push object; call 0x407b20`, where TH17 has 0x476a60 and
0x407230), the same place TH12's verified read feeds - and all four numbers are in range for the
file order ShotFiles.hpp measured. So TH16's row is landed as the numbers the site reads. TH14's is
too, on the strength of the same shape.

The measured result is two more titles reaching further, with a wall that names itself:

| title | the run | the error now |
| ----- | ------- | ------------- |
| th16 | 35 s, 20714 frames, stage 0 / phase 1 | `battle update failed: -1007 unsupported MSG opcode MSG opcode 28` |
| th17 | 35 s, 20596 frames, stage 2 / phase 1 | `battle update failed: -1007 unsupported MSG opcode MSG opcode 28` |
| th14 | 36 s, 374638 frames, stage 0 / phase 0 | `original demo resource missing` |
| th18 | 35 s, 9161 frames, stage 0 / phase 0 | `invalid TH11 session selection` |

TH18 does not reach the battle at all (its title screen is still the wall section 373 named), so the
portrait did not change it either way, and TH14's wall is the missing demo resource, not the
message.

That wall is the same for title 16 and title 17, and it is the *next* reading: MSG opcode 28.
The corpus tool for exactly this already exists (`tools/th-msg-opcodes.py` censuses the opcodes each
title's own .msg files use), and the port carries TH13's handler of that number as a row with the
address in the title's image (`Dialogue.cpp`); the generation's handler is the same kind of
measurement, one operand list per title.

## 377. Every title's messages carry their own command set, and the census names the next wall

Section 376 left titles 16 and 17 at the same named wall: `unsupported MSG opcode 28`. A number in
a message is a property of the corpus a title ships, so the first reading is the corpus itself,
before any code: `tools/th-msg-payloads.py` walks every `.msg` file of every title and records
which numbers exist, with which payloads.

| title | messages | MSG 28 | MSG 29 | 28 decoded as two floats | 29 values |
| ----- | -------- | ------ | ------ | ------------------------ | --------- |
| th12 | 55 files, 9163 commands | **none** | **none** | - | - |
| th13 | 41 files, 6331 commands | 823 x 8 bytes | 185 x 4 bytes | 823 of 823 inside +-4096 | 0..3 |
| th14 | 55 files, 8427 commands | 1116 x 8 bytes | 143 x 4 bytes | 1116 of 1116 | 0..3 |
| th16 | 40 files, 7378 commands | 1022 x 8 bytes | 103 x 4 bytes | 1022 of 1022 | 0..3 |
| th17 | 79 files, 15494 commands | 2125 x 8 bytes | 578 x 4 bytes | 2125 of 2125 | 0..7 |
| th18 | 44 files, 11910 commands | 1605 x 8 bytes | 193 x 4 bytes | 1605 of 1605 | 0..3 |

Two things follow, both measured. Every one of the 6691 payloads under 28 decodes as two finite
floats no larger than 4096 - pairs like (112,288) and (224,144), the positions a message hands to a
drawn character - which is exactly how TH13's own handler reads the same command. And every payload
under 29 is a value below 8, inside the four bits TH13's handler puts into the style flags; TH13's
own 29s range over 0..3, which are the ones that mask selects. The generation therefore needs
neither a new meaning for 28 nor a second mask for 29, and the port's rows for both stop excluding
it: they were gated to TH13, they now cover every title whose messages contain them, and TH12 - which
has neither number - keeps falling through to its `default` exactly as before.

The machine code was asked for the same shape with `tools/th-msg-op-body.py`, which decodes each
image's whole `.text` and matches the window of TH13's handler (28: `fld [P+4] / fstp [S+X] /
fld [P+8] / fstp [S+Y]`; 29: `mov R,[P+4] / add R,R / add R,R / ... and R,mask`). The control is
TH13 itself: it must report 0x428c8e writing +0x194 and +0x198 and 0x429c2d selecting 0x3c - the
two addresses the port already carried - and it must not report them for a shape that is not there.
It finds both, and exactly one of each in a 656 KB `.text`. The generation has none of that
sequence, which is why the rows above are corpus rows: their own images say the command exists with
that payload, their own messages say what it holds, and the pair the port keeps is written by
nothing else.

| title | the run | the error now |
| ----- | ------- | ------------- |
| th16 | 35 s, 18055 frames, stage 2 / phase 1 | `Missing text animation` |
| th17 | 36 s, 18193 frames, stage 2 / phase 1 | `battle update failed: -1005 ` |

The census also names the rare commands that come after: title 16's messages contain MSG 34 and 35
once each, title 18's contain 36 twenty-four times, and title 14 carries 30 and 32, none of which
the port reads yet.

Two things in the table above are worth naming as the next work. Title 16's `Missing text animation`
is the port looking for a text animation a title does not have (the string is the port's own), and
title 17's failure carries an **empty** message - `battle update failed: -1005` with nothing after
the number, which is a gap in the port's own reporting, not in the title. Both are read the way
every wall here is: from the title's own data and the route that reaches them.

## 378. A wall has to name the animation it failed on

Section 377 ended with two walls, and both were poor reports before they were walls. Title 17's was
`battle update failed: -1005` with an *empty* reason; title 16's was one sentence,
`Missing text animation`, shared by three different gaps. The routes were read first:

- `GameSession.cpp:228` prints `battle->last_error` and `battle->error`. `GameBattle.cpp` sets a
  sentence of its own at the stage, player, ECL, spell, HUD and dialogue sites, but its two
  animation-manager sites (the overlay walk before the control tick and the main walk at its end)
  set the code -1005 alone, so the tail the session printed was empty.
- `FontDevice::text` checked `!ready||!vm.sprite||!vm.resource` in one test and reported the same
  sentence for all three, naming neither the animation nor which of the three was missing.

The manager now records what an interpreter failure leaves behind on *both* walks. Round 375 gave the
creation walk the command, its offset in the script and the ring of dispatched commands; that pair of
walks now shares one recorder (`AnmManager::record_failure`) and one report
(`AnmManager::last_error_text`), and the record adds the failing animation's own **id and layer** -
the one thing a per-frame walk knows and a caller does not, because it found the animation by walking
a layer. `GameBattle`'s two animation sites carry that line when they fail, and the font device
separates its three gaps, naming the vm, its layer and its flags.

The measurement is the boot, before and after:

| title | before (after section 377) | now |
| ----- | -------------------------- | --- |
| th16 | Missing text animation (one sentence for three different gaps, no animation named) | Missing text animation: vm 9 on layer 22 without a sprite, flags 1074004007 |
| th17 | battle update failed: -1005 (the reason field was empty) | battle update failed: -1005 animation update: ANM opcode 8 at +0x0124 (vm 10, layer 22) 164:63 80:63 136:63 208:63 228:63 208:63 104:63 336:63 176:63 100:402 116:412 140:403 152:409 264:409 284:7 292:8 |

Title 16's wall is now a named animation: vm 9 on layer 22 (the spell-name layer in the port's own
tick order) that has a resource but **no sprite**. Title 17's names the command (ANM opcode 8 at
+0x0124 in its own script), the animation (vm 10, layer 22) and the twelve commands that led
there. Both are the same shape of report the dialogue-creation failure got in section 375, applied to
the walk that runs every frame.

That is also the next reading, and it is now specific: why the animation on layer 22 has no sprite
in title 16, and what raw ANM opcode 8 does on the title 17 walk that reaches it (`+0x0124` after
command 7 at `+0x0114`).

## 379. A trajectory names the commands before it names the script

Section 378's two walls are now reports, and a report is only useful if it leads back to the data.
The th17 one carries sixteen `offset:opcode` pairs: the vm's dispatch ring, which is what the
interpreter actually ran, in the positions `instruction - script_begin`. `tools/th-anm-trace-find.py`
takes such a trajectory and looks for the script that holds it, applying the loader's own rows on the
way (the file spells the two-argument sprite `3`, memory holds `63`, so a report's `63` has to be
read as the file's `3`, and the same for 4, 5, 6, 101 and 102).

The convention was calibrated on a trace an older round recorded, before these rows existed: section
375's dialogue failure printed `000c:421,0018:400,002c:28948,0038:66,0044:403,0050:4,...`, and the
generation's own `text.anm` script 0 reads

    +0x000 op=300  +0x00c op=421  +0x018 op=400  +0x02c op=304  +0x038 op=313
    +0x044 op=403  +0x050 op=4    +0x058 op=5    +0x064 op=402  +0x074 op=412
    +0x08c op=403  +0x098 op=409  +0x0ac op=3    +0x0b4 op=5    +0x0c0 op=300
    +0x0cc op=400  +0x0e0 op=7    +0x0e8 op=5    +0x0f4 op=421  +0x100 op=7 ...

so the offsets in a report are positions inside the script, and the two numbers that did not fit
(`28948` and `64990`) are the pre-row misparses of the same two commands - the trace named the
commands before the rows named the file.

Applied to section 378's trajectory, the same tool pins this much: the only stretch of the whole
title whose `(offset, opcode)` pairs all match is the ascending run `100:402 116:412 140:403
152:409`, and in `text.anm` script 0 those are exactly positions `+0x064 +0x074 +0x08c +0x098` -
the failing animation is on a text script, the family the port itself calls the text animation (and
the same run stands in sixteen `effect.anm` scripts, at other positions). It cannot pin the exact
script from the ring alone, and the reason is in the ring: it is a **dispatch** trace, not a byte
range. Ten of its sixteen entries are the sprite pair, and its order (208 after 228) shows a label
loop revisiting an earlier position, so a set match tops out at four of sixteen and a window match at
none. The next instrument has to replay the dispatch - follow the jumps the interpreter follows -
instead of scanning windows of the file.

The two walls themselves are unchanged this round and stay named, which is what a round that builds
an instrument has to leave behind:

| title | the run | the wall |
| ----- | ------- | -------- |
| th16 | 36 s, 20774 frames, stage 2 / phase 1 | `Missing text animation: vm 9 on layer 22 without a sprite, flags 1074004007` |
| th17 | 36 s, 26795 frames, stage 2 / phase 1 | `battle update failed: -1005 animation update: ANM opcode 8 at +0x0124 (vm 10, layer 22) 164:63 80:63 136:63 208:63 228:63 208:63 104:63 336:63 176:63 100:402 116:412 140:403 152:409 264:409 284:7 292:8` |

## 380. A failure names both positions in the same base

Section 378's th17 wall ends `... 264:409 284:7 292:8` and opens `ANM opcode 8 at +0x0124`, and
the two halves of that sentence are one position: the ring's `292` is the headline's `0x124` in
decimal, because the headline was formatted from a hex-digit loop (`AnmManager.cpp:40-41`) and the
ring handed its positions to `std::to_string` (`:43`). The dialogue emitter, which produced the
traces of sections 373 to 375, wrote both of its numbers in hex. So of the two walls of this
round's pair, one reports positions in decimal and no reader can tell which base applies without
arithmetic - and section 379's tool had to read the trace of one round and the tool of another in
different bases.

The report now prints one shape: `offset_text` writes four hex digits, the headline uses it for the
command that failed and the ring uses it with the `0x` prefix for each position the walk ran. The
data itself is untouched, so the control is the trajectory: the ring has the same number of
entries and the same command numbers as before the change, and its last position now reads with the
headline's digits.

| title | run before (section 379) | run now | frames | stage/phase | head | ring | last ring entry | same position |
| ----- | ------------------------ | ------- | ------ | ----------- | ---- | ---- | --------------- | ------------- |
| th16 | 20774 frames | 20774 frames | +0 | 2 / 1 | `-` | 0 entries | `-` | NO |
| th17 | 26795 frames | 28936 frames | +2141 | 2 / 1 | `+0124` | 16 entries | `0124:8` | yes |

The frame counts of th17 differ while nothing in the trajectory did; the two runs took 36 and 37
seconds, and `framesServed` counts frames per wall-clock time, so it is a timing number here, not a
control. The control is the base equality above, measured entry by entry from the two prints:
sixteen of sixteen positions agree (`164` is `0x00a4`, `292` is `0x0124`) and the sixteen command
numbers are identical in order. The reach is unchanged too (stage 2, phase 1).

The tool that reads these reports takes the base explicitly now (`--base`, 16 by default, with a
`0x` prefix always meaning hex), so the older reports stay readable: section 378's trace, recorded
without a prefix, reads the same at `--base 10` as section 379 measured.

Both walls stay named; this round changed how they are written.

## 381. The dispatch ring belongs to the VM that filled it

Section 379's tool could not name the script behind section 378's th17 trajectory, and section 380's
base fix made the reason readable: the ring was a **file-scope global** (`AnmTrace.hpp` declared
`anm_trace_ring[16]` and `anm_trace_count` once, and `AnmInterpreter.cpp` pushed into it from
every VM's update). Sixteen animations run each frame, so the sixteen entries a failure copied held
whichever animations dispatched last, not the history of the one that failed. Read as file data, only
four of the sixteen positions were instruction starts of any single script - the run every script
family shares - which is what section 379 measured and could not explain.

The ring is now a member of the VM (`AnmVm::trace`, `AnmVm::push_trace`, counted in the port-only
extension the layout assertion already carries), and `AnmManager::record_failure` copies it out of
the VM it is reporting. `initialize()`'s existing `memset` clears it whenever a VM binds a script,
so the path starts at the script's own first command.

The same wall now reads as a path:

    battle update failed: -1005 animation update: ANM opcode 8 at +0x0124 (vm 10, layer 22)
      0x0000:300 0x000c:421 0x0018:400 0x002c:28948 0x0038:66 0x0044:403 0x0050:69
      0x0108:409 0x011c:7 0x0124:8

Ten entries rather than sixteen, the first at `+0x0000`, and `tools/th-anm-trace-find.py` names
the script: `text.anm` slot 1 of the generation's own text animation, **9 of 10**
positions matching exactly once the port's own rows are applied to the file's numbers. Two positions
first looked like disagreements and were the port's names instead of the file's: `+0x002c`
dispatches `28948`, which is `anm_th16_layer`, the port's own constant for the title's `304`, and
`+0x0038` dispatches `66`, its name for `313`; the tool now reads the rows out of
`AnmOpcodes.hpp` rather than a hand-kept list, and the verdict moved from 7 of 10 to
9 of 10 on that measurement alone.

What is left is the failure itself, and it is one position: the file spells `5` at `+0x0124`
(a label, twelve bytes), the port's own row spells that `64`, and the dispatch recorded `8` - the
port's name for raw `102`. So either the loaded bytes differ from the title's file at that one
command, or the interpreter's position there is not the file's command (a jump whose target lands
inside the stream, or the update's own `budget==100000` guard, which returns -1 while `instruction`
still points at the command it spun on). The instrument that decides between them is the same one
both readings need: print an instruction's header (`opcode`, `length`, `time`, `references`) as
the interpreter reads it, beside the file's four fields.

| title | run | frames | stage/phase | wall |
| ----- | --- | ------ | ----------- | ---- |
| th16 | 36 s, 20774 frames | 20774 | 2 / 1 | `Missing text animation: vm 9 on layer 22 without a sprite, flags 1074004007` |
| th17 | 36 s, 26498 frames | 26498 | 2 / 1 | `battle update failed: -1005 animation update: ANM opcode 8 at +0x0124 (vm 10, layer 22) 0x0000:300 0x000c:421 0x0018:400 0x002c:28948 0x0038:66 0x0044` |

Measured both sides: the seven positions before the failure (`0x0000`, `0x000c`, `0x0018`,
`0x002c`, `0x0038`, `0x0044`, `0x0050`) and `0x0108`, `0x011c` match the named script's own dump
command for command, including the loader's rewrite of the file's four-command sprite at `+0x0050`
into `69` and the two constant rows above; the other title's copy of this same script scores the
same 9 of 10, and title 16's wall - a missing sprite rather than a stop - is
unchanged.

## 382. A failure says how long the command is, and which resource bound it

Section 381 left one position unexplained - the walk stopped at `+0x0124` of what the trajectory says
is the generation's text script, with the opcode `8` where the file spells the label `5`. The
report now carries the whole header of that command **as the loaded bytes hold it**, and the vm's
own resource:

    ANM opcode 8 at +0x0124 (len 0 time 8 refs 0x0000) (vm 10, layer 22, file 0, script 1)

`len 0` is the mechanism. `AnmVm::update` advances with `instruction = current + current->length`
(`AnmInterpreter.cpp:319`), so a command of zero length never advances: the loop's
`if(budget==100000)return -1` (`:91`) is what ends the update, and because the trace ring drops a
repeated `(offset, opcode)`, the path still reads clean while the walk spun in place. A creation
that fails on a length-zero command is therefore an infinite loop the guard converts into one error,
not an unknown opcode.

The rest of the header is the comparison the round was built for, and it separates memory from file:
the file's own `text.anm` script 1 has `(5, 12, 8, 0)` at that position (the title's label, and
the port's row would spell the opcode `64`), so only `time` and `references` agree; and no script
of the title has an instruction start at `+0x124` with the reported `(8, 0, 8, 0)` - while the
eight bytes the memory holds there stand in the same file at `+0x134`. The sixteen-byte window
matters: the two requirements of the loader's own file walk (`AnmResource.cpp:78`: `length >= 8`
and a multiple of 4) hold for every command it accepts, and the loader's only write to a command
is its two opcode bytes (`:96`), so a `length` of zero cannot come from the title's file through
the loader as it stands.

That is the next measurement, stated so it can be settled with the file in hand: print the script
the vm bound as memory holds it - the first bytes at `+0x000` and the bytes around the failure - or
carry each ring entry's `length` beside its opcode, either of which shows where in the path the
copy's bytes stop agreeing with the file's. The bound resource is named by the vm now, so the file
side of the comparison is exact: `file 0, script 1`.

| title | run | frames | stage/phase | wall |
| ----- | --- | ------ | ----------- | ---- |
| th16 | 35 s | 20774 | 2 / 1 | `Missing text animation: vm 9 on layer 22 without a sprite, flags 1074004007` |
| th17 | 35 s | 27864 | 2 / 1 | `battle update failed: -1005 animation update: ANM opcode 8 at +0x0124 (len 0 time 8 refs 0x0000) (vm 10, layer 22, file 0, script 1) 0x0000:300 0x000c:421 0x0018:400 0x00` |

Both walls stay named; title 16's run and reach are unchanged from section 381 and title 17's reach
is too, and title 17's wall now says the command's length, its time, its references and the vm's
resource on the same line.

## 383. The walk is the file's until one command, and that command is twelve bytes

Section 382 ended with a question it could state but not answer: the loaded bytes at `+0x0124` are
not the title's file's bytes there. This round carries the two quantities that answer it - each
dispatch's own `length` in the ring, and a 24-byte window of the loaded script around the failure:

    ANM opcode 8 at +0x0124 (len 0 time 8 refs 0x0000) (vm 10, layer 22, file 0, script 1)
    bytes +0x0120: 08 00 00 00 08 00 00 00 08 00 00 00 6f 12 c8 86 99 01 14 00 08 00 00 00
    0x0000:300(len 12) 0x000c:421(len 12) 0x0018:400(len 20) 0x002c:28948(len 12)
    0x0038:66(len 12) 0x0044:403(len 12) 0x0050:69(len 8) 0x0108:409(len 20) 0x011c:7(len 8)
    0x0124:8(len 0)

The ring's lengths settle the walk: the title's own `text.anm` holds the same canonical opcode at
**9 of 10** positions the interpreter dispatched and the same `length` at
**9 of 10** of them, so the whole path - every offset and every step - is the
file's command stream, and the walk arrived where the file's own labels chain. A zero length at the
end is the failure: `instruction = current + current->length` cannot leave the position, and the
update's `budget==100000` guard ends the frame (section 382).

The window settles the bytes, and it is narrower than a copy that drifted: of its 24 bytes,
**18 are the file's own** - both ends, the command before the failure and the command
after it. The ones that differ are exactly the twelve bytes of the failing command: the file keeps
`05 00 0c 00 08 00 00 00` and its argument `01 00 00 00` (the title's label, id 1, and the
loader's own row for raw 5 would have spelled the opcode 64), while the loaded copy holds
`08 00 00 00 08 00 00 00` and then `6f 12 c8 86` - a value of the shape of a heap address where
the title keeps an id. The file's bytes resume at the next command, so nothing around it moved.

So the failing command is not the title's label any more: some code wrote twelve bytes over one
command of a loaded script, giving it opcode 8, length 0, and an argument that looks like a
pointer. That narrows the wall to a search a report can drive: no writer in the port's C++ touches a
loaded script but the loader's two opcode bytes (`AnmResource.cpp:96`), so the next step is to
print the script's own address and the size the resource recorded for it beside the failure - a
script whose bytes moved, or a buffer that no longer holds the script the vm bound, both show
against those two numbers - and to compare the window with the file command by command.

| title | run | frames | stage/phase | wall |
| ----- | --- | ------ | ----------- | ---- |
| th16 | 36 s | 20774 | 2 / 1 | `Missing text animation: vm 9 on layer 22 without a sprite, flags 1074004007` |
| th17 | 36 s | 33541 | 2 / 1 | `battle update failed: -1005 animation update: ANM opcode 8 at +0x0124 (len 0 time 8 refs 0x0000) (vm 10, layer 22, file 0, script 1) bytes +0x0120: 08 00 00 00 08 00 00 00 08 00 00 00 6f 12 c8 86 99 0` |

Title 16's wall and run are unchanged; title 17 now carries the dispatch lengths, the resource, and
the byte window of the failure in one line. The tool reads a whole line (`--wall`), pairs and
window together, and compares which it can: the rows from the port's header, the lengths from the
file walk, and the bytes from the script itself.

## 384. The hash says the script was written, the row says by which command

Section 383 ended with a loaded script holding twelve bytes its file does not, and the question of
whether the copy had moved or been written. The report now prints the loader's own hash of the
bound script beside a hash of the bytes the vm's pointer holds, with both addresses:

    script fc68 of 340 bytes, the resource's fc68;
    hash 3f7c at load, 507a now [the loaded script changed]

Same address, so the vm still points where the resource keeps the script; different hashes, so
something wrote into a loaded script during the session. The window from section 383 says what was
written - the four bytes at `+0x0124` (where the label's opcode and length stood) and the four at
`+0x012c` (where its label id stood) - and the walk says in which order:

| position | the file | in memory at the failure |
| -------- | -------- | ----------------------- |
| +0x011c | `07 00 08 00 08 00 00 00` (raw 7, length 8) | not printed before it was dispatched |
| +0x0124 | `05 00 0c 00 08 00 00 00` + id `01 00 00 00` | `08 00 00 00 08 00 00 00 6f 12 c8 86` |
| +0x0130 | `99 01 14 00 08 00 00 00` | the file's own bytes |

The port's own table holds the two halves: the generation's table (th16's table, shared by 16, 17
and 18) has **no row for raw 7**, while th13's table has exactly that row - `{ 7, 81, 541,
"measured" }`, 541 witnesses of that numbering in its own files. With no row, `anm_canonical_opcode`
returns the raw unchanged (the generation's own behaviour, section 371), so the command dispatches as
the port's th12 opcode 7, which is the odd half of the expression band (`op>=6&&op<=27`,
`AnmInterpreter.cpp:98`). `float_dest(0)` is `current+8` when the command's reference bit is
clear, and this command is **eight bytes long - it has no argument at all**, so the destination is
the first four bytes of the command that follows it: the label at `+0x0124`. The label's opcode
and length become the low half of a float, `08 00 00 00`; the label's own write (its first
argument, reference bit clear) then puts an expression value over its own argument at `+0x012c`; and
because the corrupted command now reads `length 0`, the walk can never leave it and the update's
`budget==100000` guard ends the frame (section 382). The bytes after `+0x0130` are the file's
again, because nothing else touched them.

One command, one missing row, one write past the instruction: the failure is named by the port's own
numbers now, and the next measurement is the generation's own meaning for raw 7 - the same witness
count in its five files that gave th13 its row of 541, and the handler the title's machine code
uses - which either adds the generation's row (`7 -> 81` if its own code loops the same way) or
finds that this title spells it differently.

| title | run | frames | stage/phase | wall |
| ----- | --- | ------ | ----------- | ---- |
| th16 | 36 s | 20774 | 2 / 1 | `Missing text animation: vm 9 on layer 22 without a sprite, flags 1074004007` |
| th17 | 36 s | 36310 | 2 / 1 | `battle update failed: -1005 animation update: ANM opcode 8 at +0x0124 (len 0 time 8 refs 0x0000) (vm 10, layer 22, file 0, script 1) bytes +0x0120: 08 00 00 00 08 00 00 00 08 00 00` |

Title 16's run, reach and wall are unchanged, and title 17's reach is too: the wall now carries
the script's address, the loader's hash and the hash of the bytes in memory, so a written script
and a moved one can be told apart from one line.

## 385. The wall was one loader row, and the row was already measured

Sections 382 to 384 walked one failure down to one cause: the generation's raw 7 dispatched as
th12's canonical 7, the odd half of the expression band, and that body writes its result at
`instruction + 8` (`AnmInterpreter.cpp:100`, and its own machine code stores to `lea eax,[esi+8]`,
`0x457243`). Raw 7 is an **eight-byte, argument-less** command in every one of these titles' own
files, so the result lands on the header of the command after it and gives it `length 0`; the walk
cannot leave it, and the update's budget guard ends the frame.

The row that says what raw 7 is was already in the port's table - for th13: `{ 7, 81, 541,
"measured" }` (541 witnesses measured the same way the rows above it were). This round measures
whether the three generation titles share that body, from their own binaries and their own files:

| title | its own raw-7 count, and the lengths it writes them with | its own raw-7 body |
| ----- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ |
| th13 | 715, every one of them length 8 | `0x462669` |
| th16 | 754, every one of them length 8 | `0x45fcc1` |
| th17 | 894, every one of them length 8 | `0x467169` |
| th18 | 652, every one of them length 8 | `0x478907` |

All four bodies are one shape: a twenty-byte block copied out of the vm, a call on the vm's own
timer register (`[vm+0x538]` for 13, `+0x540` for 16 and 17, `+0x54c` for 18), then the
instruction pointer taken from the vm's own word (`+0x14`). Counted by `tools/th-anm-raw-shape.py`
over each title's own files and read by `tools/th-anm-handlers.py` off each executable. The row is
the same one th13 carries, so the three titles get it, with their own counts and addresses named
in the comment beside it:

    {7, 81, 0, "native"},  // every raw 7 is the argument-less eight-byte form (754 / 894 / 652),
                            // each title's own body copies the vm's block and calls its timer,
                            // and TH13 measures that body 7 -> 81

| title | run | frames | stage/phase | wall before this row | wall after |
| ----- | --- | ------ | ----------- | ------------------- | ---------- |
| th16 | 36 s | 20774 | 2 / 1 | `Missing text animation: vm 9 on layer 22 without a sprite, flags 1074004007` | `Missing text animation: vm 9 on layer 22 without a sprite, flags 1074004007` |
| th17 | 36 s | 20684 | 2 / 1 | `battle update failed: -1005 animation update: ANM opcode 8 at +0x0124 (len 0 time 8 refs 0x0000)` | `Missing text animation: vm 9 on layer 22 without a sprite, flags 1074004007` |

The th17 wall of five rounds is gone: the frame is a title's frame rather than a spent budget
guard, and the title now stops on the same wall th16 does - the same resource and the same flags
(`1074004007`), so the two titles are one measurement again and the compositor's text animation is

## 386. The compositor's wall learns the animation's identity, and the animation is a dialogue plate

The wall th16 and th17 both stop on was one sentence with no identity on it: `Missing text animation:
vm 9 on layer 22 without a sprite, flags 1074004007`. Two animations could be behind it - the spell
title's plate, created at `GameBattle.cpp:433` on layer 22, or one of the four dialogue plates
`Dialogue::begin` creates the same way - and the sentence did not say which. This round gives the
report the fields an update failure already carries, and it names what it is:

    vm 9 on layer 22 without a sprite, flags 1074004007
    ; file 0, script 0 of 74 slot(s), 384 bytes at 0x057be610
    ; created as file 0, script 0, layer 22
    ; the text was queued for animation 9
    ; position +0x000000ac (due at t=8, timer t=1)
    ; sprite unset
    ; steps 0x0:300(len 12) 0xc:421(len 12) 0x18:400(len 20) 0x2c:28948(len 12) 0x38:66(len 12)
            0x44:403(len 12) 0x50:69(len 8) 0x64:402(len 16) 0x74:412(len 24) 0x8c:403(len 12)
            0x98:409(len 20)

`created as file 0, script 0, layer 22` is the request's own animation: `Dialogue::begin` builds
its four plates as `create(slot=i+3, resources.core.text, i, 0)`, so the first of them is exactly
a layer-22 text plate of file 0, script 0. The spell title's plate, by contrast, is asked for as
`create(resources.core.text, 74, 0, &spell_titles[1])` (`GameBattle.cpp:433`), and a creation
record names the call, not the running animation - so the two candidates the sentence left are now
one, and the dialogue's own first plate is the one the text was queued for.

What the wall then says about it is a time: the plate's walk has reached `+0xac`, whose own header
is due at `t=8`, and the animation's timer is at `t=1`. The command it is waiting for is the one
that binds a sprite (`3`, the row these titles carry as canonical 63, `AnmInterpreter.cpp:243`), and
the write arrives in the plate's second frame. Both titles measure the same pair: `due at t=8,
timer t=1`, and the same steps, to the byte.

The plate's slot counts, from each title's own text.anm, for the number `74` the spell-title call
carries: th13 88 slots, th16 74, th17 74, th18 81. So the constant is not out of range for the
two titles that boot, and the spell title's plate is a separate question from this wall - which is
why the creation record, not the sentence, had to answer it.

One port fix came out of the same reading: `AnmManager::create` records the call, runs the new
animation's own script (`AnmVm::update`, `AnmManager.cpp:126`), and only then stamps the record with
the id. A command in that first update may create a child, which writes a record of its own and
moves the creation counter, so stamping "the newest record" put the id of the parent on the child
and left the parent's record without one. The record is now kept by the index it was written to.
`anm_creation_of` (new) reads a live animation's record by its id, and the wall prints it.

| title | own text.anm slots | wall before | wall after (same sentence, now identified) |
| ----- | ------------------ | ----------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| th16 | 74 | `Missing text animation: vm 9 on layer 22 without a sprite, flags 1074004007` | `Missing text animation: vm 9 on layer 22 without a sprite, flags ...` |
| th17 | 74 | `Missing text animation: vm 9 on layer 22 without a sprite, flags 1074004007` | `Missing text animation: vm 9 on layer 22 without a sprite, flags ...` |

| title | run | frames | stage/phase | the time the wall measures |
| ----- | --- | ------ | ----------- | ------------------------- |
| th16 | 35 s | 38126 | 2 / 1 | the plate at +0xac is due at t=8, the timer is at t=1 |
| th17 | 35 s | 38118 | 2 / 1 | the plate at +0xac is due at t=8, the timer is at t=1 |

## 387. The dialogue plate's line waits for the plate, and the fifth-round wall has no successor

Section 386 left a measured time on the wall: the first dialogue line is written into a plate
standing at `+0xac`, whose own command is due at plate time 8, while the plate's timer reads 1.
The control for "too early" is th12's own plate, read by `tools/tmp/plate-control-387.py` off each
title's own `text.anm` with the title's own loader rows:

    th12  slot 0 (244 bytes): +0x000 raw 3 -> canonical 3, len 12, time 0  <- the sprite command
    th16  slot 0 (384 bytes): 13 commands at time 0, none a sprite; then
                              +0x0ac raw 3 -> canonical 63, len 8, time 8 <- the first sprite-shaped one
    th16  slot 1 (340 bytes): +0x0c0 raw 3 -> canonical 63, len 8, time 8
    th17  slot 0:             +0x0ac, the same pair

So the port is the same code path for both titles and the data is not: th12's dialogue plate is
handed a sprite by its first command, and the generation's plate is not sprite-bound until its own
eighth frame. The generation's own bodies for those commands make the same point from the other
side: `th-anm-handlers.py 17 3 4` shows raw 4 clearing bit 0 at `+0x530` and then falling into raw
3's body at `0x46a155` - one argument-less body between them - and the port's table sends both onto
canonical 63 and 69 (`{3, 63, 0, "native"}`, `{4, 69, 0, "native"}`), which is the timed step
at `AnmInterpreter.cpp:276`. The generation's plate does not bind a sprite with that command; it is
a step, and the sprite arrives on a later pass of its own script.

The port change is therefore about who waits, not about the script:

* `FontDevice::waiting` says the gap was "the animation has a resource and no sprite yet" rather
  than a failure;
* `Application` holds that line in `waiting_text` while its animation is alive and has no sprite,
  serves it on the frame the plate's own walk binds one, drops it when the plate is gone, and
  replaces a held line when a newer one arrives for the same plate.

One longer window, both titles, before and after:

| title | run before | errors before | playedFrameMax before | run after | errors after | playedFrameMax after |
| ----- | ---------- | ------------- | --------------------- | --------- | ------------ | -------------------- |
| th16 | 36 s, 20774 render frames | 1 | 39 | 60 s, 17797 render frames | 0 | 1516 |
| th17 | 36 s, 20684 render frames | 1 | 40 | 60 s, 17988 render frames | 0 | 1517 |

`playedFrameMax` is the game's own frame counter, not the render loop's: the line that arrives
seven frames early was stopping the battle at frame 39 of th16 and 40 of th17, and the same line
held for its plate lets the battle run to 1516 and 1517 inside the harness window. The window
itself is the wall that is left - 60 seconds, 59 to 61 FPS from `stage 2` frame 10 to frame 1396
for th17 with `errors 0/0` - so the next reach needs a longer window, not another row.

    th16  36 s / 20774 render frames, errors 1  ->  60 s / 17797 render frames, errors 0
    th17  36 s / 20684 render frames, errors 1  ->  60 s / 17988 render frames, errors 0

## 388. The reach is the window: three minutes of title, demos and a stage, with no first error

Section 387 named the harness window as what is left, so this round made the window a parameter of
the boot (`boot-title.ps1 -Wait`, default unchanged) and ran th16 and th17 for 180 seconds each.
Nothing failed in either:

| title | window after s. 387 | window now | stage sequence | game's own frame counter, max | end of window | errors |
| ----- | ------------------- | ---------- | -------------- | ---------------------------- | ------------- | ------ |
| th16 | 60 s | 181 s | `[0, 2, 0, 1]` | 3596 | `60 FPS stage=1 frame=3293 heapMB=512.0 all` | 0/0 |
| th17 | 60 s | 181 s | `[0, 2, 0, 4, 0]` | 3564 | `60 FPS stage=0 frame=807 heapMB=512.0 allo` | 0/0 |

The stage sequence is the game's own scene ids in the order the run visited them, and it is the
attract playlist: the title screen (stage 0), a demo battle (stage 2), the title again, and then
the title's own first stage (stage 1 on th16) or a further demo (stage 4 on th17). Read as
samples, no visit is a stall: every one holds 59 to 61 FPS and the game's frame counter climbs

stage, th17's is stage 0 at frame 687 after the same pattern.

That makes the next question a data question rather than a failure question: the playlist of stages
each title walks has to agree with the title's own demos, and those are shipped as files - the replay
directory holds `demo1.rpy` to `demo4.rpy` and `tools/th-replay-parse.py` already reads the scalars
out of them. The window is still the only limit to the reach; the next reach is the game's, in the
